how: compare side by side with `ffmpeg -i hero.mp4 -i shot.mp4 -filter_complex "[0:v][1:v]hstack" out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Match by numbers
what: compare YAVG/UAVG/VAVG (and YLOW/YHIGH) of hero and shot, then move levels/balance until they agree
how: loop signalstats over both files: `ffmpeg -i f.mp4 -vf "signalstats,metadata=mode=print:file=m.txt" -frames:v 1 -f null -` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Colour-patch mapping with colormap
what: colormap takes the video plus source and target patch streams (e.g. a chart shot under each camera) and maps colours (up to 64 patches, relative or absolute, euclidean/weuclidean kernel)
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -i src_chart.png -i tgt_chart.png -filter_complex "[1]loop=-1:1:0[s];[2]loop=-1:1:0[d];[0][s][d]colormap=patch_size=64x64:nb_patches=24:type=relative[o]" -map "[o]" -t 2 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24 with ffmpeg colorchart images)

name: Histogram matching in Python
what: skimage `match_histograms(image, reference, channel_axis=-1)` matches each channel's cumulative histogram to a reference. Wikipedia: it suits two images of the same place under different sensors or light
how: `/home/user/tools/venv/bin/python -I -c "from skimage import io; from skimage.exposure import match_histograms; ..."` on exported frames (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Match HLG and SDR cameras scene-referred
what: BT.2408: use scene-referred mapping to match BT.709/BT.2020 SDR cameras with HLG cameras, because both signals represent scene light. Display-referred mapping would make them mismatch
how: when mixing phone HLG with SDR clips, convert the SDR into HLG scene-light, not by look.

name: Skin can drift after shots are balanced
what: lenses and lighting differ, so skin can still differ between shots after primaries. Colourists isolate skin and match it as a separate step
how: a skin qualifier pass (975) per shot after the hero match.

name: Grade the group, not each clip, afterwards
what: once shots share a baseline, Frame.io says global changes go on an adjustment layer, node or nested sequence for all of them at once
how: in ffmpeg, apply the same baked Hald/cube (967) to every matched clip.

name: PQ basics
what: SMPTE ST 2084 (Dolby, 2014, BT.2100 in 2016): signal 0–1 = 0–10,000 cd/m², absolute. No visible banding at 12 bits, where a power law would need 15. Base of HDR10, HDR10+ and Dolby Vision. Not backward compatible with BT.1886
how: tag `transfer=smpte2084`.

name: PQ code values for common levels
what: computed from the ST 2084 inverse EOTF: 100 cd/m² ≈ 0.508, 203 ≈ 0.581, 1000 ≈ 0.752 of signal

name: HLG basics
what: BBC/NHK, ARIB STD-B67, in BT.2100. The lower half of the signal is a gamma (square-root) curve and the upper half logarithmic. No metadata. Reference white sits at signal 0.5. Royalty-free
how: tag `transfer=arib-std-b67` with bt2020 primaries and 10-bit.

name: HLG on SDR screens
what: HLG is backward compatible with SDR UHDTV that understands BT.2020. On Rec.709-only displays it looks desaturated with hue shifts, so broadcasters do a colour space conversion for HD simulcast
how: tone-map/convert phone HLG before sharing to SDR-only platforms.

name: HDR format table
what: HDR10 = PQ + static ST 2086 + MaxCLL/MaxFALL. HDR10+ = HDR10 + per-scene ST 2094-40. Dolby Vision = PQ (profiles 5, 7, 8.1, 10.1) or HLG (8.4) + per-frame RPU. HLG = no metadata
how: identify with the two ffprobe commands (801/802).

name: Identify HDR flavour from ffprobe output
what: smpte2084 + mastering + content light = HDR10. Plus "HDR Dynamic Metadata SMPTE2094-40" = HDR10+. "DOVI configuration record" = Dolby Vision (dv_profile/compat id). arib-std-b67 = HLG. dv_profile=5 with unknown/ipt-c2 tags = DV profile 5
how: grep ffprobe `-show_frames` and `-show_streams` output.

name: iPhone HDR is Dolby Vision 8.4 on HLG
what: Apple records DV profile 8, cross-compatibility ID 4 (HLG), 10-bit HEVC, so plain HEVC decoders see HLG
how: treat iPhone HDR clips as HLG in ffmpeg chains (`tin=arib-std-b67`).

name: DV profile 5 looks green/purple without DV
what: profile 5's base layer is proprietary IPTPQc2, so without Dolby Vision processing colours are wrong (green/purple). The zscale+tonemap chain ignores DV metadata
how: profile 5 needs libplacebo (applies RPUs, needs Vulkan, missing here).

name: HDR10 static metadata units
what: mastering display primaries/white in units of 0.00002 and luminance in 0.0001 cd/m². MaxCLL = brightest pixel, MaxFALL = highest frame average, both in cd/m²

name: Encode HDR10 with x265 inside ffmpeg
what: set the VUI tags plus master-display, max-cll, hdr10-opt (block QP tuning for PQ, use with AQ) and repeat-headers
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -c:v libx265 -pix_fmt yuv420p10le -x265-params "colorprim=bt2020:transfer=smpte2084:colormatrix=bt2020nc:master-display=G(13250,34500)B(7500,3000)R(34000,16000)WP(15635,16450)L(10000000,1):max-cll=1000,400:hdr10-opt=1:repeat-headers=1" out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24; ffprobe showed both side data blocks)

name: Copy HDR10 numbers from the source, never invent them
what: the mastering peak is a property of the grade and MaxCLL/MaxFALL are measured from content. When a source has none, leave them out
how: read the fractions from ffprobe frame side data (802) and convert ×50000 / ×10000 for x265.

name: One glint sets MaxCLL
what: MaxCLL is one number for the whole file from its brightest pixel, so a single specular highlight can set it. MaxFALL is the average-facing value. Dolby Vision/HDR10+ exist because static values can't fit both dark and bright scenes
how: don't panic at a high MaxCLL, and check MaxFALL for overall brightness.

name: Read MaxCLL with ffprobe
what: the frame side data fields max_content and max_average are MaxCLL and MaxFALL
how: `ffprobe -v error -select_streams v:0 -show_frames -read_intervals "%+#1" -show_entries frame_side_data=max_content,max_average -of default=nw=1 in.mp4`

name: HLG encode: no HDR10 metadata
what: encode HLG 10-bit with bt2020/bt2020nc/arib-std-b67 and don't add mastering metadata unless the source has it. x265 also offers `atc-sei` and `pic-struct`, which it marks "required for HLG signalling"
how: `-x265-params "colorprim=bt2020:transfer=arib-std-b67:colormatrix=bt2020nc:atc-sei=18:pic-struct=0"` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: ffmpeg 7.0+ passes HDR10 metadata through; 6.1 here did not
what: Encode Wiki: since 7.0 a plain transcode passes mastering and content-light metadata to libx264/libx265/libsvtav1. Here (6.1) the SDR output of a PQ file carried no mastering metadata
how: on 6.1, re-add HDR10 values with -x265-params when re-encoding HDR (ffprobe check tested here 2026-10-24)

name: HDR10+ and Dolby Vision need extra tools
what: libx265 drops HDR10+: extract with hdr10plus_tool and pass `dhdr10-info=metadata.json`. Dolby Vision: `-dolbyvision 1` with libx265 writes profile 8.x (needs VBV), or extract the RPU with dovi_tool. Profile 7 must be converted to 8.1 first
how: needs hdr10plus_tool and dovi_tool (missing).

name: YouTube HDR upload spec
what: 10 or 12 bit. Rec.2020 primaries, Rec.2020 NCL matrix, PQ or HLG. PQ files should carry ST 2086 and MaxCLL/MaxFALL, or YouTube assumes a Sony BVM-X300. Recommended codecs VP9 Profile 2, AV1, HEVC. ProRes/DNxHR/10-bit H.264 work at high bitrates
how: encode with 999 (PQ) or 1003 (HLG).

name: PQ shadows hold hidden noise
what: YouTube: PQ spends much of its range on shadows, so dark noise masked by highlights may be cleaned (or look compressed) after upload. Denoise before rendering for more control
how: denoise the HDR master before the x265 pass.

name: HDR reference monitor targets (Netflix)
what: SDR: Rec.709, D65, BT.1886 gamma 2.4, ≤0.05 nit black, 100 nits, 2000:1. Dolby Vision HDR: P3, D65, PQ, 0.005 nit black, 1000 nits, 200,000:1. Surround D65 at 5 nits, viewing distance 3–3.2 picture heights
how: our cloud box has no reference display, so state "graded by scopes, not on a reference monitor" when delivering.

name: Netflix HDR originals master in Dolby Vision
what: Netflix derives Dolby Vision, HDR10 and SDR streams from one Dolby Vision IMF. Metadata (colour encoding, mastering display, aspect ratio) must be accurate
how: for client HDR work, ask for the delivery spec before choosing HDR10 vs DV.

name: Washed-out grey = curve mismatch, not a bad encode
what: a naive `scale,format=yuv420p` reads PQ/HLG codes as SDR gamma and squeezes BT.2020 into BT.709 with no tone map, so the clip looks grey. Higher bitrate changes nothing
how: always tone-map (1011).

name: Strip HDR side data after tone mapping
what: Encode Wiki: ffmpeg passes mastering/content-light metadata to the encoder even after tone mapping, so the SDR file still claims HDR. Delete it in the chain
how: `ffmpeg -i hdr.mkv -vf "zscale=t=linear:npl=100,format=gbrpf32le,zscale=p=bt709,tonemap=hable:desat=0,zscale=t=bt709:m=bt709:r=tv,format=yuv420p,sidedata=mode=delete:type=MASTERING_DISPLAY_METADATA,sidedata=mode=delete:type=CONTENT_LIGHT_LEVEL" -c:v libx264 -crf 18 sdr.mkv` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: npl sets what becomes SDR white
what: `npl=100` maps 100 cd/m² in the source to SDR white. Encode Wiki says raising it darkens the result. The media-os guide says raising it brightens
how: measured here on an HLG clip through the hable chain: YAVG 77 at npl=100 and 64 at npl=400, so higher npl = darker (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Tell zscale the HLG input curve
what: for HLG sources one guide sets `tin=arib-std-b67` in the linearising zscale
how: `ffmpeg -i hlg.mp4 -vf zscale=t=linear:tin=arib-std-b67:npl=100,format=gbrpf32le,zscale=p=709,tonemap=hable:desat=0,zscale=t=709:m=709:r=limited:d=error_diffusion,format=yuv420p -c:v libx264 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: tonemap operators per the docs
what: clip: perfect accuracy in range, distorts out of range. linear: stretch by param. gamma: log fit (param default 1.8). reinhard: keeps overall brightness, flattens detail (param default 0.5). hable: keeps dark and bright detail, slightly darkens. mobius: keeps in-range colour (param default 0.3 = linear-to-mobius transition)
how: e.g. `tonemap=reinhard:param=0.5:desat=2` and `tonemap=clip` (both tested here 2026-10-24)

name: tonemap desat and peak
what: `desat` (default 2.0) turns super-highlights toward white, and 0 disables it. `peak` overrides the signal peak when embedded metadata is unreliable
how: `tonemap=mobius:param=0.3:peak=10` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Automatic tone mapping is a compromise
what: a fixed curve that suits one scene clips or dulls another, so watch the result on an SDR display. An official SDR version, when it exists, is usually better
how: ask the client for their SDR master before converting HDR yourself.

name: libplacebo is the higher-quality path (needs Vulkan)
what: libplacebo does tone and gamut mapping in one filter, uses mastering metadata, does peak detection (`peak_detect`, `percentile` default 99.995), offers tonemapping like `bt.2390`/`spline` and gamut modes (perceptual default, clip, relative, saturation, darken, warn ...), and applies DV RPUs
how: needs a Vulkan device. Here `-init_hw_device vulkan` failed (VK_ERROR_INCOMPATIBLE_DRIVER), so it is missing.

name: HLG→PQ is transcode vs convert
what: BT.2408: a transcode (HLG EOTF → PQ inverse EOTF) gives identical light only on a display of the same peak, and diffuse white moves with the assumed HLG display peak. Converting at a 1000 cd/m² reference keeps brightness consistent. Avoid cascaded conversions
how: `ffmpeg -i hlg.mp4 -vf zscale=tin=arib-std-b67:t=smpte2084:npl=1000,format=yuv420p10le -c:v libx265 -x265-params colorprim=bt2020:transfer=smpte2084:colormatrix=bt2020nc out.mp4` ran here (tested here 2026-10-24); whether zscale applies the 1000-nit reference OOTF was not verified.

name: SDR→HDR10 mapping (MovieLabs)
what: decode SDR with BT.1886 (gamma 2.4, Lw 100, Lb 0), convert BT.709→BT.2020 (BT.2087 M2), multiply linear light by 2.0 (white → 200 cd/m²), encode with PQ inverse EOTF. Metadata: BT.709 primaries, mastering max 200 / min 0, MaxCLL 200, MaxFALL 0 (unknown)
how: steps only. No ffmpeg chain for this was verified here (a zscale attempt failed).

name: Put SDR graphics at Graphics White
what: BT.2408: map SDR graphics directly at 75% HLG / 58% PQ so they don't look too bright and dull the video. Use display-light mapping to keep brand colours, scene-light mapping to match in-scene signs
how: check title cards on the HDR waveform against 58% PQ.

name: White subtitles in HDR at ≥75%
what: ZDF's grading guideline asks pure white text (subtitles, credits) be at least 75% (203 cd/m² on a 1000 cd/m² monitor), adjusted to the background
how: same check as 1020 for captions on HDR deliveries.

name: PQ on a BT.709 monitor looks dim and washed out
what: BT.2408: PQ fed to a BT.709 monitor is dim, desaturated and hue-shifted. A down-mapping 3D LUT allows viewing but not critical HDR judgement
how: preview HDR here only through a tone-mapped proxy, and label it so.

name: Check SDR derived from HDR for detail loss
what: static HDR→SDR down-mappers are tuned to reference levels. Content far from HDR Reference White can lose detail (skin, text) in the derived SDR
how: after 1011, look at faces and captions on the SDR waveform.

name: ACES pipeline parts
section: ACES, OCIO and colour space transforms
what: Input Transform (IDT: camera → ACES), Reference Rendering Transform (RRT: scene → display-referred with an S-curve), Output Device Transform (ODT: to Rec.709/P3/Rec.2020). In practice RRT+ODT are combined as the Output Transform
how: map these names to the CST/LUT steps you do in ffmpeg (conversion LUT = input, look, display LUT = output).

name: ACES colour spaces
section: ACES, OCIO and colour space transforms
what: ACES2065-1: linear, AP0, archive/interchange. ACEScg: linear AP1 for CG/VFX. ACEScc/ACEScct: log AP1 for grading. ACEScct adds a toe like film log, which gives a milky lift in shadows. ACES white is (0.32168, 0.33767)
how: grade in ACEScct, render CG in ACEScg.

name: ACES transform types
section: ACES, OCIO and colour space transforms
what: CSC (colour space conversion), Input, Output (RRT+ODT, token RRTODT before ACES 2), InvOutput (display-referred back to ACES), Look (LMT)
how: an inverse output transform is how you bring a finished Rec.709 graphic into an ACES grade.

name: Netflix ACES settings in Resolve
section: ACES, OCIO and colour space transforms
what: use ACEScct unless you need ACEScc. ODT Rec.709 for SDR (100 nit BT.1886 monitor), P3-D65 ST2084 (1000 nits) for HDR. Keep ACES Mid Gray Luminance at 15.00. ODT None outputs ACES2065-1
how: follow for any client asking for an ACES Resolve project.

name: ffmpeg is weak at colour space conversion
section: ACES, OCIO and colour space transforms
what: the ORI encoding guidelines recommend OCIO-based tools (Nuke, oiiotool, or the ffmpeg OCIO filter) with the ACES config, writing PNG/TIF/DPX intermediates for ffmpeg
how: `oiiotool ... --colorconvert acescg srgb --dither -o out.#.png` (needs oiiotool, missing)

name: ffmpeg 8.1 OCIO filter
section: ACES, OCIO and colour space transforms
what: `ocio=input=...:output=...` or `display=...:view=...` with built-in configs like `ocio://studio-config-v1.0.0_aces-v1.3_ocio-v2.1`. Output format must be RGB (rgb48, gbrpf32le ...), then convert to YCbCr with scale
how: needs ffmpeg 8.1 built with libopencolorio (missing; local is 6.1)

name: CST is a signal contract
section: ACES, OCIO and colour space transforms
what: Resolve's Color Space Transform has four fields (input space, input gamma, output space, output gamma) that must describe the real signal. Take camera gamut/log from metadata or documentation, not from how contrasty the viewer looks
how: the same rule for picking an ffmpeg conversion LUT: confirm the camera profile first.

name: Tone mapping ≠ gamut mapping
section: ACES, OCIO and colour space transforms
what: in a CST, tone mapping handles luminance/dynamic range (Clip, Simple, Luminance Mapping, DaVinci, Saturation Preserving) and gamut mapping handles colours outside the target gamut. Check one on the waveform, the other on vectorscope/CIE
how: after an ffmpeg HDR→SDR chain, check waveform (894) and ciescope (880) separately.

name: CST Clip vs Luminance Mapping
section: ACES, OCIO and colour space transforms
what: a forum explanation: Clip leaves in-gamut colours unchanged and flattens out-of-gamut ones to the edge (detail lost). Luminance Mapping brings everything in, so in-gamut colours like skin also shift slightly
how: expect the same trade-off between `tonemap=clip` and the curve operators.

name: One colourist's output CST settings
section: ACES, OCIO and colour space transforms
what: Frame.io author: Tone Mapping = Luminance Mapping, Custom Max Input 10,000 nits, Max Output 100, Gamut Mapping = Saturation Compression, Apply Forward OOTF on, so highlights decelerate instead of clipping
how: Resolve-only. Use as a starting point when a client sends a Resolve project.

name: Grade before the output transform
section: ACES, OCIO and colour space transforms
what: forum advice: in a wide timeline space (DWG/Intermediate) the output CST's tone mapping catches highlights, so pushing gain before the CST blows out less than after it
how: in ffmpeg, put exposure/levels before the log→709 LUT, not after.

name: RCM vs ACES
section: ACES, OCIO and colour space transforms
what: both are scene-referred colour management for the same problem. Resolve Color Management is simpler outside ACES-mandated work and keeps the familiar control feel. RCM also helps editors: assign each log clip its Input Color Space and it looks normal
how: for a Resolve client, assign input spaces per camera instead of LUT-ing in the timeline.

name: Timeline colour space changes how tools feel
section: ACES, OCIO and colour space transforms
what: Resolve: Rec.709 feels familiar for SDR, and log/wide spaces (Cineon, LogC, DWG) suit film-style workflows. For HDR delivery choose a wide space. Default Input Color Space doesn't affect RAW or clips with embedded colour metadata
how: decide the working space before grading, and don't switch mid-project.

name: QuickTime plays 1-1-1 video at gamma ~1.96
what: AVFoundation uses ~1.96 as video gamma (2.45/1.25) and converts to the 2.2 display buffer on macOS 10.6+. A 75% grey bar (191) reads ~198 on screen. Pixel values read off the screen differ from the file
how: don't judge Mac QuickTime screenshots as truth, and judge with scopes on decoded frames.

name: Resolve 1-2-1 tags and re-encoders
what: Resolve exports Rec.709 gamma 2.4 timelines with 1-2-1 tags. With "Use Mac Display Color Profiles for Viewers" on (after macOS 10.14.6), QuickTime matches the viewer. Re-encoding with HandBrake turns tags into 1-1-1 and the match breaks
how: the article ties the QuickTime match to the 1-2-1 tag, so check with ffprobe that a re-encode still has color_transfer unknown (2) before sending it to a Mac client.

name: Display P3 EDR on Macs
what: Apple calls Display P3 values above nominal white EDR, which Resolve and Nuke use to show HDR on Mac screens
how: an HDR preview on a MacBook is EDR, not a reference HDR monitor.

name: Tagged colour bars test a player
what: Apple's QuickTime Test Pattern files test black crush, gradients, 100%/75% bars (matrix) and quantised gradient (gamma), and the bars themselves must be nclc-tagged
how: make tagged bars with ffmpeg: `ffmpeg -f lavfi -i smptehdbars=size=1280x720 -t 2 -c:v libx264 -color_primaries bt709 -color_trc bt709 -colorspace bt709 bars.mp4` (only the smptehdbars source was tested here) and check them in the client's player.

name: See a preset's real numbers with a dry run
section: HyperFrames presets: what each one really sets
what: a preset name hides its values; a dry run prints the fully expanded payload (adjust, details, effects) without touching the file, so you know what you are applying
how: in the project folder run `npx hyperframes@0.8.188 media-treatment --project . --file index.html --selector '#hero' --grading '<json>' --dry-run --json` with `{"preset":"<id>"}` and read the `after` object (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: "neutral" preset clears the grade
section: HyperFrames presets: what each one really sets
what: the `neutral` preset is not a mild look: a dry run of `{"preset":"neutral"}` returns `action: "clear"` and `after: null`, i.e. it removes `data-color-grading`
how: use it (or `--clear`) to strip a treatment before re-applying a different one (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Preset tuning values are absolute
section: HyperFrames presets: what each one really sets
what: in a recipe payload, `adjust` values are absolute values in the final payload, not deltas added to the preset; manual controls live inside `adjust`/`details`/`effects`, never top level
how: write `{"preset":"skin-soft","intensity":0.58,"adjust":{"highlights":-0.08}}`, not `"highlights"` at top level

name: Unknown keys and out-of-range values are rejected
section: HyperFrames presets: what each one really sets
what: media-treatment validates before writing: `adjust.warmth` failed with "unsupported key(s): warmth" and `effects.bloom: 4` failed with "must be a finite number from 0 through 3"
how: run the dry run first; fix the reported key instead of hand-editing the HTML attribute (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Product Polish base
what: for filmed or photographed products: intensity 0.7 with exposure 0.01, contrast 0.06, highlights -0.10, shadows 0.04, whites 0.02, blacks -0.03, vibrance 0.03, saturation 0.02; temperature/tint stay 0 unless a cast is visible, and no grain, vignette, blur or pixelate for catalogue media
how: `npx hyperframes@0.8.188 media-treatment --project . --file index.html --selector '#hero' --grading '<json>' --dry-run --json` with that payload (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Product Polish rejection rules
what: reject a result that clips white packaging, muddies black products, shifts a known brand colour, hides texture or makes labels harder to read; if the source already has accurate colour and clean endpoints, leave pixels unchanged and polish with framing or motion, and report that choice
how: compare before/after sheets; skip `--apply` when the source wins

name: UI footage gets no grade
what: for literal app, website, dashboard, terminal or slide pixels the default payload is none; a global grade shifts brand colours, status colours, charts and tiny text together
how: polish UI with crop, scale, pacing, cursor emphasis or DOM overlays outside the captured pixels; if a stylised UI look is requested, state that exact UI colour is no longer preserved

name: Film Memory flicker
what: the Film Memory treatment adds a gentle exposure pulse, not a flash: author `--hf-color-grading-exposure: 0` inline and move it through a finite irregular sequence within -0.03..0.03, in `sine.inOut` segments of about 0.45-0.8 s, returning near the start
how: `tl.to("#hero",{"--hf-color-grading-exposure":0.02,duration:0.6,ease:"sine.inOut"},t)` steps on the registered paused timeline; no randomness, timers or onUpdate

name: Film Memory gate weave limits
what: keep x/y drift within 0.15% of the shorter composition edge, rotation within 0.03 degrees and scale 1.005-1.01 so edges never show; weave is slight mechanical drift, not handheld shake
how: for 1080 px height that is at most about 1.6 px of x/y; tween `x`, `y`, `rotation`, `scale` on the media wrapper with finite sine.inOut steps

name: Film Memory is not stock emulation
what: the recipe is for warm memories and restrained flashbacks and must be described as an HF film-memory treatment, not camera-stock emulation; don't add dust, scratches, light leaks or halation unless an owned component exists and the story needs it
how: report it with that wording; reach for 8mm Home Movie when material artifacts are wanted

name: Creator Camcorder bounds
what: tune only inside: intensity 0.55-0.8, contrast 0.03-0.1, saturation -0.12..-0.02, grain 0.04-0.12, chromaBleed 0.35-0.7, vignette 0.03-0.1; blur and pixelate stay 0, and square pixels, scanlines, RGB splitting and tracking noise are other visual languages, not defaults
how: `npx hyperframes@0.8.188 media-treatment --project . --file index.html --selector '#hero' --grading '<json>' --dry-run --json` with the recipe payload, then change one value inside its range (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Camcorder HUD block
what: explicit recording-device language comes from the Registry block `camcorder-hud`; its paused timeline derives the counter and REC blink from composition time, so preview, scrub and render agree
how: `npx hyperframes@0.8.188 add camcorder-hud --dir . --no-clipboard --json` (installs `compositions/camcorder-hud.html`, default 4 s, 1920x1080); edit date/time/mode there; the installed file loads GSAP from cdn.jsdelivr, so point it at `assets/vendor/gsap-3.14.2.min.js` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Source-to-camera reveal needs two layers
what: global grading intensity fades only primary correction and LUT output, not the camcorder effects; for a visible switch from clean to camera, use two synchronized media layers and a finite opacity crossfade on the paused timeline
how: duplicate the `<video>` (same src/data-start), grade only the top copy, tween its `opacity` 0 to 1

name: VHS Playback: use the whole combination
what: start from the complete recipe, not `tapeDamage` alone; tapeDamage owns line jitter, time-base wobble, bottom-edge head switching, luma bandwidth loss, ghosting, noise and dropouts, chromaBleed separately cuts horizontal chroma detail
how: `npx hyperframes@0.8.188 media-treatment --project . --file index.html --selector '#hero' --grading '<json>' --dry-run --json` with the recipe payload or `{"preset":"vhs-playback"}` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: VHS digital stage only tears rows
what: in the VHS recipe the digital glitch stage is used only for rare horizontal row tears: digitalGlitchColorSplit, Pixelate, BlockAmount, BlockDisplacement and BlockOpacity stay 0; blur, CRT curvature, pixelation and the camera HUD stay off
how: keep those keys at 0 when tuning `digitalGlitch` (0.2-0.4) and `digitalGlitchLineTear` (0.04-0.1)

name: VHS rejection checks
what: inspect dense consecutive frames and reject hard edge tearing, face smearing, frozen noise, square blocks, blank borders or a bottom disturbance that competes with the subject; global intensity does not fade tape damage
how: render a draft and step through frames; for a source-to-tape reveal crossfade two synchronized layers

name: "Old home video" is not automatically VHS
what: for "make it feel like an old home video", compare 8mm and VHS language against the source first; never infer that every old-video request means VHS
how: build two candidates (`home-movie-8mm` and `vhs-playback`) and pick from before/after evidence

name: 8mm filmArtifacts owns only dust and scratches
what: in the 8mm recipe `filmArtifacts` (0.35-0.7) adds deterministic sparse dust and short scratches; colour, vignette and grain come from the preset/details, weave from the host timeline (within 0.15% of the short edge, 0.03 deg, scale 1.005-1.015, 0.6-1 s sine.inOut steps)
how: `npx hyperframes@0.8.188 media-treatment --project . --file index.html --selector '#hero' --grading '<json>' --dry-run --json` with the 8mm payload; reject constant dust, persistent scratches, pumping, exposed edges or muddy highlights (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Editorial Halftone screens
what: a real four-angle CMYK raster with fixed C/M/Y/K angles 15/75/0/45 degrees, separate ink coverage and a warm paper base; tune only amount (0.75-1) and size (0.15-0.55) and judge at final output resolution because browser zoom misrepresents the screen
how: `npx hyperframes@0.8.188 media-treatment --project . --file index.html --selector '#hero' --grading '<json>' --dry-run --json` with `{"intensity":1,"adjust":{"contrast":0.04,"saturation":0.04},"effects":{"halftone":0.94,"halftoneSize":0.36}}`; keep captions as DOM above the media (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Two-Ink Editorial Print
what: maps warm midtones to vermilion, deep/cool shadows to teal and shared dark coverage to a dark overprint on warm paper, with 15/75-degree screens and a slight registration offset; never combine it with `halftone` or a duotone LUT
how: `npx hyperframes@0.8.188 media-treatment --project . --file index.html --selector '#hero' --grading '<json>' --dry-run --json` with `{"intensity":1,"adjust":{"contrast":0.08,"highlights":-0.06,"shadows":0.04},"effects":{"twoInkPrint":1,"twoInkPrintSize":0.42}}` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Monochrome Screen Print shapes
what: `monoScreen` builds monochrome dot/shape/line artwork; `monoScreenShape` 0-4 = circle, square, diamond, triangle, line; keep size and spread within 0.15-0.55 and use a two-colour palette
how: `npx hyperframes@0.8.188 media-treatment --project . --file index.html --selector '#hero' --grading '<json>' --dry-run --json` with `{"effects":{"monoScreen":1,"monoScreenSize":0.35,"monoScreenShape":4},"palette":["#111319","#f2ecdc"]}` (line screen) (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Engraved Illustration
what: `engraving` translates luminance into directional engraved lines; keep the calibrated base and tune spacing 0.25-0.6, contrast 0.3-0.65, wave 0-0.35; reject broken contours or lines that flicker across frames
how: `npx hyperframes@0.8.188 media-treatment --project . --file index.html --selector '#hero' --grading '<json>' --dry-run --json` with the recipe's engraving payload and palette `["#101216","#f3eddf"]` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Crosshatched Sketch
what: layered hand-hatched lines that keep the subject contour; tune spacing 0.18-0.5, edge detail 0.3-0.7, wave 0.1-0.45; reject dense black fill or shimmer stronger than the sketch language
how: `npx hyperframes@0.8.188 media-treatment --project . --file index.html --selector '#hero' --grading '<json>' --dry-run --json` with the recipe's crosshatch payload (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: CRT Display needs more than curvature
what: curvature alone is geometry; pair `crtCurvature` (0.08-0.28) with restrained scanlines (0.18-0.45) and slight channel separation (0-0.12), and only when the media is shown as an old monitor or game screen
how: `npx hyperframes@0.8.188 media-treatment --project . --file index.html --selector '#hero' --grading '<json>' --dry-run --json` with `{"effects":{"crtCurvature":0.2,"scanlines":0.35,"scanlineCount":0.17,"scanlineSoftness":1,"chromaticAberration":0.08}}` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Terminal ASCII vs Editorial ASCII
what: a real shader 5x7 glyph field: Terminal = `asciiSize` 0.08, `asciiInvert` 1, palette dark `#020605` + green `#38ff78`; Editorial = size 0.066, invert 0, palette `#0b0d0d`/`#eee9db`; keep ascii 0.75-1 and size 0.04-0.15
how: `npx hyperframes@0.8.188 media-treatment --project . --file index.html --selector '#hero' --grading '<json>' --dry-run --json` with either payload (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: ASCII style and rotation controls
what: beyond the recipes, the capability catalogue lists `asciiStyle` 0-7, `asciiColor` 0-1 and `asciiRotation` 0-1 for the ASCII effect
how: `npx hyperframes@0.8.188 media-treatment --project . --file index.html --selector '#hero' --grading '<json>' --dry-run --json` with `{"effects":{"ascii":1,"asciiStyle":3,"asciiRotation":0.5}}` validated; judge the result in a render (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Ordered dither is Bayer, not error diffusion
what: the realtime `dither` effect uses a stable 4x4 Bayer threshold and an explicit dark-to-light palette; never call it Floyd-Steinberg or Atkinson. Warm Print: `ditherSize` 0.25 with `#17121a,#824c50,#e09873,#f7ddb1`; Electric Ink: size 0.4 with six colours `#080717 ... #aafae0`
how: `npx hyperframes@0.8.188 media-treatment --project . --file index.html --selector '#hero' --grading '<json>' --dry-run --json` with either payload (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Palette order inverts the mapping
what: `palette` takes 2-6 exact `#RRGGBB` colours in authored order; the runtime validates but does not reorder, so reversing the array inverts the tone mapping
how: a reversed Warm Print palette also passed the dry run, so check the render, not the validator (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Classic dither palettes
what: owned ramps: `noir` `#000000,#ffffff`; `ink-paper` `#1a1a2e,#f5f5dc`; `terminal` `#001100,#00ff00`; `amber-glow` `#1a0f00,#ffcc00`; `handheld-green` `#0f380f,#306230,#8bac0f,#9bbc0f`. The name is a shortcut; persist the colours in `palette`
how: `npx hyperframes@0.8.188 media-treatment --project . --file index.html --selector '#hero' --grading '<json>' --dry-run --json` with `{"effects":{"dither":1,"ditherSize":0.3},"palette":["#0f380f","#306230","#8bac0f","#9bbc0f"]}` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Mood dither palettes
what: `golden-hour` `#1a1205,#4a3510,#8b6914,#d4a017,#fff8dc`; `deep-sea` `#0a1628 ... #a8dce8`; `arctic-night` `#0a0a14 ... #cae8ff`; `synthwave` `#120458,#7b2cbf,#e040fb,#ff6ec7,#fff59d`; `vaporwave` `#1a0a2e,#3d1a5c,#ff71ce,#01cdfe,#fffb96`; `forest` `#1a2e1a ... #c8e6c8`; synthwave is a deliberate stylisation, not polish
how: `npx hyperframes@0.8.188 media-treatment --project . --file index.html --selector '#hero' --grading '<json>' --dry-run --json` with the golden-hour or synthwave list (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Mono dither palettes: sepia and blueprint
how: put the list in `palette` with `effects.dither` 0.7-1, `ditherSize` 0.1-0.5

name: Exact error diffusion bakes a file
what: Floyd-Steinberg, Atkinson (higher contrast, early Macintosh), Jarvis-Judice-Ninke (smoother), Stucki, Burkes, Sierra variants need every block's error from earlier blocks, so they bake a new image/MP4 instead of running in the shader
how: `node .claude/skills/media-use/scripts/dither.mjs --input clip.mp4 --out clip.atk.mp4 --algorithm atkinson --palette '#17121a,#824c50,#e09873,#f7ddb1' --point-size 3`, then `npx hyperframes media-use resolve --from clip.atk.mp4 --type video --project .` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Error-diffusion controls
what: `dither.mjs` also takes `--brightness` 0.5-2, `--contrast` 0.5-2 (default 1.2) and `--detail` 0.1-1 (diffused-error strength); video output uses the source average frame rate as CFR. Don't process PQ/HLG footage without an SDR tone-map decision
how: `node .claude/skills/media-use/scripts/dither.mjs --help` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Organic light leak block
what: a finite deterministic CSS/GSAP overlay with one rise, peak and full recovery that scales to its placed duration; for one motivated memory beat, not a looping texture
how: `npx hyperframes@0.8.188 add organic-light-leak-overlay --dir . --no-clipboard --json` (default 4 s); fix its CDN GSAP src; reject clipped faces, unmotivated warm wash or black from a wrong blend mode (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Bloom effect controls
what: `effects.bloom` adds thresholded glow around bright regions, range 0-3 (recommended 0.55) with `bloomRadius` 1-100 (default 8); it is a multipass effect
how: `npx hyperframes@0.8.188 media-treatment --project . --file index.html --selector '#hero' --grading '<json>' --dry-run --json` with `{"effects":{"bloom":0.55,"bloomRadius":8}}` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Animate bloom seek-safely
what: bloom is one of the animatable controls: author `style="--hf-color-grading-bloom: <start>"` inline and tween `--hf-color-grading-bloom` on the registered paused timeline; once set, the CSS property overrides the payload's bloom value
how: `tl.to("#hero",{"--hf-color-grading-bloom":1.2,duration:0.8},t)`; no frame-zero `tl.set`, timers or onUpdate

name: Kuwahara painterly effect
what: edge-preserving painterly smoothing with radius, sharpness and saturation controls; multipass and animatable via `--hf-color-grading-kuwahara`
how: `npx hyperframes@0.8.188 media-treatment --project . --file index.html --selector '#hero' --grading '<json>' --dry-run --json` with `{"effects":{"kuwahara":1,"kuwaharaRadius":0.1429,"kuwaharaSharpness":0.3125,"kuwaharaSaturation":0.5}}` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Channel separation with an angle
what: `chromaticAberration` offsets colour channels by `chromaticAngle` (0-1); recommended 0.15
how: `npx hyperframes@0.8.188 media-treatment --project . --file index.html --selector '#hero' --grading '<json>' --dry-run --json` with `{"effects":{"chromaticAberration":0.15,"chromaticAngle":0.25}}` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Full digital glitch
what: `digitalGlitch` composes tears, blocks and colour splits; its recommended apply set is glitch 0.55, colorSplit 0.25, lineTear 0.25, pixelate 0.15, blockAmount 0.5, blockDisplacement 0.25, speed 0.5
how: `npx hyperframes@0.8.188 media-treatment --project . --file index.html --selector '#hero' --grading '<json>' --dry-run --json` with that payload (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Multipass cost check
what: Blur, Bloom and Kuwahara are multipass; cost follows treated pixel area, and more than two simultaneously visible full-frame multipass layers needs a continuous playback check on the target machine
how: simplify or pre-render the stack if playback drops frames; don't claim a universal cap

name: Animatable grading properties
what: only these may be tweened: `--hf-color-grading-intensity` 0-1, `-lut-intensity` 0-1, `-exposure` -2..2, `-blur` 0-1, `-bloom` 0-3, `-kuwahara`, `-pixelate`, `-ascii`, `-dither` (each 0-1)
how: `npx hyperframes@0.8.188 media-treatment --capability animation --json` prints this list; put the first value inline in `style`, then finite `tl.to()` keyframes (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Fade a LUT in over time
what: `--hf-color-grading-lut-intensity` animates the LUT strength alone (0-1), separate from overall intensity
how: inline `style="--hf-color-grading-lut-intensity:0"` on the graded `<video>`, then `tl.to("#hero",{"--hf-color-grading-lut-intensity":0.85,duration:1.5},t)`

name: Grading order in the shader
what: the processing order is adjust, wheels, curves, hueCurves, secondaries, lut, details, effects
how: `npx hyperframes@0.8.188 media-treatment --capability grading --json` prints it; plan a look in that order (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Colour wheels payload
what: shadows/midtones/highlights each take `hue` (degrees 0-360), `amount` 0-1 and `level` -1..1; the catalogue example is shadows hue 205 amount 0.08, highlights hue 35 amount 0.06
how: `npx hyperframes@0.8.188 media-treatment --project . --file index.html --selector '#hero' --grading '<json>' --dry-run --json` with `{"wheels":{"shadows":{"hue":205,"amount":0.08,"level":0},"highlights":{"hue":35,"amount":0.06,"level":0}}}` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: RGB curves payload
what: master/red/green/blue curves take normalized `[input, output]` points, 2-16 per curve, endpoints implicit but counted toward the 16
how: `npx hyperframes@0.8.188 media-treatment --project . --file index.html --selector '#hero' --grading '<json>' --dry-run --json` with `{"curves":{"blue":[[0,0.06],[1,0.94]]}}` (blue shadows up, blue highlights down) (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Hue curves payload
what: `hueVsHue` (delta -180..180 deg), `hueVsSaturation` and `hueVsLuma` (delta -1..1) take `[hueDegrees, delta]` points, 3-16 per curve
how: `npx hyperframes@0.8.188 media-treatment --project . --file index.html --selector '#hero' --grading '<json>' --dry-run --json` with `{"hueCurves":{"hueVsSaturation":[[180,0],[210,0.15],[240,0]]}}` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: HSL secondaries payload
what: up to four ordered selections, each with a key (hue centre/range/softness, saturation min/max/softness, luma min/max/softness) and a correction (hueShift, saturation, luma, temperature, tint)
how: `npx hyperframes@0.8.188 media-treatment --project . --file index.html --selector '#hero' --grading '<json>' --dry-run --json` with the catalogue example (hue centre 215, range 25) (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: One selector can patch many clips
what: a selector matching several images/videos patches every match, merged into each element's own grading; run `--clear` first for an identical look, or add `--selector-index` to patch only one
how: `npx hyperframes media-treatment --selector ".clip" --grading '<json>' --apply --json` and read `count`

name: Analyze before correcting
what: `--analyze` returns luma percentiles (yMin, yLow, yAvg, yHigh, yMax), saturation average, shadow/highlight clip risk, source colour metadata, HDR/LOG warnings and a bounded suggested patch without changing the file; the patch is a starting point, not an automatic neutralisation of intentional colour
how: `npx hyperframes@0.8.188 media-treatment --project . --file index.html --selector '#hero' --analyze --json` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Named bold looks must read clearly
what: when the owner names VHS, glitch, ASCII, halftone, camcorder, print or engraving, apply the signature effects strongly enough to read unmistakably; correction and polish stay restrained
how: for a named look start at the recipe's base, not its low end

name: At most two candidates
what: when more than one lane fits, generate at most two candidates and choose from before/after evidence; ordinary correction starts with one, and stacking effects to look sophisticated is out
how: two entries in `grades.json`, then `grade-compare`

name: "Too many shadows and boring" means correction first
what: the owned feedback table says: lift shadows and protect highlights, then compare one restrained preset; add mild contrast or vibrance only if frames justify it; never infer retro texture, HUD or palette effects
how: `{"adjust":{"shadows":0.1,"highlights":-0.06}}` then compare against `soft-boost`

name: "Keep brand colours exact"
what: leave UI/logo pixels unchanged and use framing and motion; only a demonstrated exposure-only correction is allowed, never a stylised preset, palette or LUT
how: no `data-color-grading` on the logo/UI media

name: Grain and vignette belong in the payload
what: use the canonical `details`/`effects` fields for vignette, grain, blur and pixelate; don't duplicate them on treated media with CSS filters, SVG turbulence, opacity or decorative DOM overlays
how: `{"details":{"vignette":0.1,"grain":0.08}}` instead of a grain/vignette overlay block on the same clip

name: Vignette shape controls
what: besides `vignette` 0-1, `details` has `vignetteMidpoint` (default 0.5), `vignetteRoundness` -1..1 (default 0) and `vignetteFeather` (default 0.65); grain has `grainSize` (default 0.25) and `grainRoughness` (default 0.5)
how: `npx hyperframes@0.8.188 media-treatment --project . --file index.html --selector '#hero' --grading '<json>' --dry-run --json` with `{"details":{"vignette":0.2,"vignetteRoundness":1,"vignetteFeather":0.9}}` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Grade-split-reveal component
what: the Registry has `grade-split-reveal`: the same picture flat and finished with a hard edge sweeping between them, pausing mid-way to compare, then committing to the graded look; both sides are real HF grading through the WebGL shader
how: `npx hyperframes catalog grade` lists it; install with `npx hyperframes add grade-split-reveal --dir . --no-clipboard --json`

name: A Hald CLUT is a 3D LUT stored as pixels
section: Making and using LUTs (Hald CLUT, .cube, HyperFrames)
what: each pixel holds one cube entry (its colour is the output value), laid out row by row across a square image; it is an ordinary PNG
how: treat Hald PNGs as LUTs, never as photos (don't resize, re-encode lossy or colour-manage them)

name: Identity Hald from ffmpeg
section: Making and using LUTs (Hald CLUT, .cube, HyperFrames)
what: `haldclutsrc` makes an identity Hald CLUT; level N gives an N*N*N by N*N*N picture, each component coded on a 1/(N*N) scale: level 8 = 512x512 (a 64-point cube), level 6 = 216x216 (36-point)
how: `ffmpeg -f lavfi -i haldclutsrc=8 -frames:v 1 hald8.png` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Turn any grade into a LUT
section: Making and using LUTs (Hald CLUT, .cube, HyperFrames)
what: open the identity image in any editor, apply the grade and save; the result is that grade as a LUT, which is how you get a LUT out of software with no LUT export
how: grade the identity with an ffmpeg chain: `ffmpeg -i hald8.png -vf "curves=preset=cross_process" -frames:v 1 hald_cp.png` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Keep spatial effects off the Hald
section: Making and using LUTs (Hald CLUT, .cube, HyperFrames)
what: a LUT can only change colour, contrast, brightness and gamma; grain, noise reduction, vignetting or sharpening applied to the Hald PNG can corrupt the LUT
how: grade the Hald with colour-only filters (curves, colorbalance, eq, lut3d); add grain/vignette later on the video

name: Apply a Hald to video
section: Making and using LUTs (Hald CLUT, .cube, HyperFrames)
what: `haldclut` takes the video as first input and the Hald as second; the Hald can be a picture or a whole video stream
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -i hald_cp.png -filter_complex "[0:v][1:v]haldclut" -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Prove the Hald round trip
section: Making and using LUTs (Hald CLUT, .cube, HyperFrames)
what: an untouched identity Hald should give back the source; here identity `haldclut` vs source measured PSNR 50.68 dB average, so differences are interpolation rounding only
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -i hald8.png -filter_complex "[0:v]format=rgb24,split[a][b];[b][1:v]haldclut[c];[c][a]psnr" -f null -` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Animated CLUT stream
section: Making and using LUTs (Hald CLUT, .cube, HyperFrames)
what: the docs build an identity Hald stream altered over time (`hue=H=2*PI*t...`, `curves=cross_process`) saved with a lossless codec; haldclut applies it frame by frame and, after the CLUT stream ends, keeps applying its last picture (`repeatlast` default 1)
how: `ffmpeg -f lavfi -i haldclutsrc=8 -vf "hue=H=2*PI*t:s=sin(2*PI*t)+1, curves=cross_process" -t 2 -c:v ffv1 clut.nut` then `[0:v][1:v]haldclut` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Use only the first CLUT frame
section: Making and using LUTs (Hald CLUT, .cube, HyperFrames)
what: `clut=first` processes only the first frame of the CLUT input (default `all`)
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -i clut.nut -filter_complex "[0:v][1:v]haldclut=clut=first" out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Hald with a built-in preview
section: Making and using LUTs (Hald CLUT, .cube, HyperFrames)
what: ffmpeg uses the biggest square from the top-left of the Hald picture and ignores right/bottom padding, so you can pad the Hald with SMPTE bars before/after the effect as a visual label
how: the docs' `pad=iw+320 ... smptebars=s=320x256 ... curves=color_negative` example made `clutprev.png`, and that padded file still applied cleanly with `haldclut` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Hald to .cube converter (Python)
section: Making and using LUTs (Hald CLUT, .cube, HyperFrames)
what: a Hald PNG's pixels in row-major order are the .cube entries (red fastest), so conversion is a relabelling; here a level-8 Hald became `LUT_3D_SIZE 64` and `lut3d` with it matched `haldclut` at 57.75 dB PSNR
how: `python3 hald2cube.py hald_cp.png look.cube` (script in this session's scratch folder: reads the PNG with PIL, writes `LUT_3D_SIZE n` then one `r g b` line per pixel) (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: lut3d formats and interpolation
section: Making and using LUTs (Hald CLUT, .cube, HyperFrames)
what: `lut3d` reads .3dl (After Effects), .cube (Iridas), .dat (DaVinci), .m3d (Pandora) and .csp (cineSpace); interp can be nearest, trilinear, tetrahedral, pyramid or prism
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf "lut3d=file=look.cube:interp=tetrahedral" out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: 1D LUT for a pure tone curve
section: Making and using LUTs (Hald CLUT, .cube, HyperFrames)
what: `lut1d` applies a 1D .cube or .csp with nearest, linear, cosine, cubic or spline interpolation; a 1D LUT changes each channel's curve only
how: write `LUT_1D_SIZE 1024` + 1024 `v v v` lines (here a 0.8 gamma lift) and run `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf "lut1d=file=lift.cube:interp=cubic" out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: LUT strength in ffmpeg
section: Making and using LUTs (Hald CLUT, .cube, HyperFrames)
what: ffmpeg's LUT filters have no intensity option; mixing the LUT result over the original with `blend` opacity gives a partial strength
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -i look.png -filter_complex "[0:v]format=gbrp,split[a][b];[b][1:v]haldclut,format=gbrp[g];[g][a]blend=all_mode=normal:all_opacity=0.6" out.mp4` (command ran; 0.6 is an example) (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Hald CLUTs on stills with ImageMagick
section: Making and using LUTs (Hald CLUT, .cube, HyperFrames)
what: IM's `-hald-clut` takes an image and a Hald and returns a new image of the input's size; `hald:8` generates an identity
how: `convert hald:8 hald8.png` and `convert frame.png look.png -hald-clut out.png` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Ingest your own .cube into HyperFrames
section: Making and using LUTs (Hald CLUT, .cube, HyperFrames)
what: `media-use resolve --type lut --from` validates a cube before registering it under `.media/luts/`; an ffmpeg-made 64-point cube ingested as `lut_001`
how: `npx hyperframes@0.8.188 media-use resolve --type lut --from look.cube --project . --json`, then `{"lut":{"src":".media/luts/lut_001.cube","intensity":0.85}}` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: HyperFrames cube size limit is 64
section: Making and using LUTs (Hald CLUT, .cube, HyperFrames)
what: the LUT contract is a 3D .cube with max cube size 64; a level-9 Hald (729 px, 81-point cube) was rejected with "LUT_3D_SIZE 81 exceeds max 64"
how: build Halds at level 8 or lower for HF (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Parametric LUT from numbers
section: Making and using LUTs (Hald CLUT, .cube, HyperFrames)
what: `--params` builds a deterministic cube (buildCube) from controls such as contrast and temperature
how: `npx hyperframes@0.8.188 media-use resolve --type lut --params '{"contrast":0.2,"temperature":-0.3}' --project . --json` wrote `.media/luts/lut_002.cube` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Parametric LUTs can't be film stocks
section: Making and using LUTs (Hald CLUT, .cube, HyperFrames)
what: buildCube math cannot reproduce real film stocks or emulsion transforms; for those, use a CDN-backed scanned .cube entry or ingest a real scanned cube
how: `resolve --type lut --from scanned.cube`; never call a `--params` cube a stock emulation

name: Library LUTs work offline
section: Making and using LUTs (Hald CLUT, .cube, HyperFrames)
what: each `luts/index.json` look has a CDN `url` plus a `params` fallback used offline (`--local-only`) or when the download fails; `film-fade` (blacks 0.35, shadows 0.18, contrast -0.28, temperature 0.16, saturation -0.12, intensity 0.75) resolved here via params-fallback
how: `npx hyperframes@0.8.188 media-use resolve --type grade --intent "film fade" --project . --json --local-only` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: List LUT candidates before comparing
section: Making and using LUTs (Hald CLUT, .cube, HyperFrames)
what: `resolve --type grade --candidates` lists reusable LUT/grade entries (project and global scope) to copy into a `grades.json`
how: `npx hyperframes@0.8.188 media-use resolve --type grade --candidates --intent "cinematic" --project . --json` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: grade-compare with LUT files
section: Making and using LUTs (Hald CLUT, .cube, HyperFrames)
what: besides `--grades` (JSON array of `{label, grading}`), `grade-compare` takes `--luts a.cube,b.cube` and prepends the ungraded frame as an "original" cell unless `--no-baseline`
how: `npx hyperframes@0.8.188 grade-compare --for frame.png --luts .media/luts/grade_001.cube,.media/luts/lut_001.cube --project . --out cmp.png --json` (3 cells) (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Never read a .cube into context
section: Making and using LUTs (Hald CLUT, .cube, HyperFrames)
what: a 33-point cube is about 36k lines of numbers with no readable signal; judge it with grade-compare and read `.media/index.md` or `luts/index.json` for its description
how: `head -1 look.cube` at most (size line)

name: Don't bake a LUT for shader controls
section: Making and using LUTs (Hald CLUT, .cube, HyperFrames)
what: don't generate or hand-edit a LUT merely to combine controls the realtime shader already owns (adjust, wheels, curves, secondaries); keep those as editable JSON
how: use a LUT only for transforms outside the preset vocabulary

name: RawTherapee film HaldCLUT collection
section: Making and using LUTs (Hald CLUT, .cube, HyperFrames)
what: RawTherapee's Film Simulation tool uses HaldCLUT PNG/TIFF reference images, one per look, mostly based on classic film stocks (Pat David's G'MIC film emulation work); the shared `HaldCLUT.zip` is 402 MB
how: not downloaded (size); if the owner wants it, fetch from rawtherapee.com/shared, convert the needed level-8 PNG with `hald2cube.py`, and check licence first

name: Kodak Portra 400
section: Film stocks: what each one looks like (reference for matching)
what: warm and natural; reviews call its saturation restrained (Kodak claims "exceptional"), skin tones are its reputation, one reviewer notes a slight magenta bias in skin, and shadows may lean blue or blue-green; latitude about -1 to +3 stops
how: brief it as warm, restrained saturation, cool-leaning shadows; check skin on a real frame with `grade-compare`

name: Portra 400 defining traits
section: Film stocks: what each one looks like (reference for matching)
what: three things to nail: soft highlight roll-off (highlights fade rather than clip), restrained saturation (warm, not vivid), warm shadows on the orange/amber side
how: HF controls that correspond: `adjust.highlights` negative, modest `saturation`, `wheels.shadows` toward a warm hue; compare candidates on a frame

name: Portra 160
section: Film stocks: what each one looks like (reference for matching)
what: soft, muted, pastel; less saturated than Portra 400 and 800; Kodak promises neutral skin, reviews find it warm; takes overexposure well, underexposure looks muddy
how: treat as the low-saturation member of the Portra family when briefing

name: Portra 800
section: Film stocks: what each one looks like (reference for matching)
what: warm and more saturated than Portra 400 for most reviews, with vibrant reds, yellows and oranges; Print Grain Index 48 vs 37 for Portra 400
how: more grain and saturation than Portra 400 when matching

name: Kodak Ektar 100
section: Film stocks: what each one looks like (reference for matching)
what: highly saturated with vivid blues, greens and reds; skin is the weak point (faces can look redder); Print Grain Index under 25, below visibility in a 4x6 print
how: if matching Ektar on people, watch faces for red shift with a skin secondary (`secondaries` key around the skin hue)

name: Kodak Gold 200
section: Film stocks: what each one looks like (reference for matching)
what: warm, golden-to-orange tint and saturated colours by Kodak's account; adds yellow to light greys in cool light and can turn orange when underexposed; Print Grain Index 44
how: brief as warm consumer film; don't confuse with Portra's restraint

name: Kodak UltraMax 400
section: Film stocks: what each one looks like (reference for matching)
what: saturated consumer colour, usually called warm, punchier in colour and contrast than Portra 400 in a lab side-by-side; Print Grain Index 46
how: reference for a punchy everyday-snapshot look

name: Kodak ColorPlus 200
section: Film stocks: what each one looks like (reference for matching)
what: warm and fairly muted for most reviews, very close to Gold 200 in a controlled side-by-side; reds and pinks pop slightly more than blues and greens
how: reference for budget-film warmth

name: Kodak Ektachrome E100
section: Film stocks: what each one looks like (reference for matching)
what: E-6 slide film: neutral balance and moderately enhanced saturation per Kodak, some reviews find it cool; overexposed areas may shift cooler and shadows warmer; latitude about half a stop either way; RMS 8
how: brief as clean, slightly cool, careful highlights

name: Ektachrome E100 Lightroom recipe
section: Film stocks: what each one looks like (reference for matching)
what: slightly cool white balance (temp down 300-800 K), highlights -30 to -70, contrast +10 to +25, blacks -10 to -25, vibrance +10 to +20 with saturation 0 to +5, blue hue toward cyan and blue luminance down, mild S-curve, light grain 10-25 (Lightroom units)
how: the matching HF controls are `adjust.temperature`, `highlights`, `contrast`, `blacks`, `vibrance`, `hueCurves.hueVsHue`/`hueVsLuma` around blue, `curves.master`, `details.grain` — values must be re-chosen by eye, units differ

name: Ektachrome skin needs protection
section: Film stocks: what each one looks like (reference for matching)
what: E100 pushes warm tones toward magenta, the tone curve does more than the contrast slider, and slide film has almost no latitude above the exposure point
how: protect skin with an HSL secondary and set highlights before anything else

name: Kodak Kodachrome 64
section: Film stocks: what each one looks like (reference for matching)
what: warm with rich reds and deep neutral blacks in photographers' accounts; skies blue, sometimes cyan; contrast slightly higher than Ektachrome; RMS 10; K-14 processing ended in January 2011
how: reference for warm-red vintage slides

name: Fujifilm Velvia 50
section: Film stocks: what each one looks like (reference for matching)
what: extremely saturated with deep blues and a lean toward magenta/purple; high contrast steepening toward the shadows; narrow latitude (about 5 stops); RMS 9
how: reference for hyper-saturated landscapes; don't use for skin

name: Fujifilm Provia 100F
section: Film stocks: what each one looks like (reference for matching)
what: neutral and faithful, slightly cool, saturated but less than Velvia; "Standard" contrast in Fujifilm's chart; RMS 8
how: reference for neutral slide film

name: Fujifilm Astia 100F
section: Film stocks: what each one looks like (reference for matching)
what: soft, subdued colour and natural skin, warmer than Provia 100F; Fujifilm rates its contrast "Soft", mostly in the highlights; RMS 7
how: reference for soft fashion/portrait slide film

name: Fujifilm Superia X-TRA 400
section: Film stocks: what each one looks like (reference for matching)
what: cool, with strong greens and blues; reviews often report a magenta cast; shadows turn green when underexposed
how: reference for the "Fuji consumer" cool-green look

name: Fujifilm Pro 400H
section: Film stocks: what each one looks like (reference for matching)
what: neutral to cool with deep greens and blues, pastel when overexposed; minty greens with cyan undertones; very tolerant of overexposure; discontinued 2021 (its fourth cyan-sensitive layer)
how: the wedding "airy" reference; overexposure is part of the look

name: Pro 400H overexposed a stop
section: Film stocks: what each one looks like (reference for matching)
what: a wedding favourite: bright, airy, pastel greens and soft skin, overexposed a stop; low contrast, fine grain
how: exposure up first (`adjust.exposure`), then lower contrast

name: Fujifilm Eterna (film simulation)
section: Film stocks: what each one looks like (reference for matching)
what: inspired by motion-picture film: more muted colours and flatter contrast than other film simulations, made to give video room in post
how: reference for a muted, low-contrast base before a creative grade

name: Eterna in its own words
section: Film stocks: what each one looks like (reference for matching)
what: Fujifilm's development story: in cinema, saturation is suppressed so no particular colour stands out, and the tonality is wide to deliver the atmosphere of the scene
how: keep saturation down and contrast gentle when the brief says "cinema, not photo"

name: Kodak Vision3 500T
section: Film stocks: what each one looks like (reference for matching)
what: tungsten-balanced: natural colour under 3200 K, blue to teal in daylight without a Wratten 85 filter; low-contrast camera negative (slope about 0.5) made for scanning and grading
how: reference for night/interior cinema negative

name: Kodak Vision3 250D
section: Film stocks: what each one looks like (reference for matching)
what: daylight-balanced cinema negative: accurate, nuanced colour; scans often come out warm; low contrast in ECN-2 (slope about 0.5)
how: reference for daylight cinema negative

name: Kodak Vision3 50D
section: Film stocks: what each one looks like (reference for matching)
what: natural, accurate colour with praised skin tones; Kodak's finest-grain motion-picture film; sources disagree on saturation
how: reference for the cleanest daylight negative

name: CineStill 800T
section: Film stocks: what each one looks like (reference for matching)
what: Vision3 500T without its rem-jet backing: natural under warm lamps, blue to teal in daylight, red to orange halos around bright lights because light reflects back into the red-sensitive layer next to the base
how: halation is the signature; see the halation section

name: CineStill 800T traits
section: Film stocks: what each one looks like (reference for matching)
what: a good emulation shows: cool tungsten balance strongest in the shadows with skin leaning slightly cyan, warm halation around the lights (not white bloom), lifted blacks, moderate organic grain, soft contrast; made for night content with point lights, wrong for product videos and tutorials
how: pick night clips with practical lights before choosing this look

name: CineStill 400D
section: Film stocks: what each one looks like (reference for matching)
what: daylight film: soft palette, natural saturation, warm skin per CineStill; scans often warm, sometimes mint-green
how: reference for warm daylight negative

name: Kodak Tri-X 400
section: Film stocks: what each one looks like (reference for matching)
what: contrasty B&W with deep blacks and visible grain (RMS 17); more sensitive to violet/blue than the eye, so skies come out pale and skin and reds slightly darker
how: to darken skies Kodak gives daylight filter factors of 2 (No. 8 yellow), 2.5 (No. 15 deep yellow) and 8 (No. 25 red); in post the matching control is the red/blue weights of `colorchannelmixer` or ffmpeg `monochrome` (see B&W items)

name: Ilford HP5 Plus
section: Film stocks: what each one looks like (reference for matching)
what: subtle tones and visible grain; skies lighter than the eye sees them; in the archive's test its curve made skin 5.7 L* darker than luminance
how: reference for documentary B&W

name: Fujifilm Acros II
section: Film stocks: what each one looks like (reference for matching)
what: very fine grain (RMS 7), crisp highlights, blues a little darker than on most panchromatic films
how: reference for clean, fine-grain B&W

name: Ilford Delta 3200
section: Film stocks: what each one looks like (reference for matching)
what: grain everywhere, shadows that block up at EI 3200, highlights that hold; renders blue lighter and skin darker (6.3 L* in the archive's test)
how: reference for night/concert B&W

name: Kodak Double-X 5222
section: Film stocks: what each one looks like (reference for matching)
what: cinema B&W: vintage look with rich blacks and visible cubic grain (RMS 14)
how: reference for classic movie B&W

name: Kodak Aerochrome III (infrared false colour)
section: Film stocks: what each one looks like (reference for matching)
what: infrared prints as red, green as blue, red as green; healthy foliage turns magenta to red, skies deep blue to almost black, water very dark; always shot through a yellow filter
how: reference only; no infrared capture or false-colour tool exists here

name: LomoChrome Purple
section: Film stocks: what each one looks like (reference for matching)
what: false colour: greens turn purple, blues green or teal, yellows pink, reds mostly stay red (per Lomography)
how: reference for a hue-rotation look; `hueCurves.hueVsHue` is the matching control

name: Lomography Redscale XR
section: Film stocks: what each one looks like (reference for matching)
what: strong red-orange cast as if a red filter were on the lens, because light passes the base first and blue is weakened; more light means less effect
how: reference for a redscale brief

name: Polaroid Color 600 / i-Type
section: Film stocks: what each one looks like (reference for matching)
what: warm with pink highlights and green shadows and a limited colour range; high contrast, virtually grainless but soft
how: reference for instant-film briefs

name: Fujifilm Instax Mini
section: Film stocks: what each one looks like (reference for matching)
what: saturated but natural; vivid reds and greens, dark blues; high contrast with short latitude; no visible grain but soft
how: reference; cooler-looking than Polaroid in comparisons

name: Agfa Vista 200
section: Film stocks: what each one looks like (reference for matching)
what: high saturation; reviews disagree on warmth; fairly contrasty; RMS 4.3
how: reference for vivid consumer film

name: Kodak 2383 print stage
section: Film stocks: what each one looks like (reference for matching)
what: in the photochemical chain the negative was printed onto a print stock, for decades usually Kodak Vision 2383; the print supplied most of the contrast and its dye crossover gave cool shadows and warm highlights; Resolve ships 2383 LUTs built for Cineon film-log footage
how: a print look on normally exposed footage usually wants +0.3 to +0.7 EV so skin doesn't sink (`adjust.exposure`)

name: Eastman Color Negative II 5247 (early 70s)
section: Film stocks: what each one looks like (reference for matching)
what: early-1970s film was dominated by Kodak 5247, giving warmer, more saturated colours with deep shadows and fine grain; The Holdovers recreated that era on an ALEXA Mini
how: reference for a 70s-period brief

name: Four pillars of film emulation
section: Film stocks: what each one looks like (reference for matching)
what: The Holdovers' team treated film emulation as colour response, grain, halation and gate weave, not surface illusions
how: check each pillar separately: grade (LUT/adjust), `details.grain`, a halation pass, weave on the wrapper

name: Matrix look, colourist version
what: low saturation of about 30%, green pushed into shadows and (more) midtones, a little yellow in the highlights so it isn't monochrome, then key the skin and bring it back to a normal skin tone on the vectorscope
how: HF controls in that order: `adjust.saturation` down, `wheels.shadows`/`midtones` toward green, `wheels.highlights` toward yellow, then a `secondaries` skin key with a correcting `hueShift`

name: Matrix green, don't overdo the tint
what: the green sits mostly in shadows and midtones and skin should read as "a bit sick", not lime; tint around -15 to -20 (v8eo units), -40 looks like night vision, and raising saturation makes skin radioactive; offices, stairwells and fluorescent light suit it
how: keep the green in the split/wheels, not in global saturation

name: Matrix real-world blue
what: the Zion/ship scenes go blue and cold (temperature -20, split shadow `#101c2c`, highlight `#b8c4cc`, grain 20 in v8eo units); cutting between green and blue worlds makes an edit feel like it has a story
how: two looks on two scene groups; `wheels` toward blue for the second

name: Why the Matrix is green
what: the green tint nods to the monochrome green of command-line computing, and the film runs against the usual healthy yellow/orange skin rendering
how: use green-tinted skin only when the story is "inside a system"

name: Mexican filter: know the criticism
what: a yellow/sepia or overly warm grade used to signal hot, arid places such as Mexico, starting with Traffic (2000); it is criticised for washing out darker-skinned faces and stereotyping the places shown
how: don't apply a blanket yellow wash to a real place or client footage; if warmth is wanted, protect skin with a secondary

name: Traffic: one palette per storyline
what: Soderbergh gave each thread its own colour: Mexico a desaturated yellow, Judge Wakefield's story icy blue, the DEA storyline bright and multicoloured
how: for a multi-thread edit, assign one HF payload per thread and apply it with one selector per thread

name: David Fincher desaturated look
what: precise, desaturated (55-65%), a yellow-green cast in shadows and midtones, deep but never crushed shadows, cool blue-cyan highlights, subtle digital-looking grain and no halation or bloom at all
how: keep `effects.bloom` 0; desaturate and split green shadows/cool highlights with `wheels`

name: Fincher variants by film
what: Se7en is the most extreme bleach-bypass version (saturation 42, contrast 138); The Social Network adds a Boston-winter blue cast (temperature -12); Zodiac is slightly warmer; The Killer is cooler and slicker (v8eo units)
how: one base payload, then per-film overrides of temperature/saturation/contrast

name: Blade Runner 2049: Las Vegas orange
what: thick orange dust where everything goes soft and almost monochrome; low contrast (haze), high temperature, fade for fake atmosphere, bloom, split highlight `#ffb050` (v8eo units); commit to one colour per scene
how: warm `wheels.highlights` strongly, contrast down, `effects.bloom`; check nothing in frame stays blue/green

name: Blade Runner 2049: Los Angeles blue
what: cold grey-blue wet nights lit by signs; low saturation so the neon is the only strong colour (that is what separates it from a cyberpunk game), halation on neon
how: cool base, saturation down, halation pass on lights only

name: Dune desert palette
what: desert ochre, amber, sand and terracotta kept short of orange; restrained teal in night/interior shadows; film-like highlight fade, low-to-moderate saturation, near-invisible grain, wide tonal range; no halation, no bloom
how: warm wheels without pushing to orange, `highlights` down to keep sky/sand separation

name: Villeneuve variants
what: Sicario: the Dune recipe with less warmth and saturation and more contrast; Arrival: overcast, grey-green, mysterious (Eterna base, slightly cool and green, low saturation)
how: reuse one desert payload and lower temperature/saturation for Sicario

name: Euphoria purple shadows
what: the one trait that matters most: shadows magenta-purple, not blue or teal; saturated complementary contrast, heavy bloom so skin glows, red-orange halation on every light, subtle chromatic aberration (2-4 v8eo), lifted cool blacks
how: `wheels.shadows` toward purple hue, `effects.bloom`, small `chromaticAberration`

name: Wong Kar-wai warm vs green
what: tungsten warmth (reds, oranges, ambers) in interiors against a saturated green-yellow cast in the shadows, heavy red-orange halation on lamps, neon and candles, lifted blacks behind a veil, visible grain
how: `wheels.highlights` warm, `wheels.shadows` toward green, halation pass, `details.grain`

name: Step-printing smear (Wong Kar-wai)
what: v8eo approximates step printing by slowing the clip, then layering the same clip on itself at 40% opacity offset by 2 frames; it is not real step printing
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -filter_complex "[0:v]format=gbrp,split[a][b];[b]setpts=PTS+2/30/TB[d];[a][d]blend=all_mode=normal:all_opacity=0.4:shortest=1" out.mp4` (30 fps clip; slow it first) (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Sofia Coppola dreamy pastel
what: bleached pastels at low-to-moderate saturation, creamy (not amber) warmth, heavy fade so pure black almost never appears, gauzy bloom on highlights, fine grain, and a slight green-yellow tint in the shadows
how: lifted `blacks`, low `saturation`, `effects.bloom`, `wheels.shadows` toward green-yellow

name: A24 approach
what: not one recipe but an approach: desaturated, limited palette (two or three colour families per scene), subtly cool blue-green shadows, natural highlights with no crushed blacks or clipped whites, earth tones (browns, olives, ochres)
how: pick the two or three colour families first; lift blacks slightly

name: A24 per-film notes
what: Moonlight: neon-saturated nights, heavy blue cast with skin-warm highlights; Lady Bird: warm Sacramento daylight; Midsommar: blown-out unnerving daylight with no vignette; The Lighthouse: high-contrast B&W in a near-square frame
how: use as briefing vocabulary with the owner

name: Oppenheimer: keep the blacks down
what: if you change one thing, make it the blacks: phone footage lifts shadows to grey, Nolan's sit low and fall into darkness; warm, not teal-and-orange; B&W scenes harsher with more contrast
how: `adjust.blacks`/`shadows` negative; for the B&W parts `mono-clean`-style contrast

name: Ghibli live-action mood
what: vivid but not saturated (selective saturation via split toning, not a global push), soft warm golden light, painted-looking skies, lifted open shadows, soft bloom like a watercolour wash, almost no grain; green, natural subjects and train windows suit it, concrete and fluorescent interiors fight it
how: choose footage first; small `effects.bloom`, shadows up, grain 0

name: Y2K digicam look
what: harsh on-camera flash (centre brighter, skin near the flash blown), slight blue in the shadows from CCD sensors, heavy bloom/halation on bright spots, fine slightly chromatic sensor noise, reds slightly oversaturated, soft focus, strong flash vignette
how: `effects.bloom` high, `details.vignette` strong, small `chromaticAberration`, grain

name: Wes Anderson palette rules
what: pastel primaries (pinks, mints, butter yellows, dusty blues) at moderate saturation with hues shifted toward chalk, deliberately flat contrast with almost no deep shadow, slight warmth (Moonrise Kingdom the cool faded exception), heavy matte so pure black almost never appears, fine grain and never a vignette
how: `details.vignette` 0, lifted `blacks`, low contrast

name: Wes Anderson five-step grade
what: after a base correction: compressed dynamic range, contrast, saturation, warm/cool separation, then teal and orange
how: follow that order on a balanced shot

name: Cyberpunk is a restriction
what: a narrow palette: cyan-blue shadows, hot magenta-pink highlights and almost nothing warm in between, on a deep blue-black base; reference hexes: shadows `#0a1f3d` to `#123a5e`, midtones `#2b2f3a`, highlights `#d61f8a` to `#ff3fa4`, one sparing amber accent `#ffb347`; avoid orange/yellow elsewhere
how: `wheels.shadows` toward cyan, `wheels.highlights` toward magenta, saturation of other hues down with `hueCurves.hueVsSaturation`

name: Cyberpunk safety checks
what: isolate practical neon signs with HSL qualifiers, add controlled glow, protect skin on a separate node, and check the vectorscope so saturated cyan and magenta don't clip in Rec.709 delivery
how: skin `secondaries` key + `effects.bloom`; render a frame and look at the neon edges

name: Cyan-magenta gradient map
what: one Photoshop cyberpunk recipe: B&W conversion with more contrast, then a gradient map from cyan `#00D4FF` (shadows) to magenta `#FF00C8` (highlights) in Soft Light at 55%
how: ffmpeg version of that map: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -filter_complex "[0:v]format=gbrp,split[a][b];[b]colorchannelmixer=.3:.4:.3:0:.3:.4:.3:0:.3:.4:.3,lutrgb=r='val':g='212*(1-val/255)':b='255-55*val/255'[m];[a][m]blend=all_mode=softlight:all_opacity=0.55" out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Horror: keep a little colour
what: horror rarely goes fully monochrome: a sickly green or cold blue-grey cast keeps a scene feeling wrong, while full desaturation removes information
how: desaturate partly, never to 0, and add a green or blue-grey cast

name: Horror green as decay
what: green is also the colour of mold; mottled green makes a whole frame look rotten, as in the squalid settings of the Saw franchise
how: green `wheels.midtones` on grimy locations only

name: Green as "the colour of fear"
what: by 1931 green and horror were linked strongly enough that Universal reportedly marketed Dracula's green tint as "the color of fear"; German expressionist films used green tint for forests, night and dread
how: briefing history for a green-tinted horror title

name: Moody blue
what: cool the temperature, push shadows to blue harder than for teal-and-orange, a smaller cool push in midtones, protect the orange band so faces don't die, lift the black point a little (crushed blacks plus heavy blue reads as an error), cut global saturation 10-20%
how: HF order: `adjust.temperature`, `wheels.shadows`/`midtones`, skin `secondaries`, `adjust.blacks` up, `saturation` -0.1..-0.2

name: Moody is not dark
what: true moody editing keeps visible shadows, warm but restrained highlights, muted greens and blues, balanced midtones and preserved dynamic range; the difference between moody and muddy is always in the highlights and shadows
how: check `--analyze` clip risk after a moody grade

name: Dark-and-moody in two curve handles
what: the Phlearn guide: in Curves, move the bottom-left point up and right and the top-right point in and down, the same two points per R/G/B channel, then a corrective pass
how: HF `curves.master` with a lifted first point and lowered last point, e.g. `[[0,0.06],[1,0.92]]` (example values), validated with the dry run (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Golden hour in post
what: warm overall slightly and fix any green cast, push highlights toward yellow-orange (carries most of the look), hold shadows slightly cool (real golden hour has cool shadows; skipping this looks like a sepia filter), lift the red curve's top, soften the highlight roll-off, lift yellow saturation/luminance
how: `wheels.highlights` warm + `wheels.shadows` slightly blue + `curves.red` top lifted

name: What golden hour can't fake
what: post reproduces the colour (warm highlights, cool shadows, soft roll-off) but not the direction and length of shadows, which are geometry; it fights hard midday light and fluorescent interiors
how: only fake golden hour on overcast or soft-light footage

name: Bright and airy wedding grade
what: four moves from neutral: shadows lifted 15-25 IRE above true black, a gentle amber push on highlights, greens and blues pulled to pastels while skin oranges/pinks are kept, exposure 0.5-1 stop brighter than neutral; moody-dark weddings are the opposite (crushed cool shadows, 1-1.5 stops under)
how: `adjust.exposure` up, `blacks` up, `wheels.highlights` amber, `hueCurves.hueVsSaturation` down around green/blue

name: Pastel base grade
what: one node: lift blacks slightly, pull gain down a touch, saturation to about 30-35 (Resolve scale), a cool-to-warm split tone in lift and gain, protect skin with a Hue vs Sat curve, check the vectorscope
how: lifted `blacks`, `saturation` well down, `wheels` cool shadows/warm highlights, `hueCurves.hueVsSaturation` lifting the skin hue

name: Pastel is not faded film
what: pastel keeps saturation low everywhere and leans to candy colours (pinks, lavenders, mints, butter yellows); faded film lowers contrast and lifts blacks like an old print and can stay saturated; skipping the contrast step gives a foggy, undersaturated mess
how: set contrast first, then the pastel colour choice

name: High-contrast look
what: S-curve first, bring black and white points just to the limits and back off (watch the waveform, clipping can't be undone), then cut saturation 5-10% because contrast raises perceived saturation, then check skin hue (contrast pushes faces to red)
how: `curves.master` S, then `adjust.saturation` -0.05..-0.1

name: Teal and orange through the blue curve
what: Luttie's order: neutralise white balance, shadows toward cyan/blue (about 5-10% of the wheel), highlights toward orange by about half that, orange saturation up slightly with hue a degree or two toward red, then lift the blue curve's shadow end and pull its highlight end down ("the split that makes the look, more than the wheels"), gentle S-curve last
