how: `curves.blue` like `[[0,0.05],[1,0.95]]` (example values; ffmpeg `curves=blue='0/0.05 1/0.95'` also ran) (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Teal-orange: when to avoid
what: skip it when the background is already warm (sunset, wood-panelled interior: the frame turns muddy) and on documentary or product work where accurate colour matters
how: check the background colour before choosing it

name: Modernised teal-orange
what: the separation is fine, the intensity dates it: put warmth in the highlights only (highlight hue about 40-50 at low saturation) instead of warming every range
how: warm `wheels.highlights` at a small amount, no global temperature

name: Split the split-tone
what: a colourist's alternative: put the high end and the low end on separate nodes, remove neutrals from the low end so grey/black things don't turn blue, keep neutrals in the high end so whites go creamy
how: in HF, use a `secondaries` selection with a minimum saturation for the cool push instead of a global shadow wheel

name: Cross-processing look
what: developing slide film in C-41 (or negative in E-6) gave a marked colour shift and contrast change; the digital start: red channel shallow S (down about 25% along, up about 75%), blue channel reverse S, optionally green, then an overall S or reverse S for contrast
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf "curves=red='0/0 0.25/0.18 0.75/0.82 1/1':blue='0/0.1 0.25/0.3 0.75/0.7 1/0.9'" out.mp4` (example amounts; ffmpeg also has `curves=preset=cross_process`) (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Bleach bypass via a desaturated overlay
what: duplicate the image, desaturate the copy, put it on top in Overlay; strength by the copy's levels or opacity. Alternative: desaturated copy with contrast below, original on top in Color mode
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -filter_complex "[0:v]format=gbrp,split[a][b];[b]hue=s=0[g];[a][g]blend=all_mode=overlay" out.mp4` (add `:all_opacity=0.5` for less) (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Bleach bypass in three adjustment layers
what: saturation about -40, contrast about +40, then Photoshop's Bleach Bypass colour lookup at about 30% opacity because full strength was overblown (example values for one image)
how: HF `adjust.saturation`/`contrast` plus the library `bleach-bypass` LUT at low `lut.intensity`

name: Orton glow
what: Michael Orton blended a well-exposed and an overexposed slide, the overexposed one blurred; darktable's soften module copies this with size (blur), saturation and brightness of the overexposed copy and a mix where 50% is an equal blend
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -filter_complex "[0:v]format=gbrp,split[a][b];[b]exposure=exposure=1,gblur=sigma=10[o];[a][o]blend=all_mode=average" out.mp4` (1 EV, sigma 10 are examples) (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Silent-film tint vs tone
what: tinting dyes the whole film so what would be white becomes coloured; toning replaces the silver and colours the darkest areas, leaving whites largely untouched
how: tint = grey image multiplied by a colour: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -f lavfi -i color=c=0x4060c0:s=640x360:d=2 -filter_complex "[0:v]hue=s=0,format=gbrp[g];[1:v]format=gbrp[c];[g][c]blend=all_mode=multiply:shortest=1" out.mp4`; tone-like = same with `all_mode=screen` and a dark colour (both ran) (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Silent-film tint meanings
what: common tints in order: amber for daylight interiors (night amber for lit night exteriors), orange for night interiors, yellow ("Sunshine") only for daylight exteriors, blue for moonlit night, sepia tone popular in 1930s-50s westerns, red for fire and fury, lavender for romance/dusk/dawn, rose for low-key night interiors, green for mysterious or sea scenes
how: pick the tint colour for the multiply pass from this list

name: Tint names as moods
what: a vintage tint ad: Azure = reserve and distance (cold, formal interiors); Nocturne = night, murky interiors, sadness and dark intrigue; Purplehaze = dim, hazy, dreamy; Fleur de Lis = ceremonial, royal
how: use as a mood vocabulary when the owner asks for an old-film chapter

name: Nosferatu tint LUTs
what: one colourist built three tint LUTs from Nosferatu (1922) stills: yellow for daylight, pink for twilight, green for night, over a B&W dye-density base, mixed so a clip can fade from day to twilight to night. (Wikipedia's caption shows a blue-tinted night scene from the same film, so prints differ.)
how: three tinted versions of a B&W clip crossfaded on the timeline

name: Sepia from the ffmpeg docs
what: ffmpeg's documented sepia simulation is a colour-channel-mixer matrix

name: Technicolor three-strip
what: made famous by The Wizard of Oz; its quirks delivered posterised primary colours; PremiumBeat recreates it in Resolve by splitting the image into red, green and blue with splitter nodes and recombining
how: reference only here; a channel split/recombine needs a node tool (Resolve) that the repo lacks

name: Sin City: shot in colour, graded to near-B&W
what: Rodriguez shot everything in colour on HDCAM SR 4:4:4 with two monitors on set, one in colour and one desaturated with pushed contrast to make lighting choices; he admitted some greyscale instead of pure black-and-white, which gives more detail and a silvery depth
how: keep a colour master; for a single held colour use ffmpeg `colorhold` (keeps one colour, rest grey): `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf "colorhold=color=red:similarity=0.3:blend=0.0" out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: B&W virtual colour filters
what: film photographers used red filters to darken skies and make clouds pop, orange to smooth skin, green to lighten foliage; digital channel mixing does the same maths, so start at the channel mixer, push contrast further than in colour, and add a real grain pass
how: ffmpeg `monochrome` is a "custom colour filter" grey conversion: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf "monochrome=cb=-0.3:cr=0.3:size=1" out.mp4` (cb/cr set the filter spot, -1..1) (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Indian skin tones
what: Indian skin ranges from very fair to deep brown with warm, neutral or cool undertones (melanin, hemoglobin, carotene); keep skin on the vectorscope skin line without pushing to red or magenta, isolate skin with qualifiers, and avoid LUTs designed for Western skin
how: a `secondaries` skin key before any creative LUT on the owner's clients

name: Build a "digital film stock" first
what: Annapurna Studios' supervising colourist spends the first days building highlight roll-off, skin tones, mid-tone contrast and shadow distribution as a base "digital film stock", including a shadow roll-off that holds blacks just above absolute zero, then does the rest in the base grade
how: make one shared base payload for the whole film before per-scene looks

name: Palette from the story setting (Dangal)
what: Dangal's DoP and colourist tested skin tones and costumes in pre-production and derived the palette from the setting, shooting mostly in natural light to look raw and real
how: for client films, set the palette from place and period before choosing a LUT

name: Music videos grade for identity
what: films grade for naturalism with sparing departures; music videos grade for identity: a teal-orange wash, a mono treatment, a saturated push in one channel or a film-emulation look
how: pick one signature look per music video and keep it across every shot

name: Music video: two passes
what: build a stable image first (organise by camera, lighting setup and scene, correct), then shape its personality, so a creative node never hides an exposure or white-balance problem
how: correction payload per clip group, then one shared look

name: Look reference categories
what: a practical music-video look reference separates mood, lighting, colour (wardrobe, design, skin, grade direction), camera and texture (grain, halation, haze, diffusion) references
how: ask the owner for one reference per category before grading

name: Bloom vs halation
what: bloom is a soft, neutral glow from bright areas into neighbouring darks, wider and gentler than halation, mostly from the lens (dust, coating flaws, reflections between elements); halation happens inside the film when light reflects off the base and re-exposes it from behind, so it is red-orange and hugs the highlight
how: use a neutral blurred-highlight pass for bloom and a red-only tight pass for halation; don't use one for the other

name: Bloom only from real highlights
what: Silver Halide finds the real highlights, blurs only those and adds the result back over the sharp image; a pass over the whole frame just looks hazy
how: threshold, blur, add: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -filter_complex "[0:v]format=gbrp,split[a][b];[b]curves=all='0/0 0.75/0 1/1',gblur=sigma=12[g];[a][g]blend=all_mode=addition" out.mp4` (0.75 threshold and sigma 12 are examples) (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Bloom amount per stock
what: Silver Halide's engine values: Vision3 C41 cross 0.25, Kodak 2383/2393 print 0.2, Vision3 500T 0.2, Fuji 3510 print 0.18, Kodachrome 64 0.1, Fuji Sensia 0.08, Fuji Astia 100F and Ilford FP4 0.05; print stocks bloom more than slide/B&W stocks in their library
how: keep `effects.bloom` low for slide/B&W looks, higher for print looks (relative use only; their units are not HF's)

name: Bloom threshold and amount
what: Luttie's bloom: amount 5-20 = subtle believable softness, 40+ = deliberate dreamlike (music video, fashion); threshold default 75 means only the top 25% of tones bloom; lower it to reach into upper midtones, raise it for only speculars and light sources
how: in the ffmpeg bloom pass the threshold is the curves knee (`0.75/0`); in HF tune `bloom` and `bloomRadius` and judge a render

name: What bloom fixes
what: digital highlights clip abruptly; bloom softens hard speculars (jewellery, wet surfaces, windows), waxy bright skin (low bloom at a high threshold) and contained-looking practical lights and neon
how: for skin use a high threshold and low amount

name: Halation controls
what: amount 10-20 is most convincing ("when you're not sure it's there"), 60+ is stylised; radius sets how far down into the highlights the tint reaches; hue default warm red-orange (~10), about 40 for golden amber, about 350 for a pinker Kodak-style halation
how: colour the halation pass by the hue you need before screening it back

name: Where halation shows
what: backlit subjects (hair and rim lights, subjects against windows), street and night practicals, golden-hour highlights and bright skin patches; in CineStill 800T it shows most when a light source stands against a dark background
how: apply halation only to clips with such sources

name: Halation is the red layer
what: light reflected from the inner camera surfaces is filtered of high frequencies (blue and green) and backlights mostly the red emulsion layer, the closest to that surface; stocks differ with their anti-halation layer
how: build halation from the red channel only (`lutrgb=g=0:b=0` on the highlight copy)

name: Vision3 500T has no red halos
what: with its anti-halation protection intact, Vision3 500T showed none of CineStill 800T's red glow; Kodak says its AHU structure controls halation even better than rem-jet
how: don't add halation when the brief says "Vision3 500T" as opposed to "CineStill 800T"

name: Free halation from edge detect
what: the free-Resolve method: a node in Screen composite mode with an Edge Detect effect so only bright edges are picked up and coloured
how: ffmpeg equivalent of those two steps: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -filter_complex "[0:v]split[a][b];[b]edgedetect=low=0.1:high=0.4,format=gbrp,lutrgb=g=0:b=0,gblur=sigma=4[e];[a]format=gbrp[a2];[a2][e]blend=all_mode=screen" out.mp4` (thresholds/sigma are examples) (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Two pro halation builds
what: Mixing Light describes one method that converts LogC to linear, isolates highlights with a curve and recombines through a Layer Mixer, and another that builds a matte from an edge detect, a grown luma key and a Key Mixer
how: for log footage, do the highlight isolation after a linear conversion, not on the display image

name: Dreamy glow by screen blend
what: duplicate the image, blur the bright parts and screen them back over the original; it softens the clinical sharpness of digital sensors for romantic sequences
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -filter_complex "[0:v]format=gbrp,split[a][b];[b]curves=all='0/0 0.6/0 1/1',gblur=sigma=20[g];[a][g]blend=all_mode=screen" out.mp4` (example values) (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Glow vs halation sliders
what: RapidRAW defines Glow as soft "halation" around bright tones (picks bright pixels, blurs them, blends back) and Halation as a stronger, colour-warm bloom around very bright highlights emulating film's red/orange halo
how: use the neutral blurred pass for "glow" requests and the red pass for "halation" requests

name: Glow by range, spread, warmth
what: Adobe Camera Raw's Glow has Range (which tones are targeted), Spread (how far beyond them it goes) and Warmth (blue to orange), plus styles Diffusion, Bloom and Halation
how: the same three choices in ffmpeg: threshold knee in `curves`, `gblur` sigma, and the colour of the glow copy

name: Bloom includes diffusion filters
what: Dehancer's bloom is light dispersion at contrasting boundaries from the optics, amplified in the emulsion, most prominent with vintage lenses and diffusion filters such as Pro-Mist
how: a Pro-Mist request is a bloom/glow request in post

name: Black Pro-Mist character
what: even at its lowest density (1/8) it adds diffusion and a little halation that warms the image without distorting skin tones; it slightly reduces contrast and highlights, smooths wrinkles and blemishes, and becomes more apparent from 1/4 up
how: if mimicking it in post, keep bloom low and add a slight contrast drop; bright-and-airy wedding crews use a Black Pro-Mist 1/4 on set

name: Light trails with lagfun
what: ffmpeg `lagfun` slowly updates darker pixels so short flashes of light appear longer (decay 0-1, default 0.95)
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf "lagfun=decay=0.95" out.mp4` for neon/lights streaking on a music beat (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Temporal soft blend with tmix
what: `tmix` mixes successive frames with weights; the docs' example averages 7 frames
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf "tmix=frames=7:weights='1 1 1 1 1 1 1'" out.mp4` (smears motion; use on short dreamy inserts) (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Anamorphic streak flare block
what: the Registry's `vfx-anamorphic-flare` draws bright points each throwing the long horizontal blue-violet streak of an anamorphic lens, from measured constants (0.3 high-pass, 80 horizontal taps at quarter resolution, samples/3 gain, tint 0x7a8aff)
how: `npx hyperframes add vfx-anamorphic-flare --dir . --no-clipboard --json` as an overlay, not a grade

name: Grain scale is set by the 48 µm aperture
section: Grain, gate weave and film breath
what: every datasheet granularity is measured through a 48 µm aperture, which projects to about 3.7 px at 1920 wide for Super 35, 7.5 px for Super 16 and 2.6 px for 35 mm stills (7.4 / 14.9 / 5.1 px at 3840)
how: use those as the target grain feature size in pixels for the delivery raster

name: Grain scale doubles with the raster
section: Grain, gate weave and film breath
what: a grain setting dialled in on a 1920 timeline is wrong by a factor of two at 3840, the most common grain mistake; set grain at delivery resolution or scale the size parameter
how: in HF re-check `details.grainSize` after changing composition size; in ffmpeg add grain after the final `scale`

name: Super 16 = double grain scale, same intensity
section: Grain, gate weave and film breath
what: 16 mm is often the same emulsion enlarged twice as much, so Vision3 500T in Super 16 gets the same intensity and about 2x (24.89/12.35 = 2.02) the grain scale of Super 35
how: for a "16mm" brief double the grain size, don't just raise the amount

name: RMS granularity ladder
section: Grain, gate weave and film breath
what: published diffuse RMS (48 µm): Pro 400H 4, Acros 100 7, Ektachrome E100 8, Kodachrome 25 9, Kodachrome 64 10, Double-X 5222 14, Kodachrome 200 16; RMS is linear, so ratios between stocks are meaningful, but no absolute plugin value follows from it
how: use the ratios to set relative grain amounts between looks; calibrate absolute values by eye

name: Why 8mm looks grainier
section: Grain, gate weave and film breath
what: grain particles are roughly the same size in 8, 16 and 35 mm; the smaller frame makes them huge relative to the picture once blown up to a screen
how: grain size, not amount, carries the gauge difference

name: Grain follows brightness
section: Grain, gate weave and film breath
what: real grain isn't uniform: Luttie's grain is strongest in the midtones and fades toward pure black and white, while v8eo describes Portra's grain as heavier in the shadows and lighter in the highlights; both reject a flat noise overlay
how: ffmpeg `noise` has no tone-dependent option (its docs list only strength, seed and flags), so prefer HF `details.grain` (deterministic film grain) for film looks

name: Grain goes on top of the grade
section: Grain, gate weave and film breath
what: grade first; grain sits on top of the colour work, as in a darkroom
how: grain last in the ffmpeg chain; in HF the shader order already puts details after the LUT

name: ffmpeg noise options
section: Grain, gate weave and film breath
what: `noise` takes strength 0-100 per component (`alls`) and flags `a` (averaged temporal, smoother), `p` (mixed with a semi-regular pattern), `t` (changes every frame), `u` (uniform, otherwise gaussian); the docs' example is `alls=20:allf=t+u`
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf "noise=alls=20:allf=t+u" out.mp4`; omit `t` and the pattern freezes (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Grain in AV1: synthesis instead of encoding
section: Grain, gate weave and film breath
what: SVT-AV1 film grain synthesis denoises the input, estimates a grain model in flat areas (autoregressive, from source minus denoised) and signals its parameters so the decoder re-adds grain; adaptive film grain (default on) varies the grain block size with resolution to reduce patterns
how: `ffmpeg -i graded.mp4 -c:v libsvtav1 -preset 10 -crf 35 -svtav1-params film-grain=8 out.mkv` ran here (SVT-AV1 1.7.0); check the result on the target player (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Gate weave is mechanical, film breath is exposure
section: Grain, gate weave and film breath
what: Dehancer separates gate weave (frame movement in the gate) from film breath (frame-to-frame changes in exposure, contrast and colour from uneven coating, shutter instability and development); film breath is most pronounced on Super 8, even fresh and well developed
how: for an 8mm look use both: HF weave on the wrapper plus the Film Memory exposure pulse

name: Weave needs a slight scale-up
section: Grain, gate weave and film breath
what: to displace the image without revealing frame edges it must be scaled slightly, and that resampling can soften the image a little
how: HF recipes keep weave scale at 1.005-1.015 for exactly this reason

name: Weave in fractions of a pixel
section: Grain, gate weave and film breath
what: Kdenlive's frei0r Gate Weave moves the frame randomly with an interval and max horizontal/vertical movement up to 10, taking fractions that give subtle pixel colour mixes
how: frei0r plugins are not installed here (ffmpeg lists the `frei0r` filter, no plugin dir), so use HF GSAP weave (checked here 2026-10-24: `ffmpeg -filters | grep frei0r`)

name: Reference-based weave
section: Grain, gate weave and film breath
what: The Holdovers' team motion-tracked actual 35 mm film and applied that data to their digital footage for "a little subtle gate weave throughout the show"
how: if the owner has a real film clip, track its drift and reuse those offsets in GSAP keyframes

name: What VHS really did
section: VHS, tape and analog video looks (ffmpeg route)
what: VHS recorded brightness and colour as separate signals with very different bandwidth (luma about 3 MHz, chroma about 0.4 MHz), so colour had roughly a tenth of the horizontal detail and smeared sideways across edges that stayed fairly crisp; the defining artifact is colour bleed, not static
how: degrade chroma more than luma

name: VHS artifacts in order of importance
section: VHS, tape and analog video looks (ffmpeg route)
what: 1 horizontal colour bleed (blur chroma only, horizontally), 2 red/blue offset of two or three pixels, 3 slight overall softness (under a pixel), 4 fine tape noise mostly in the darks with a horizontal streak, 5 head-switching noise in a few lines at the bottom
how: chroma-only horizontal blur: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf "format=yuv444p,gblur=sigma=6:sigmaV=0:planes=6,format=yuv420p" out.mp4`; offset: `rgbashift=rh=-3:bh=3`; softness: `gblur=sigma=0.6` (all ran) (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: What to leave out of VHS
section: VHS, tape and analog video looks (ffmpeg route)
what: scanlines come from a CRT, not the tape (wrong for "tape on a modern screen"); constant rolling/tracking errors mean a broken tape (intermittent is convincing); date stamps belong to the camcorder look, not a commercial tape
how: add scanlines/curvature only for "tape on a CRT someone filmed"

name: VHS order of operations
section: VHS, tape and analog video looks (ffmpeg route)
what: soften slightly, bleed colour horizontally, offset red and blue, add tape noise, then crop or add head-switching noise; anything imitating the display goes after all of this; a channel offset applied before a displacement gets dragged along and reads as a bad encode
how: keep the ffmpeg chain in that order

name: VHS signal-chain recipe
section: VHS, tape and analog video looks (ffmpeg route)
what: finish in 4:3 at 29.97 or 25 fps; scale to about 640x480 and back up (detail loss first); blur only the colour channels horizontally (3-6 px) and shift red 1-3 px right; lift blacks, clip highlights, lower saturation except skin and reds; streaky horizontal noise, not film grain; a head-switching strip on the bottom 6-10 lines; a tracking band once or twice per scene; date stamp last in a blocky, slightly soft font
how: first steps: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf "crop=ih*4/3:ih,scale=640:480,format=yuv444p,gblur=sigma=4:sigmaV=0:planes=6,format=yuv420p,rgbashift=rh=2,fps=30000/1001" out.mp4` (ran: 640x480 at 30000/1001) (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: VHS resolution
section: VHS, tape and analog video looks (ffmpeg route)
what: the tape stored roughly 240 lines of horizontal detail for brightness and far less for colour, so edges go soft and colours smear sideways, especially reds
how: scale down and back up before any artifact: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf "scale=320:-2:flags=bilinear,scale=640:360:flags=bilinear" out.mp4` (ran; pick the down-size by eye) (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: VHS vs glitch
section: VHS, tape and analog video looks (ffmpeg route)
what: the VHS effect is a medium (a whole shot that looks like tape, constant mostly gentle artifacts); a glitch is an event (the image breaks for a moment, often with digital blocks). Scratches, dust and burns belong to damaged film, never to tape
how: never add `filmArtifacts` to a VHS look; use `digitalGlitch` only as a short event

name: VHS colour drift and timestamp
section: VHS, tape and analog video looks (ffmpeg route)
what: tapes drifted warm toward red and magenta as they aged and VHS clipped highlights aggressively; mute and warm the palette; a period timestamp in a blocky pixel font in orange or yellow is the fastest "camcorder" cue; leaving it too clean or widescreen gives it away
how: warm/magenta `wheels`, highlights clipped, 4:3 crop (`crop=ih*4/3:ih` ran: 480x360 from 640x360) (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Balance and crop before the VHS style
section: VHS, tape and analog video looks (ffmpeg route)
what: a VHS node chain separates degradation from decoration: balance the shot, crop to 4:3, colour-cast look, blur only the chroma for bleed, then scanlines/tracking, tape noise and vignette; skipping balance and crop is the most common reason a VHS grade looks like a sticker
how: run correction first, then the VHS chain

name: Why VHS is used in films
section: VHS, tape and analog video looks (ffmpeg route)
what: memory (family camcorder = birthdays and living rooms; a cut to tape works like a flashback), evidence (amateur video feels unauthored: found-footage horror), period match (No, 2012, shot on U-matic cameras to cut with real 1988 ads) and unease
how: pick the VHS look only when one of these reasons applies

name: Chroma shift without RGB split
section: VHS, tape and analog video looks (ffmpeg route)
what: `chromashift` moves only the chroma planes (cb/cr horizontally and vertically, edge smear/warp), unlike `rgbashift` which moves R/G/B
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf "chromashift=cbh=3:crh=-3" out.mp4` keeps luma edges in place (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Count variable-delta frames with vfrdet
what: vfrdet reports how many frames had a variable vs constant pts delta, plus min/max/average delta when any varied
how: Run it before choosing a CFR target: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf vfrdet -an -f null -` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Equal rate fields do not prove CFR
what: r_frame_rate is only a base-rate guess and avg_frame_rate an estimate; equal values do not prove constant frame rate, so read the decoded frame times across the clip and do not pick the target from the average alone
how: Dump every frame time and compare neighbours: `ffprobe -v error -select_streams v:0 -show_frames -show_entries frame=best_effort_timestamp_time -of csv=p=0 in.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Per-frame log with showinfo
what: showinfo prints, per frame, n, pts_time, interlace mode i (P/T/B), iskey, picture type (I/P/B) and plane checksums, mean and stdev, without changing the video
how: Use it to see keyframes, field flags and odd timestamps around a damaged spot: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf showinfo -f null - 2>&1 | grep pts_time | head` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: List duplicated frames with mpdecimate debug
what: There is no "dupedetect" filter; mpdecimate at loglevel debug prints a drop/keep line with pts_time for every frame it considers a duplicate
how: Count or grep the drop lines: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf mpdecimate -loglevel debug -an -f null - 2>&1 | grep -c ' drop '` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Find frozen stretches with freezedetect
what: freezedetect logs freeze_start/duration/end when the picture shows no significant change for duration d (default 2 s) against noise tolerance n (default -60 dB / 0.001)
how: Lower d to catch short freezes: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf freezedetect=n=-60dB:d=0.5 -an -f null -` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Find black dropouts with blackframe
what: blackframe reports frames where at least amount % (default 98) of pixels are below threshold (default 32), with frame number and timestamp, and exports lavfi.blackframe.pblack
how: Needs loglevel info or higher: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf blackframe=amount=98:threshold=32 -an -f null -` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Spot tape dropouts with signalstats TOUT
what: signalstats stat=tout flags temporal outliers, pixels unlike their same-field neighbours, such as video dropouts, head clogs or tape tracking problems in digitised analog video
how: Read the per-frame TOUT value: `ffprobe -v error -f lavfi -i "movie=in.mp4,signalstats=stat=tout" -show_entries frame_tags=lavfi.signalstats.TOUT -of csv=p=0` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Spot dropout concealment with signalstats VREP
what: stat=vrep finds vertical line repetition; uncommon in analog captures, so in digitised tape it can mean a dropout compensator concealed damage
how: Same probe, VREP tag: `ffprobe -v error -f lavfi -i "movie=in.mp4,signalstats=stat=vrep" -show_entries frame_tags=lavfi.signalstats.VREP -of csv=p=0` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Log per-frame brightness and change (YAVG, YDIF)
what: signalstats logs YAVG (average luma) and YDIF (average difference to the previous frame) per frame, among YMIN/YMAX, U/V and saturation stats
how: Read both for a flickering clip, before and after a fix: `ffprobe -v error -f lavfi -i "movie=in.mp4,signalstats" -show_entries frame_tags=lavfi.signalstats.YAVG,lavfi.signalstats.YDIF -of csv=p=0` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Score blockiness with blockdetect
what: blockdetect measures blocking artifacts without changing frames (no-reference measure by Muijs and Kirenko); period_min/max set the grid search range, default 3-24
how: Docs example searches periods 8-32: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf blockdetect=period_min=8:period_max=32 -an -f null -` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Score blur with blurdetect
what: blurdetect measures blurriness (Marziliano no-reference metric); block_width/height/pct limit it to the most significant blocks
how: Docs example: 80% of the most significant 32x32 blocks: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf blurdetect=block_width=32:block_height=32:block_pct=80 -an -f null -` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Measure spatial and temporal information (siti)
what: siti computes ITU-T P.910 SI/TI scores (a legacy implementation of a superseded edition); print_summary=1 prints summary stats
how: Docs command: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf siti=print_summary=1 -f null -` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Telecine shows up as repeated fields in idet
what: In idet's summary, telecine appears as Top or Bottom "Repeated Fields" in roughly two of every five frames; true interlaced video combs every moving frame instead
how: Run idet over a moving section and read the Repeated Fields line: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf idet -an -f null - 2>&1 | grep -E "Repeated|frame detection"` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Per-frame idet verdicts
what: idet sets per-frame metadata (single/multiple current_frame, repeated.current_frame); the docs inspect the first 360 frames with metadata=print
how: Docs command: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -filter:v idet,metadata=mode=print -frames:v 360 -an -f null -` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Clean wrong interlace flags with idet
what: analyze_interlaced_flag=N makes idet check the interlaced flag on N frames; an accurate flag is kept, an inaccurate one is cleared, a cheap way to clean the flag
how: Place it before a deint=interlaced deinterlacer: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf idet=analyze_interlaced_flag=20,yadif=deint=interlaced -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Do not trust container field flags
what: Flags are often wrong (especially DVD rips); deinterlacing with the wrong field order makes motion step backward and forward, so when idet and the container disagree, test both orders on a pan and keep the smooth one
how: Read the stream flag, then compare with idet: `ffprobe -v error -select_streams v:0 -show_entries stream=field_order -of csv=p=0 in.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Find black borders with cropdetect
what: cropdetect prints recommended crop values for the non-black area; limit (default 24) is the black threshold, round (default 16; 2 for even sizes), skip initial frames (default 2)
how: Docs pattern with metadata print: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf cropdetect=limit=24:round=2,metadata=mode=print -an -f null - 2>&1 | grep crop= | tail -1` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Find an embedded picture with cropdetect mvedges
what: mode=mvedges finds the playing video from motion vectors plus edge pixels; motion vectors come from mestimate or from the decoder with -flags2 +export_mvs
how: Docs command: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf mestimate,cropdetect=mode=mvedges,metadata=mode=print -an -f null - 2>&1 | grep crop= | tail -1` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Reset cropdetect when a logo spoils it
what: reset_count=N restarts detection after N frames; useful when channel logos distort the detected area (0 = never reset, keep the largest area)
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf cropdetect=reset_count=30,metadata=mode=print -an -f null - 2>&1 | grep -c crop=` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Bounding box of non-black pixels
what: bbox prints the box containing all luma values above min_val (default 16)
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf bbox=min_val=16 -an -f null - 2>&1 | grep -m1 x1` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Scene-change scores with scdet
what: scdet sets lavfi.scd.score per frame and logs cuts above threshold (good values 8-14, default 10); sc_pass=1 passes only the scene-change frames
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf scdet=threshold=10 -an -f null -` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Stop at the first error: -xerror
what: -xerror makes ffmpeg stop and exit on error, so a corrupt file fails fast instead of being decoded through
how: Exits non-zero on our damaged test TS (that is the point): `ffmpeg -xerror -v error -i in.ts -f null -` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Exit code 69 when too many frames fail
what: -max_error_rate sets the fraction of failed frame decodes (0-1, default 2/3) above which ffmpeg returns exit code 69; processing still continues
how: `ffmpeg -max_error_rate 0.0 -v error -i in.ts -f null -; echo exit=$?` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Strict damage check: -err_detect explode
what: The err_detect decoder flags include crccheck, bitstream, buffer and explode (abort decoding on minor error detection); careful/compliant/aggressive tighten what counts as an error
how: Here (ffmpeg 6.1) it still exited 0 on a damaged TS while logging the errors, so read the log, or use -xerror for a non-zero exit: `ffmpeg -v error -err_detect explode -i in.ts -f null -` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Abort when nothing gets written
what: -abort_on empty_output stops when no packets reached the muxer; empty_output_stream does it per output stream
how: `ffmpeg -abort_on empty_output -i in.mp4 -c copy out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Show only what changed between frames: tmix -1 2 -1
what: Docs example tmix=frames=3:weights="-1 2 -1":scale=1 shows only temporal differences (weights -1 3 -1 is a simple temporal convolution)
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf "tmix=frames=3:weights=-1 2 -1:scale=1" -c:v libx264 -crf 18 diff.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Keep phone timestamps as they are: -fps_mode passthrough
what: -fps_mode passthrough passes each frame with its demuxer timestamp; cfr duplicates/drops to an exact rate; vfr passes frames but drops ones that would share a timestamp; auto (default) picks cfr or vfr by muxer
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -fps_mode passthrough -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: CFR conversion cannot bring back missing pictures
what: Converting VFR to CFR only duplicates or drops frames; it cannot restore lost pictures or work out the right lip sync. If original and copy are off by the same fixed amount, changing the frame rate will not fix it
how: Compare start, middle and end of the original and a short CFR test copy in the same player first.

name: VFR to CFR with audio kept on the same timeline
what: Put fps=<rate> on the video chain and aresample=async=1 on the audio chain: fps alone gives constant video beside audio that still has the recorder's hole in it; async=1 fills holes with silence and trims overlaps
how: Source-given filtergraph: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -filter_complex "[0:v]fps=25[v];[0:a]aresample=async=1[a]" -map "[v]" -map "[a]" -c:v libx264 -crf 18 -c:a aac out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: What the number in aresample=async means
what: async=1 only inserts silence or trims samples; values above 1 also allow stretching/squeezing by up to that many samples per second; inserting/trimming starts when the gap exceeds 0.1 s (min_hard_comp default). In MP4 a clock-speed mismatch may not show in timestamps, so async cannot fix it
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -af aresample=async=1000 -c:v copy out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Growing drift is a speed problem, not an offset
what: If audio matches at the start and gets worse toward the end, it is drift; -itsoffset only shifts by a fixed amount. Measure the gap near the end and correct the audio speed: 0.5 s late at 600 s gives (600+0.5)/600 = 1.00083
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -af atempo=1.00083 -c:v copy out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Drop duplicate frames and keep the audio
what: mpdecimate removes near-duplicate frames; with variable-rate output the remaining frames keep their timestamps, so the audio stays usable (the answer used -vsync vfr, now -fps_mode vfr)
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf mpdecimate -fps_mode vfr -c:v libx264 -crf 18 -c:a copy out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Cut frozen parts out of a video-only clip
what: mpdecimate plus setpts=N/FRAME_RATE/TB rebuilds smooth timestamps after the duplicates are gone; mpdecimate works only on video, so drop the audio or it goes out of sync
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf mpdecimate,setpts=N/FRAME_RATE/TB -an out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Tune mpdecimate thresholds
what: A frame is dropped when no 8x8 block differs by more than hi (default 64*12) and no more than frac (default 0.33) of blocks differ by more than lo (default 64*5); one user detected duplicates more aggressively with hi=64*32:lo=64*24:frac=0.05
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf mpdecimate=hi=64*32:lo=64*24:frac=0.05 -fps_mode vfr -an out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Limit how many frames mpdecimate may drop in a row
what: max (mode 0) sets the maximum consecutive drops when positive, or the minimum interval between drops when negative; keep ignores that many similar frames before dropping starts
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf mpdecimate=max=2:keep=1 -fps_mode vfr -an out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Periodic duplicates: decimate, not mpdecimate
what: mpdecimate is heuristic and may skip some duplicates; decimate removes exactly one frame per cycle, so it suits only regularly repeating duplicates (one user had 1 duplicate after every 5 good frames). decimate needs CFR input
how: cycle=N drops one frame in every N: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf decimate=cycle=6 -an -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: decimate on partly duplicated footage
what: decimate mixed=1 says only part of the input needs decimating; the output then becomes variable frame rate
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf decimate=mixed=1 -an -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mkv` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Pad the start when video begins after audio
what: fps start_time=0 assumes the first PTS is 0, padding the beginning with copies of the first frame when video starts after audio, or trimming negative-PTS frames
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf fps=fps=30:start_time=0 -c:v libx264 -crf 18 -c:a copy out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: fps rounding and the last frame
what: fps round chooses PTS rounding (zero, inf, down, up, near = default); eof_action=pass passes the last frame through if the input duration has not been reached
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf fps=fps=30:round=near:eof_action=pass -an -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Named rates in fps: ntsc, pal, film, ntsc_film
what: fps accepts source_fps, ntsc (30000/1001), pal (25), film (24) and ntsc_film (24000/1001) in its expression
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf fps=fps=ntsc -an -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Input -r ignores the file's timestamps
what: As an input option, -r ignores stored timestamps and generates CFR timestamps at the given rate (for image inputs prefer -framerate). Use it to re-time a clip whose timestamps are wrong; the duration changes
how: `ffmpeg -r 18 -i in.mp4 -an -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: -r with stream copy can make an invalid file
what: With -c copy, output -r only tells the muxer the rate; nothing is dropped or duplicated, and the file may be invalid if it does not match the packet timestamps (see the setts bitstream filter instead)
how: Re-encode when you need a real rate change.

name: Clamp a wrongly detected huge frame rate: -fpsmax
what: -fpsmax caps the auto-set output rate, useful when the input rate is detected wrongly high
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -fpsmax 30 -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Rewrite packet timestamps without re-encoding: setts
what: The setts bitstream filter sets PTS/DTS/duration from expressions (N, PTS, DTS, PREV_OUTPTS, ...); docs example sets PTS equal to DTS, not recommended when B-frames are involved
how: Docs example on the audio stream: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -c copy -bsf:a setts=pts=DTS out.mkv` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Regenerate missing PTS while remuxing MKV
what: For "Timestamps are unset in a packet" / "Can't write packet with unknown timestamp", +genpts generates missing PTS from DTS during a stream copy
how: `ffmpeg -fflags +genpts -i in.mp4 -c copy repaired.mkv` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Ignore corrupt DTS: +igndts+genpts
what: igndts drops DTS when PTS is set; combined with genpts it gives clean presentation timestamps when DTS is corrupt and seeking gets stuck
how: `ffmpeg -fflags +igndts+genpts -ss 1 -i in.mp4 -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Seek a broken file on the output side
what: -ss before -i relies on the index; after -i ffmpeg decodes from the start and discards up to the point: slower, but accurate when timestamps are broken
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -ss 1 -c:v libx264 -crf 18 -c:a aac out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Repair once, then seek fast
what: For many seeks, remux the damaged file once with ignore_err and genpts, then use normal fast input seeking on the repaired copy
how: `ffmpeg -err_detect ignore_err -fflags +genpts -i in.mp4 -c copy fixed.mp4 && ffmpeg -ss 1 -i fixed.mp4 -c copy part.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Keep the original timestamps: -copyts
what: -copyts keeps input timestamps without sanitising (start offset kept); -start_at_zero with it shifts them to start at zero
how: `ffmpeg -copyts -start_at_zero -i in.mp4 -c copy out.mkv` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Shift leading negative timestamps: avoid_negative_ts
what: avoid_negative_ts make_zero shifts so the first timestamp is 0; make_non_negative only removes leading negatives; all streams move by the same amount so sync is kept
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -c copy -avoid_negative_ts make_zero out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Stop drops caused by noisy timestamps
what: -frame_drop_threshold (in frames, default -1.1) sets how far behind a frame may be before it is dropped; one use is avoiding framedrops with noisy timestamps
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -frame_drop_threshold 4 -fps_mode cfr -r 30 -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Timestamp discontinuity threshold
what: -dts_error_threshold sets the seconds of timestamp jump above which ffmpeg drops the PTS/DTS, for formats that do not allow discontinuities
how: `ffmpeg -dts_error_threshold 1 -i in.ts -c copy out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: minterpolate motion estimation direction
what: me_mode=bidir estimates vectors forward and backward for each source frame; bilat (default) estimates them directly for the interpolated frame
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf minterpolate=fps=30:mi_mode=mci:me_mode=bidir -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: minterpolate search algorithm and block size
what: me picks the search (esa, tss, tdls, ntss, fss, ds, hexbs, epzs default, umh); mb_size (default 16) and search_param (default 32) set block size and search range
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf minterpolate=fps=30:mi_mode=mci:me=umh:mb_size=8:search_param=32 -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Keep minterpolate scene detection on clips with cuts
what: At a scene change, motion vectors point in random directions; scd=fdiff (default) replaces those interpolated frames by duplicates, scd_threshold default 10
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf minterpolate=fps=30:mi_mode=mci:scd=fdiff:scd_threshold=10 -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Blend-interpolate with the framerate filter
what: framerate makes new frames as a linear interpolation of two source frames inside interp_start..interp_end (default 15..240), with scene detection (scene default 8.2). It is not for interlaced media: deinterlace first
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf framerate=fps=30 -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: AI interpolation on CPU: RIFE ncnn
what: rife-ncnn-vulkan is a portable RIFE build (no CUDA/PyTorch); -g -1 selects CPU; input is a folder of frames, output 2x frames by default. Here 6 frames of 320x180 became 12 in 0.5 s with -g -1
how: Needs rife-ncnn-vulkan (missing; we downloaded release 20221029 for the test). README workflow: decode frames, interpolate, encode at double rate: `mkdir -p in_frames out_frames && ffmpeg -v error -i in.mp4 in_frames/frame_%08d.png && rife-ncnn-vulkan -i in_frames -o out_frames -m rife-v4.6 -g -1 && ffmpeg -v error -framerate 24 -i out_frames/%08d.png -c:v libx264 -crf 20 -pix_fmt yuv420p out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: RIFE to an exact frame count
what: rife-ncnn-vulkan -n sets the target frame count (default N*2) and -s the time step (0-1), so 12 fps can become 2.5x more frames for 30 fps
how: Needs rife-ncnn-vulkan (missing). Tested 6 frames to 15: `mkdir -p f o && ffmpeg -v error -i in.mp4 -frames:v 6 f/%08d.png && rife-ncnn-vulkan -i f -o o -n 15 -m rife-v4.6 -g -1 && ls o | wc -l` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: RIFE threads and test-time augmentation
what: -j load:proc:save sets threads for decode, interpolation and encode (default 1:2:2; README suggests 4:4:4 for many small images, 2:2:2 for large); -x enables spatial TTA, -z temporal TTA, -u UHD mode
how: Needs rife-ncnn-vulkan (missing). `mkdir -p f o && ffmpeg -v error -i in.mp4 -frames:v 4 f/%08d.png && rife-ncnn-vulkan -i f -o o -m rife-v4.6 -g -1 -j 4:4:4 -x && ls o | wc -l` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: RIFE model 4.6 vs 4.4
what: SVP notes model 4.6 gives higher quality but is about 10-15% slower than 4.4, and 4.4 needs a little less memory
how: Pick with -m rife-v4.6 (folder in the ncnn release).

name: Undo telecine judder: dejudder cycle
what: dejudder removes judder from partially telecined content (e.g. after pullup); cycle 4 = film to NTSC (24 to 30), 5 = PAL to NTSC (25 to 30), 20 = a mixture; output may become VFR
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf dejudder=cycle=4 -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Real-ESRGAN on a CPU-only box via Mesa lavapipe
what: The portable realesrgan-ncnn-vulkan needs no CUDA/PyTorch but does need a Vulkan device; with Mesa's llvmpipe (lavapipe) Vulkan driver it ran here on CPU: one 160x90 frame to 320x180 in 7.9 s
how: Needs realesrgan-ncnn-vulkan + apt mesa-vulkan-drivers (missing). README_ubuntu frame workflow: extract, upscale, merge with original audio: `mkdir -p tmp_frames out_frames && ffmpeg -v error -i in.mp4 -vf scale=160:90 -frames:v 2 -qscale:v 1 -qmin 1 -qmax 1 -fps_mode passthrough tmp_frames/frame%08d.jpg && realesrgan-ncnn-vulkan -i tmp_frames -o out_frames -n realesr-animevideov3 -s 2 -f jpg && ffmpeg -v error -i out_frames/frame%08d.jpg -i in.mp4 -map 0:v:0 -map 1:a:0 -c:a copy -c:v libx264 -r 30 -pix_fmt yuv420p -shortest out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Real-ESRGAN ncnn model choice
what: The ncnn release ships realesr-animevideov3 (default, x2/x3/x4, for anime video), realesrgan-x4plus (general) and realesrgan-x4plus-anime; -n picks the model, -s the scale (2, 3, 4)
how: Needs realesrgan-ncnn-vulkan (missing). General-photo model on one frame: `ffmpeg -v error -i in.mp4 -vf scale=96:54 -frames:v 1 s.png && realesrgan-ncnn-vulkan -i s.png -o s4.png -n realesrgan-x4plus -s 4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Real-ESRGAN tiles and block seams
what: -t sets tile size (>=32, 0 = auto); the ncnn build crops the image into tiles and stitches them, which can introduce block inconsistency vs the PyTorch version; -x enables TTA mode
how: Needs realesrgan-ncnn-vulkan (missing). `ffmpeg -v error -i in.mp4 -vf scale=160:90 -frames:v 1 s.png && realesrgan-ncnn-vulkan -i s.png -o s2.png -n realesr-animevideov3 -s 2 -t 64` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Real-ESRGAN Python features the ncnn build lacks
what: The Python inference script supports --outscale (arbitrary scale, a further LANCZOS4 resize), --face_enhance (GFPGAN), -t tile, alpha, gray and 16-bit images; realesr-general-x4v3 adds -dn denoise strength to avoid over-smoothing. The ncnn build does not support outscale
how: Needs the realesrgan Python package and weights (missing).

name: Lanczos taps: param0
what: In libswscale, lanczos is a windowed sinc whose number of taps is set by param0 (default 3)
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf scale=1280:720:flags=lanczos:param0=5 -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Bicubic B and C: param0/param1
what: bicubic is a BC-spline (Mitchell-Netravali); B and C are param0 and param1, default 0.0 and 0.6
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf scale=1280:720:flags=bicubic:param0=0:param1=0.5 -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Gaussian and spline scalers
what: gauss has a sharpness param0 (default 3.0); spline is an unwindowed natural bicubic spline; area averages and equals bilinear when upscaling
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf scale=1280:720:flags=spline -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Accurate rounding and full chroma interpolation
what: Scaler flags accurate_rnd (accurate rounding), full_chroma_int (full chroma interpolation) and full_chroma_inp (full chroma input) can be added to the algorithm flag
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf scale=1280:720:flags=lanczos+accurate_rnd+full_chroma_int -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Choose the scaler dither
what: sws_dither sets dithering: auto (default), none, bayer, ed (error diffusion), a_dither, x_dither
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf scale=1280:720:flags=lanczos:sws_dither=ed -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Keep aspect and even sizes with -2
what: If one of w/h is -n, scale computes it from the aspect ratio and makes it divisible by n
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf scale=1280:-2:flags=lanczos -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Pixel-art magnifiers: xbr, hqx, epx
what: xbr (2/3/4x, edge-detection rules), hqx (hq2x-hq4x by Maxim Stepin) and epx (2x/3x) are magnification filters designed for pixel art
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf xbr=n=2 -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Nearest-neighbour scaling
what: point/neighbor is plain point sampling (nearest neighbour)
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf scale=iw*4:ih*4:flags=neighbor -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: zscale resize kernels and dither
what: zscale (z.lib) offers point, bilinear (default), bicubic, spline16, spline36, spline64 and lanczos; param_a is the lanczos tap count or bicubic b; dither none/ordered/random/error_diffusion
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf zscale=w=1280:h=720:filter=spline36:dither=error_diffusion,format=yuv420p -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Interlace-aware scaling: interl=1
what: scale interl=1 forces interlaced-aware scaling, -1 decides from the frame flags (default 0); Encode Wiki: deinterlace before scaling, because resizing blends the two fields
how: Here `scale=720:-2:interl=1` crashed ffmpeg 6.1 (signal 11) on a TFF H.264 test clip, so deinterlace first instead.

name: ffmpeg sr / dnn_processing need a DNN backend
what: sr (SRCNN/ESPCN) and dnn_processing need ffmpeg built with TensorFlow, OpenVINO, LibTorch or ONNX Runtime plus a model file; our ffmpeg 6.1 has none of them
how: Needs a DNN-enabled ffmpeg build (missing); use Real-ESRGAN ncnn instead.

name: Do not scan 8mm higher than about 1024x768
what: An 8mm frame holds limited detail; Jim Battle found 1920x1080 just shows the grain clearly and calls more than 1024x768 overkill for 8mm
how: Ask for SD/1024-class scans, save the pixels for restoration.

name: Pick a denoiser by speed and type
what: ffmpeg-user summary: atadenoise very fast, temporal only, no motion compensation; hqdn3d fast spatial+temporal, low-pass that blurs at extreme settings; nlmeans very slow; bm3d very very slow; vaguedenoiser slow, spatial wavelet, pretty good; dctdnoiz very very slow, blurs too much; fftdnoiz slow, limited temporal, may ring; owdenoise very very very slow; removegrain fast, limited use
how: Licences in the same list: hqdn3d and owdenoise GPL; atadenoise, nlmeans, bm3d, vaguedenoiser, dctdnoiz and fftdnoiz LGPL.

name: Test denoisers on representative frames first
what: Pick a couple of representative frames, try several denoise filters and options on them, and keep what works for that footage; nlmeans if you are patient, atadenoise or hqdn3d for speed
how: `ffmpeg -ss 1 -i in.mp4 -frames:v 1 -vf vaguedenoiser f_vague.png && ffmpeg -ss 1 -i in.mp4 -frames:v 1 -vf hqdn3d f_hq.png` (tested here 2026-10-24)
refs: Super User accepted answer, https://superuser.com/questions/1547426, checked 2026-10-24

name: hqdn3d parameter defaults
what: hqdn3d luma_spatial defaults 4.0; chroma_spatial 3*ls/4; luma_tmp 6*ls/4; chroma_tmp luma_tmp*cs/ls; it aims to make still images really still and improve compressibility
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf hqdn3d=luma_spatial=4 -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: VHS chroma bleed: chroma-only hqdn3d
what: claude-mods suggests, for VHS-style chroma bleed, a mild chroma-only denoise with a slight desaturation
how: Source-given chain: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf "hqdn3d=0:6:0:6,eq=saturation=0.92" -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: nlmeans patch and research sizes for chroma
what: nlmeans s strength 1-30 (default 1), p patch (odd, default 7), r research window (odd, default 15); pc and rc set them for chroma (0 = automatic)
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf nlmeans=s=3:p=7:r=9:pc=5:rc=7 -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Basic bm3d
what: bm3d (Block-Matching 3D) is very sensitive to sigma (default 1); docs basic example: sigma=3:block=4:bstep=2:group=1:estim=basic. group=1 means no block matching
how: Our ffmpeg 6.1 rejects block=4 (range 8-64 there), so block=8: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf bm3d=sigma=3:block=8:bstep=2:group=1:estim=basic -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: bm3d on luma only
what: planes=1 filters only the first (luma) plane
how: block=8 because 6.1 needs 8-64: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf bm3d=sigma=3:block=8:bstep=2:group=1:estim=basic:planes=1 -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Two-stage bm3d (basic, then final)
what: estim=final uses a second (reference) stream for block matching; docs run a basic pass and feed it as reference to a final pass with group=16
how: Docs filtergraph, with block=8 for 6.1: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf "split[a][b],[a]bm3d=sigma=3:block=8:bstep=2:group=1:estim=basic[a],[b][a]bm3d=sigma=3:block=8:bstep=2:group=16:estim=final:ref=1" -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: bm3d with an nlmeans pre-filter
what: Docs variant: nlmeans makes the reference stream for the final bm3d stage
how: block=8 for 6.1; took about 6 min on this 2 s 640x360 clip: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf "split[a][b],[a]nlmeans=s=3:r=7:p=3[a],[b][a]bm3d=sigma=3:block=8:bstep=2:group=16:estim=final:ref=1" -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Wavelet denoise: vaguedenoiser
what: vaguedenoiser (CDF 9/7 wavelet) should smooth and reduce noise without blurring features; threshold default 2, method garrote (default), soft or hard; hard tolerates a higher threshold before looking overfiltered
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf vaguedenoiser=threshold=4:method=hard -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: vaguedenoiser decomposition, percent and bayes
what: nsteps (1-32, default 6) cannot exceed what the frame size allows (about 8 for 640x480); percent (default 85) gives partial denoise; type=bayes makes the threshold depend on each decomposition
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf vaguedenoiser=nsteps=5:percent=70:type=bayes -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Overcomplete wavelet denoise: owdenoise
what: owdenoise depth 8-16 (default 8; larger denoises lower frequencies more, slower), luma_strength and chroma_strength 0-1000 (default 1)
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf owdenoise=depth=8:ls=4:cs=4 -t 0.5 -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: 3D FFT denoise with neighbour frames: fftdnoiz
what: fftdnoiz sigma (0-30, default 1), amount, block (default 32), overlap (0.2-0.8, default 0.5), method wiener/hard; prev/next add temporal frames (default 0). Very high sigma with low overlap may block
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf fftdnoiz=sigma=6:prev=1:next=1 -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: DCT denoise: dctdnoiz
what: dctdnoiz drops DCT coefficients below 3*sigma (docs: dctdnoiz=4.5, same as e='gte(c, 4.5*3)'); n=4 uses 16x16 blocks (docs call dctdnoiz=15:n=4 violent); not designed for real time
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf dctdnoiz=4.5 -t 0.5 -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: removegrain median mode
what: removegrain is a spatial denoiser for progressive video with modes 0-24 per plane; mode 4 clips to the 4th min/max of the 8 neighbours, equivalent to a median filter; mode 1 clips to their min/max
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf removegrain=m0=4:m1=4:m2=4 -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: removegrain blur and line-sensitive modes
what: Modes 11/12 are a [1 2 1] blur, 20 a 3x3 average, 19 the average of the 8 neighbours, 5-9 line-sensitive clipping, 17 clips with opposite-neighbour pairs; 23/24 "reputed useless"
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf removegrain=m0=17:m1=11:m2=11 -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Spatial median with its own radius
what: median picks the median pixel in a rectangle: radius (1-127), radiusV (0 = same as radius), percentile 0.5 (0 = minimum, 1 = maximum)
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf median=radius=1 -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Temporal median: tmedian
what: tmedian picks the median pixel over successive frames (radius 1-127, default 1; percentile like median)
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf tmedian=radius=1 -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Average frames: tmix
what: tmix mixes successive frames with weights; docs average 7 frames with tmix=frames=7:weights="1 1 1 1 1 1 1"
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf "tmix=frames=7:weights=1 1 1 1 1 1 1" -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Chroma noise only: chromanr
what: chromanr averages chroma from neighbours whose summed Y/U/V difference is under thres (default 30); luma is copied; sizew/sizeh radius (default 5); stepw/steph speed it up
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf chromanr=thres=30:sizew=5:sizeh=5:stepw=2:steph=2 -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: atadenoise frame count and serial mode
what: atadenoise s = frames averaged (odd 5-129, default 9); a=p parallel (default, aborts early on the first big change) or s serial (keeps checking the other side); per-plane 0a/0b... thresholds; 0s=0 disables a plane
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf atadenoise=s=15:a=s -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Edge-preserving smoothing: bilateral
what: bilateral smooths while preserving edges; sigmaS spatial (0-512, default 0.1), sigmaR range (0-1, default 0.1); filters only the first plane by default
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf bilateral=sigmaS=4:sigmaR=0.1:planes=7 -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Smooth flat areas only: smartblur threshold
what: smartblur blurs without touching outlines; luma_threshold 0 filters everything, 1..30 only flat areas, -30..0 only edges; luma_strength -1..0 sharpens instead
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf smartblur=lr=1.5:ls=0.8:lt=10 -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Shape adaptive blur: sab
what: sab luma_radius 0.1-4, pre-filter radius 0.1-2, luma_strength 0.1-100 (max pixel difference still considered); chroma values follow luma unless set
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf sab=lr=1.5:lpfr=1:ls=1 -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Guided filter smoothing
what: guided is an edge-preserving smoother (radius 1-20, default 3; eps default 0.01; mode basic/fast with sub); with guidance=on a second same-size input is the guide, which the docs mention for dehazing and detail transfer
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf guided=radius=3:eps=0.01 -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: pp temporal noise reducer
what: libpostproc's pp filter (still in our ffmpeg 6.1, removed from current docs) has tn/tmpnoise with three thresholds (larger = stronger); docs example pp=default/tmpnoise|1|2|3
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf "pp=default/tmpnoise|1|2|3" -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Keep intended grain: -tune grain
what: For intentional film grain, do not denoise; encode with -tune grain instead
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -c:v libx264 -tune grain -crf 18 -c:a copy out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Restoration order of operations
what: claude-mods order: deinterlace, denoise, deband, stabilize, grade, sharpen, encode; stabilize after denoise because noise defeats motion estimation
how: Apply the steps in that order on one chain.

name: Weak small-block deblock
what: deblock removes blocking artifacts; filter weak/strong (default strong), block 4-512 (default 8); docs example deblock=filter=weak:block=4
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf deblock=filter=weak:block=4 -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Stronger deblock thresholds
what: alpha (default 0.098) detects at the exact block edge, beta/gamma/delta (default 0.05) near it; higher = more deblocking, 0 disables; docs example with alpha=0.12:beta=0.07:gamma=0.06:delta=0.05, planes=1 luma only, planes=6 chroma only
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf deblock=filter=strong:block=4:alpha=0.12:beta=0.07:gamma=0.06:delta=0.05:planes=1 -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: pp7 deblocking
what: pp7 is an spp variant (7-point DCT); qp forces 0-63 (else the stream QP), mode hard/soft/medium (default medium; soft = better deringing, blurrier)
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mpg -vf pp7=qp=8:mode=medium -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: spp quality levels
what: spp compresses/decompresses at several shifts and averages; quality 0-6 (default 3; each step about halves speed), mode hard (default)/soft; use_bframe_qp may cause flicker
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mpg -vf spp=quality=4:qp=8 -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: fspp strength
what: fspp is a faster spp; quality 4-5, strength -15..32 (lower = more detail and artifacts, higher = smoother and blurrier; 0 = PSNR-optimal)
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mpg -vf fspp=quality=4:strength=4:qp=8 -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: uspp with Snow encodes
what: uspp actually encodes/decodes each shift with Snow (spp uses an MJPEG-like DCT); quality 0-8; not available in ffmpeg 5.0-6.0 (works in our 6.1)
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mpg -vf uspp=quality=1:qp=8 -t 0.3 -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: pp deblock and dering subfilters
what: pp subfilters hb/vb (horizontal/vertical deblock, difference default 32, flatness 39), ha/va accurate versions, dr dering; presets de (hb|a,vb|a,dr|a), fa fast, ac high quality; docs example pp=de/-al
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mpg -vf pp=de/-al -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Luma-only pp deblocking
what: Subfilter option y/nochrom filters luma only; a/autoq follows quality commands; docs example pp=hb|y/vb|a
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mpg -vf "pp=hb|y/vb|a" -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Decoder error concealment: -ec
what: ec sets the decoder's concealment: guess_mvs (iterative motion vector search, slow), deblock (strong deblock on damaged macroblocks), favor_inter (predict from the previous frame)
how: `ffmpeg -ec guess_mvs+deblock+favor_inter -i in.ts -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Deband in 10-bit before encoding
what: An 8-bit frame has no in-between values, so convert to 10-bit before deband and keep -pix_fmt yuv420p10le on the output, or ffmpeg may negotiate back to 8-bit
how: Encode Wiki command: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf "format=yuv420p10le,deband" -c:v libsvtav1 -crf 30 -pix_fmt yuv420p10le output.mkv` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: deband thresholds and blur
what: 1thr..4thr per plane 0.00003-0.5 (default 0.02): higher fixes stronger banding but flattens more detail; range default 16; blur=0 requires all four neighbours under threshold, touching less real detail
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf deband=1thr=0.015:2thr=0.015:3thr=0.015:blur=0 -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: deband coupling and direction
what: coupling=1 changes a pixel only if all components are banded; direction sets the angle of compared pixels (negative = exact; -PI/2 picks only the same column)
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf deband=coupling=1:direction=-3.14159 -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Banding that appears only in your encode
what: If the source is clean and the encode bands, the encoder flattened the gradient: encode at 10-bit (even from 8-bit), use a lower CRF, and consider grain
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -c:v libx264 -pix_fmt yuv420p10le -crf 16 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Deband only the shots that band
what: Too high a threshold blurs dark texture, grain and skin; start low, apply to the scenes that band and check the others for damage
how: Limit it with timeline editing (enable=): `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf "deband=enable='between(t,0,1)'" -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Single rate or double rate
what: Double rate (one frame per field, 50/59.94 fps) keeps all captured motion and suits sports and fast movement; single rate (send_frame) discards half the temporal information but is fine at moderate motion when you must keep the source rate
how: bwdif defaults to double rate; add mode=send_frame for single rate: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf bwdif=mode=send_frame -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Force the field order when flags lie
what: yadif/bwdif parity tff/bff overrides auto detection; with unknown parity they assume top field first
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf bwdif=mode=send_field:parity=tff -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Deinterlace only flagged frames
what: deint=interlaced makes yadif/bwdif touch only frames marked interlaced (deint=all is default); Encode Wiki: leave deint alone unless you trust the flags
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf yadif=mode=send_frame:deint=interlaced -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: yadif without the spatial check
what: yadif modes 2/3 (send_frame_nospatial, send_field_nospatial) are like 0/1 but skip the spatial interlacing check
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf yadif=mode=send_field_nospatial -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: BBC Weston 3-field deinterlacer: w3fdif
what: w3fdif uses BBC R&D coefficients (filter=complex default, or simple), outputs one frame per field by default, and takes field dominance from the frame; if wrong, put setfield before it
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf setfield=tff,w3fdif=filter=complex:mode=field -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Edge-slope deinterlacer: estdif
what: estdif is spatial-only, interpolating missing lines by edge slope tracing; rslope, redge, ecost/mcost/dcost tune the matching; interp 2p/4p (default)/6p
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf estdif=mode=frame:interp=6p -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Neural edge-directed deinterlace: nnedi
what: nnedi needs the nnedi3_weights.bin file (from dubhater/vapoursynth-nnedi3); field af/a/t/b/tf/bf; nsize, nns, qual, etype, pscrn (prescreener, default new) tune it
how: Weights downloaded for the test (13.6 MB): `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf nnedi=weights=nnedi3_weights.bin:field=af -t 0.5 -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: See what kerndeint touches: map=1
what: kerndeint (Donald Graft adaptive kernel) has thresh (default 10, 0 = every pixel); map=1 paints pixels above the threshold white; sharp=1 and twoway=1 add sharpening
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf kerndeint=map=1 -frames:v 1 kd_map.png` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Motion-compensated deinterlace: yadif=1,mcdeint
what: mcdeint needs one field per frame as input, so it follows yadif=1/3; mode fast/medium/slow/extra_slow; parity default bff; qp smooths the vector field
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf yadif=1,mcdeint=mode=fast:parity=tff -t 0.5 -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Inspect fields: separatefields
what: separatefields splits each frame into its fields: half height, twice the rate and frame count; use setfield first if the dominance is wrong
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf separatefields -frames:v 4 field_%02d.png` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Keep one field only: field
what: field type=top/bottom extracts a single field cheaply by stride arithmetic; output frames are marked progressive
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf field=type=top,scale=iw:ih*2 -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Mark the field order: setfield
what: setfield sets the interlace property (auto, bff, tff, prog) without changing pixels; it affects how later filters such as fieldorder or yadif treat the frame
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf setfield=bff,yadif -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Change field order: fieldorder
what: fieldorder shifts the picture one line to change field order (default tff); useful to or from PAL DV, which is bottom field first; unflagged input is left alone
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf fieldorder=bff -c:v libx264 -flags +ildct+ilme -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: PAL film captured with the wrong field order: phase
what: phase delays interlaced video by one field to fix PAL movies captured with the opposite field order to the transfer; modes t, b, a, u and the analysing T, B, A (default), U
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf phase=mode=A -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Simple IVTC: fieldmatch,decimate
what: fieldmatch rebuilds progressive frames but does not drop duplicates, so a decimate after it completes inverse telecine; docs example for TFF
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf fieldmatch=order=tff:combmatch=none,decimate -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: IVTC with a deinterlace fallback
what: fieldmatch marks frames it cannot match as interlaced; yadif=deint=interlaced fixes only those before decimate. kfrn saw some artefacts with deint=interlaced and preferred plain yadif on their DVD
how: Docs/Encode Wiki chain: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf fieldmatch,yadif=deint=interlaced,decimate -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: IVTC for mixed 30i and 24p content
what: decimate only works on CFR input; for mixed telecined (30 fps) and progressive 24 fps content the docs give dejudder,fps=30000/1001,fieldmatch,decimate
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf dejudder,fps=30000/1001,fieldmatch,decimate -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Ignore subtitles or logos while field-matching
what: fieldmatch y0/y1 define a band of lines excluded from the match decision (subtitles, a logo); equal values disable it
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf fieldmatch=y0=300:y1=359,decimate -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: fieldmatch safety vs matching
what: mode pc is safest against jerkiness but outputs combed frames where a good match existed in damaged sections; pcn_ub almost always finds a match at the most jerkiness risk; default pc_n. pc is fastest
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf fieldmatch=mode=pcn_ub,decimate -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Field-match on a cleaned copy, output from the clean source
what: ppsrc=1 treats the first input as pre-processed (e.g. denoised) for matching and takes fields from the second, clean input, keeping the output lossless
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -filter_complex "[0:v]split[a][b];[a]hqdn3d[p];[p][b]fieldmatch=ppsrc=1,decimate" -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Rainbowing breaks field matching
what: fieldmatch mchroma=0 excludes chroma from match comparisons when chroma is badly damaged (heavy rainbowing); chroma=0 (default) already leaves chroma out of the combed-frame decision
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf fieldmatch=mchroma=0,decimate -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Tune combed-frame detection
what: cthresh (default 9, good range 8-12) sets how visible combing must be; combpel (default 80) how many combed pixels per blockx x blocky (default 16) window declare a frame combed
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf fieldmatch=cthresh=10:combpel=80,yadif=deint=interlaced,decimate -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Pattern-free IVTC: pullup
what: pullup looks ahead instead of locking to a pattern and handles mixed hard-telecine, 24000/1001 and 30000/1001 content; set the output rate (e.g. -r 24000/1001) to avoid duplicates
how: Docs NTSC example: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf pullup -r 24000/1001 -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: pullup junk margins and strict breaks
what: jl/jr (units of 8 px) and jt/jb (units of 2 lines) ignore junk at the edges (default 8 px each side); sb=1 reduces mismatched frames but may drop too many in fast motion, -1 matches more easily; mp picks the metric plane
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf pullup=jl=1:jr=1:jt=4:jb=4:sb=1 -r 24000/1001 -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Exact inverse of a known pulldown: detelecine
what: detelecine undoes a telecine whose pattern is known (same pattern string as the telecine filter, default 23); start_frame fixes a cut stream's position in the pattern
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf detelecine=first_field=top:pattern=23 -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Pulldown patterns for odd film rates
what: telecine pattern examples: NTSC 24p 23 (classic) or 2332 (preferred), 20p 33, 18p 334, 16p 3444; PAL 24p 222222222223 (Euro pulldown), 16p 33333334. detelecine takes the same strings
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf telecine=pattern=334 -c:v libx264 -flags +ildct+ilme -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Do not IVTC with -r 24
what: fps=24 or -r 24 drop frames on a schedule without matching fields: combed frames stay and clean ones are lost
how: Use fieldmatch/decimate or pullup instead.

name: Check an IVTC result
what: A correct IVTC gives exactly four fifths of the frames at 24000/1001 with the same duration; credits, titles and inserted 30i video do not follow the pattern and need separate handling
how: Count frames before/after: `ffprobe -v error -count_frames -select_streams v:0 -show_entries stream=nb_read_frames -of csv=p=0 in.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Soft telecine needs nothing undone
what: Soft telecine stores 24p with repeat-field flags (many NTSC film DVDs); ignore the flags and you already have clean 24p. Hard telecine bakes the pulldown into frames and needs IVTC
how: (repeatfields is a different tool: it hard-repeats fields based on the repeat_field flag.)

name: Progressive content stored as fields
what: Most PAL film DVDs (25p as 50i) only comb when fields are mismatched; field-match and weave, no interpolation needed
how: Try fieldmatch without decimate: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf fieldmatch -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Shimmering thin lines after bobbing
what: Remaining combing means wrong field order or a missed mode; shimmer on thin lines is normal for single-pass bobbing and is what QTGMC's stabilisation reduces
how: Check scrolling text, thin horizontal lines and fast pans after deinterlacing.

name: QTGMC is the quality ceiling
what: QTGMC (motion-compensated, with noise handling and temporal stabilisation) is the community's highest-quality deinterlacer but much slower; one MiniDV archivist's 504 blind comparisons ranked QTGMC slower_default first
how: Needs VapourSynth + vs-jetpack QTempGaussMC (missing).

name: Block deinterlacers inside pp
what: pp also has deinterlacers: lb linear blend (1 2 1), li linear interpolation, ci cubic interpolation, md median, fd ffmpeg (-1 4 2 4 -1), l5 FIR low-pass (-1 2 6 2 -1)
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf pp=lb -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Print fieldmatch combed metrics
what: fieldmatch combdbg=pcn or pcnub forces and prints the combed metrics for those matches (micout in TFM/VFM terms)
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf fieldmatch=combdbg=pcn,decimate -an -f null - 2>&1 | grep -m3 -i fieldmatch` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: See what vidstab measures: show=1
what: vidstabdetect show=1 (or 2) draws the measurement fields and transforms on the output frames
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf vidstabdetect=shakiness=5:show=1:result=tr.trf -c:v libx264 -crf 23 show.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Virtual tripod: lock to one reference frame
what: vidstabdetect tripod=N compares every frame to reference frame N to keep the view absolutely still; use tripod=1 in vidstabtransform too (equivalent to relative=0:smoothing=0). Frames before the reference are not stabilized
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf vidstabdetect=tripod=1:result=tr.trf -f null - && ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf vidstabtransform=input=tr.trf:tripod=1 -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Low-contrast footage: mincontrast and stepsize
what: mincontrast (0-1, default 0.3) discards measurement fields below that contrast; stepsize (default 6) sets the search step, with 1-pixel resolution around the minimum
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf vidstabdetect=mincontrast=0.2:stepsize=4:result=tr.trf -f null -` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Readable transform file
what: fileformat=ascii writes human-readable transforms; binary (default) is about 40% smaller
how: Not available in our ffmpeg 6.1 build ("Option not found"); newer builds only.

name: Average instead of Gaussian path: optalgo=avg
what: vidstabtransform optalgo chooses the camera-path optimisation: gauss (default, Gaussian low-pass) or avg (averaging transformations)
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf vidstabdetect=result=tr.trf -f null - && ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf vidstabtransform=input=tr.trf:optalgo=avg -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Cap vidstab corrections
what: maxshift limits translation in pixels and maxangle rotation in radians (degree*PI/180); -1 (default) means no limit
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf vidstabdetect=result=tr.trf -f null - && ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf vidstabtransform=input=tr.trf:maxshift=20:maxangle=0.05 -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Black borders instead of previous-frame fill
what: vidstabtransform crop=keep (default) fills exposed borders from the previous frame; crop=black fills them black
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf vidstabdetect=result=tr.trf -f null - && ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf vidstabtransform=input=tr.trf:crop=black:optzoom=0 -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Adaptive zoom so no border ever shows
what: optzoom=2 picks an adaptive zoom so no borders are visible, changing at most zoomspeed % per frame (0-5, default 0.25); optzoom=1 (default) is a static zoom; zoom adds on top
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf vidstabdetect=result=tr.trf -f null - && ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf vidstabtransform=input=tr.trf:optzoom=2:zoomspeed=0.5 -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Bicubic resampling in vidstab
what: interpol: no, linear (horizontal only), bilinear (default), bicubic (slow)
