how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf vidstabdetect=result=tr.trf -f null - && ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf vidstabtransform=input=tr.trf:interpol=bicubic -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Dump vidstab global motions
what: vidstabtransform debug=1 raises verbosity and writes the detected global motions to global_motions.trf
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf vidstabdetect=result=tr.trf -f null - && ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf vidstabtransform=input=tr.trf:debug=1 -f null - && ls global_motions.trf` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Deinterlace before stabilising, in both passes
what: vid.stab has no notion of fields: combing is measured as image content. Put the same deinterlacer before vidstabdetect and vidstabtransform; double-rate (yadif=1) is fine if both passes use it
how: README commands: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf yadif,vidstabdetect -f null - && ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf yadif,vidstabtransform,unsharp=5:5:0.8:3:3:0.4 out_stabilized.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: 10-bit 4:2:2 into vidstab: convert first
what: The vid.stab README says 10-bit 4:2:2 must be downsampled to 8-bit 4:2:0 to avoid chroma shift or colour bleed: format=yuv420p before vidstabtransform
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mov -vf format=yuv420p,vidstabdetect -f null - && ffmpeg -i in.mov -vf format=yuv420p,vidstabtransform -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out_stabilized.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Concatenated input and vidstab
what: Concatenated input (-f concat) can present irregular timestamps; check that both passes report the same frame count before blaming stabilisation
how: Compare `-count_frames` on both pass inputs.

name: Zoomed stabilise recipe with mild sharpen
what: claude-mods pass 2 example: vidstabtransform zoom=2 to crop the wobble margin, smoothing=24, then unsharp=5:5:0.6
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf vidstabdetect=shakiness=6:accuracy=15:result=transforms.trf -f null - && ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf vidstabtransform=input=transforms.trf:zoom=2:smoothing=24,unsharp=5:5:0.6 -c:v libx264 -crf 19 stable.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: deshake search range
what: deshake rx/ry set the maximum movement searched, 0-64 px (default 16)
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf deshake=rx=32:ry=32 -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: deshake: search only a static area
what: x, y, w, h limit the motion search to a rectangle, useful when subjects moving in frame would be mistaken for camera motion; drawbox can show the box
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf deshake=x=0:y=0:w=200:h=120 -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: deshake edge fill
what: edge chooses how blank edges are filled: blank, original, clamp, mirror (default)
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf deshake=edge=clamp -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: deshake block size, contrast and speed
what: blocksize 4-128 (default 8); only blocks with contrast above contrast (1-255, default 125) are used; search=less is less exhaustive than the default; filename writes a motion log
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf deshake=blocksize=16:contrast=100:search=less:filename=ds.log -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Gyro-data stabilisation: Gyroflow
what: Gyroflow stabilises from the gyroscope/accelerometer data that GoPro, Sony, Insta360 and others record, with rolling-shutter correction, lens correction, adaptive zoom and editor plugins (GPL-3.0)
how: Needs Gyroflow (missing).

name: Gyroflow with slow-motion (VFR) clips
what: Motion data is real-time; if 120 fps was recorded as 30 fps slow motion, enter the real-time rate (exact NTSC values like 119.88) so Gyroflow stretches the motion data
how: Needs Gyroflow (missing).

name: Gyroflow low-pass for drone vibration
what: A low-pass filter on IMU data removes high-frequency vibration (e.g. drone motors); usual values 30-70 Hz
how: Needs Gyroflow (missing).

name: Rolling-shutter jello without gyro data
what: Efenstor's rsvs (OpenCV, CPU) targets jello; methods 1 JelloComplex2 (default) to 5 FullFrameTransform2; jello methods suit handheld static viewpoints; --test shows motion vectors. Code licence is unclear (personal use only)
how: Needs rsvs (missing).

name: Straighten a tilted horizon: rotate
what: rotate takes an angle in radians (clockwise; degrees*PI/180), fillcolor (default black, none = no background), and rotw()/roth() for an output size that contains the rotated frame
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf "rotate=2*PI/180:ow='rotw(2*PI/180)':oh='roth(2*PI/180)'" -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Keystone fix: perspective
what: perspective corrects video not shot perpendicular to the screen; x0..y3 are the four corners (top-left, top-right, bottom-left, bottom-right); sense=source maps those points to the corners
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf perspective=x0=20:y0=10:x1=W-20:y1=0:x2=0:y2=H:x3=W:y3=H:sense=source -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: lenscorrection: the formula and its limits
what: r_src = r_tgt*(1 + k1*(r_tgt/r_0)^2 + k2*(r_tgt/r_0)^4), r_0 half the diagonal; k1/k2 in [-1,1]; cx/cy the centre (default 0.5); OpenCV calibration can give k1/k2, otherwise trial and error
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf lenscorrection=cx=0.5:cy=0.5:k1=-0.2:k2=-0.02 -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Use bilinear interpolation in lenscorrection
what: lenscorrection defaults to nearest interpolation, which Daniel Playfair Cal found visibly aliased; i=bilinear is the other option; fc sets the colour of unmapped pixels (default black@0)
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf lenscorrection=k1=-0.2:k2=-0.02:i=bilinear:fc=black -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: GoPro k1/k2 starting points
what: Posted values: Hero 3/2 class k1=-0.227:k2=-0.022; Hero 5/6 k1=-0.18:k2=0.006. One tester found most posted values poor, so treat them as a start for trial and error
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf lenscorrection=k1=-0.18:k2=0.006 -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Fisheye to flat with v360 and the camera's FOV
what: v360 converts between standard projections using input FOV values (e.g. stereographic input sg with ih_fov/iv_fov from the maker's FOV table) to output flat; lowering output d_fov removes unmapped areas. His own command also had pitch=-90
how: Tested without pitch: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf v360=input=sg:ih_fov=122.6:iv_fov=94.4:output=flat:d_fov=121:w=640:h=360 -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: v360 fisheye FOV: diagonal vs horizontal
what: id_fov is the diagonal field of view, not horizontal/vertical; set ih_fov and iv_fov to the camera's real FOV (a 180-degree fisheye is not 360)
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf v360=fisheye:equirect:ih_fov=180:iv_fov=180 -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: v360 interpolation quality
what: v360 interp: near, line (default), lagrange9, cube, lanc, sp16, gauss, mitchell; more complex methods need much more memory
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf v360=input=fisheye:output=flat:ih_fov=150:iv_fov=100:d_fov=110:interp=lanc -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: lensfun: database-driven lens correction
what: lensfun wraps the lensfun library with a camera/lens database (it had a GoPro HERO5 Black entry); it was slower but more accurate than lenscorrection, with scale to show the whole input. Not in our ffmpeg build
how: Needs ffmpeg built with --enable-liblensfun (missing).

name: Reverse lens vignetting
what: vignette mode=backward brightens toward the edges to reverse a vignette; there is no automatic detection of the lens angle (set angle, x0, y0); dither on by default
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf vignette=angle=PI/5:mode=backward -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Shift misaligned chroma: chromashift
what: chromashift moves chroma-blue (cbh/cbv) and chroma-red (crh/crv) planes; edge smear, default or warp
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf chromashift=cbh=-2:crh=2:edge=smear -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Shift R, G, B separately: rgbashift
what: rgbashift moves red/green/blue/alpha planes horizontally (rh, gh, bh, ah) and vertically (rv, gv, bv, av), edge smear/default/warp
how: Undo the +4/-4 shift of our test clip: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf rgbashift=rh=-4:bh=4:edge=smear -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: deflicker averaging modes
what: deflicker removes temporal luminance variation with a moving average of size 2-129 frames (default 5); modes am, gm, hm, qm, cm, pm, median; bypass=1 only computes metadata
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf deflicker=size=7:mode=median -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Auto-levels with temporal smoothing: normalize
what: normalize stretches each channel's range; smoothing=N rolling frames reduces flicker when small dark/bright objects enter, like camera auto-exposure; independence=0 links channels and preserves hue
how: Docs example: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf normalize=blackpt=black:whitept=white:smoothing=50:independence=0 -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Histogram equalisation for degraded captures only
what: histeq is useful only for degraded or poorly captured video with a compressed intensity range; strength default 0.2, intensity 0.21 caps wash-out, antibanding weak/strong adds tiny noise against banding
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf histeq=strength=0.2:intensity=0.21:antibanding=weak -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Tame dangerous flashes: photosensitivity
what: photosensitivity reduces flashes for viewers with epilepsy: frames (default 30), threshold (default 1, lower is stricter), skip, blend (0 duplicates the last good frame, 1 blends up to the threshold), bypass
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf photosensitivity=frames=30:threshold=1 -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Projector-and-camera transfers bake in flicker
what: Filming a projection captures at the camera rate whatever the projector does: speed errors and flicker get locked into the file, plus hot spots, gate cropping (up to 20%) and keystone; frame-by-frame scanning avoids this
how: Ask for a frame-by-frame scan, not a real-time transfer.

name: Dehaze: no built-in filter here
what: Our ffmpeg has no dehaze filter; the guided filter docs mention dehazing only with a separately generated guidance image (He et al. guided filtering)
how: Two-input form: `guided=guidance=on` with a guide stream.

name: Truncated phone MP4 ("moov atom not found"): untrunc
what: untrunc rebuilds the missing index of a truncated mp4/m4v/mov/3gp using a healthy reference video, ideally from the same camera; the anthwlock fork is faster, handles >2 GB and GoPro/Sony XAVC. Here it recovered 1.17 s from a 2 s clip cut to 60%
how: Needs untrunc (missing; built here from source with system libav). Output is <broken>_fixed.mp4: `untrunc ok.mp4 in.mp4 && ffprobe -v error -show_entries format=duration -of csv=p=0 in.mp4_fixed.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Pick the right untrunc reference
what: The reference must match device or app, resolution, frame rate, codec and encoder settings; content and length do not matter (10 s is enough). Expect to lose the last few seconds before the interruption
how: Best reference: another clip from the same session.

name: ffmpeg cannot rebuild a missing moov
what: Remuxing with +genpts or -movflags faststart fails on a truncated MP4 with "moov atom not found"; that needs untrunc and a template file
how: Recognise the error, switch tools.

name: Damaged sectors: rescue the bytes first
what: If the OS cannot read parts of the file, ffmpeg cannot help; copy it with a tool that skips bad areas (ddrescue), then try ffmpeg -err_detect ignore_err with stream copy
how: `ffmpeg -err_detect ignore_err -i in.ts -c copy video_fixed.mkv` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Drop corrupt packets while copying
what: Second attempt for an interrupted recording: +discardcorrupt discards corrupted packets and +igndts ignores DTS while copying
how: `ffmpeg -fflags +discardcorrupt+igndts -i in.ts -c copy out_recovered.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Rebuild an AVI index by remuxing
what: ffmpeg rebuilds a broken AVI index during a plain stream-copy remux
how: `ffmpeg -i in.avi -c copy out_fixed.avi` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Probe deeper when streams are not found
what: probesize (default 5,000,000 bytes) and analyzeduration (default 5 s) control probing; raise both when ffmpeg cannot find stream info
how: `ffmpeg -analyzeduration 200M -probesize 200M -i in.ts -c copy out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Keep only keyframes from a damaged stream
what: Input -discard nokey discards all frames except keyframes at the demuxer (not all demuxers support it)
how: `ffmpeg -discard nokey -i in.ts -c:v libx264 -crf 18 keys.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Decode only keyframes: -skip_frame nokey
what: Decoder option skip_frame nokey discards everything but keyframes (also noref, bidir, nointra); fast for keyframe thumbnails of a long or damaged file
how: `ffmpeg -skip_frame nokey -i in.mp4 -fps_mode vfr key_%03d.png` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Fix DivX packed B-frames
what: mpeg4_unpack_bframes unpacks DivX-style packed B-frames, which are not valid MPEG-4 and can break decoding when copied to mp4/ts
how: Docs command: `ffmpeg -i in.avi -codec copy -bsf:v mpeg4_unpack_bframes out.avi` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: MP4 H.264 into TS: annex B
what: h264_mp4toannexb converts length-prefixed H.264 to start codes, needed for MPEG-TS; ffmpeg inserts it automatically for mpegts and raw h264 output
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -codec copy -bsf:v h264_mp4toannexb out.ts` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: ADTS AAC into MP4: aac_adtstoasc
what: Raw AAC uses ADTS headers; packaging into MP4 needs aac_adtstoasc or the header write fails
how: `ffmpeg -i in.ts -c copy -bsf:a aac_adtstoasc out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Fix the aspect flag without re-encoding
what: h264_metadata sample_aspect_ratio rewrites the SAR in the H.264 VUI during a stream copy
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -c copy -bsf:v h264_metadata=sample_aspect_ratio=1/1 out_sar_fixed.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Crop garbage edges in the bitstream
what: h264_metadata crop_left/right/top/bottom set the SPS cropping offsets in pixels (some sizes cannot be represented with subsampled or interlaced video)
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -c copy -bsf:v h264_metadata=crop_bottom=8 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Override wrong rotation metadata
what: -display_rotation (degrees counter-clockwise) overrides the file's rotation; with transcoding and -autorotate the rotation is applied in filtering; -noautorotate turns automatic rotation off
how: `ffmpeg -display_rotation 90 -i in.mp4 -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Damage a copy to test your repair chain
what: The noise bitstream filter damages or drops packets without breaking the container, for testing error resilience; docs example drops non-key video packets after 30 s
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -c copy -bsf:v noise=amount=-1:drop='gt(pts*tb\,1)*not(key)' damaged.mkv` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Show damaged DV blocks: dv_error_marker
what: dv_error_marker replaces DV blocks marked damaged with a colour; sta selects which error-status codes (default 0xFFFE = all non-zero)
how: `ffmpeg -i in.dv -c copy -bsf:v dv_error_marker=color=magenta marked.dv` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Record so a crash leaves a playable file
what: A fragmented MP4 stays decodable if writing is interrupted, while a normal MP4 is undecodable if not finished; enable with movflags +frag_keyframe (or frag_duration/frag_size). Downside: less compatible
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -c copy -movflags +frag_keyframe+empty_moov frag.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Ignore broken MP4 edit lists
what: The mov demuxer applies edit lists by default; ignore_editlist=1 ignores them (advanced_editlist only works when edit lists are honoured)
how: `ffmpeg -ignore_editlist 1 -i in.mp4 -c copy out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Re-mux to fix seeking; keyframes need a re-encode
what: Forcing new keyframes requires re-encoding (choose the codecs, or ffmpeg uses the container default); if you only need seeking, re-muxing to .mp4 can solve it without transcoding
how: `ffmpeg -i in.ts -c copy remux.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Fill a gap with cloned frames: tpad
what: tpad adds frames before/after the stream: start/stop counts or start_duration/stop_duration; mode add (solid colour) or clone (copies of the first/last frame)
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf tpad=stop_mode=clone:stop_duration=1 -an -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Replace a run of bad frames: freezeframes
what: freezeframes replaces frames first..last with frame number replace taken from the second input
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -i in.mp4 -filter_complex "[0:v][1:v]freezeframes=first=24:last=36:replace=23" -an -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Cut by frame number and reset timestamps
what: trim start_frame/end_frame count frames, start/end use timestamps; trim does not change timestamps, so add setpts=PTS-STARTPTS for output starting at zero; chain trims to require all constraints
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf trim=start_frame=10:end_frame=40,setpts=PTS-STARTPTS -an -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: DV double captures: DVRescue A/B semantics
what: In DVRescue repair, file A is the reference timeline and B only donates frames to fill damage inside A; it never makes A longer, so extra material in B needs stitching, not repair
how: Needs DVRescue (missing).

name: Before capturing old tapes
what: Fully rewinding a tape to the end and back before capture reduced artifacts on long-stored MiniDV tapes; a TI-chipset FireWire card avoided dropped frames; Scenalyzer created unmarked missing frames, WinDV was cleanest
how: Capture-side checklist, applies before any repair.

name: Mask VHS head-switching noise with black
what: Masking the bottom noise with black keeps the aspect ratio; cropping and stretching risks aspect damage and aliasing (digitalFAQ staff). fillborders mode=fixed fills edge rows with a constant colour without changing size
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf fillborders=bottom=10:mode=fixed:color=black -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: How many lines the head-switching band takes
what: Typical bands: VHS SP bottom 4-10 lines, VHS EP/LP 6-16 (wider), S-VHS consumer 4-8, Hi8/Video8 6-14, U-matic 2-4, Betacam SP 2 or less, MiniDV/Digital8 none. It sits at a fixed position on virtually every frame; dropouts are intermittent streaks anywhere; TBC errors tear the whole picture
how: Measure on a 2-minute test capture at 100% zoom before choosing the mask.

name: Crop and re-pad the frame (M6WIQ VHS script)
what: The M6WIQ Linux VHS script crops 10 px width and 14 px height then pads back to the original size so the head-switching lines are hidden
how: Source-given crop/pad: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf "crop=(iw-10):(ih-14):3:0, pad=iw+10:ih+14:(ow-iw)/2:(oh-ih)/2" -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)
refs: M6WIQ VHS capture on Linux, https://www.m6wiq.uk/2022/11/vhs-capture-linux/, checked 2026-10-24

name: Crop the band and keep 4:3 exactly
what: For a 720x480 NTSC capture: 16 px of side bars carry no picture (704 active); removing 6 bottom lines needs 25 side pixels in total off, giving 695x474; removing 4 lines needs 22, giving 698x476. Then scale to any 4:3 size
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf crop=695:474:12:0,scale=640:480,setsar=1 -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: M6WIQ VHS clean-up chain order
what: The M6WIQ script runs fieldorder, bwdif (mode=1, deint=all), nlmeans noise reduction, zscale (to 960x720 bicubic), unsharp, the crop/pad mask, then setsar=1:1
how: Tested with simple values for the unnamed variables: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf "fieldorder=tff,bwdif=mode=1:parity=tff:deint=all,nlmeans,zscale=w=960:h=720:filter=bicubic,format=yuv420p,unsharp,crop=(iw-10):(ih-14):3:0,pad=iw+10:ih+14:(ow-iw)/2:(oh-ih)/2,setsar=1:1" -t 0.5 -c:v libx264 -crf 23 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)
refs: M6WIQ VHS capture on Linux, https://www.m6wiq.uk/2022/11/vhs-capture-linux/, checked 2026-10-24

name: Keep a lossless interlaced master
what: M6WIQ keeps two files per tape: a raw interlaced capture (huffyuv, -flags +ilme+ildct, 4:3) and a deinterlaced, cleaned MP4 for normal use
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -c:v huffyuv -flags +ilme+ildct -aspect 4:3 -an master.avi` (tested here 2026-10-24)
refs: M6WIQ VHS capture on Linux, https://www.m6wiq.uk/2022/11/vhs-capture-linux/, checked 2026-10-24

name: A TBC or DVD-recorder passthrough steadies capture
what: An S-VHS deck with built-in TBC is ideal; without one, a mid-2000s Panasonic DVD recorder's "frame adjusters" work similarly in passthrough. An EasyCAP gave unusable results; M6WIQ then used a Hauppauge USB-Live2 on Linux
how: Hardware choice before any software repair.
refs: M6WIQ VHS capture on Linux, https://www.m6wiq.uk/2022/11/vhs-capture-linux/, checked 2026-10-24

name: Dot crawl and rainbows: dedot
what: dedot reduces cross-luminance (dot crawl) and cross-colour (rainbows); m=dotcrawl+rainbows; lt/tl tune luma, tc/ct chroma (lower ct / higher tc = more rainbow reduction)
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf dedot=m=dotcrawl+rainbows -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Composite-era 4:3 pixels: set SAR explicitly
what: M6WIQ ends with setsar=1:1 after scaling to square-pixel 960x720, so players do not re-stretch the image
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf scale=640:480,setsar=1:1 -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)
refs: M6WIQ VHS capture on Linux, https://www.m6wiq.uk/2022/11/vhs-capture-linux/, checked 2026-10-24

name: Know the true film speed
what: Normal 8 was usually shot at 16 or 18 fps, Super 8 at 18 (sometimes 24), 16mm mostly 24; very old 8mm used 9 or 12 fps. Film shot at 18 and shown at 25 runs about 40% too fast; 16 at 25 more than 50%
how: A person's walking pace reveals the right speed; set it scene by scene when unknown.

name: Re-time a frame-per-frame scan to its real rate
what: Files playing at the original 16/18/24 fps give a 1:1 representation with no intermediate frames; input -r ignores the stored timestamps and assigns the rate you give
how: `ffmpeg -r 18 -i in.mp4 -an -c:v libx264 -crf 18 film18.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Blended frames come from projector transfers
what: Recording an 18 fps projection at 25 fps creates blended frames showing two images at once; adding duplicate frames (18 to 25) is sharper but slightly jerky on pans
how: Prefer a frame-by-frame scan; convert the rate last.

name: Ask the scanner for one frame per film frame
what: Ask for one video frame per film frame, progressive, no pulldown, in a lightly compressed or lossless codec (ProRes, MJPEG, huffyuv, lagarith), and test a 10-frame sample first; do the rate conversion after editing
how: Order spec for a transfer house.

name: Emulsion vs base scratches
what: A scratch on the emulsion side often shows as a blue streak and is real damage (fix in post); a base-side scratch shows dark when projected and a wet-gate transfer fills it during capture
how: Decide wet-gate rescans before digital fixes.

name: Undo a known 18 fps pulldown
what: If 18p film was telecined to NTSC with pattern 334, detelecine with the same pattern returns the progressive frames
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf detelecine=pattern=334 -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: AI dust and scratch removal is still immature
what: TheUnduster (macOS, GPL-3.0, ONNX detector + LaMa inpainting) ships an untrained fixture detector, so detection misses real dust until a model is trained
how: Needs a dust/scratch tool (missing).

name: Hide a dead or hot pixel with delogo
section: Dead pixels, logos and burned-in marks
what: delogo interpolates a small rectangle from its surroundings; a 2x2 box over a stuck pixel fixed it visually, and the whole job scripts and parallelises well
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf delogo=x=299:y=199:w=4:h=4 -c:v libx264 -crf 18 -c:a copy out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Several dead pixels: chain delogo
section: Dead pixels, logos and burned-in marks
what: Chain one delogo per pixel; find x,y by exporting a frame and reading coordinates in GIMP; one user saw a slight washed-out look; preview with ffplay before encoding
how: `ffmpeg -ss 1 -i in.mp4 -frames:v 1 frame.png && ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf "delogo=x=299:y=199:w=4:h=4,delogo=x=10:y=120:w=2:h=2" -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)
refs: Ask Ubuntu accepted answer, https://askubuntu.com/questions/706933, checked 2026-10-24

name: Find the delogo box: show=1
section: Dead pixels, logos and burned-in marks
what: delogo show=1 draws a green rectangle on the outermost pixels used, to set x, y, w, h
how: `ffmpeg -ss 1 -i in.mp4 -vf delogo=x=540:y=20:w=80:h=40:show=1 -frames:v 1 box.png` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Mask-shaped logo removal: removelogo
section: Dead pixels, logos and burned-in marks
what: removelogo fills pixels marked non-zero in a same-size bitmap; make it from a black frame with the logo via threshold and one or two erosions; marking too many pixels hurts less than missing some
how: `ffmpeg -ss 1 -i in.mp4 -vf "drawbox=x=0:y=0:w=iw:h=ih:color=black:t=fill,drawbox=x=536:y=16:w=88:h=48:color=white:t=fill,format=gray" -frames:v 1 mask.png && ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf removelogo=f=mask.png -c:v libx264 -crf 18 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Blur over a rectangle: cover_rect
section: Dead pixels, logos and burned-in marks
what: cover_rect covers a found rectangle by interpolating the surroundings (mode=blur, default) or with a supplied yuv420 image; docs pair it with find_rect
how: Docs command shape: `find_rect=newref.pgm,cover_rect=cover.jpg:mode=cover`.

name: Read `ffmpeg -h filter=NAME` before copying options from the online docs
what: the online page documents a newer ffmpeg than our 6.1.1, and option values differ: online `adynamicequalizer` lists modes like `cutbelow`/`cutabove`, but 6.1.1 only accepts `mode=listen|cut|boost` plus a separate `direction=downward|upward`; `mode=cutabove` fails with "Unable to parse option value"
how: `ffmpeg -hide_banner -h filter=adynamicequalizer` and use the values it prints (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Find which options can change while the file plays
what: options marked `T` in `ffmpeg -h filter=NAME` accept runtime commands; the command name is the option name
how: `ffmpeg -hide_banner -h filter=afftdn | grep -E "sample_noise|gain_smooth"` shows the `T` flag column (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Change a filter setting at a set time with asendcmd
what: `asendcmd` sends `TIME TARGET COMMAND ARG` to a later audio filter, e.g. raise de-noise strength only where a noisy shot starts
how: `ffmpeg -i noisy.wav -af "asendcmd=c='5.0 afftdn nr 20',afftdn=nr=8" out.wav` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Keep a list of timed commands in a file
what: `asendcmd=f=FILE` reads intervals like `4.0 volume@b volume 0.3;`; name the target instance with `@name`
how: `echo "4.0 volume@b volume 0.3;4.4 volume@b volume 1.0;" > cmds.txt` then `ffmpeg -i sp.wav -af "asendcmd=f=cmds.txt,volume@b=1" out.wav` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Teach afftdn the noise from a noise-only stretch
what: `sample_noise` start/stop commands capture a noise profile from the input; the docs' example learns from the first 0.4 s. On our noisy clip (pauses at -42.9 dB) this took pauses to -55.0 dB with speech level unchanged (-18.6 -> -18.8 dB)
how: `ffmpeg -i noisy.wav -af "asendcmd=0.0 afftdn sn start,asendcmd=0.4 afftdn sn stop,afftdn=nr=20:nf=-40" out.wav` - put the start/stop times on a pause with no speech (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: afftdn's default noise model is white noise
what: `noise_type` defaults to white; on our pink-noise + hum clip plain `afftdn` only moved pauses from -42.9 to -43.8 dB, while on a white-noise clip it gave -44.8 -> -49.3 dB. Learn a profile (above) when the noise is not white
how: compare `ffmpeg -i noisy.wav -af afftdn a.wav` and the sample-noise command, then measure the pauses (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Set afftdn's noise floor near the real noise level
what: `nf` (default -50 dB, range -80 to -20) is the measured noise floor the filter works from. With a profile learned from 0-1.5 s at nr=20 our pauses came out at -53.2 dB (nf=-30), -50.5 (nf=-40), -44.5 (nf=-50), -43.1 (nf=-60): a floor set far below the actual noise did almost nothing
how: measure a pause first: `ffmpeg -i in.wav -af "atrim=0:1.5,astats=measure_perchannel=RMS_level+Noise_floor:measure_overall=none" -f null -`, then try nf a little above that value (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Listen to what afftdn removes
what: `output_mode=noise` (`om=n`) passes only the removed noise; if words are audible in it, the setting is eating speech
how: `ffmpeg -i noisy.wav -af "afftdn=nr=12:om=n" removed.wav` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Let afftdn follow a changing floor
what: `track_noise=1` (`tn=1`) adjusts the noise floor automatically during processing; the docs pair it with a very low starting floor. On our steady test noise it changed little (-42.9 -> -42.9 dB at nr=10), so keep it for noise that really changes
how: `ffmpeg -i in.wav -af "afftdn=nr=10:nf=-80:tn=1" out.wav` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Smooth afftdn gains against "music noise"
what: `gain_smooth` (`gs`, 0-50, default 0) smooths the gain of neighbouring frequency bins and is meant to reduce random music-noise artefacts. On a white-noise clip nr=24 gave pauses -49.7 dB without and -52.1 dB with gs=15
how: `ffmpeg -i in.wav -af "afftdn=nr=24:gs=15" out.wav` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Give afftdn a hand-made 15-band noise profile
what: `noise_type=custom` reads `band_noise`: 15 values separated by space or `|`
how: `ffmpeg -i in.wav -af "afftdn=nt=c:bn='-40 -40 -42 -44 -46 -48 -50 -50 -52 -54 -56 -58 -60 -60 -60'" out.wav` (ran here; values are an example, not a measured profile) (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Residual floor and adaptivity in afftdn
what: `residual_floor` (`rf`, default -38 dB) sets where the reduced noise sits; `adaptivity` (`ad`, 0-1, default 0.5) sets how fast per-bin gains adapt: 0 is instant, higher is slower
how: `ffmpeg -i in.wav -af "afftdn=nr=20:rf=-30" a.wav` and `afftdn=nr=12:ad=0.9` (both tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Link the noise floor across mics in a multichannel file
what: `noise_link` (`nl`) chooses whether each channel uses its own floor (`none`) or the min/max/average of all channels (default `min`)
how: `ffmpeg -i twomic.wav -af "afftdn=nr=10:nl=average" out.wav` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: afftdn output is late by about 25 ms here
what: cross-correlating input and output showed the sample-noise afftdn result 1200 samples (25.0 ms at 48 kHz) behind the input. That matters when the cleaned track is mixed back with the dry track or another mic
how: trim the head after the filter: `...,afftdn=nr=20:nf=-40,atrim=start_sample=1200,asetpts=PTS-STARTPTS` (re-measured lag 0) (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: anlmdn patch and research sizes, and its noise-only output
section: Other de-noisers in ffmpeg and Python
what: `anlmdn` compares patches (`p`, 1-100 ms, default 2 ms) inside a research area (`r`, 2-300 ms, default 6 ms); `o=n` outputs only the removed noise; `m` is a smooth factor (default 11)
how: `ffmpeg -i noisy.wav -af "anlmdn=s=0.001:o=n" removed.wav`, `anlmdn=s=0.001:p=0.004:r=0.015:m=15` (both ran here) (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Wavelet de-noise with afwtdn
section: Other de-noisers in ffmpeg and Python
what: `afwtdn` reduces broadband noise with wavelets; `sigma` sets strength and is most usefully given in dB (e.g. -45dB); `percent` (default 85) is partial de-noising. Plain sigma=-45dB moved our pauses -42.9 -> -44.2 dB
how: `ffmpeg -i noisy.wav -af "afwtdn=sigma=-45dB" out.wav` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: afwtdn profile and adaptive modes
section: Other de-noisers in ffmpeg and Python
what: `profile` uses the first input frame as the noise profile (very poor if that frame has non-noise); `adaptive` re-detects noise frames and uses them as profile. On our clip (2 s of noise first): profile=1 -> pauses -59.3 dB, adaptive=1:percent=70 -> -51.2 dB, speech level unchanged
how: `ffmpeg -i noisy.wav -af "afwtdn=sigma=-45dB:profile=1" out.wav` - only when the file starts on pure noise (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: arnndn needs a real model file
section: Other de-noisers in ffmpeg and Python
what: `arnndn` (recurrent-network speech de-noise) has a required `model` option; the `.rnnn` files are in richardpl/arnndn-models (std.rnnn is the one bundled with Xiph RNNoise; the others are by Gregor Richards). With std.rnnn our pauses went -42.9 -> -65.6 dB, speech -18.6 -> -18.8 dB
how: `curl -sSLO https://raw.githubusercontent.com/richardpl/arnndn-models/master/std.rnnn` then `ffmpeg -i noisy.wav -af "arnndn=m=std.rnnn" out.wav` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Pick the rnnoise model by signal and noise type
section: Other de-noisers in ffmpeg and Python
what: GregorR's table maps expected signal (general / voice / speech; "voice" includes laughter and other non-speech sounds) against expected noise (general / recording): e.g. speech + recording noise = somnolent-hogwash, voice + recording = beguiling-drafter, general + recording = conjoined-burgers, general + general = marathon-prescription. In richardpl's repo the files are named by those initials (sh, bd, cb, mp, lq). On our test sh.rnnn gave pauses -55.7 dB vs -65.6 dB for std.rnnn: compare models on your own clip
how: `for m in std sh; do ffmpeg -i in.wav -af arnndn=m=$m.rnnn out_$m.wav; done` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Blend arnndn with the original
section: Other de-noisers in ffmpeg and Python
what: `mix` (-1 to 1, default 1) sets how much filtered signal goes out; mix=0.7 gave pauses -52.4 dB instead of -65.6 dB. Negative values keep the removed noise, and `mix=-1` lets you hear exactly what was taken out
how: `arnndn=m=std.rnnn:mix=0.7` and `arnndn=m=std.rnnn:mix=-1` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: arnndn output is late by 10 ms here
section: Other de-noisers in ffmpeg and Python
what: cross-correlation put the arnndn result 479-480 samples (10 ms at 48 kHz) behind the input
how: `arnndn=m=std.rnnn,atrim=start_sample=480,asetpts=PTS-STARTPTS` re-aligned it to 0 samples (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Measure what a de-noiser does to the speech, not just the noise
section: Other de-noisers in ffmpeg and Python
what: `asdr`, `asisdr` and `apsnr` compare two time-aligned streams (processed vs clean reference) and print dB per channel. Aligned results here: noisy input SDR 22.9 dB, profile-afftdn 25.1 dB, arnndn 11.2 dB - arnndn removed more noise but changed the speech more. Un-aligned output gives nonsense (arnndn read -3.3 dB before the 480-sample trim)
how: `ffmpeg -i processed.wav -i clean.wav -filter_complex "[0][1]asdr" -f null -` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Adaptive self-reference de-noise with anlms
section: Other de-noisers in ffmpeg and Python
what: the docs' noise-reduction example filters the input with a copy of itself delayed by a fixed amount. It ran here, but on our clip it also pulled the speech down by about 24 dB (-18.6 -> -42.6 dB), so check the level before trusting it
how: `ffmpeg -i in.wav -af "asplit[a][b],[a]adelay=32S:all=1[a],[b][a]anlms=order=128:leakage=0.0005:mu=.5:out_mode=o" out.wav` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Adaptive filters that take a second (reference) stream
section: Other de-noisers in ffmpeg and Python
what: `anlms`/`anlmf` and `arls` adapt the 1st input toward the "desired" 2nd input; `out_mode` picks input, desired, output, noise or error. Useful when a separate noise-reference recording exists
how: `ffmpeg -i main.wav -i ref.wav -filter_complex "[0][1]arls=order=16:out_mode=o" out.wav` (ran here; no quality claim) (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: noisereduce: stationary spectral gating with a noise clip
section: Other de-noisers in ffmpeg and Python
what: the Python package `noisereduce` (MIT per its package metadata) gates noise per frequency band; with `stationary=True` and a noise-only clip as `y_noise` it took our pauses to -74.8 dB with speech -1.3 dB
how: `uv pip install --target pylib --no-deps noisereduce` (pure Python; numpy/scipy are in /home/user/tools/venv), then `nr.reduce_noise(y=y, sr=sr, stationary=True, y_noise=y[:int(1.5*sr)])` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: noisereduce non-stationary mode can cost speech level
section: Other de-noisers in ffmpeg and Python
what: the default (`stationary=False`) keeps updating the noise threshold over time (`time_constant_s`, default 2.0); on our steady-noise clip it reached -76.7 dB pauses but dropped speech by about 11 dB. Use it for changing noise and check levels
how: `nr.reduce_noise(y=y, sr=sr)` vs the stationary call, then measure (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: noisereduce prop_decrease for partial reduction
section: Other de-noisers in ffmpeg and Python
what: `prop_decrease` is the proportion to reduce the noise by (1.0 = 100%); 0.7 gave pauses -54.5 dB instead of -74.8 dB
how: `nr.reduce_noise(y=y, sr=sr, stationary=True, y_noise=noise, prop_decrease=0.7)` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: agate: reduce noise between lines instead of muting it
what: below `threshold` the gate divides the level by `ratio`, down to the floor set by `range` (default 0.06125; 0 turns it into an expander); `attack` and `release` level the change. With range=0.25 our pauses dropped about 12 dB (-42.9 -> -55.0 dB) and speech was untouched
how: `ffmpeg -i in.wav -af "agate=threshold=0.05:range=0.25:attack=10:release=250" out.wav` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: agate detection and knee
what: `detection` is `rms` (default) or `peak`; `knee` (1-8, default 2.83) curves the threshold so reduction starts more softly
how: `agate=threshold=0.05:range=0.1:detection=peak:knee=4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: A gate threshold must sit above the noise
what: the docs' compand noise gate opens at about -50 dB; our noise is at -43 dB, so it changed nothing (pauses stayed -42.9 dB). Measure the pause level first and set the gate between noise and speech

name: Key a gate from a filtered copy
what: `sidechaingate` processes the 1st stream from the level of the 2nd; filtering the key (the docs' example cuts the lows) stops rumble from opening it. Keying from a 300 Hz high-passed copy gave pauses -56.9 dB
how: `ffmpeg -i in.wav -af "asplit[m][k];[k]highpass=f=300[k2];[m][k2]sidechaingate=threshold=0.04:range=0.2:release=300" out.wav` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: compand as a downward expander
what: the docs give an expander transfer curve for compand that pushes low levels further down

name: adeclick: detection threshold and the "save" method
what: lower `threshold` (1-100, default 2) means more samples are treated as impulsive noise; `method=save` (`m=s`) leaves non-interpolated samples unchanged, while the default overlap-add slightly changes even good samples
how: `ffmpeg -i clicks.wav -af "adeclick=t=4:m=s" out.wav` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: adeclick window, overlap and burst
what: `window` (10-100 ms, default 55), `overlap` (50-95%, default 75; higher removes more but is much slower) and `burst` (0-10%, default 2; fuses detected samples that are close together)
how: `ffmpeg -i clicks.wav -af "adeclick=w=20:o=90:b=4" out.wav` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: See clicks and clipping in a waveform picture
what: `showwavespic` draws the whole file as one image; `filter=peak` draws peak values instead of averages, so single-sample spikes show
how: `ffmpeg -i clicks.wav -lavfi "showwavespic=s=1600x300:filter=peak" wave.png` and look at the PNG (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Mouth De-click: run it twice
what: iZotope's Mouth De-click targets clicks and lip smacks; higher Sensitivity can damage plosives, Frequency Skew at zero or above targets mid-frequency mouth clicks, Click Widening extends the repair for lip smacks with a decay, and a second pass often catches quieter clicks masked by louder ones
how: needs iZotope RX (missing, paid); in ffmpeg the nearest tool is `adeclick` (above)

name: De-click algorithm choice and "clicks only" listening
what: RX De-click offers Single band (narrow digital clicks), Multi-band periodic, Multi-band random, and Low latency (mouth clicks other modes miss); "Output clicks only" outputs the difference so you hear what is removed
how: needs iZotope RX (missing); ffmpeg has no clicks-only output for adeclick, so subtract by ear

name: Short click: interpolate under 4000 samples
what: RX Interpolate repairs individual clicks below 4000 samples by synthesizing a replacement from the selection; RX's Instant Process uses Interpolate for selections under 4000 samples and De-click settings above
how: needs iZotope RX (missing)

name: Longer damage: Spectral Repair instead of De-click
what: with a time selection, RX Spectral Repair gives better results than De-click on corrupted segments longer than 10 ms; Attenuate (vertical) is unlimited in length, Attenuate horizontal/2D and Replace up to 10 s, Pattern and Partials+Noise up to 4 s
how: needs iZotope RX (missing)

name: Attenuate over speech, Replace over room tone
what: for a creak under a line, iZotope's editor attenuated the noise where it overlapped dialogue and replaced it with surrounding audio where only room tone was present
how: needs iZotope RX Spectral Repair (missing)

name: De-crackle after De-click
what: crackle is many quiet, close-together clicks; RX De-crackle works better after De-click has removed the worst clicks; RX also lists it for dry-mouthed spoken word
how: needs iZotope RX (missing)

name: Audacity click tools and their size limits
what: Click Removal needs a selection longer than 4096 samples (about 93 ms at 44.1 kHz), may miss broad clicks of 10 ms or more, and does not remove soft crackle (use Noise Reduction for that); Repair fixes a selection of at most 128 samples from the audio either side
how: needs Audacity (missing, free GPL); in ffmpeg use `adeclick` on whole stretches

name: Audition: Automatic Click Remover vs DeClicker
what: Automatic Click Remover runs in real time in the Effects Rack/Multitrack and applies several scan-and-repair passes automatically; DeClicker (Diagnostics) lets you review detected clicks and choose which to fix but must be run several times for the same reduction
how: needs Adobe Audition (missing, paid)

name: Paste clean "air" over small noises
what: dialogue editor Brad Semenoff sets RX's paste preferences to "To Selection" so he can copy full-bandwidth clean air from one place and paste it over clicks or birds elsewhere
how: needs iZotope RX (missing); the ffmpeg equivalent is a room-tone patch with `amix` (see the fill section)

name: Run de-plosive before any high-pass
what: RX De-plosive looks for plosives between 20 and 80 Hz, so a file already high-passed may defeat detection; plosives usually sit 20-300 Hz and can reach 500 Hz (set Frequency Limit just above them)
how: needs iZotope RX (missing); in our chains keep `highpass` after any plosive fix

name: Sensitivity before strength on plosives
what: in RX De-plosive, Sensitivity affects results more than Strength; to keep speech quality, raise Sensitivity and lower Strength
how: needs iZotope RX (missing)

name: Which letters pop
what: plosives come from stopping and suddenly releasing air; the low-frequency boom happens most with p, b, d, t and k
how: listen for low thumps on those consonants; find them as bright low-frequency blobs with `showspectrumpic=start=0:stop=500`

name: A dynamic low-shelf in ffmpeg 6.1 syntax
what: `adynamicequalizer` can detect with a lowpass and act with a lowshelf, cutting only while the detector is over threshold (6.1: `mode=cut`)
how: `ffmpeg -i in.wav -af "adynamicequalizer=dftype=lowpass:dfrequency=150:tftype=lowshelf:tfrequency=150:mode=cut:threshold=20:attack=1:release=60:range=8" out.wav` (ran here; values not tuned on real pops) (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Find the hum frequency on a spectrogram
what: `showspectrumpic` with `start`/`stop` limits the picture to a frequency range, so 50/60 Hz and harmonics are easy to read
how: `ffmpeg -i in.wav -lavfi "showspectrumpic=s=800x400:start=0:stop=500:legend=1" hum.png` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Notch each harmonic with its own width
what: Audacity's manual: notch the fundamental (60 Hz North America, 50 Hz UK and most other countries), find further spikes with a spectrum plot, use a higher Q on higher harmonics, and a Q between 2 and 10 generally works for mains hum
how: `anequalizer=c0 f=50 w=4 g=-30 t=0|c0 f=100 w=4 g=-20 t=0` (ran here; per-band f, width in Hz, gain) (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Narrow notches ring
what: a higher Q makes a notch narrower but adds longer "tails" (ringing) to its impulse response; minimum-phase filters put the ringing after the transient where it is more easily masked, linear-phase filters add pre-ringing and latency
how: use the widest notch that removes the hum; ffmpeg `bandreject`/`equalizer` are two-pole IIR filters

name: Static vs dynamic de-hum
what: RX De-hum Static suits simple hum with few harmonics that doesn't overlap speech; Dynamic suits hum with more than a dozen harmonics, inharmonic tones, buzz reaching high frequencies or hum overlapping speech; "Output hum only" helps tune Q and slope
how: needs iZotope RX (missing)

name: Notch first, compress last around noise reduction
what: Audacity advises notch filtering and click removal before Noise Reduction, and compression after it; RX likewise uses De-hum Dynamic before Voice/Spectral De-noise
how: order a chain as `bandreject...,adeclick,afftdn...`

name: FIR notch with firequalizer adds 10 ms
what: `firequalizer` takes a gain curve from `gain_entry`; its `delay` option defaults to 0.01 s, and our output was 480 samples (10 ms) late even with `zero_phase=on` written to WAV
how: `firequalizer=gain_entry='entry(40,0);entry(48,-30);entry(52,-30);entry(60,0)'` then `atrim=start_sample=480,asetpts=PTS-STARTPTS` if it must stay aligned (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Steep rumble cut with asubcut
what: `asubcut` cuts below `cutoff` (2-200 Hz) with a selectable `order` (3-20, default 10), a steeper roll-off than `highpass`
how: `ffmpeg -i in.wav -af "asubcut=cutoff=80:order=20" out.wav` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Gentler high-pass with one pole
what: `highpass` rolls off 6 dB per pole per octave; default is 2 poles, `p=1` gives a gentler 6 dB/octave slope
how: `ffmpeg -i in.wav -af "highpass=f=100:p=1" out.wav` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Check and remove DC offset before noise reduction
what: Adobe says Noise Reduction works best on audio with no DC offset; `astats` reports `DC_offset`; a 20 Hz high-pass or `dynaudnorm=correctdc=1` removes it. A test with `dcshift=0.05` read 0.050022 and the high-passed version ran clean
how: `ffmpeg -i in.wav -af "astats=measure_perchannel=DC_offset:measure_overall=none" -f null -` then `highpass=f=20` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Single-tone buzz or many-harmonic buzz
what: RX suggests Spectral Repair Attenuate (vertical, 1024-4096 bands) for an occasional single-tone buzz and Spectral De-noise's tonal controls for buzz with harmonics up the spectrum
how: needs iZotope RX (missing); in ffmpeg notch a single tone with `bandreject=f=F:width_type=q:w=10`

name: Detect clipping with astats
what: `Peak_count` counts how often the signal hits its min/max level and `Flat_factor` measures flat runs at the peaks; our deliberately clipped test read Peak level 0.0003 dB, Flat factor 32.6, Peak count 32858
how: `ffmpeg -i in.wav -af "astats=measure_perchannel=Peak_count+Flat_factor+Peak_level:measure_overall=none" -f null -` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: adeclip threshold, histogram and method
what: `threshold` (default 10) and `hsize` (histogram size, default 1000): higher values make clip detection less aggressive; `method=save` keeps non-interpolated samples unchanged
how: `ffmpeg -i clip.wav -af "volume=-6dB,adeclip=t=5:n=1500:m=s" out.wav` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Save de-clipped audio as 32-bit float
what: de-clipping raises peaks above the old clip level; RX notes restored intervals above 0 dBFS survive if saved as 32-bit float. Our adeclip output written as `pcm_f32le` read a peak of +5.2 dBFS (a 16-bit file would clip it again)
how: `ffmpeg -i clip.wav -af adeclip -c:a pcm_f32le out.wav`, then lower gain later (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Set de-clip threshold just under the clip level, per side if needed
what: RX's histogram shows clipping as a line across the meter; set Threshold just below where peaks pile up, and unlink positive/negative thresholds for one-sided clipping (their example shears at -13 dB only on the positive side)
how: needs iZotope RX (missing); in ffmpeg read `Min_level`/`Max_level` from `astats` to see if clipping is one-sided

name: Hear only the esses the de-esser takes
what: `deesser` output mode `s=e` passes only the detected ess, `s=o` the de-essed signal, `s=i` the input
how: `ffmpeg -i in.wav -af "deesser=i=0.4:s=e" ess_only.wav` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Listen to adynamicequalizer's detector band
what: `mode=listen` outputs only the isolated detection signal, which helps place `dfrequency` on the harsh band before switching to `mode=cut`
how: `ffmpeg -i in.wav -af "adynamicequalizer=dfrequency=6500:mode=listen" det.wav` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Band de-essing with adynamicequalizer (6.1 syntax)
what: detector and target can sit on the same band; in 6.1 use `mode=cut:direction=downward`; `auto=on` picks the threshold from the detector
how: `adynamicequalizer=dfrequency=6500:dqfactor=2:tfrequency=6500:tqfactor=2:mode=cut:direction=downward:threshold=10:range=6` and `...:mode=cut:auto=on` (both ran here; not tuned on a real voice) (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Classic vs spectral de-ess
what: RX Classic mode attenuates sibilants with a broadband gain envelope; Spectral mode attenuates only the high frequencies where sibilance is active (a multiband compressor with dozens of bands); the Cutoff frequency is the lower boundary of detection; Fast speed fixes high-frequency pumping, Slow keeps transients
how: needs iZotope RX (missing); ffmpeg `deesser` and `adynamicequalizer` are the local options

name: ML dialogue de-reverb needs no learning pass
what: RX Dialogue De-reverb separates reverb from dialogue without learning a profile; Reduction sets the dB cut of the reverb part, higher Sensitivity removes more but adds artifacts, Ambience Preservation keeps background noise from being cut with the reverb
how: needs iZotope RX (missing); locally `clean_voice.py --dereverb`

name: One module that splits voice, reverb and noise
what: RX 11 Dialogue Isolate separates dialogue, noise and reverberation into three components with separate Voice/Reverb/Noise gain faders; lower Sensitivity keeps clarity but leaves more noise. Best/Offline quality is Advanced only
how: needs iZotope RX (missing)

name: Parallel EQ amount with `mix`
what: `equalizer` (and the other biquad filters) take `mix` 0-1 for how much filtered signal is used, a quick way to soften a move
how: `ffmpeg -i in.wav -af "equalizer=f=3000:t=q:w=1:g=6:m=0.5" out.wav` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Tilt a dull or bright voice with tiltshelf
what: `tiltshelf` boosts or cuts lows and does the opposite to highs around `f` (default 3000 Hz), like a hi-fi tone control
how: `ffmpeg -i in.wav -af "tiltshelf=g=-3:f=1500" out.wav` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Draw an EQ curve point by point
what: `firequalizer` interpolates between `entry(f,g)` points (the docs' custom example: 0 dB at 100 Hz, -4 at 400, -6 at 1000, 0 at 2000)
how: `firequalizer=gain_entry='entry(100,0); entry(400, -4); entry(1000, -6); entry(2000, 0)'` (ran here; output 10 ms late, see the FIR note) (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: EQ one mic of a two-mic file
what: `anequalizer` bands start with `cN` for the channel, so boom (c0) and lav (c1) in one stereo file can get different EQ
how: `ffmpeg -i twomic.wav -af "anequalizer=c1 f=4000 w=2000 g=4 t=1" out.wav` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Add missing highs with an exciter, sparingly
what: `aexciter` creates harmonics above `freq` (default 7500 Hz) instead of just boosting; Thunderbird Sound uses an exciter, sparingly, to give clean ADR the grit of a production lav
how: `ffmpeg -i in.wav -af "aexciter=amount=2:freq=6000" out.wav` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Same EQ plug-in on boom and lav
what: a film mixer keeps the same EQ type on boom and lavalier tracks because different EQ algorithms can shift phase differently between the tracks
how: in ffmpeg use the same filter (e.g. `equalizer`) on both channels

name: EQ-match at 10-40%, not 100%
what: RX EQ Match copies one selection's spectrum to another (lav to boom, location to ADR); a 100% match can sound unnatural, and 10-40% is often enough
how: needs iZotope RX (missing)

name: Proximity effect only on directional mics
what: bass rises as a directional (cardioid-family) mic gets close to the mouth; omni capsules do not show it, and the more directional the mic the stronger it is
how: if a close VO is boomy, check the mic pattern before EQ

name: Four EQ zones for matching ADR
what: Thunderbird Sound's map: 100-250 Hz tubby/boomy, 250-800 Hz boxy, 800 Hz-4 kHz clarity (too much = "telephone"), 4 kHz+ sparkle (studio ADR often has too much here); use gentle cuts where ADR differs from production
how: `equalizer=f=F:t=q:w=1:g=-2` per zone, A/B against the production line

name: Steeper filters to match production
what: to match production, Thunderbird Sound sometimes high-passes ADR as high as 200 Hz and low-passes it as low as 5 kHz
how: `highpass=f=200,lowpass=f=5000` as a starting experiment, by ear

name: Where to look for fill, in order
what: Idyll Sounds' priority: fill per shot crossfaded into the dialogue; near the moment; same clip; same location; room tone recorded per setup; other takes of the shot; other shots in the location; synthesized fill; library room tone (absolute last resort, mono)
how: pull pauses from the same clip first with `atrim`

name: Stitch small silences into one fill
what: collect tiny pauses (between lines, right after "action") and join them with tiny equal-power crossfades
how: `ffmpeg -i in.wav -i in.wav -i in.wav -filter_complex "[0]atrim=0.1:1.0,asetpts=PTS-STARTPTS[p];[1]atrim=17.0:18.2,asetpts=PTS-STARTPTS[q];[2]atrim=0.3:1.2,asetpts=PTS-STARTPTS[r];[p][q]acrossfade=d=0.02:c1=qsin:c2=qsin[pq];[pq][r]acrossfade=d=0.02:c1=qsin:c2=qsin" fill.wav` (2.96 s out) (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Make fill loopable: add a reversed copy
what: duplicate the stitched fill and reverse the duplicate; for plain broadband noise that is usually enough
how: `ffmpeg -i fill.wav -i fill.wav -filter_complex "[1]areverse[r];[0][r]acrossfade=d=0.05:c1=qsin:c2=qsin" loopfill.wav` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Make fill loopable: swap the halves
what: cut the fill in the middle into A and B, put B before A and crossfade the B-A joint, so the loop point is the original continuous middle
how: `ffmpeg -i fill.wav -i fill.wav -filter_complex "[0]atrim=0:0.8,asetpts=PTS-STARTPTS[A];[1]atrim=start=0.8,asetpts=PTS-STARTPTS[B];[B][A]acrossfade=d=0.03:c1=qsin:c2=qsin" loopfill.wav` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: acrossfade gotcha: feed the file twice, not through asplit
what: in ffmpeg 6.1.1 `[0]asplit[x][y]` followed by `[B][A]acrossfade` (later part first) produced a 0.023 s file instead of 1.57 s; the same graph with the file given as two `-i` inputs worked. Cutting in normal order (`[a][b]`) from one asplit worked
how: use `-i fill.wav -i fill.wav` whenever the second-in-time piece must play first (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: AIRFILL: room tone as a convolution impulse
what: a tiny sample of production room tone used as the impulse of a convolution reverb, fed with pink noise, gives perfectly steady (but sterile) fill; Idyll credits Douglas Murray
how: `ffmpeg -f lavfi -i "anoisesrc=c=pink:a=0.1:r=48000:d=6" -i tone.wav -filter_complex "[0][1]afir=dry=0:wet=1" airfill.wav`, then match its level to the real tone (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Name fill after the shot it came from
what: Idyll names fill like "5B-T3.Boom Fill A", adds a tag (AF, IZ, AM) when synthesized, and makes Fill B etc. for different moments; a fill can serve another take of the same setup if the background doesn't change
how: name scratch fills `scene-take-mic-fillA.wav` in the scratchpad

name: Don't slather fill over a scene
what: Brad Semenoff: fill eases transitions but too much makes the scene noisier; he prefers hand-built fill from bits between lines (natural movement) and uses RX Ambience Match only as a last resort or for M&E centre fill
how: fill only the holes and the clip heads/tails

name: Ambience Match: static vs complex, and it only adds
what: RX Ambience Match learns a noise floor and generates matching ambience; Static suits steady room tone/AC/fans, Complex generates moving ambience (new random result each render); it cannot reduce ambience already present (use Spectral De-noise for that)
how: needs iZotope RX Advanced (missing); locally use stitched fill or AIRFILL

name: Generated ambience is usually too loud
what: with Ambience Match's "Output Ambience Only" Idyll usually has to trim it down by about 2-4 dB, and adds handles for crossfades
how: after making AIRFILL, lower it with `volume=-3dB` and compare with the real pauses

name: Learn ambience without fades in the selection
what: iZotope warns against learning Ambience Match from audio containing fades (Pro Tools fade dither, worst at 16-bit, throws off the noise-floor detection)
how: take tone samples from unfaded source audio, before any `afade`

name: Record room tone with the dialogue chain untouched
what: same mic, polar pattern, distance, angle, input, gain, sample rate and room state; don't switch off a fan that ran during the take; about a minute gives far more choice
how: ask for a minute of quiet before moving any mic

name: Patch a gap without changing the runtime
what: overwrite the gap instead of inserting audio, so later words stay in sync; soften both boundaries with short fades
how: mute the gap and lay tone under it in place: `ffmpeg -i in.wav -i tone.wav -filter_complex "[0]volume=0:enable='between(t,5,5.6)'[m];[1]atrim=0:0.7,afade=t=in:d=0.05,afade=t=out:st=0.65:d=0.05,adelay=4950:all=1[f];[m][f]amix=inputs=2:normalize=0:duration=first" out.wav` (duration unchanged) (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: amix sums at full level only with normalize=0
what: `amix` scales inputs by default (`normalize` enabled); for laying fill under dialogue, the docs' example uses `normalize=0` with `weights`
how: `amix=inputs=2:duration=first:dropout_transition=0:weights="1 0.25":normalize=0` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Start the fill level at the surrounding background
what: begin with the room-tone level close to the background on both sides of the patch and lengthen fades only until the join disappears; no fade rescues tone that is brighter, louder or rhythmically different
how: read the pause level on both sides with `astats=measure_perchannel=RMS_level`, set the patch `volume` to match (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Re-check fills after compression and loudness
what: compression, limiting and loudness changes lift the background between phrases and can expose a loop or mismatch that seemed harmless
how: listen to and measure patched pauses again on the final render

name: Bridge two takes with different floors
what: for a modest difference, a little of the noisier take's room tone laid under the cleaner take at low level lets the two floors meet; a large mismatch needs a different editing decision
how: `amix=inputs=2:normalize=0:weights="1 0.3"` with the noisier take's tone

name: Fade a noisy background in and out with tone
what: when a recording's background noise would pop in with the first word, use clean room tone to fade the noise in before the line and out after it
how: `afade=t=in:d=0.5` on a tone clip placed before the line with `adelay`, mixed with `amix ... normalize=0`

name: Pull clip handles to find tone
what: handles are the extra recording before and after each clip; the picture editor should include them in the OMF/AAF so the dialogue editor can extend a clip edge into clean room tone
how: when a client sends an export, ask for handles; locally keep the full camera clip and `atrim` wider than the edit

name: Extend a loopable fill to any length
what: `aloop` repeats samples (`loop=-1` infinite, `size` max samples); trim the result to the gap
how: `ffmpeg -i loopfill.wav -af "aloop=loop=-1:size=2e6,atrim=0:6" fill6s.wav` (6.0 s out) (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Pull the background out to use as tone
what: iZotope's editor runs Dialogue Isolate the other way round (keep noise, remove dialogue) when she needs extra room tone. Locally, `audio-separator --single_stem Instrumental` keeps only the non-voice stem (45 s for our 18 s clip with MDX-Net Voc FT)
how: `/home/user/tools/venv/bin/audio-separator in.wav -m UVR-MDX-NET-Voc_FT.onnx --model_file_dir /home/user/tools/sep-models --single_stem Instrumental --output_format WAV --output_dir out/` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Build fill as a mono centre track
what: a film mixer describes fill tracks as mono ambience of the same location sent to the centre channel; they cover ADR noise jumps, smooth takes and are needed for the M&E
how: render fill as mono (`-ac 1`)

name: Room tone also matches recordings from different rooms
what: iZotope's example: lines recorded in two rooms sounded different; de-noising the odd line and laying the original room tone under it hid the change
how: `afftdn` on the odd line, then `amix ... normalize=0` with the scene's tone

name: Duplicating a short noise sample doesn't improve a profile
what: Audacity: Noise Reduction calculates noise statistics, so repeating the same short block adds nothing; it needs at least 2048 samples and longer is better
how: learn afftdn profiles from the longest clean pause you have

name: Duck one breath by its time range
what: many ffmpeg filters take a generic `enable` expression; `volume=0.3:enable='between(t,4.0,4.4)'` lowered just that 0.4 s by 10.4 dB (-18.5 -> -28.9 dB) and left the rest untouched
how: `ffmpeg -i in.wav -af "volume=0.3:enable='between(t,4.0,4.4)'" out.wav`; chain several for several breaths (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Breath ducking as one volume expression
what: with `eval=frame` the volume expression is evaluated per frame and can use `t`
how: `ffmpeg -i in.wav -af "volume='if(between(t,4,4.4),0.3,1)':eval=frame" out.wav` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Target mode beats fixed gain for breaths
what: RX Breath Control detects breaths by harmonic structure, not level; Gain mode cuts every breath by the same dB (quiet breaths can vanish, loud ones stay), Target mode only pulls breaths above a target level, which sounds more natural; "Output breaths only" checks detection
how: needs iZotope RX (missing); locally duck only the loud breaths by hand with `volume ... enable`

name: Replace an unwanted breath with room tone, not silence
what: for voice-over where the speaker is off camera, a breath can be cut and the hole filled with clean room tone instead of hard cuts out and in
how: the runtime-safe patch command in the fill section, with the breath's times (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Collect breaths and efforts to reuse
what: while first watching the film, Brad Semenoff notes scenes where he can "steal" breaths and efforts from production to use elsewhere
how: log good breaths (time + clip) during the first listen

name: speechnorm: four strengths from the docs
what: `speechnorm` expands/compresses each half-cycle toward a peak target; the docs list weak (`e=3:r=0.00001:l=1`), moderate (`e=6.25:r=0.00001:l=1`), strong (`e=12.5:r=0.0001:l=1`) and very strong (`e=25:r=0.0001:l=1`) presets
how: `ffmpeg -i in.wav -af "speechnorm=e=6.25:r=0.00001:l=1" out.wav` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: speechnorm with an RMS target
what: option `rms` (`m`, default 0 = off) sets the highest allowed RMS level instead of only the peak target

name: dynaudnorm without pumping up the noise
what: `threshold` (`t`) skips frames below a level so digital noise is not amplified; `framelen` (default 500 ms) and `gausssize` (default 31, odd) set how fast gain follows; smaller gausssize behaves more like a compressor
how: `ffmpeg -i in.wav -af "dynaudnorm=f=250:g=15:t=0.05:m=6" out.wav` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: dynaudnorm compress factor
what: `compress` (`s`, 0-30, default off) adds soft-knee thresholding; smaller values compress harder and values below 3.0 can distort audibly
how: `dynaudnorm=f=500:g=31:s=5` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: List every pause with times
what: `silencedetect` logs silence_start/end when the level stays below `noise` for at least `duration`; `mono=1` checks each channel separately (handy for two mics). On our clip at -40 dB / 0.1 s it found the pauses at 5.23-5.38, 6.53-6.79, 11.77-12.21 s
how: `ffmpeg -i in.wav -af "silencedetect=n=-40dB:d=0.1" -f null - 2>&1 | grep silence_` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: silenceremove: cap every pause at a set length
what: `silenceremove` with negative `stop_periods` works through the whole file, `stop_duration` is the pause length that triggers it and `stop_silence` keeps up to that much of each pause
how: `ffmpeg -i in.wav -af "silenceremove=stop_periods=-1:stop_duration=0.6:stop_threshold=-38dB:stop_silence=0.3" out.wav` (18.34 -> 17.67 s here) (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Trim the dead head of a take but keep a lead-in
what: `start_periods=1` trims leading silence; `start_silence` keeps up to that many seconds of it
how: `ffmpeg -i in.wav -af "silenceremove=start_periods=1:start_threshold=-50dB:start_silence=0.2" out.wav` (18.34 -> 16.23 s) (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: silenceremove timestamps: write vs copy
what: `timestamp=write` (default) rewrites timestamps; `timestamp=copy` leaves kept frames at their original times
how: `silenceremove=stop_periods=-1:stop_duration=0.5:stop_threshold=-50dB:timestamp=copy` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Retime by compressing or decompressing pauses
what: Inside the Edit's two core moves: if a character talks too slowly, shorten pauses between words and phrases; if too fast, add space so the meaning can breathe
how: get pause times from `silencedetect`, then cut with `atrim`+`acrossfade` or pad with fill

name: Keep a pause between sentences
what: Larry Jordan: there is a slight pause between the end of one sentence and the start of the next; when picture cuts make one clip's audio crash into the next, recreate that pause
how: `apad=pad_dur=0.3` on the first line, or fill

name: Cut mid-word on hard consonants
what: Podcast Engineering School: when an edit must fall inside a word (e.g. a restated word with odd inflection), cut on hard consonants like t, k, p
how: zoom with `showwavespic` on the word, cut at the consonant burst with `atrim` + 5-20 ms `acrossfade`

name: Cut on a later word or a syllable
what: it can be easier to cut on the 2nd or 3rd word of a sentence, or on a syllable, than on the first word; repeats spoken while laughing are nearly impossible to edit
how: try several cut points against the retake before settling

name: Cut after the breath, not before
what: a sound editor lists cutting after the breath instead of before it, and cutting on plosives or hard consonants, as useful filler-edit moves
how: place the out-point after the inhale so the next line keeps its breath

name: Break filler clusters and patterns, not every filler
what: remove clusters ("um, uh, you know"), shorten extended fillers to normal length (under one second), and remove enough of a speaker's signature filler that the pattern is no longer noticed
how: list fillers from the transcript, cut clusters first

name: Transcript-driven word cut in ffmpeg
what: cut out a phrase using Whisper word times (adjusted to the real pause from silencedetect) and join with a short equal-power crossfade
how: `ffmpeg -i sp.wav -filter_complex "[0]asplit[x][y];[x]atrim=0:6.53[a];[y]atrim=start=8.32,asetpts=PTS-STARTPTS[b];[a][b]acrossfade=d=0.02:c1=qsin:c2=qsin" out.wav` removed "one of the two small steamers" (18.34 -> 16.53 s) (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Salvage a take with one bad word
what: Apple's dialogue tips: if someone mumbles a single word, salvage the rest of the take instead of dropping the whole take
how: cut the replacement word with `atrim` and drop it in with short crossfades; check lip sync

name: Use alts sparingly and label them
what: Brad Semenoff replaces as little as possible with alternate takes, colour-labels the alt clip and keeps the original muted underneath
how: keep the replaced original as a separate muted file next to the edit

name: Text-based editing in Premiere
what: Premiere transcribes clips and cutting, copying or pasting text trims and moves the clips on the timeline; Find/Replace works in the transcript
how: needs Adobe Premiere (missing); locally edit from Whisper JSON as above

name: Descript's filler detection is English only
what: Descript detects "um", "uh", "you know" and similar fillers in the script so each can be removed or kept; the feature currently works on English transcripts only and uses AI credits on current plans
how: for Hindi/Urdu clips find fillers in the Whisper transcript instead

name: Get per-word times and confidence
what: `--word_timestamps True` adds `words` with start, end and probability to each JSON segment
how: `/home/user/tools/venv/bin/whisper in.wav --model small --language en --word_timestamps True --output_format json --fp16 False` (75 s for our 18 s clip on CPU) (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Whisper word times are approximate: snap cuts to real pauses
what: our first word was stamped 1.80 s while silencedetect showed speech starting at 2.30 s, and a word end at 6.42 s while the pause began at 6.53 s; Whisper discussion #435 notes timestamps tend to start before the word is spoken
how: take the cut times from `silencedetect` near each Whisper time (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Flag doubtful words by probability
what: word `probability` in the JSON marks weak recognitions; in our clip the place names scored 0.43-0.77 while ordinary words were mostly above 0.9
how: `[w for s in j['segments'] for w in s['words'] if w['probability']<0.8]` and check those by ear (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Find long gaps from word times
what: subtract each word's end from the next word's start to list pauses for tightening
how: `gaps=[(W[i]['word'],W[i+1]['word'],W[i+1]['start']-W[i]['end']) for i in range(len(W)-1)]` found 0.36-0.6 s gaps here (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Steer spellings with --initial_prompt
what: a prompt can steer Whisper toward particular spellings or style; with the prompt "A steamer on the Scottish loch." our transcript changed "lock" to "loch"
how: `whisper in.wav --model small --initial_prompt "Names: FireCraft, Lifesteal, ..."` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Prompt every window, at a cost
what: `--carry_initial_prompt True` prepends the initial prompt to every internal decode call; the help warns it may reduce the effectiveness of `condition_on_previous_text`
how: add it only when names keep slipping later in long files

name: Stop repetition loops
what: `--condition_on_previous_text False` stops feeding the previous text as a prompt; the help says the text may become inconsistent across windows but the model is less prone to failure loops
how: `whisper in.wav --condition_on_previous_text False ...`

name: Skip silence that triggers hallucinations
what: `--hallucination_silence_threshold N` (requires `--word_timestamps True`) skips silent periods longer than N seconds when a possible hallucination is detected
how: `whisper in.wav --word_timestamps True --hallucination_silence_threshold 1` (ran here) (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Expect invented text over non-speech
what: a study found about 1% of Whisper transcriptions contained entire hallucinated phrases; another found Whisper-large-v3 often turns non-speech into filler-like words, with 55.2% of non-speech audios transcribed as "so"
how: check transcript words that fall inside `silencedetect` pauses

name: Transcribe only part of a file
what: `--clip_timestamps start,end,...` processes just those ranges; 2-9 s of our clip took 16.6 s instead of 75 s for the whole file
how: `whisper in.wav --model small --clip_timestamps 2,9 --output_format txt` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: When Whisper treats a segment as silence
what: a segment counts as silence only if the no-speech probability is above `--no_speech_threshold` (0.6) AND decoding already failed `--logprob_threshold` (-1.0); failures also come from `--compression_ratio_threshold` (2.4) and trigger temperature fallback (+0.2)
how: tune these only after checking a problem file; defaults from the help

name: Pick the Whisper model by speed
what: six sizes; relative speed vs large on an A100: tiny ~10x, base ~7x, small ~4x, medium ~2x, turbo ~8x (an optimized large-v3); `.en` models do better for English, mostly at tiny/base; turbo is not trained for translation
how: our cache holds `small.pt` (~/.cache/whisper); pass `--model small` to avoid a big download

name: Separate the voice before transcribing over music
what: repo lesson: Whisper on a long song misses sung stretches; separate vocals first, transcribe with condition_on_previous_text False, and align script lines with an in-order DP, never greedy first-match
how: `clean_voice.py --fast` or audio-separator first; DP pattern in `library/templates/website-promo/dp_align.py`

name: Forced alignment for tighter word times
what: WhisperX refines Whisper timestamps with wav2vec2 forced alignment and adds VAD and pyannote diarization; words without characters in the alignment dictionary (e.g. "2014." or "£13.60") get no timing, and overlapping speech is handled poorly
how: needs WhisperX (missing, BSD-2)

name: Faster Whisper on CPU
what: faster-whisper (CTranslate2, MIT) is up to 4x faster than openai/whisper for the same accuracy with less memory, and supports 8-bit quantization on CPU
how: needs faster-whisper (missing)

name: Voice activity detection with Silero VAD
what: MIT-licensed, supports 8 kHz and 16 kHz, one 30+ ms chunk takes under 1 ms on one CPU thread, trained on over 6000 languages
how: needs silero-vad (missing; torch is already in the venv)

name: Choose the mic by tone, noise and echo
what: Frame.io's questions: which recording has the fuller, more realistic tone (not tinny, not muffled), which is less noisy (lavs may add clothing rustle), and which is less echoey; send all mics to the sound studio because another may be easier to improve
how: split dual-mono camera audio with `channelsplit` and A/B each mic

name: One mic per scene, swap only for a problem line
what: use the same mic for a whole scene, but swap in another recording for one line if the better mic has a hiccup there (e.g. a lav rustle)
how: keep the alternate mic aligned underneath so the swap is a simple cut

name: Grade each mic: good, usable, poor
what: April Tucker listens scene by scene: good (close, present, not too noisy), usable if necessary (minor placement/noise/correctable tech issue), poor (hard to understand, distant, very noisy, dropouts)
how: write the grade per mic in the edit notes before cutting

name: Boom or lavs: when lavs win
what: for two characters in a quiet scene a well-placed boom may be preferred; if they yell over each other, lavs give the mixer control to favour one line; a lav with constant cloth rubbing pushes you to the boom
how: decide per scene, not per line

name: Keep usable alts muted or on X tracks
what: Tucker leaves a good second mic muted on an active track or moves it to an "X" (alt) track so the mixer can find it; only completely unusable mics are deleted
how: keep alternate mic WAVs next to the edit, named `X-...`

name: Same mic choice for the same location
what: when a location returns across scenes shot at the same time, reuse the same mic choice so the mixer can reuse settings
how: note "location -> mic" in the project notes

name: Why two mics sound hollow together
what: sound travels about 34 cm per millisecond, so a distance difference becomes a time offset and summing gives comb-filter notches (hollow, thin); it is most obvious in a mono sum and vanishes when either track is soloed
how: always test the mono sum: `pan=mono|c0=0.5*c0+0.5*c1,volumedetect` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: The 3:1 mic rule
what: place the second mic at least three times further from the first than the first is from the source, so the level difference keeps cancellation inaudible; a film mixer avoids mixing two ADR mics that don't follow the 1:3 rule
how: when two mics must be blended, check the rule first

name: Flip polarity only for reversed signals
what: inverting polarity flips the whole waveform; it fixes reversed wiring and some close pairs but cannot fix a time offset, which needs a delay. Our test pair with one channel inverted summed to -91 dB (near total cancellation); after flipping it summed to -19.9 dB
how: `stereotools=phaser=1` (flip right) or `pan=stereo|c0=c0|c1=-1*c1`, then re-check the mono sum (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Measure the delay between two mics and line them up
what: delay between mic signals can be estimated with signal processing (e.g. cross-correlation, GCC-PHAT) and corrected with a compensating delay; estimation errors cause flanging. Our scipy cross-correlation found exactly the 72-sample (1.5 ms) offset we built in; `adelay` takes sample counts with `S`
how: `scipy.signal.correlate(b, a, mode='full', method='fft')`, argmax minus (n-1) = lag, then `adelay=72S|0` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Delay a mic by distance
what: `compensationdelay` delays by `mm`/`cm`/`m` at a given `temp` (default 20 °C); the docs note about 30 cm between mics puts one in antiphase. cm=51 gave a 71-sample (1.48 ms) shift here
how: `ffmpeg -i boom.wav -af "compensationdelay=cm=51" out.wav` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Log out-of-phase stretches automatically
what: `aphasemeter` with `phasing=1` logs mono and out-of-phase sequences (angle threshold default 170°) lasting at least `duration`; on our inverted pair it logged `out_phase_start: 2.28`
how: `ffmpeg -i pair.wav -af "aphasemeter=video=0:phasing=1:duration=1" -f null -` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Boom left, lav right, then look at phase
what: a mixer routes the lav and boom to a stereo bus (one left, one right) and checks them on a phase scope; a sudden dip in body or low mids usually means the two are slipped or out of phase, and nudging fixes tone without EQ
how: `join=inputs=2:channel_layout=stereo:map=0.0-FL|1.0-FR` then `aphasemeter` or `channelsplit,axcorrelate=size=1024:algo=fast` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Read correlation between channels
what: `axcorrelate` outputs normalized windowed cross-correlation: 1 = highly correlated, 0 = unrelated, -1 = out of phase (cancel). Our aligned pair averaged -1.0 dB (near 1); the inverted pair hit the -1 end
how: `ffmpeg -i pair.wav -af "channelsplit,axcorrelate=size=1024:algo=fast" corr.wav` then `astats` on corr.wav (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Split dual-mono camera audio into separate mics
what: `channelsplit` makes one stream per channel; `pan=mono|c0=c1` keeps only the right channel
how: `ffmpeg -i in.wav -filter_complex "channelsplit=channel_layout=stereo[L][R]" -map "[L]" boom.wav -map "[R]" lav.wav` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: High-pass the lav to reduce overlap
