what: Sonniss gives away yearly GDC bundles (2026: 7.47 GB+, 347+ files; 2024: 27.5 GB+): royalty-free, commercially usable, no attribution, unlimited projects for life, under Sonniss' own licence (not CC0)
how: fine for SFX in client videos; keep a copy of the licence page next to the files.

name: Avoid BBC Sound Effects for paid work
what: the 16,000 BBC sound effects are BBC copyright under the RemArc licence: personal, educational or research use, credit required; commercial use is not allowed
how: skip BBC files for the owner's promos and client edits.

name: Repo SFX licence
what: the 21 bundled SFX files in `.claude/skills/media-use/audio/assets/sfx/` are from Pixabay under the Pixabay Content License (free, commercial, no attribution required)
how: use them freely; their per-file durations and placement hints are in `manifest.json`.

name: media-use searches Openverse first
what: the repo's SFX engine searches Openverse per cue (CC0 and CC BY only, never NC/SA/ND), prefers clips up to 15 s and CC0 over CC BY when close, and falls back to the bundled library; anonymous use allows 20 searches a minute and 200 a day
how: name cues concretely (`glass shatter`, not `dramatic sound`); because the owner wants no-credit audio, keep only results whose `license` is `cc0`.

name: Free convolution IRs: Voxengo
what: Voxengo's free reverb impulses (44.1 kHz 16-bit WAV) may be used royalty-free for any purpose including commercial, but not sold or redistributed
how: download the zip, keep it in the scratchpad or `library/` (not shared publicly), use with `afir` (see #2120).

name: Free IRs under MIT: Conner's library
what: a public library of 738 impulse responses (~1 GB: rooms, gear, objects, instruments) under the MIT License
how: download a release zip from the linked repo; keep the MIT notice with it.

name: Name SFX files with UCS
what: the Universal Category System filename is `CatID_FXName_CreatorID_SourceID`, blocks separated by `_` (used only between blocks); CatID comes from the UCS list (e.g. `DOORWood`), keep its case; FXName ideally under 25 characters
how: name library files like `WHSH_Fast Pass_FC_FireCraft.wav` (CatID from the official list).

name: UCS is public domain and frozen at 8.2
what: UCS (82 categories, 753 subcategories per ucs-tools) is a public-domain initiative; 8.2 was announced as the final category update (8.2.1 minor update Jan 2024)
how: download the category list once and keep it beside `library/sfx/`.

name: Level SFX by loudness, not only peak
what: peak (dBFS) says whether a file can clip, and packs often normalize to about −1 dBFS; LUFS says how loud it sounds, and two files with the same peak can differ a lot; level mixed-source sounds to a common target, then balance categories
how: measure with `ffmpeg -i x.wav -af ebur128=peak=true -f null -` (tested here 2026-10-24: a synthesized whoosh read I −32.0 LUFS, peak −17.8 dBFS).

name: Keep a personal hit library
what: build a personal library of 10-15 whooshes, risers and impacts you like and reuse them; most editors work from a curated library and build custom hits only when nothing fits
how: keep favourites in `library/sfx/` with names by length and use (see #2016), listed in `library/README.md`.

name: Name presets by length, not vibe
what: save designed FX as "Riser 2bar", "Riser 4bar", "Downlifter", "Sub Drop", "Impact Boom"; mid-session "Riser 4bar dark" beats a fancy name
how: name the generated files the same way, e.g. `riser_4bar_72bpm.wav`.

name: Peak one frame after the picture
what: place an SFX so its peak lands one frame after its picture (light arrives before sound; early feels wrong sooner than late); most files peak after their start
how: read the hit time with `npx hyperframes audio <file> --json`, then set `data-start` = picture frame time + 1/30 s − peak offset.

name: Which sound for which picture event
what: repo table: click only on a real cursor click, whoosh on a scene cut or a large card moving fast, soft key tick for text arriving letter by letter, pop for a badge/chip/number landing, riser into impact once per film on the payoff
how: list every visible event in the storyboard and assign at most one of these.

name: No synthesized dings in HyperFrames films
what: the repo sound rules say "No synthesised tones, chimes or dings"; hits sit 3-6 dB over the bed, and a bed with most energy under 150 Hz plays as nothing on a phone
how: use library chimes/pings for UI moments; keep synthesized tones (this file's lavfi recipes) as layers or raw material, not as the visible "ding".

name: Rotate takes of repeated sounds
what: the same whoosh on every cut is the most common tell; rotate two or three takes
how: make variants with `ffmpeg -i hit.wav -af "asetrate=44100*1.06,aresample=44100" hit_b.wav` (±6 %; tested here 2026-10-24 for 0.94/1.0/1.06) or pick other library files.

name: SFX volume ~0.35 under voice and music
what: the media-use rule is SFX volume about 0.35, sitting under narration and BGM; a missing effect is skipped, never a render blocker
how: start `<audio data-volume="0.35">` for SFX, then adjust by measurement.

name: Air pass vs rush into a hit
what: an "air pass" (air moving past with nothing at the end) can be slid either side of the edit point; a "rush into a hit" puts the rush before the cut and the hit on the first frame after it
how: air pass for soft cuts; rush+hit for reveals: end the rush at the cut frame, start the impact clip on the next frame.

name: Rising swell = seconds of warning
what: a rising swell (noise climbing and thickening until it stops at the top) is for when the audience needs several seconds of warning that something is about to change; a 5-second swell can also fill dead air before anything happens
how: a 3-5 s noise riser (#2068) ending on the change; for an intro, start it at 0 s under the title.

name: Downward fall reads as an ending
what: a tone sliding down and gaining weight reads as an ending, where a rising sound reads as an arrival, so it is the natural close of a sequence
how: put a downlifter (#2073) or sub drop (#2074) under the last shot, not the first.

name: Short swish for small elements
what: a light quick brush of air is sized for small elements (a title card); a full rush on a title card sounds like far more than what moves
how: use 120-250 ms swishes (#2058) for titles and chips, long whooshes only for whole-frame moves.

name: Transitions set the pace
what: short swishes read as light and quick, a heavy fall reads as final; the chosen transitions tell the audience how fast the piece means to move
how: pick one transition family per video's pace and stay with it.

name: Off-screen arrival with sound alone
what: a rush ending on a dull hit implies something arriving from outside the frame; nothing has to be animated
how: lay a whoosh + soft impact over a static shot where an off-screen event is implied.

name: Match the whoosh to the move
what: a whoosh/swoosh fits a whip pan or fast-moving scenes better than a riser or slow-motion effect; keep transition SFX lower than BGM and dialogue, and don't overuse them
how: whoosh on whip pans and fast slides; risers only before reveals.

name: Match energy, loosely match style
what: a slow gentle text fade doesn't need an aggressive impact; bright energetic edits want sharper, more digital whooshes, moody cinematic edits deeper, more organic ones
how: choose whoosh brightness by the grade and pace, not by the subject.

name: Duck the bed under each big hit
what: sidechain or manually duck the music slightly under each major hit so whooshes/impacts read; keep it subtle: fast attack, 50-150 ms release, 3:1-6:1
how: `ffmpeg -i music.wav -i hit.wav -filter_complex "[0]aformat=channel_layouts=stereo[m];[1]aformat=channel_layouts=stereo,asplit[k][h];[m][k]sidechaincompress=threshold=0.05:ratio=4:attack=1:release=100[d];[d][h]amix=inputs=2:normalize=0" out.wav` (tested here 2026-10-24).

name: Music cut-off before a key line
what: trailers cut the music to leave a big auditory space before a quote (Cruella trailer at 0:20) and cut scenes to the beat so impacts work like a light switch
how: stop the bed (5 ms fade) one beat before the key line; put impacts on beat-aligned cuts.

name: Long tails carry into silence
what: before a switch to silence, long drawn-out tails carry the viewer forward and keep attention a little longer
how: let the last impact's reverb tail (#2120) run 1-3 s into the silent section instead of cutting it.

name: Place many cues in one ffmpeg call
what: delay each SFX to its time and mix without normalization, padded to the video length
how: `ffmpeg -i vid.mp4 -i whoosh.wav -i pop.wav -i hit.wav -filter_complex "[1]adelay=400:all=1[a];[2]adelay=1200:all=1[b];[3]adelay=2000:all=1[c];[a][b][c]amix=inputs=3:normalize=0,apad=whole_dur=3[s]" -map 0:v -map "[s]" -c:v copy -c:a aac -shortest out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24).

name: Verify cue positions with silencedetect
what: silence ends mark where each cue begins
how: `ffmpeg -i out.mp4 -af "silencedetect=n=-45dB:d=0.1" -f null - 2>&1 | grep silence_` (tested here 2026-10-24: cues placed at 0.4/1.2/2.0 s reported silence_end 0.46, 1.20, 2.03 s — the whoosh file's own lead-in shows as +0.06 s).

name: Verify cue positions with librosa onsets
what: `librosa.onset.onset_detect(..., units='time')` lists hit times of a mix
how: extract audio (`ffmpeg -i out.mp4 -vn out.wav`), then in `/home/user/tools/venv/bin/python`: `librosa.onset.onset_detect(y=y, sr=sr, units='time')` (tested here 2026-10-24: found 0.51, 1.21, 2.07 s for cues at 0.4/1.2/2.0 s).  [librosa 1.0.0 docstring in /home/user/tools/venv: `units : {'frames', 'samples', 'time'}`]

name: Find picture cuts to hang whooshes on
what: `scdet` writes scene-change times as metadata
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf "scdet=threshold=10,metadata=print:file=scdet.txt" -f null -`, then read `lavfi.scd.time` lines (tested here 2026-10-24 on a 2-clip join: 1 cut found) and place whooshes per #2021.

name: Four layers: sub, body, detail, tail
what: sub = low weight you feel (0.5-2 s), body = midrange that says what it is (0.5-2 s), detail = high-frequency specifics (short, inside the body), tail = room/distance (1-4 s); a single library file disappoints because it tries to do all four
how: build hero impacts from four files on separate tracks/lanes.

name: Balance order for a layer stack
what: set the body first as anchor, bring the sub in under it, add detail lower so it flavours, let the tail run past the others, roll off lows of detail/body if the sub carries the bottom; mute layers one at a time to hear each one's job
how: in HyperFrames use separate `data-track-index` lanes per layer and adjust `data-volume`.

name: Align transients, let detail arrive a hair late
what: align layer transients to the same frame so they read as one event; the tail can extend and a detail layer can arrive slightly late for texture
how: same `data-start` for all layers; detail +5-20 ms if wanted.

name: Impact timing map
what: transient 0-10 ms (mostly high frequencies), body 10-100 ms (mid frequencies, material character), sub below 80 Hz concurrent with the body, tail 100 ms+; a body delayed 20-30 ms feels "explosive"
how: for an explosive variant, `adelay=25:all=1` the body layer before mixing.

name: Filter each impact layer to its band
what: high-pass the transient layer at 2 kHz (maybe 4 kHz), low-pass the sub at 60-80 Hz (rumble above 120 Hz fights the body), band-pass the body roughly 150 Hz-2 kHz, and notch body energy at 200 Hz 6-12 dB if it masks the sub
how: body: `ffmpeg -i hit.wav -af "highpass=f=150,lowpass=f=2000,equalizer=f=200:t=q:w=4:g=-9" body.wav` (tested here 2026-10-24).

name: Split one hit into bands with acrossover
what: `acrossover` splits audio into bands that sum back flat
how: `ffmpeg -i hit.wav -filter_complex "acrossover=split=150 2500:order=4th[l][m][h]" -map "[l]" low.wav -map "[m]" mid.wav -map "[h]" high.wav` (tested here 2026-10-24); per-band output gain is option `gain` in local ffmpeg 6.1 (`gain=1.5 1 0.5`, tested), named `gains` in the current docs.

name: Synthesized click transient
what: a sine with instant attack and 2 ms decay at 4 kHz makes a clean click to shape a transient layer
how: `ffmpeg -f lavfi -i "aevalsrc='sin(2*PI*4000*t)*exp(-t/0.002)':d=0.02:s=44100" click4k.wav` (tested here 2026-10-24).

name: Stagger several transients
what: soft click at 0, harder crack 2-3 ms later, a wide panned transient pair ~5 ms later for complexity without losing definition
how: `[crack]adelay=2.5:all=1`, `[pair]adelay=5|6` then mix with `amix=normalize=0` (tested here 2026-10-24).

name: Sub layer: sine, phase-aligned, checked in mono
what: use a sine or triangle for sub layers (saw/square harmonics invade the body); at 50 Hz a 5 ms offset is a 90° shift, so align zero-crossings and check in mono; tune the sub to the key, or below 30 Hz where pitch perception is minimal
how: mono check `pan=mono|c0=0.5*c0+0.5*c1` (tested here 2026-10-24).

name: Sub pitch envelope: an octave in 50 ms
what: a quick one-octave drop over 50 ms then sustain emphasizes the impact; an exponential drop sounds more natural than linear; starting high and dropping adds weight, starting low and rising adds urgency
how: `ffmpeg -f lavfi -i "aevalsrc='0.9*sin(2*PI*(45*t+90*0.05/log(2)*(1-pow(2,-t/0.05))))*exp(-t*2.5)':d=1.5:s=44100" -af lowpass=f=80 sub.wav` (tested here 2026-10-24; measured 59→45 Hz).

name: Reverb per layer, none on the sub
what: tight room 0.3-0.8 s on the body, long hall 2-5 s on mids/highs only, no reverb on the sub (it builds up and muddies later hits); reverb pre-delay 20-80 ms keeps the attack, 100 ms+ suggests distance
how: convolve only the body/high layers with a synthetic IR (#2120) and leave the sub dry.

name: Whoosh = moving filter on noise
section: Whooshes, risers, downlifters and sub drops
what: start with white or pink noise and sweep a band-pass or low-pass quickly up and back down (or just up); the filter movement, not the noise, makes the whoosh
how: `ffmpeg -f lavfi -i "anoisesrc=d=0.8:c=pink:r=44100:a=0.5" -af "asendcmd=c='0.0-0.8 [expr] bandpass f 300+3500*sin(PI*TI)',bandpass=f=300:w=1.2:t=o,afade=t=in:d=0.4:curve=qsin,afade=t=out:st=0.4:d=0.4:curve=qsin" whoosh.wav` (tested here 2026-10-24; measured centroid 2.9→5.5→3.3 kHz).

name: asendcmd [expr] sweeps a filter per frame
section: Whooshes, risers, downlifters and sub drops
what: inside an `asendcmd` interval, the `[expr]` flag evaluates the argument with `TI` (0→1 across the interval), so any filter with a `frequency` command can be swept
how: `asendcmd=c='0.0-0.6 [expr] lowpass f 200+6000*sin(PI*TI)',lowpass=f=200` (tested here 2026-10-24); avoid commas inside the expression (use `exp(log(a)*TI)` instead of `pow(a,TI)`; a `\,` escape failed here).

name: Neutral cinematic whoosh recipe
section: Whooshes, risers, downlifters and sub drops
what: pink noise → HPF 30-50 Hz 24 dB/oct → band-pass sweep 300 Hz→5 kHz, Q 0.8-1.5 → envelope 120 ms attack, 15 ms hold, 420 ms release → light saturation (the source also adds 4 Hz random AM at 10 % and a 0.3-0.8 s room at 5-15 %, not done here)
how: `ffmpeg -f lavfi -i "anoisesrc=d=0.6:c=pink:r=44100:a=0.6" -af "highpass=f=40,highpass=f=40,asendcmd=c='0.0-0.555 [expr] bandpass f 300*exp(log(5000/300)*TI)',bandpass=f=300:t=q:w=1.2,volume='if(lt(t,0.12),t/0.12,if(lt(t,0.135),1,max(0,1-(t-0.135)/0.42)))':eval=frame,asoftclip=type=tanh" whoosh.wav` (tested here 2026-10-24; centroid rose 1.8→5.8 kHz).

name: Whoosh envelope ranges
section: Whooshes, risers, downlifters and sub drops
what: length 300 ms-1.5 s (UI shorter, cinematic longer), attack 50-300 ms, peak hold 0-60 ms, release 150-900 ms; add 1-3 dB slow random level variation (2-8 Hz) so it isn't flat
how: set these in the `volume=...:eval=frame` envelope of #2054.

name: Noise colour for whooshes
section: Whooshes, risers, downlifters and sub drops
what: white = equal power per Hz, bright/hissy (sci-fi, fast); pink = ~1/f, fuller, more wind-like; brown = low-heavy, can get boomy, high-pass it
how: `anoisesrc` colours `white|pink|brown|blue|violet|velvet` (tested here 2026-10-24 for white/pink/brown/velvet).

name: Filter ranges for whoosh sweeps
section: Whooshes, risers, downlifters and sub drops
what: band-pass centre ~200 Hz→6 kHz for broad cinematic whooshes; Q 0.5-2 for natural wind, 2-8 for stylized "laser-swish"; high shelf +2 to +8 dB above 4-8 kHz on approach, down on exit
how: in #2052 set `t=q:w=1` (natural) or `w=5` (stylized).

name: UI swipe whoosh for phones
section: Whooshes, risers, downlifters and sub drops
what: 120-250 ms swish: white noise → steep band-pass 1-6 kHz → fast envelope; keep energy in 1.5-5 kHz where small speakers reproduce, no sub
how: `ffmpeg -f lavfi -i "anoisesrc=d=0.2:c=white:r=44100:a=0.6" -af "highpass=f=1000,highpass=f=1000,lowpass=f=6000,lowpass=f=6000,volume='sin(PI*t/0.2)':eval=frame" swipe.wav` (tested here 2026-10-24).

name: High-pass whooshes at 30-50 Hz
section: Whooshes, risers, downlifters and sub drops
what: a whoosh rarely needs energy below 40-60 Hz unless it is a deliberate "sub swoop"; start with a 24 dB/oct HPF at 30-50 Hz; uncontrolled sub steals headroom and triggers limiters
how: `highpass=f=40,highpass=f=40` (two 2-pole stages; each is 12 dB/oct per the docs' 6 dB per pole) (tested here 2026-10-24).

name: Doppler matters on tones, not on noise
section: Whooshes, risers, downlifters and sub drops
what: real pass-by Doppler is noticeable on tonal parts (engines, whistles), not purely broadband noise; for noise whooshes the motion cues are level envelope, spectral tilt and inter-channel cues
how: add a tonal layer if you want audible Doppler (#2188); otherwise sweep filters and pan.

name: Bounded randomness for whoosh variants
section: Whooshes, risers, downlifters and sub drops
what: randomize sweep time ±15 %, end frequency within 4-7 kHz, modulation depth 8-14 % to get variants that still match
how: loop #2054 with `d` and the end frequency drawn per variant in a shell/Python loop.

name: Big trailer whoosh in three layers
section: Whooshes, risers, downlifters and sub drops
what: 1.2 s: air (pink noise band-pass 250 Hz→4.5 kHz, mild saturation), body (noise through a "large metal tube" IR, HPF 60 Hz, LPF 6-8 kHz), edge (white noise burst high-passed at 2 kHz, 150-250 ms, near the peak)
how: build the air layer with #2054, the body with `afir` + an IR (#2120), the edge with a short `anoisesrc` + `highpass=f=2000`.

name: Two band-passes in parallel for a swish
section: Whooshes, risers, downlifters and sub drops
what: a short swish: noise into two parallel band-pass filters with different Q, both driven by the amplitude envelope with different ranges, plus a low-pass after
how: `... asplit[a][b];[a]asendcmd=c='0.0-0.4 [expr] bandpass f 800+3000*sin(PI*TI)',bandpass=f=800:t=q:w=0.8[x];[b]asendcmd=c='0.0-0.4 [expr] bandpass f 1500+5000*sin(PI*TI)',bandpass=f=1500:t=q:w=4[y];[x][y]amix=inputs=2:normalize=0,lowpass=f=9000` (tested here 2026-10-24).

name: Flanger for a "magic" whoosh
section: Whooshes, risers, downlifters and sub drops
what: a flanger emphasizes movement in stylized whooshes (try different LFO rates)
how: `ffmpeg -i whoosh.wav -af "flanger=delay=3:depth=6:speed=2:regen=40" magic.wav` (tested here 2026-10-24).

name: Whoosh sources beyond noise
section: Whooshes, risers, downlifters and sub drops
what: base whooshes on ambience recordings (character), cymbals (bright swells that exaggerate the peak), synthesized noise, and reversed cymbals; layer several and sync their peaks
how: reverse a CC0 cymbal with `areverse` and stack it under a noise whoosh with matched peak.

name: Layered volume automation shapes a whoosh
section: Whooshes, risers, downlifters and sub drops
what: sculpt fades at start and end; layering several volume automations gives precise control of rise and tail; subtle pitch rises raise tension, drops release it
how: multiply two `volume=...:eval=frame` envelopes in series.

name: Four-layer whoosh with Doppler moves
section: Whooshes, risers, downlifters and sub drops
what: automate volume, panning and pitch to emulate Doppler, layer a sub oscillator, a reversed crash cymbal and a reversed snare
how: pitch/pan moves per #2188, sub from #2050, reversed hits with `areverse`.

name: Noise riser: high-pass sweep 200 Hz→8 kHz
section: Whooshes, risers, downlifters and sub drops
what: white noise, highpass swept from ~200 Hz to 8 kHz, long amp attack; match length to the music: 2 bars at 128 BPM ≈ 3.75 s, 4 bars 7.5 s
how: `ffmpeg -f lavfi -i "anoisesrc=d=3.75:c=white:r=44100:a=0.5" -af "asendcmd=c='0.0-3.75 [expr] highpass f 200*exp(log(40)*TI)',highpass=f=200,volume='pow(t/3.75,2)':eval=frame,highpass=f=180,afade=t=out:st=3.745:d=0.005" riser.wav` (tested here 2026-10-24).

name: Tonal riser: saw climbing an octave
section: Whooshes, risers, downlifters and sub drops
what: slide a saw under the noise with a pitch envelope climbing one octave over the same duration; a tonal riser pulls harder than plain noise
how: `ffmpeg -f lavfi -i "aevalsrc='0.3*(2*mod(110*3.75/log(2)*(pow(2,t/3.75)-1),1)-1)*pow(t/3.75,2)':d=3.75:s=44100" -af highpass=f=180 saw_riser.wav` (tested here 2026-10-24; 110→220 Hz exponential).

name: Exponential pitch curves sound less stock
section: Whooshes, risers, downlifters and sub drops
what: most of the riser's pitch movement belongs in the final bar (lazy start, steep finish); for downlifters fall fast first then a long lazy tail; symmetric curves sound like stock sounds
how: use `exp()`/`pow()` pitch laws in `aevalsrc` (as in #2069) instead of linear chirps.

name: Riser gets wetter as it climbs
section: Whooshes, risers, downlifters and sub drops
what: automate the reverb mix upward during the riser; a sound getting wetter signals "something is coming" even quietly
how: mix dry riser with an `afir` wet copy whose `volume` rises with `t` (`volume='t/3.75':eval=frame` on the wet branch).

name: High-pass risers at 150-200 Hz
section: Whooshes, risers, downlifters and sub drops
what: riser low end argues with the bassline for no benefit; high-pass around 150-200 Hz, give a light sidechain to the kick, and keep them quieter than instinct says (if the listener notices the riser as its own sound, it is too loud)
how: end every riser chain with `highpass=f=180`.

name: Downlifter = riser reversed
section: Whooshes, risers, downlifters and sub drops
what: white noise, filter sweeping down, pitch sinking, reverb drying up; keep downlifters 6-10 dB below risers
how: `ffmpeg -i riser.wav -af "areverse,volume=-8dB" downlifter.wav` (areverse tested here 2026-10-24).

name: Sub drop recipe
section: Whooshes, risers, downlifters and sub drops
what: one sine, no filter, pitch diving 1-2 octaves over 1-2 s, fired on the downbeat, starting around G1-C2; audition in mono and on small speakers and stop the fall around 35-40 Hz (below 30 Hz nobody hears it)
how: `ffmpeg -f lavfi -i "aevalsrc='0.8*sin(2*PI*65.4*1.5/log(65.4/37)*(1-exp(-t*log(65.4/37)/1.5)))*min(1,(1.5-t)/0.3)':d=1.5:s=44100" -af "afade=t=in:d=0.005" subdrop.wav` (tested here 2026-10-24; measured 63→39 Hz).

name: Impact boom = oversized kick
section: Whooshes, risers, downlifters and sub drops
what: low boom: a sine with a quick pitch envelope dropping an octave in 100-200 ms; add a white-noise burst with fast decay and generous reverb; a third textured layer is easier to take from a recording
how: boom `aevalsrc='0.9*sin(2*PI*(55*t+55*0.15/log(2)*(1-pow(2,-t/0.15))))*exp(-t*3)':d=1.2` (measured 90→55 Hz), splash `anoisesrc=d=1:c=white:a=0.7,volume='exp(-t*12)':eval=frame` into `afir` with a synthetic IR, then `amix=weights='1 0.5':normalize=0,alimiter=limit=0.89:level=0` (all tested here 2026-10-24).

name: Riser over 1-4 s into a reveal
section: Whooshes, risers, downlifters and sub drops
what: an oscillator sweeping up in pitch over 1-4 s, often with rising volume and some noise, builds anticipation before a reveal or drop
how: `ffmpeg -f lavfi -i "aevalsrc='0.5*sin(2*PI*(200*t+300*t*t))*pow(t/3,2)':d=3:s=44100" -af "afade=t=out:st=2.995:d=0.005" riser.wav` (tested here 2026-10-24; measured 390→1860 Hz).

name: Riser into the drop, not the bundled file blindly
section: Whooshes, risers, downlifters and sub drops
what: the bundled `riser.mp3` is 10.03 s and its manifest says trigger at climax − 10.03 s, but CLAUDE.md measured its crest at 3.47 s and silence after 4.5 s
how: trust the measurement: `data-media-start` so 3.47 s lands on the hit.

name: Trailer sub boom = hit through a low-pass
section: Whooshes, risers, downlifters and sub drops
what: sub booms contain only sub frequencies (60 Hz down to 20 Hz and below, felt more than heard); make one by putting a huge hit through a low-pass; use sparingly (act one, stop-downs, the end)
how: `ffmpeg -i hit.wav -af "lowpass=f=60,lowpass=f=60,volume=6dB" subboom.wav` (tested here 2026-10-24).

name: Distant hit: taiko + 500 Hz cut + 8 s plate
section: Whooshes, risers, downlifters and sub drops
what: a distant hit keeps more highs than a sub boom; one recipe: taiko roll, high-cut everything above 500 Hz, into an 8-second plate reverb; use it to introduce a new section, not the biggest change
how: `ffmpeg -i hit.wav -i ir8s.wav -filter_complex "[0]lowpass=f=500,lowpass=f=500,apad=pad_dur=8[d];[d][1]afir" distant.wav` with an 8 s synthetic IR (#2120) (tested here 2026-10-24).

name: Swish hit = reverse tail into the hit
section: Whooshes, risers, downlifters and sub drops
what: a swish hit is a large hit with a rise before it; the "swish" just has to be a reverse tail into the attack (a reversed drum or synth works)
how: `ffmpeg -i hit.wav -af "areverse,afade=t=in:d=0.5" pre.wav` then `ffmpeg -i pre.wav -i hit.wav -filter_complex "[0][1]concat=n=2:v=0:a=1" swishhit.wav` (tested here 2026-10-24).

name: Pre-impact element 100-500 ms
section: Whooshes, risers, downlifters and sub drops
what: a reversed part of the impact, a rising sweep or a building noise before the hit creates anticipation; 100-500 ms usually works
how: trim the reversed pre-hit of #2080 to 0.1-0.5 s with `atrim`.

name: Impact variations at five intensities
section: Whooshes, risers, downlifters and sub drops
what: make full, medium (less sub/body, shorter tail), light (transient-focused), sub-only and transient-only versions so not every moment gets maximum force
how: export layer subsets from the same stack (#2041) as separate files.

name: Parallel compression on the impact stack
section: Whooshes, risers, downlifters and sub drops
what: copy the mixed impact through heavy compression (10:1, fast attack/release), blend under the original; limit the final at about −1 dB
how: `ffmpeg -i impact.wav -filter_complex "asplit[a][b];[b]acompressor=threshold=-30dB:ratio=10:attack=1:release=50:makeup=6[c];[a][c]amix=inputs=2:weights='1 0.35':normalize=0,alimiter=limit=0.89:level=0" out.wav` (tested here 2026-10-24).

name: Don't fast-compress transient layers
section: Whooshes, risers, downlifters and sub drops
what: fast-attack compression clamps the initial peak and reduces impact; use slow attack 30-100 ms or parallel compression
how: `acompressor=attack=50` on transient layers.

name: Think in four slots: frequency, sustain, tail, transient
section: Whooshes, risers, downlifters and sub drops
what: trailer designer advice: think in those four layers and don't stack too many in the same slot or the sound gets muddy; max out the layers, clean unneeded frequencies and make space between elements with sidechain ducking
how: one file per slot, EQ each, duck the bed under the stack (#2034).

name: Build impacts bottom to top
section: Whooshes, risers, downlifters and sub drops
what: start with a kick or taiko, cut its highs, add metal or orchestral percussion for highs, EQ every layer individually; the Ableton example uses distorted kick, high percussion, processed cymbal, sub and an atmosphere
how: `lowpass=f=200` the kick layer, `highpass=f=2000` the metal layer, mix.

name: Distort, then EQ and compress
section: Whooshes, risers, downlifters and sub drops
what: distortion is effective on cinematic sounds but adds many overtones, so EQ and compress after it; compress elements and limit the final sound
how: `asoftclip=type=tanh,equalizer=...,acompressor,alimiter` in that order.

name: Braaam starting point
section: Whooshes, risers, downlifters and sub drops
what: the braaam is a low-register brass sound (popular since the Inception trailers); record a long loud low note around C1-C2 and stack octaves (C0, C1, C2)
how: needs a brass sample library (missing; see Missing tools); with a CC0 brass note, stack octaves with `asetrate` copies at 0.5x and 2x.

name: Bass drop as transition
section: Whooshes, risers, downlifters and sub drops
what: the trailer "bass drop/bass bend" (from dubstep and drum'n'bass) transitions from something big to weighty dialogue, like an old record scratch
how: sub drop (#2074) under the last frame of the action, dialogue after.

name: Phase-check layered impacts
section: Whooshes, risers, downlifters and sub drops
what: when stacking two or three impact samples, align the transients so they trigger together and don't cancel each other's frequencies
how: zoom the waveform (`showwavespic`, #2234) and nudge with `adelay` in ms.

name: Mids first, then lows, then highs
section: Whooshes, risers, downlifters and sub drops
what: start with a mid-range sound as the primary, stack a low sound for weight, sprinkle a high-frequency sound for clarity
how: pick the body file first, then add sub and detail.

name: Fix clashing layers by cutting the other layer
section: Whooshes, risers, downlifters and sub drops
what: solo each layer to find its dominant range; if two layers both peak at the same frequency, cut that frequency on the other by 2-3 dB
how: `equalizer=f=400:t=q:w=2:g=-3` on the layer that should yield.

name: Steep crossover between layers
section: Whooshes, risers, downlifters and sub drops
what: split layers by band (example kick: sub low-passed ~100 Hz, body 100-400 Hz, click high-passed ~2 kHz) and cut steeply: 24 dB/oct makes a real handoff, 6 dB/oct leaves both in the crossover region
how: `acrossover=split=100 400 2000:order=4th` (24 dB/oct per the docs).

name: Compare with references, rest your ears
section: Whooshes, risers, downlifters and sub drops
what: imitate the shape of reference sounds you like, and re-listen to yesterday's work after a long break because you get used to wrong sounds
how: keep a reference clip next to the edit and A/B at matched loudness (#2018).

name: Mouth pop: 380 Hz sine sliding up 12 semitones in 70 ms
what: Notify Sound's "Mouth Pop" is a 380 Hz sine with a +12 semitone slide over 0.07 s; a negative slide gives a falling plop (Cork Pop body at 420 Hz); most of a pop happens in the first few hundredths of a second
how: `ffmpeg -f lavfi -i "aevalsrc='0.8*sin(2*PI*380*0.07/log(2)*(pow(2,t/0.07)-1))*exp(-t*50)':d=0.09:s=44100" -af "afade=t=in:d=0.001,afade=t=out:st=0.085:d=0.005" pop.wav` (tested here 2026-10-24; measured 409→855 Hz).

name: Sharp vs round pop = attack time
what: Balloon Pop: white noise, attack 0.0005 s (a wide crack); Pop Up: triangle wave, attack 0.003 s (rounded front edge)
how: set the `afade=t=in:d=` to 0.0005 for sharp, 0.003 for round.

name: Cork pop needs its airy tail
what: the tail is the escaping pressure; without it the pop reads as a click
how: don't trim the tail of cork/bubble pops; trim it on UI pops.

name: Pop = fast attack, short tail
what: a pop is short and bright with a fast attack and little sustain; the transient says "something happened", then the tail should get out of the way, or it stops acting as punctuation
how: `afade=t=out` the last 20-30 ms of pops longer than 0.3 s.

name: Sticker and emoji pops
what: Pop Up and Mouth Pop mark a word, sticker or emoji landing in a motion-graphics video; Bubble Up marks a panel opening, Bubble Down closing
how: pop on chip/badge landings (see #2022); pair rising pops with opens, falling with closes.

name: When not to use UI sound
what: sound is usually unsuitable for frequently performed actions, users who asked for no interruptions, and UIs needing privacy; silence gives other elements focus
how: in app-demo videos, sound only the key actions, not every tap.

name: Sound only as a supplement
what: users may be in noisy places, have sound off, hearing loss, or no speakers, so sound must supplement visuals, never carry the only signal
how: every SFX'd event in a video also has a visual change (pairs with the sound-off test).

name: Urgency sets duration, volume, character
what: a sound's duration, volume and character should follow the event's urgency; avoid sounds that annoy after repetition; keep them distinct and succinct
how: short soft cues for info, longer brighter cues only for alerts in a demo.

name: Custom notification sound for identity
what: a default notification sound says nothing about where it comes from; a custom one identifies the app
how: for a brand promo (e.g. FireCraft), reuse one signature ping across videos.

name: Camera shutter from scissors
what: Pixel's shutter sound is based on a recording of scissors opening and closing, not a camera
how: record or find a CC0 scissors snip for a phone-camera moment.

name: Match the shutter to the camera
what: phone capture: short polite click; DSLR: firmer click with mirror slap; film camera: gears and a winding stop; close-ups punchy and direct, distant ones softer
how: pick the shutter sample by the camera in shot.

name: Mechanical motion-graphics layer template
what: tracks for clicks/stops, motors/servos, gears/ticks, air/whooshes, impacts/weight, sweeteners and a shared reverb return keep revisions easy
how: map them to fixed `data-track-index` lanes in HyperFrames.

name: Noise click (tested command only)
what: a 30 ms decaying noise burst
how: `ffmpeg -f lavfi -i "aevalsrc='(random(0)*2-1)*exp(-t*800)':d=0.03:s=44100" click.wav` (tested here 2026-10-24; no claim about how it sounds).

name: Beep every second from `sine`
what: `sine` with `beep_factor` adds a periodic beep every second at b times the carrier (doc example `sine=220:4:d=5`)
how: `ffmpeg -f lavfi -i "sine=f=600:b=2:d=4:r=44100" beeps.wav` (tested here 2026-10-24); note the repo rule against synthesized dings in films (#2023).

name: Robot announcer placeholder with flite
what: ffmpeg's `flite` source speaks text (voices include `kal` and `slt`; output 16 kHz here)
how: `ffmpeg -f lavfi -i "flite=text='Season two starts now':voice=kal" -af aresample=44100 vo_temp.wav` (tested here 2026-10-24); only for timing drafts — real voice per CLAUDE.md voice rules.

name: Beds vs specifics
what: beds are groups of layered sounds that set the base (room tone, wind, crickets, traffic washes) and can carry the scene's emotion; specifics are distinct to the location (vehicles); establish backgrounds at the top of every scene and never let them overpower intimate moments
how: one bed lane for the whole scene + specifics placed on visible/plausible events.

name: Two to four ambience layers per scene
what: build at least two to four layers, match one quiet layer to the original dialogue's tone, place specific sounds in the gaps between lines, balance with level, EQ, panning and reverb
how: e.g. room tone + distant city + one specific (car horn) between lines.

name: Ambience must not pump between edits
what: ambience should run smoothly under the scene without pumping in and out between dialogue edits; it is the steady bed that hides cuts
how: run the bed as one continuous clip across all dialogue cuts of a scene.

name: Pink for water, brown for rumble
what: white noise contains all frequencies and suits subtractive sculpting; pink is more natural and good for water sounds; brown generates low frequencies, ideal for rumble and room tones
how: `anoisesrc=c=white|pink|brown` (tested here 2026-10-24).

name: Synthetic stereo room tone
what: room tone is often just filtered noise: noise into two EQ filters at slightly different frequencies around 300 Hz gives a small stereo effect
how: `ffmpeg -f lavfi -i "anoisesrc=d=5:c=brown:a=0.3:seed=1" -f lavfi -i "anoisesrc=d=5:c=brown:a=0.3:seed=2" -filter_complex "[0]bandpass=f=290:w=1:t=o[l];[1]bandpass=f=310:w=1:t=o[r];[l][r]join=inputs=2:channel_layout=stereo" roomtone.wav` (tested here 2026-10-24).

name: Fan / ventilation from noise + LFO
what: noise low-passed around 110 Hz for rumble, an LFO on its amplitude for rotation
how: `ffmpeg -f lavfi -i "anoisesrc=d=4:c=white:a=0.6" -af "lowpass=f=110,lowpass=f=110,tremolo=f=6:d=0.6,volume=3" fan.wav` (tested here 2026-10-24; tremolo = sine LFO, the source used a TwoSines shape).

name: Distant helicopter: moving notch on brown noise
what: brown noise into a bell EQ with negative gain (a notch) whose centre is moved by an LFO gives a rotor sound
how: `ffmpeg -f lavfi -i "anoisesrc=d=4:c=brown:a=0.7" -af "asendcmd=c='0.0-4.0 [expr] equalizer f 400+300*sin(2*PI*TI*4*5)',equalizer=f=400:t=q:w=2:g=-20" heli.wav` (tested here 2026-10-24).

name: Cloth foley from pink noise
what: pink noise into a band-pass whose centre is modulated to mimic movement, then EQ toward a friction sound, with amplitude driven together
how: `ffmpeg -f lavfi -i "anoisesrc=d=1.5:c=pink:a=0.6" -af "asendcmd=c='0.0-1.5 [expr] bandpass f 1500+1200*sin(2*PI*TI*3)',bandpass=f=1500:w=1:t=o,volume='0.5+0.5*sin(2*PI*t*2)':eval=frame" cloth.wav` (tested here 2026-10-24).

name: Seamless ambience loop with acrossfade
what: make a loop whose end flows into its start: take seconds 1-6 and crossfade its last second with seconds 0-1
how: `ffmpeg -i amb.wav -af "atrim=1:6,asetpts=N/SR/TB" a.wav; ffmpeg -i amb.wav -af "atrim=0:1,asetpts=N/SR/TB" b.wav; ffmpeg -i a.wav -i b.wav -filter_complex "[0][1]acrossfade=d=1:c1=qsin:c2=qsin" loop.wav` (tested here 2026-10-24; 5.0 s loop). Splitting one input inside a single `filter_complex` produced an empty file here; separate files worked.

name: Loop an ambience to length
what: `-stream_loop N` loops an input (−1 = infinite); `aloop` loops samples in the graph
how: `ffmpeg -stream_loop 3 -i loop.wav -t 12 bed.wav` (tested here 2026-10-24; `-stream_loop -1` with a WAV did not finish within 120 s here, so use a finite count) or `-af "aloop=loop=2:size=220500"` (tested).

name: Reverb from a synthetic noise-burst IR (afir)
what: `afir` convolves the first stream with an IR stream (up to 60 s; doc example: input + IR wav → reverb). Without an IR file, a decaying noise burst works as a synthetic IR
how: IR: `ffmpeg -f lavfi -i "anoisesrc=d=1.5:c=white:a=0.5:seed=7" -af "volume='exp(-t*4)':eval=frame,lowpass=f=6000" ir.wav`; reverb: `ffmpeg -i dry.wav -i ir.wav -filter_complex "[0]apad=pad_dur=1.5,asplit[a][b];[b][1]afir[w];[a][w]amix=inputs=2:weights='1 0.35':normalize=0" wet.wav` (tested here 2026-10-24; the synthetic IR is a tested command, not a judged room).

name: Decay time = RT60
what: reverb time is usually the time to drop below −60 dB (RT60); short decay = small space, long = big; in real spaces highs die faster than lows
how: for an exponential IR `exp(-t*k)`, amplitude falls 60 dB at t = 6.91/k (k=4 → ~1.7 s; k=0.86 → ~8 s, used for #2079) and low-pass the IR to darken the tail.

name: Pre-delay changes size and distance
what: pre-delay (time between dry sound and first reflections) affects perceived room size and distance and separates direct sound from reverb for clarity; avoid slap-back
how: delay only the wet branch: `[w]adelay=20:all=1` before `afir`.
refs: Apple Logic Pro Space Designer, https://support.apple.com/guide/logicpro-ipad/main-parameters-lpipe9ff881d/ipados, checked 2026-10-24

name: More wet = farther
what: the further away a source, the quieter the direct sound compared with its reverb, so raising reverb level pushes it back
how: raise the second `amix` weight for distant sounds.

name: Early-reflection spacing = room size
what: greater spacing of early reflections makes the virtual room sound bigger
how: with `aecho`, wider tap spacing (`aecho=0.8:0.7:30|70|110:0.5|0.4|0.3` vs `10|20|30`) (aecho tested here 2026-10-24).

name: aecho doc presets
what: ffmpeg's own examples: `aecho=0.8:0.88:60:0.4` doubles instruments; `0.8:0.88:6:0.4` (very short) gives a metallic robot; `0.8:0.9:1000:0.3` open-air mountains; `0.8:0.9:1000|1800:0.3|0.25` one more mountain
how: `ffmpeg -i v.wav -af "apad=pad_dur=3,aecho=0.8:0.9:1000|1800:0.3|0.25" canyon.wav` (pad so the echoes aren't cut; tested here 2026-10-24).

name: Switch IRs with afir nbirs
what: `afir` can hold several IR streams (`nbirs`, up to 32) and pick one with `ir` (changeable at runtime)
how: `ffmpeg -i dry.wav -i small.wav -i big.wav -filter_complex "[0]apad=pad_dur=1[d];[d][1][2]afir=nbirs=2:ir=1" out.wav` (tested here 2026-10-24).

name: Reverse reverb (swell into a word)
what: copy the phrase, reverse it, add 100 % wet long reverb, print it, reverse again so the tail precedes the voice, then align with a fade-in just before the original; it also works with delays
how: `ffmpeg -i v.wav -i ir.wav -filter_complex "[0]atrim=0:0.8,asetpts=N/SR/TB,apad=pad_dur=1.5,areverse[r];[r][1]afir=dry=0:wet=1,highpass=f=300,areverse" swell.wav`, then place the swell so it ends where the word starts (`adelay` on the dry) (tested here 2026-10-24).

name: Reverse-reverb details
what: end the isolated snippet on a vowel for a cleaner swell, cut the reverb's lows to reduce mud, and automate pan/volume of the swell to blend
how: the `highpass=f=300` in #2127 is that low cut; trim the snippet at a vowel.

name: Reverse delay swell variant
what: the reversed-reverb trick also works with delays
how: `ffmpeg -i v.wav -af "atrim=0:0.6,asetpts=N/SR/TB,apad=pad_dur=1.2,areverse,aecho=0.8:1:120|240|360|480:0.6|0.45|0.3|0.2,areverse" swell_delay.wav` (tested here 2026-10-24).

name: Reverse and pitch for horror
what: reversing and pitch-shifting make natural sounds surreal; time-stretching and (reversed) reverbs/delays add the other-worldly touch; metal/wood squeaks, whistling wind and voices are good ghostly sources
how: `areverse,rubberband=pitch=0.7` on a CC0 creak (both tested here 2026-10-24).

name: areverse needs a trimmed input
what: `areverse` buffers the whole clip in memory; trim first (`atrim=end=5,areverse`)
how: always `atrim` before `areverse` on long files (tested here 2026-10-24).

name: Landline phone recipe
section: Futz: phone, radio, TV, PA, walkie
what: HPF 300 Hz and LPF 3.4 kHz, both 24 dB/oct; a 4-6 dB peak at 1.5-2 kHz; hard compression (fast attack, 6-10 dB gain reduction, release 60-150 ms); light distortion after the filter, then a second 3.4 kHz low-pass (distortion leaks energy above the band); mono; no reverb
how: `ffmpeg -i v.wav -af "highpass=f=300,highpass=f=300,lowpass=f=3400,lowpass=f=3400,equalizer=f=1700:t=q:w=1.5:g=5,acompressor=threshold=-30dB:ratio=8:attack=5:release=100:makeup=4,asoftclip=type=tanh,lowpass=f=3400,lowpass=f=3400,aformat=channel_layouts=mono" phone.wav` (tested here 2026-10-24).

name: Why 300-3400 Hz
section: Futz: phone, radio, TV, PA, walkie
what: the analog phone channel carried about 300-3400 Hz; once digital it was sampled 8,000 times a second (content up to 4 kHz), 8 bits → 64 kbit/s; modern wideband calls carry roughly 50 Hz-7 kHz with digital artifacts instead
how: `aresample=8000,aresample=44100` after the band-pass imitates the 8 kHz rate (tested here 2026-10-24).

name: Slope decides phone vs "bass cut"
section: Futz: phone, radio, TV, PA, walkie
what: at 12 dB/oct a 300 Hz HPF leaves 200 Hz only 7.8 dB down (still chesty); 24 dB/oct gives 14.3 dB, 48 dB/oct 28.2 dB; a 24 dB/oct LPF at 3.4 kHz puts 6 kHz 19.8 dB down and 8 kHz 29.7 dB down
how: cascade two `highpass`/`lowpass` (2-pole each) for 24 dB/oct, four for 48.

name: Phone corner off the singer, not a preset
section: Futz: phone, radio, TV, PA, walkie
what: a voice at 110 Hz loses its fundamental to a 300 Hz HPF but keeps its pitch (the ear uses harmonic spacing); a 220 Hz voice loses only 11.1 dB of its fundamental, so move the HPF to 400 Hz (−20.8 dB) or 500 Hz (−28.5 dB) for higher voices
how: `highpass=f=400,highpass=f=400` for higher voices.

name: Band-pass makes the voice peakier
section: Futz: phone, radio, TV, PA, walkie
what: on their test line the 24 dB/oct band-pass dropped RMS 4.20 dB but peak only 1.84 dB (crest factor 13.25→15.61 dB), so compression is needed twice over; budget 4-5 dB make-up
how: compare `astats` RMS/peak before and after (astats tested here 2026-10-24).

name: Phone check: sweep and mono
section: Futz: phone, radio, TV, PA, walkie
what: solo the effect and sweep a narrow boost: anything answering below 250 Hz or above 4 kHz means soft slopes; sum to mono and it should not change; A/B against a real phone voice memo
how: check the band on a spectrogram: `ffmpeg -i phone.wav -lavfi "showspectrumpic=s=640x320:fscale=log:start=50:stop=8000" spec.png` (tested here 2026-10-24).

name: Phone effect on a duplicate, crossfaded in
section: Futz: phone, radio, TV, PA, walkie
what: build it on a copy of the voice with sends off; crossfade in on a consonant at a phrase start with a 10-20 ms fade; dip the instrumental 1 dB for the length of the phone line; use it for a line or hook, not a whole verse
how: cut the voice into dry/phone pieces and join with `acrossfade=d=0.015`.

name: Phone alternative: sinc FIR band-pass
section: Futz: phone, radio, TV, PA, walkie
what: the `sinc` source makes Kaiser-windowed FIR coefficients (band-pass when hp < lp) for `afir`
how: `ffmpeg -i v.wav -f lavfi -i "sinc=hp=300:lp=3400:r=44100" -filter_complex "[0][1]afir" phone_fir.wav` (tested here 2026-10-24).

name: Futz band table by device
section: Futz: phone, radio, TV, PA, walkie
what: landline/mobile 300 Hz-3.4 kHz; mobile HD voice 100 Hz-7 kHz; small TV/clock radio 200-400 Hz to 5-8 kHz + cabinet peak 800 Hz-1.5 kHz; laptop 400 Hz-10 kHz (thin, not muffled); PA/megaphone 400 Hz-4 kHz + strong 1-2 kHz honk + real distortion; intercom/walkie 400 Hz-3 kHz + heavy compression + squelch at each transmission's top and tail; all with steep filters, 24 dB/oct+
how: e.g. TV `highpass=f=300,highpass=f=300,lowpass=f=6000,lowpass=f=6000,equalizer=f=1100:t=q:w=4:g=6,acompressor=threshold=-25dB:ratio=6`; laptop `highpass=f=400,highpass=f=400,lowpass=f=10000,lowpass=f=10000`; PA `...lowpass=f=4000,lowpass=f=4000,equalizer=f=1500:t=q:w=1.5:g=8,volume=2,asoftclip=type=hard:threshold=0.5` (all tested here 2026-10-24).

name: Walkie with squelch at both ends
section: Futz: phone, radio, TV, PA, walkie
what: intercom/walkie: 400 Hz-3 kHz, heavy compression, a noise squelch at the start and end of each transmission
how: `ffmpeg -i v.wav -f lavfi -i "anoisesrc=d=0.2:c=white:a=0.25" -filter_complex "[0]highpass=f=400,highpass=f=400,lowpass=f=3000,lowpass=f=3000,acompressor=threshold=-30dB:ratio=10:attack=2:release=60:makeup=6,agate=threshold=0.0056[v];[1]highpass=f=1000,asplit[s1][s2];[s1][v][s2]concat=n=3:v=0:a=1" walkie.wav` (tested here 2026-10-24; gate 0.0056 ≈ −45 dB from #2142).

name: Two-way radio preset numbers
section: Futz: phone, radio, TV, PA, walkie
what: a walkie preset cuts below 500 Hz and above 3 kHz, boosts the mids 6 dB, adds drive for the clipped edge and gates at −45 dB so the line is quiet between phrases
how: `highpass=f=500,lowpass=f=3000,equalizer=f=1500:t=o:w=2:g=6,asoftclip,agate=threshold=0.0056` (agate threshold is linear; 0.0056 ≈ −45 dBFS).

name: Radio distortion: analog vs digital
section: Futz: phone, radio, TV, PA, walkie
what: a bitcrusher is distortion you'd only hear on digital devices; for an analog radio feel use a 3-band EQ band-pass and then distortion, optionally a compressor before it to even out levels
how: `bandpass` + `acompressor` + `asoftclip` (analog); `acrusher` only for digital radio.

name: Futzed voice must sit in a room
section: Futz: phone, radio, TV, PA, walkie
what: the dry, centred futz is why it sounds fake; after filtering add a short reverb matching the device's room, pan to where the device is on screen, drop the level; if the camera moves, the device's sound should change too
how: futz chain → `afir` small IR at low mix → `pan` toward the device side.

name: Codec dropout sells a mobile call
section: Futz: phone, radio, TV, PA, walkie
what: a modern mobile call sounds slightly granular and metallic and occasionally drops out; one very short dropout per call does more than any EQ; gentle top-octave bitcrushing gets close
how: one dropout: `volume='if(between(t,1.2,1.32),0,1)':eval=frame` (volume eval tested here 2026-10-24).

name: Noise matched to the device
section: Futz: phone, radio, TV, PA, walkie
what: a landline has faint hum and hiss, a walkie a squelch burst, a PA room noise around it; silence between words gives the plugin away
how: mix a very low `anoisesrc` (pink, a≈0.02) under the futzed line (tested in old-radio chain here 2026-10-24).

name: Futz definition
section: Futz: phone, radio, TV, PA, walkie
what: futzing is intentional processing of a sound to fit a scene and environment (cell-phone voice, a voice inside a space suit, Darth Vader)
how: decide what device/space the voice passes through before picking filters.

name: Worldizing
section: Futz: phone, radio, TV, PA, walkie
what: Walter Murch's technique: play a recording through a speaker in a real space and re-record it with microphones so it takes on that place's acoustics; it still beats plugins
how: play the futzed file from a phone in a real room, record with another phone, use that take.

name: Old radio with iZotope-style band limits
section: Futz: phone, radio, TV, PA, walkie
what: band-limiting makes music sound like small radio speakers (wider band = bigger set), mechanical noise/dust/scratch simulate interference, and mono helps for a radio in a bar or a phone call
how: `ffmpeg -i m.wav -af "highpass=f=400,lowpass=f=4000,aformat=channel_layouts=mono" radio.wav` (tested here 2026-10-24), plus a low pink-noise layer.

name: Telephone mid boost alternative
section: Futz: phone, radio, TV, PA, walkie
what: a simpler phone recipe: LPF at 2 kHz, HPF at 500 Hz and a 1 kHz boost
how: `highpass=f=500,lowpass=f=2000,equalizer=f=1000:t=o:w=1:g=6`.

name: Next-room music recipe
what: LPF 500 Hz-2 kHz at 24 dB/oct (start ~1 kHz), drop 6-12 dB, collapse toward mono, small room reverb 0.6-1.2 s with pre-delay under 20 ms at 30-50 % mix, a small 100-200 Hz boost for wall resonance, roll off below 40 Hz; don't high-pass the low end away — the mud is the effect
how: `ffmpeg -i m.wav -i ir_small.wav -filter_complex "[0]aformat=channel_layouts=mono,lowpass=f=1000,lowpass=f=1000,equalizer=f=150:t=q:w=1:g=4,highpass=f=40,volume=-9dB,asplit[d][w];[w]adelay=15:all=1[wd];[wd][1]afir[r];[d][r]amix=inputs=2:weights='0.6 0.4':normalize=0" nextroom.wav` with a 0.9 s synthetic IR (tested here 2026-10-24).

name: Room-effect variations
what: door open: cutoff 3-4 kHz, less reverb, keep some stereo; underwater: LPF ~400 Hz with slow cutoff modulation; car outside: LPF ~250 Hz, heavy compression, slow fade as it drives away; club from the smoking area: LPF ~800 Hz, long reverb, and when the door opens automate the cutoff up 2 kHz for a bar
how: car: `lowpass=f=250,lowpass=f=250,acompressor=threshold=-30dB:ratio=8:makeup=4,afade=t=out:st=1:d=3`; club door: `asendcmd=c='1.0-2.0 lowpass f 2800;2.0 lowpass f 800',lowpass=f=800,lowpass=f=800` (both tested here 2026-10-24).

name: Muffled presets with numbers
what: Next Room 850 Hz, −8 dB, +6 dB bass, mono; Bathroom at a Party 1100 Hz, −6 dB, +4 dB, stereo; Through the Wall 600 Hz, −12 dB, +8 dB, mono; Underwater 400 Hz, −4 dB, 0 dB, low reverb; Daydream 3000 Hz, −3 dB, +2 dB; all with a 24 dB/oct low-pass and a 1.4 s small-room reverb
how: `lowpass=f=850,lowpass=f=850,lowshelf=f=120:g=6,volume=-8dB` (all four presets tested here 2026-10-24; reverb not included).

name: Phone filters steep, wall filters gentle
what: a wall is a gentle physical roll-off, a phone line a designed electronic band limit with hard edges; that is why futz advice is "steep" and through-wall advice differs
how: 2-pole (12 dB/oct) `lowpass` for walls, cascaded 4-pole for phones.

name: Through a wall: low-pass ~300 Hz, plus resonance and reflections
what: try a low-pass around 300 Hz (maybe lower); building materials resonate, so a bump somewhere 180-400 Hz (careful of 300 Hz mud), reverb/IR, or a short slap delay (early reflections tell the ear the space) help
how: `lowpass=f=300,equalizer=f=220:t=q:w=2:g=3,aecho=0.6:0.4:40:0.3`.

name: Underwater EQ by depth
what: HPF at 20 Hz (optional), the key move is a LPF at 300 Hz; go to 200 Hz for deeper, 400-500 Hz nearer the surface; add chorus after the EQ at about 4 Hz rate, 50/50 dry/wet for warble
how: `ffmpeg -i m.wav -af "highpass=f=20,lowpass=f=300,lowpass=f=300,chorus=0.5:0.5:20:0.5:4:2" underwater.wav` (tested here 2026-10-24).

name: Swim to the surface = automate the cutoff up
what: automate the underwater low-pass upward when the character surfaces; going from filtered to full spectrum feels refreshing
how: `asendcmd=c='2.0-3.0 [expr] lowpass f 300*exp(log(60)*TI)',lowpass=f=300` (tested here 2026-10-24 on pink noise; centroid 0.28→6.3 kHz across the move).

name: Underwater transition: dip the level too
what: cut highs (above ~1 kHz for "deep"), and when going from above to under water, drop the level a bit at the transition; add water sounds for depth
how: combine #2157 with `volume=-4dB` at the dive point.

name: Distance: quieter, duller, thinner
what: a sound at the back needs to be quieter and have less top end (air absorbs highs); also roll off below 150-200 Hz; use a diffuse reverb with its top rolled off; distant sounds can take more reverb
how: `ffmpeg -i v.wav -i ir.wav -filter_complex "[0]highpass=f=180,lowpass=f=3000,volume=-8dB,asplit[d][w];[w]apad=pad_dur=1.5,adelay=100:all=1[wd];[wd][1]afir,lowpass=f=4000[r];[d][r]amix=inputs=2:weights='1 0.5':duration=longest:normalize=0" far.wav` (tested here 2026-10-24).

name: Distance with filtered echoes
what: echo repeats with the top rolled off above ~4 kHz and bottom below ~200 Hz give an impression of distance; long pre-delay (90-110 ms) reverb or delay instead of reverb keeps a vocal forward
how: `ffmpeg -i v.wav -af "apad=pad_dur=1.5,asplit[a][b];[b]aecho=0.8:0.6:350|700:0.4|0.2,highpass=f=200,lowpass=f=4000[e];[a][e]amix=inputs=2:normalize=0" echo_far.wav` (tested here 2026-10-24).

name: Automated low-pass instead of a volume dip
what: a 12 or 18 dB/oct low-pass automated down while something else plays pushes a sound back more subtly than level automation
how: `asendcmd=c='1.0 lowpass f 2500;3.0 lowpass f 20000',lowpass=f=20000` (tested here 2026-10-24).

name: Darker = farther
what: highs lose more level over distance than mids, lows much less (a distant helicopter still rumbles), so a low-pass moves sounds back; bright, airy, dry sounds sit up front
how: dull background SFX with `lowpass`, keep hero SFX full-band.

name: Game-audio distance curves
what: Wwise maps distance to both volume (e.g. −17 dB at 30 m in the course example) and a low-pass curve, because highs diminish over distance
how: for an approaching object, ramp `volume` and a `lowpass` frequency together with `asendcmd`.

name: Bass travels: sub booms read as distant
what: bass travels further than highs, so a distant event sounds like it has a high-cut filter on it
how: low-pass a hit to make it read distant (#2078).

name: Ear-ringing after an explosion
what: after the explosion, low-pass all other sounds and fade in an ear-ringing tone; the trope (often credited to Saving Private Ryan) puts the audience in the character's hearing
how: `ffmpeg -i hit.wav -i bed.wav -f lavfi -i "sine=f=3500:d=4:r=44100" -filter_complex "[1]asendcmd=c='0.5-1.0 [expr] lowpass f 18000*exp(log(300/18000)*TI)',lowpass=f=18000,volume=0.6[m];[2]volume=0.06,afade=t=in:st=0.5:d=0.3,afade=t=out:st=1.5:d=2.5[r];[0]aformat=channel_layouts=mono[i];[i][m][r]amix=inputs=3:duration=longest:normalize=0" ring.wav` (tested here 2026-10-24; the 3.5 kHz tone is our choice).

name: Ring types: steady, blast, slow recovery
what: a steady ring holds; a blast ring arrives at full level with no ramp plus dull pressure underneath; a slow recovery thins out and lets the world back in
how: for "blast" skip the fade-in in #2165; for "recovery" fade the bed's low-pass back up.

name: Slow-mo SFX: an octave down, 30 % slower
section: Pitch and time: slow-mo, tape stop, creature voices
what: pitch slow-mo effects at least one octave down (about as far as you go without severe artifacts) and also time-shift them at least 30 % slower; treat backgrounds the same; add low-end elements; use a low whoosh or bass flutter into and out of slow-mo; water doesn't pitch well (try lava or mud)
how: `ffmpeg -i hit.wav -af "rubberband=pitch=0.5:tempo=0.7" hit_slomo.wav` (tested here 2026-10-24).

name: Varispeed vs independent pitch/time
section: Pitch and time: slow-mo, tape stop, creature voices
what: time stretching changes duration without pitch, pitch scaling changes pitch without duration, "pitch control" (varispeed) changes both together; varispeed is the simpler method and degrades the sound less
how: varispeed: `asetrate=44100*0.5,aresample=44100` (octave down, twice as long; tested here 2026-10-24); independent: `rubberband`.

name: Semitones from speed
section: Pitch and time: slow-mo, tape stop, creature voices
what: pitch in semitones = 12 × log2(speed): half speed is 12 semitones down and twice as long; a quarter is 24 down; a tenth −39.9
how: for n semitones use `asetrate=44100*2^(n/12)` (math checked here 2026-10-24: 0.5→−12.0, 0.25→−24.0, 0.1→−39.9).

name: rubberband pitch with formant preservation
section: Pitch and time: slow-mo, tape stop, creature voices
what: `rubberband` shifts pitch (`pitch` scale factor) and tempo independently and has `formant=preserved`
how: `ffmpeg -i v.wav -af "rubberband=pitch=0.7937:formant=preserved" v_down4.wav` (−4 semitones; tested here 2026-10-24).

name: rubberband transient and window modes
section: Pitch and time: slow-mo, tape stop, creature voices
what: options include `transients=crisp|mixed|smooth`, `detector=compound|percussive|soft`, `window=standard|short|long`, `smoothing`, `pitchq=quality|speed|consistency`
how: hits: `rubberband=tempo=0.5:transients=crisp:detector=percussive`; textures: `rubberband=tempo=0.5:transients=smooth:window=long` (both tested here 2026-10-24).

name: atempo for speed without pitch
section: Pitch and time: slow-mo, tape stop, creature voices
what: `atempo` takes 0.5-100; above 2 it skips samples instead of blending, so chain instances (`atempo=sqrt(3),atempo=sqrt(3)`)
how: `atempo=0.5` (tested here 2026-10-24).

name: Stretch and pitch for drones
section: Pitch and time: slow-mo, tape stop, creature voices
what: time-stretch existing files to make atmospheres/drones; it works best with high sample-rate sources, and recordings with lots of highs survive pitching down two or three octaves better than sub-heavy ones
how: `ffmpeg -i src.wav -af "rubberband=tempo=0.125:window=long:smoothing=on,rubberband=pitch=0.5" drone.wav` (tested here 2026-10-24).

name: High-resolution sources survive extreme pitch
section: Pitch and time: slow-mo, tape stop, creature voices
what: material recorded at high sample rates (192 kHz/24-bit, sold as 96 kHz) can be pitched and processed to extremes while keeping quality
how: prefer 96 kHz CC0 sources for heavy slow-mo/creature work.

name: Creature voice = pitch down + layered animal
section: Pitch and time: slow-mo, tape stop, creature voices
what: the core of creature voices is pitch shifting your own roar low and layering animal roars on top
how: `rubberband=pitch=0.6:formant=shifted` on the voice, then `amix` with a CC0 animal growl (pitch chain tested here 2026-10-24).

name: Tape stop: speed and pitch fall together
section: Pitch and time: slow-mo, tape stop, creature voices
what: a tape stop slows audio to a halt so pitch and speed fall together (unlike wow/flutter or a pitch bend); length a quarter note to one bar; shed speed fastest at the start; fade the last moment (≤5 ms) so it doesn't click; high-pass at 25 Hz after the stop
how: numpy: read position = cumulative sum of a speed ramp, `np.interp` the source, 5 ms end fade, `butter(2,25,'highpass')` (tested here 2026-10-24, `sk2_07/np_tests.py`).

name: Tape stop curve: exponential = straight pitch line
section: Pitch and time: slow-mo, tape stop, creature voices
what: a linear speed ramp drops slowly then off a cliff in pitch (first half = one octave, last tenth = three more); a speed decaying as e^(−t/τ) falls 17.3 semitones per τ in a straight line but never reaches zero, so you choose where to cut
how: `v = np.exp(-t/0.25)` instead of `1 - t/T` in #2176 (both tested here 2026-10-24).

name: Tape stop eats half its length of material
section: Pitch and time: slow-mo, tape stop, creature voices
what: a linear stop of length T consumes T/2 of source, so anything after is T/2 late; keep at least that much material past the stop point
how: measured here: a 1.0 s linear stop consumed 0.5 s of source (2026-10-24).

name: Tape stop length in beats
section: Pitch and time: slow-mo, tape stop, creature voices
what: set the stop in beats, not milliseconds (bar = 240/BPM s): two beats at 87 BPM is 1.379 s; the same gesture then reads right at any tempo
how: stop length = n × 60/BPM.

name: Tape start / spin-up
section: Pitch and time: slow-mo, tape stop, creature voices
what: the reverse move: speed rises from a dead stop into pitch; good as an intro into a phrase or drop
how: numpy speed ramp 0→1 (`v = t/T`, tested here 2026-10-24).

name: Where tape stops land
section: Pitch and time: slow-mo, tape stop, creature voices
what: into a drop (quick stop, a beat of silence, then the drop), ending a phrase/track, or short repeated as a stutter; it wears out fast if used on every transition
how: once per video, at the biggest section change.

name: Check a tape stop on a phone
section: Pitch and time: slow-mo, tape stop, creature voices
what: small drivers give up in the hundreds of Hz, so on a phone the second half of a stop is hats over near-silence; put the drama in the top of the ramp and finish sooner if it must work there; test on a sustained sine (period should lengthen smoothly)
how: run #2176 on `sine=f=440` and look at `showwavespic`.

name: Wow and flutter are not tape stop
section: Pitch and time: slow-mo, tape stop, creature voices
what: wow/flutter is a small ongoing pitch wobble that never stops the sound
how: a tested stand-in: `vibrato=f=0.8:d=0.05,vibrato=f=7:d=0.02` (tested here 2026-10-24; rates are our choice).

name: Frequency shift ≠ pitch shift
section: Pitch and time: slow-mo, tape stop, creature voices
what: a true frequency shift moves the whole spectrum and gives a metallic, inharmonic sound (a special effect); pitch shifting keeps harmonic relations
how: `afreqshift=shift=50` (metallic) vs `rubberband=pitch=1.06` (both tested here 2026-10-24).

name: Transposing noise in a sampler
section: Pitch and time: slow-mo, tape stop, creature voices
what: white noise can't be transposed at source (pitch doesn't change on a noise oscillator), but transposing a noise recording in a sampler gives a lo-fi effect
how: `asetrate=44100*0.5,aresample=44100` on a recorded noise file.

name: Granular textures
section: Pitch and time: slow-mo, tape stop, creature voices
what: granular synthesis chops a sound into grains (tens of ms; NI says 1-100 ms) and reassembles them; each grain gets a smooth window (Hann) because raw rectangular grains click; results tend to be cloudy, smeared, frozen or glitchy
how: numpy: 50 ms Hann grains from random positions, overlap-add at 1/4 grain hop (tested here 2026-10-24, `np_tests.py`).
refs: CMU Intro to Computer Music, https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~15322/book/ch10/03.html, checked 2026-10-24

name: Doppler formula
what: observed f = ((v_m ± v_r)/(v_m ∓ v_s)) × f0: source speed subtracted from the wave speed when approaching, added when receding
how: for a 440 Hz source at 30 m/s in air (343 m/s): 482.2 Hz approaching, 404.6 Hz receding; a numpy pass-by (delay = r/c, gain 1/r) measured 478.4 and 401.7 Hz (tested here 2026-10-24, `np_tests.py`).

name: Pass-by = pitch + level + pan
what: automate pitch up and volume up while panning in, then pitch and volume down as it moves away
how: ffmpeg approximation on a tonal source: `aformat=channel_layouts=stereo,asendcmd=c='0.0-3.0 [expr] rubberband pitch 1.12-0.24/(1+exp(-(TI-0.5)*12))',rubberband=pitch=1.12,aeval='val(0)*(1-t/3)*(0.3+0.7*exp(-pow((t-1.5)*2,2)))|val(1)*(t/3)*(0.3+0.7*exp(-pow((t-1.5)*2,2)))'` (tested here 2026-10-24).

name: Doppler needs pre-delay for far sources
what: a Doppler simulation adds an initial delay (a source a mile away arrives seconds late) that must be compensated to land the peak at a point
how: in the numpy pass-by, offset the read index by the distance delay and shift the result so the closest point lands on the frame.

name: Equal-power pan moves
what: pan automation with equal-power law; avoid hard-left-to-hard-right moves in stereo unless you want a stylized wipe (natural pass-bys arc through the field)
how: `aeval='val(0)*cos(PI/2*min(t/0.8,1))|val(0)*sin(PI/2*min(t/0.8,1))':c=stereo` (tested here 2026-10-24); keep the end angle short of 90° for a natural pass.

name: Static pan of a mono SFX
what: `pan` sets per-output-channel gains
how: `pan=stereo|c0=0.8*c0|c1=0.3*c0` (tested here 2026-10-24); use `<` instead of `=` to renormalize gains and avoid clipping.

name: Mono SFX are point sources
what: mono is the default for effects without width (footsteps, animal calls, flickering bulbs, UI beeps); they are easier to pan than stereo files and ideal for movement effects
how: keep spot SFX mono and pan them; keep beds stereo.

name: Haas zone and its numbers
what: two copies within roughly 30-40 ms fuse into one event located at the first arrival; around 2-5 ms location comes almost only from the first sound, beyond ~5 ms it gets louder and wider; the reflection can be ~10 dB louder and still not shift localization
how: `haas` filter on a mono SFX (default delays 2.05/2.12 ms; local 6.1 allows 0-40 ms): `ffmpeg -i mono.wav -af "haas=left_delay=0:right_delay=15:middle_source=left" wide.wav` (tested here 2026-10-24).

name: Haas is not mono-safe: keep it off key sounds
what: Haas-widened parts disappear or change in mono through phase cancellation; going outside 5-35 ms fixes cancellation but becomes an echo; use it only on non-critical extras; M/S widening, chorus, double-tracking or early-reflection reverbs are mono-compatible alternatives
how: never Haas the main whoosh/impact; mono-check with `pan=mono|c0=0.5*c0+0.5*c1` (tested here 2026-10-24).

name: Stereo-ising a mono sound
what: duplicate it, route hard left/right and make the copies different; the more different, the wider; delay, pitch shift and pitch modulation are the usual tools
how: `aformat=channel_layouts=stereo,adecorrelate=stages=6` (tested here 2026-10-24) or a small `chorus`.

name: Widen beds with stereowiden / extrastereo
what: `stereowiden` suppresses common signal and cross-delays L/R (defaults delay 20 ms, feedback 0.3, crossfeed 0.3, drymix 0.8); `extrastereo` scales L/R difference (m=1 unchanged, 0 mono, −1 swaps)
how: `stereowiden=delay=20:feedback=0.3:crossfeed=0.3` or `extrastereo=m=2.0` on stereo ambience (both tested here 2026-10-24); mono-check after.

name: Whoosh width and stereo micro-delays
what: stereo decorrelation with micro-delays 0.2-1.5 ms or all-pass networks widens without obvious echo; if it drops more than ~3 dB or turns hollow in mono, reduce inter-channel delay and keep energy in the mid
how: `adelay=0|1:all=0` (1 ms on the right) then mono-check RMS with `astats`.

name: Auto-pan with apulsator
what: `apulsator` modulates L/R volume with an LFO; offset_r 0.5 (default) acts as an autopanner, equal offsets as a tremolo; modes sine/triangle/square/sawup/sawdown; timing in bpm, ms or hz
how: `ffmpeg -i amb.wav -af "aformat=channel_layouts=stereo,apulsator=hz=0.5" pan.wav` (tested here 2026-10-24).

name: Headphone crossfeed options
what: `crossfeed` (strength default 0.2, cut-off near 1550 Hz), `bs2b` (profiles default 700 Hz/50, cmoy 700/60, jmeier 650/95) and `earwax` (moves headphone image in front, for 44.1 kHz stereo) reduce extreme headphone separation
how: `crossfeed=strength=0.4`, `bs2b=profile=cmoy`, `earwax` (all three tested here 2026-10-24) on an exported headphone check copy, not the master.

name: HRTF binaural placement needs SOFA files
what: `sofalizer` places virtual speakers with HRTFs from SOFA files (needs libmysofa); `headphone` needs HRIR WAVs per channel
how: needs a SOFA/HRIR file (missing; see Missing tools), then `sofalizer=sofa=/path/x.sofa:type=freq:radius=1`.

name: Ring-mod robot voice
what: ring modulation multiplies the voice by a steady sine; 30-80 Hz gives the clanging metallic sci-fi robot; lower (30) harsher and more mechanical, higher (120+) more alien
how: `ffmpeg -i v.wav -f lavfi -i "sine=f=30:r=44100:d=3.2" -filter_complex "[0][1]amultiply,volume=6" robot.wav` (tested here 2026-10-24 at 30 and 120 Hz; `sine` has amplitude 1/8, hence the gain).

name: Dalek origin: 30 Hz tape loop
what: the BBC Radiophonic ring modulator multiplied an actor's voice by a 30 Hz sine from a tape loop; its diodes added distortion; ring modulation can make speech robotic though it rarely suits melodic sounds
how: #2201 at 30 Hz plus a light `asoftclip`.

name: tremolo above 20 Hz is a ring modulator
what: ffmpeg's `tremolo` docs: below 20 Hz it is tremolo, higher frequencies make it a ring modulator
how: `tremolo=f=60:d=1` (tested here 2026-10-24).

name: FFT robotize and whisper (doc recipes)
what: `afftfilt` doc examples: robotize `real='hypot(re,im)*sin(0)':imag='hypot(re,im)*cos(0)':win_size=512:overlap=0.75`; whisper with random phase, `win_size=128:overlap=0.8`
how: `ffmpeg -i v.wav -af "afftfilt=real='hypot(re,im)*sin(0)':imag='hypot(re,im)*cos(0)':win_size=512:overlap=0.75" robot_fft.wav` (both tested here 2026-10-24).

name: Vocoder robot (monotone)
what: a vocoder measures the voice's loudness in bands (16 in VoiceFX's) and imposes it on a buzzing carrier so each syllable lands on one flat pitch; Audacity's Vocoder takes the voice in the left channel and the carrier in the right, and white-noise carrier gives a robot voice
how: no vocoder filter in ffmpeg; use Audacity's Vocoder (missing here; see Missing tools).

name: What a glitch is
what: the audible by-product of digital failure: buffer overruns, bit-depth truncation, sample-rate mismatches, corruption → stutters, zipper noise, bitcrushed distortion, granular fragments; harsh and aliased rather than warm
how: combine stutter (#2207) and crush (#2209).

name: Buffer-repeat stutter
what: repeat a short slice (Selekt: buffer-repeat at 1/32-note intervals); a glitch module records a circular buffer and loops a clock-sized slice
how: `ffmpeg -i m.wav -af "atrim=0:0.0625,asetpts=N/SR/TB,aloop=loop=15:size=2756" stutter.wav` (a 1/32 note at 120 BPM = 62.5 ms; tested here 2026-10-24).

name: Progressive bitcrush 16→4 bit
what: bitcrush progressively from 16-bit down to 4-bit over two bars for a transition
how: `acrusher` accepts commands: `asendcmd=c='0.0-4.0 [expr] acrusher bits 16-12*TI',acrusher=bits=16:mode=lin:mix=1` (tested here 2026-10-24).

name: acrusher modes
what: `acrusher` reduces bit resolution (without changing real bit depth); `mode=log` is more natural and doesn't gate quiet signals; `aa` gives softer crushing; `samples` reduces sample rate; built-in `lfo`
how: `acrusher=bits=6:mode=log:aa=1:mix=1`; rate crush `acrusher=samples=12:bits=16`; moving `acrusher=bits=8:samples=6:lfo=1:lforange=10:lforate=0.5` (all tested here 2026-10-24).

name: Bitcrush for a bad radio / broken robot
what: crushing to ~13 bit gives grit; heavier gives broken-robot sounds, a bad radio signal (like C&C radio) and digital breakup; compress before the crusher so the grit sits evenly
how: `acompressor,acrusher=bits=8:mode=log` on a futzed voice.

name: Random gating for digital dropouts (tested command only)
what: `volume` with `eval=frame` and `random()` mutes random 1024-sample frames
how: `ffmpeg -i m.wav -af "volume='gt(random(0),0.35)':eval=frame,acrusher=bits=8:samples=4" glitch.wav` (tested here 2026-10-24; no claim about how it sounds).

name: Trance gate / rhythmic chop
what: `apulsator` with `mode=square`, `offset_r=0` (both channels together) and BPM timing chops a bed in tempo
how: `apulsator=mode=square:offset_r=0:timing=bpm:bpm=120:amount=1` (tested here 2026-10-24); or `amultiply` with a square LFO from `aevalsrc='0.5+0.5*sgn(sin(2*PI*4*t))'` (tested).

name: Lo-fi gramophone ingredients
what: gramophone/lo-fi emulators combine low- and high-pass band limiting (thin, phone-like), warbly modulation (depth/rate) and hum and crackle (noise/dust)
how: `highpass=f=400,lowpass=f=4000` + `vibrato` + a low velvet-noise crackle layer (#2214) (pieces tested here 2026-10-24).

name: Velvet noise for sparse crackle (tested command only)
what: `anoisesrc` has a velvet colour with `density` (0-1, default 0.05)
how: `ffmpeg -f lavfi -i "anoisesrc=d=4:c=velvet:density=0.002:a=0.8" -af "highpass=f=1500" crackle.wav` (tested here 2026-10-24; no claim about how it sounds).

name: RIAA/vinyl emphasis curves
what: `aemphasis` applies or restores emphasis curves (Columbia, EMI, BSI 78 RPM, RIAA, CD, FM 50/75 µs); production mode applies, reproduction restores
how: `aemphasis=mode=production:type=riaa` (tested here 2026-10-24; no claim it sounds "vintage").

name: Saturation vs clipping
what: clipping distortion suits single sounds (thicker, more highs) but on complex material every frequency makes harmonics until it turns toward noise; gentler saturation suits groups and buses; saturation adds compression and harmonics (even harmonics of 100 Hz at 200, 400, 600 Hz)
how: single hits: `asoftclip=type=hard`; groups: `asoftclip=type=tanh:threshold=0.6:oversample=4` (tested here 2026-10-24).

name: Oversample nonlinear stages
what: nonlinear saturation widens bandwidth and can alias above Nyquist; whoosh guides advise oversampling (2×-8×) for aggressive drive
how: `asoftclip=...:oversample=4` (tested here 2026-10-24).

name: Transient boost survives limiting
what: boosting a snare's attack and then limiting back to the same peak does not fully cancel the perceived punch; clipping back to the peak keeps the enhancement more obviously (with more grit)
how: `crystalizer=i=4` or `aderivative` blend as a crude attack lift, then `alimiter`/`apsyclip=clip=0.7` (all tested here 2026-10-24).

name: Transient shaper vs compressor
what: a transient shaper splits attack and sustain and adjusts each (boost attack for crack, pull sustain to tighten a boomy hit) without the level-riding of a compressor
how: no dedicated transient shaper in ffmpeg; approximate attack lift with `crystalizer` and tail cut with `agate` (#2221).

name: Exciter adds missing highs
what: `aexciter` creates harmonics in a limited range (freq 2-12 kHz, default 7.5 kHz) and adds them, raising the top end differently from EQ
how: `aexciter=amount=3:drive=8.5:freq=3000` on a dull SFX (tested here 2026-10-24).

name: Cut an impact's tail with agate
section: Envelopes, dynamics and synthesis building blocks
what: `agate` reduces signal below a threshold (range, ratio, attack/release in ms)
how: `agate=threshold=0.05:range=0.001:attack=1:release=60` (tested here 2026-10-24).

name: Gate a bed by another sound
section: Envelopes, dynamics and synthesis building blocks
what: `sidechaingate` opens/closes the first input by the level of the second
how: `[bed][key]sidechaingate=threshold=0.05:range=0.1:attack=5:release=150` (both mono; tested here 2026-10-24).

name: compand hard limiter for stacked hits
section: Envelopes, dynamics and synthesis building blocks
what: doc example "Hard limiter at −6 dB": `compand=attacks=0:points=-80/-80|-6/-6|20/-6`
how: after `amix` of layers (tested here 2026-10-24).

name: alimiter: set level=0
section: Envelopes, dynamics and synthesis building blocks
what: `alimiter` uses lookahead (delay = attack) and by default auto-levels the output back to 0 dB (`level` enabled); disable it to keep your gain staging
how: `alimiter=limit=0.89:level=0` (tested here 2026-10-24).

name: amix: weights and normalize=0
section: Envelopes, dynamics and synthesis building blocks
what: `amix` normalizes inputs by default; for layered SFX with set levels use `weights` and `normalize=0` (doc example vocals 1, music 0.25)
how: `amix=inputs=3:weights='1 0.7 0.5':normalize=0` (tested here 2026-10-24).

name: Fade curves for SFX
section: Envelopes, dynamics and synthesis building blocks
what: `afade` curves include tri (default), qsin, hsin, esin, log, exp, par, qua, cub, losi, desi and more; `silence` sets the end gain of a fade-out
how: natural-sounding tail: `afade=t=out:st=0.3:d=1.2:curve=exp`; partial fade `afade=t=out:st=1:d=1:silence=0.25` (both tested here 2026-10-24).

name: Custom envelopes with volume eval=frame
section: Envelopes, dynamics and synthesis building blocks
what: `volume` evaluates an expression per frame with `t`; doc example fades after 10 s over 5 s
how: `volume='if(lt(t,1),t,if(lt(t,4),1,max(1-(t-4),0)))':eval=frame` (tested here 2026-10-24); resolution is one audio frame (1024 samples by default for lavfi sources).

name: aevalsrc chirps and exponential pitch
section: Envelopes, dynamics and synthesis building blocks
what: `aevalsrc` evaluates per-sample expressions (`t`, `n`, `s`; functions from ffmpeg-utils like `exp`, `pow`, `mod`, `random`, `sgn`); a pitch law f(t) needs its integral as phase: linear f0+k·t → `sin(2*PI*(f0*t+k*t*t/2))`
how: `aevalsrc='0.5*sin(2*PI*(200*t+300*t*t))':d=3:s=44100` (200→2000 Hz; measured 390→1860 Hz across 6 windows, tested here 2026-10-24).

name: FM tones in aevalsrc (tested command only)
section: Envelopes, dynamics and synthesis building blocks
what: phase modulation inside `sin()` gives FM sidebands
how: `aevalsrc='0.5*sin(2*PI*500*t+4*exp(-t*3)*sin(2*PI*700*t))*exp(-t*2)':d=2:s=44100` (tested here 2026-10-24; no claim about how it sounds).

name: Heartbeat for tension
section: Envelopes, dynamics and synthesis building blocks
what: a synth heartbeat: simple sine/triangle, low-pass for warmth, realistic tempo 60-100 BPM; layer soft noise or reverb for realism
how: `ffmpeg -f lavfi -i "aevalsrc='0.9*sin(2*PI*55*t)*(exp(-mod(t,0.9)*25)+0.7*gt(mod(t,0.9),0.25)*exp(-(mod(t,0.9)-0.25)*25))':d=3.6:s=44100" -af lowpass=f=150 heartbeat.wav` (~67 BPM two-thump pattern; tested here 2026-10-24).

name: Shape a sound with firequalizer curves
section: Envelopes, dynamics and synthesis building blocks
what: `firequalizer` takes a gain curve via `gain_entry='entry(f,g);...'`
how: small-speaker shape `firequalizer=gain_entry='entry(0,-40);entry(250,-30);entry(500,0);entry(4000,0);entry(8000,-30)'` (tested here 2026-10-24).

name: Tilt a whole SFX darker/brighter
section: Envelopes, dynamics and synthesis building blocks
what: `tiltshelf` boosts/cuts lows and does the opposite to highs around a centre frequency (default 3 kHz), like hi-fi tone controls
how: `tiltshelf=g=6:f=1500` (tested here 2026-10-24).

name: Spectrogram to see a sweep
what: `showspectrumpic` renders a whole file's spectrum to one image (`fscale=log`, `start`/`stop` frequency range, `legend`)
how: `ffmpeg -i whoosh.wav -lavfi "showspectrumpic=s=640x320:legend=1" spec.png` (tested here 2026-10-24), then open the PNG with Read.

name: Waveform image to check attack and tail
what: `showwavespic` draws the whole waveform (`split_channels=1` per channel); `showwaves` makes a waveform video
