how: `ffmpeg -i hit.wav -lavfi "showwavespic=s=640x160:split_channels=1" wave.png`; `-filter_complex "showwaves=s=320x120:mode=cline:rate=30"` for video (both tested here 2026-10-24).

name: Measure pitch movement with an FFT
what: split the file into windows and take each window's FFT peak (tonal sounds) or spectral centroid (noise sweeps) to confirm a riser rises and a drop falls, since Claude can't listen
how: numpy/soundfile in `/home/user/tools/venv/bin/python`: `np.fft.rfft(seg*np.hanning(len(seg)))` per segment (used for every measured number in this file, 2026-10-24).

name: Peak and RMS of an SFX
what: `astats` prints per-channel and overall Peak/RMS levels and DC offset; `volumedetect` prints mean and max volume
how: `ffmpeg -i hit.wav -af astats -f null - 2>&1 | grep -E 'Peak level dB|RMS level dB'` and `-af volumedetect` (both tested here 2026-10-24).

name: Beat times in seconds straight from the tracker
what: `beat_track` returns tempo and beat positions; `units='time'` gives seconds instead of frames, ready for cut lists
how: `/home/user/tools/venv/bin/python -c "import librosa;y,sr=librosa.load('song.wav',sr=22050);t,b=librosa.beat.beat_track(y=y,sr=sr,units='time');print(t,b[:6])"` gave 79 beats starting 0.07, 0.464, 0.836 s on a 30 s CC0 lofi clip (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: librosa's BPM reading is coarse at the default hop
what: tempo is estimated from autocorrelation of the onset envelope, measured in frames; with the default hop (512 at 22.05 kHz) an exact 120 BPM click read 117.45, with a finer hop it read closer
how: `librosa.feature.tempo(y=y,sr=sr)` gave 117.45 and `librosa.feature.tempo(y=y,sr=sr,hop_length=128)` gave 120.19 on a synthetic 120 BPM click; `npx hyperframes audio click.wav --only bpm --json` gave 120 (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Tempo = first autocorrelation peak
what: the rhythm tutorial estimates tempo from the first prominent autocorrelation peak of the onset envelope (not lag 0): a peak at about 0.4 s is 2.5 cycles/s = 150 BPM
how: BPM = 60 / lag-of-first-peak; read `librosa.feature.tempogram` to see those lags over time

name: Three detectors, three tempos: check before you cut
what: on the same 30 s lofi clip `beat_track` said 161.5, `feature.tempo` 107.67 and HyperFrames 104.8 BPM; HyperFrames' film guide warns that on calm music a tracker invents a metronome, often at double tempo
how: run both `librosa.beat.beat_track` and `npx hyperframes audio <track> --only bpm --json`; if they disagree, cut on phrases and energy changes instead (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Steer half/double tempo with start_bpm
what: `start_bpm` is the tracker's initial tempo guess
how: on the lofi clip `start_bpm=60` or `90` gave 78.3 BPM and `120` or `180` gave 161.5 BPM: try the guess that matches what you hear (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Cap the tempo with max_tempo
what: `feature.tempo` only estimates below `max_tempo` when given
how: `librosa.feature.tempo(y=y,sr=sr,max_tempo=100)` moved the lofi reading from 107.67 to 78.3 BPM (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: A tempo prior instead of a guess
what: `prior` takes a scipy distribution over BPM and overrides `start_bpm`; the plp docs show a log-normal prior centred on 120
how: `pr=scipy.stats.lognorm(loc=np.log(120),scale=120,s=1); librosa.beat.beat_track(y=y,sr=sr,prior=pr)` gave 78.3 BPM on the lofi clip (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Known BPM: only place the beats
what: pass `bpm=` and the tracker uses it instead of estimating, so you only get the beat phase
how: `librosa.beat.beat_track(y=y,sr=sr,bpm=85,units='time')` returned beats at 0.07, 0.836, 1.602 s (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: trim=False when the music never goes silent
what: by default beat_track assumes silence at the end and trims the last beats; the dynamic-tempo tutorial sets `trim=False` for audio that runs to the end
how: `librosa.beat.beat_track(y=y,sr=sr,trim=False)`; on a 16 s click both settings gave 31 beats here, so compare counts on your track (tested here 2026-10-24)
refs: librosa tutorial "Beat tracking with time-varying tempo", https://librosa.org/doc/latest/auto_tutorials/03-advanced/plot_dynamic_beat.html, checked 2026-10-24

name: Beats as a per-frame on/off array
what: `sparse=False` returns a boolean array (needed for multi-channel input)
how: `librosa.beat.beat_track(y=y,sr=sr,sparse=False)` gave 1292 frames with 79 True (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Track beats through tempo changes
what: estimate a tempo per frame with `aggregate=None` (wider `std_bpm`) and feed that array to `beat_track(bpm=...)`; the tutorial shows a static tempo drifting off an accelerating beat
how: `td=librosa.feature.tempo(y=y,sr=sr,aggregate=None,std_bpm=4); librosa.beat.beat_track(y=y,sr=sr,units='time',bpm=td,trim=False)` (tested here 2026-10-24)
refs: librosa tutorial "Beat tracking with time-varying tempo", https://librosa.org/doc/latest/auto_tutorials/03-advanced/plot_dynamic_beat.html, checked 2026-10-24

name: Autocorrelation window size changes the answer
what: `ac_size` is the autocorrelation window in seconds (8 s default)
how: on the lofi clip `ac_size=4` gave 161.5 BPM and `ac_size=16` gave 103.36 BPM: use a longer window for a steadier global tempo (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: PLP beats for drifting tempo or streaming
what: predominant local pulse finds a locally stable tempo per frame; the docs prefer it over beat_track when tempo varies a lot, and its local maxima are beat estimates
how: `p=librosa.beat.plp(onset_envelope=oe,sr=sr); bp=np.flatnonzero(librosa.util.localmax(p))` found 86 pulses in 30 s (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Limit PLP to a tempo range
what: `tempo_min`/`tempo_max` bound the permissible tempo (30-300 default)
how: `librosa.beat.plp(y=y,sr=sr,tempo_min=60,tempo_max=100)` gave 40 pulses with a median spacing of 0.766 s on the lofi clip (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Median-aggregated onset envelope
what: the beat_track docs build the envelope with `aggregate=np.median` across frequency and pass it in
how: `oe=librosa.onset.onset_strength(y=y,sr=sr,aggregate=np.median); librosa.beat.beat_track(onset_envelope=oe,sr=sr)` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Tempogram to see tempo over time
what: local autocorrelation of the onset envelope; default window 384 frames is about 8.9 s
how: `librosa.feature.tempogram(y=y,sr=sr)` gave a 384 x 1292 matrix for 30 s (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Let the owner hear the beat grid
what: the rhythm tutorial sonifies beats as a click track and plays song left, clicks right
how: `c=librosa.clicks(times=b,sr=sr,length=len(y)); sf.write('check.wav',np.stack([y,c]).T,sr)` wrote a stereo check file (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Click sound you can pick out
what: `click_freq` (default 1 kHz) and `click_duration` (default 0.1 s) set the click; the dynamic-beat tutorial uses 660 Hz and 0.25 s
how: `librosa.clicks(times=b,sr=sr,click_freq=660,click_duration=0.25,length=len(y))` (tested here 2026-10-24)
refs: librosa tutorial "Beat tracking with time-varying tempo", https://librosa.org/doc/latest/auto_tutorials/03-advanced/plot_dynamic_beat.html, checked 2026-10-24

name: Synthetic click track at an exact BPM
what: aevalsrc evaluates an expression per sample; a decaying 60 Hz burst every 60/BPM s makes a test beat for checking tools
how: `ffmpeg -f lavfi -i "aevalsrc=exprs='0.8*sin(2*PI*60*t)*exp(-30*mod(t\,0.5))':s=44100:d=16" -ac 2 click120.wav` (HyperFrames read it as 120 BPM) (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Onset times in seconds
what: `onset_detect` peak-picks the onset strength envelope; `units='time'` returns seconds
how: `librosa.onset.onset_detect(y=y,sr=sr,units='time')` found 134 onsets in the 30 s clip (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Backtrack onsets before slicing
what: `backtrack=True` rolls each onset back to the preceding energy minimum, "primarily useful when using onsets as slice points"
how: `librosa.onset.onset_detect(y=y,sr=sr,units='time',backtrack=True)` moved onsets a median 46 ms earlier on the lofi clip (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Backtrack to RMS minima
what: `onset_backtrack(events, energy)` matches events to the nearest preceding minimum of any energy function you give it
how: `rms=librosa.feature.rms(S=np.abs(librosa.stft(y)))[0]; librosa.onset.onset_backtrack(ev,rms)` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Onsets per frequency band
what: `onset_strength_multi` computes one envelope per channel range of spectrogram bins (`channels` = bin boundaries)
how: `librosa.onset.onset_strength_multi(y=y,sr=sr,channels=[0,8,32,128])` gave 3 envelopes (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: onset_detect is not a pure peak picker
what: the docs note it may favour earlier points on the rising edge of a peak; naive local maxima give far more events than really occur
how: use `onset_detect` (tuned peak_pick) rather than `librosa.util.localmax(onset_env)` for cut points

name: Kick-band onsets in HyperFrames
what: `hyperframes audio --band lo,hi` measures onsets only in that band, and `--threshold` (0-1, default 0.1) sets the strength floor
how: `npx hyperframes audio music.wav --only onsets --band 40,150 --threshold 0.3 --json` found 42 low-band hits in 30 s (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Fewer false onsets on vibrato
what: onset_strength's `max_size` applies a local max filter across frequency (Böck & Widmer vibrato suppression); 1 disables it
how: `oe=librosa.onset.onset_strength(y=y,sr=sr,max_size=3)`; on a CC0 tabla/synth clip onsets went from 80 (max_size=1) to 75 (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Energy vs spectral-flux onsets in HyperFrames
what: `hyperframes audio --onset-method` is spectral-flux by default or energy
how: on the same 20 s CC0 clip spectral-flux found 95 onsets and `--onset-method energy` 201: compare both before choosing hit points (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Studio beat file for the project's music
what: `npx hyperframes beats` finds the `<audio>` marked `data-timeline-role="music"` (or an id with music/bgm/soundtrack), tracks beats with ffmpeg and writes `beats/<audio-path>.json`; it fails and writes nothing without a steady beat
how: in a test project it wrote 51 beats (`time`, `strength`) at 104.8 BPM (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: A BPM curve, not just one number
what: `hyperframes audio --only bpm` returns a global value plus a curve point every 4 s
how: `npx hyperframes audio music.wav --only bpm,downbeats --json` gave 104.8 with points 104.3-105.4 (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Downbeats come with a confidence
what: the same call returns downbeat times, the meter and a confidence; on the lofi clip it said meter 4, confidence "low" (signal method; the beat-this/apple-mu providers were unavailable)
how: cut only on downbeats marked confident, otherwise follow sections (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Song sections from HyperFrames
what: `--only sections,onsets,moments` finds sections; the music-video guide makes each section a chapter (intro, verse, chorus, bridge, outro)
how: on the lofi clip it returned spans A 0-6.145 s and B 6.145-30 s, snapped to beats (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Snap planned cuts to the nearest tracked beat
what: read the beats JSON and move each rough cut time to the closest beat
how: `b=[x['time'] for x in json.load(open('beats/assets/music.wav.json'))['beats']]; [min(b,key=lambda t:abs(t-c)) for c in cuts]` moved 2.0/5.3/9.9 s to 1.955/5.565/9.925 s (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: k-section split of a song
what: `segment.agglomerative` partitions features into k contiguous segments and returns left boundaries (always starting at 0)
how: `C=librosa.feature.chroma_cqt(y=y,sr=sr); librosa.frames_to_time(librosa.segment.agglomerative(C,4),sr=sr)` gave 0, 2.95, 24.17, 27.14 s (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Laplacian structure segmentation (McFee & Ellis)
what: the tutorial beat-synchronises a CQT, builds a recurrence matrix (`width=3` blocks links within a bar, `mode='affinity'`), median-filters it with `timelag_filter`, combines it with an MFCC path graph, then clusters eigenvectors with k-means; boundaries are where the label changes
how: follow the tutorial code; `librosa.segment.recurrence_matrix(C,mode='affinity',sym=True)` ran here (sklearn 1.9.1 is in the venv) (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Beat-synchronous features
what: `util.sync` aggregates feature frames between beat positions so each column is one beat
how: `librosa.util.sync(librosa.feature.chroma_cqt(y=y,sr=sr),beats,aggregate=np.median)` turned 1292 frames into 81 beat columns (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Include frame 0 in beat lists
what: `util.fix_frames(beats, x_min=0)` adds the start frame so segments cover the whole song (the segmentation tutorial does this for beat times)

name: Find the loudest stretch
what: `feature.rms` gives frame energy; `times_like` maps frames to seconds
how: `rms=librosa.feature.rms(y=y)[0]; librosa.times_like(rms,sr=sr)[rms.argmax()]` gave 27.45 s on the lofi clip (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Picture of the whole song
what: showwavespic renders the waveform as one image; `split_channels=1` draws each channel
how: `ffmpeg -i song.wav -filter_complex showwavespic=s=1200x200:split_channels=1 -frames:v 1 wave.png` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Make quiet passages visible in the waveform
what: showwavespic `scale` can be lin, log, sqrt or cbrt (default linear), `filter` average or peak
how: `showwavespic=s=1200x240:colors=white:scale=sqrt` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Spectrum picture with a legend
what: showspectrumpic draws the whole file's spectrogram with time/frequency axes when `legend=1`
how: `ffmpeg -i song.wav -lavfi showspectrumpic=s=800x400:legend=1 spec.png` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Constant-Q view of notes
what: showcqt renders a musical-pitch (CQT) spectrum video; librosa's harmony tutorial explains CQT bins are geometrically spaced like notes
how: `ffmpeg -i song.wav -t 3 -filter_complex showcqt=s=640x360 -an cqt.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Find gaps and stops
what: silencedetect logs silence_start/end when level stays under the noise tolerance (default -60 dB) for at least d seconds (default 2)
how: `ffmpeg -i in.wav -af silencedetect=n=-50dB:d=1 -f null -` reported 20 to 25 s on a padded clip (prints at info level, so don't add `-v error`) (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Non-silent intervals in Python
what: `effects.split` returns (start, end) sample pairs of non-silent audio, `top_db` below the reference peak
how: `librosa.effects.split(y,top_db=40)` returned 0-20.06 s on a clip with 5 s of padding (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Trim a track's silent head and tail
what: `effects.trim` cuts segments `top_db` below the max RMS and returns the kept index; a fully uniform or silent signal is not trimmed with the default ref
how: `yt,idx=librosa.effects.trim(y,top_db=40)` cut 25.0 s to 20.06 s (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Music-video tells to avoid
section: Structure rules for cutting picture to a song (repo guides)
what: the same treatment for more than about 6 s, a spectrum bar or waveform as the main picture, and every cut on every beat
how: vary treatment per section; cut per strong beat only in rhythmic sections

name: Hits start early, reactions late
section: Structure rules for cutting picture to a song (repo guides)
what: a move that must land on a hit starts 40-190 ms early; a reaction starts 0-45 ms after; the hit itself is a 0 ms `tl.set`, because easing a hit kills it
how: `tl.set(el,{opacity:1},beat)` for the hit, `tl.to(...,beat-0.12)` for the approach

name: Words hold a beat, footage follows the section
section: Structure rules for cutting picture to a song (repo guides)
what: a word meant to be read holds at least one beat; on rhythmic sections one clip per strong beat, on calm ones one slow push from 1.0 to 1.08
how: schedule captions in whole beats from the beats JSON

name: Enter at the strongest bar, end on a bar line
section: Structure rules for cutting picture to a song (repo guides)
what: start music at the track's strongest bar rather than a quiet intro, and end on a bar line with a short fade under the end card
how: pick the entry with `--only sections` and set `data-media-start` on the `<audio>`

name: Test the opening against later 5-second sections
section: Structure rules for cutting picture to a song (repo guides)
what: for short videos don't assume the file's start is the best edit point; if it opens with a quiet build, trim from a stronger later section with a short fade-in and longer fade-out, and make sure the music covers the whole cut with no silent tail
how: re-check whenever the composition length changes

name: Library loops under a film
section: Structure rules for cutting picture to a song (repo guides)
what: library music often comes as 15-30 s loops: loop the bed to the film with a 0.4 s fade-in and a 1.5 s fade-out
how: `-stream_loop -1` or `aloop` to length, then `afade=t=in:d=0.4` and a 1.5 s `afade=t=out`

name: Sample-exact trim
section: Cutting and fitting music to length (ffmpeg, pydub)
what: atrim's `start_sample`/`end_sample` count samples, unlike `start`/`end` which read timestamps; add asetpts to restart timestamps at zero
how: `ffmpeg -i song.wav -af "atrim=start_sample=44100:end_sample=132300,asetpts=PTS-STARTPTS" bar.wav` gave exactly 2.000 s (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Chain atrims to AND their limits
section: Cutting and fitting music to length (ffmpeg, pydub)
what: with several start/end options atrim is greedy and keeps samples matching any of them; to keep only what matches all, chain several atrim filters
how: `atrim=start=10,atrim=end=20` rather than mixing both forms in one atrim

name: Fast window cut with input seeking
section: Cutting and fitting music to length (ffmpeg, pydub)
what: `-ss` before `-i` seeks the input; when transcoding, accurate seek (default) decodes and drops the part before the position
how: `ffmpeg -ss 12.5 -t 6 -i song.wav part.wav` gave 6.000 s (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Grab the real ending
section: Cutting and fitting music to length (ffmpeg, pydub)
what: `-sseof` seeks relative to the end of file (negative = earlier)
how: `ffmpeg -sseof -8 -i song.wav ending.wav` gave the last 8.000 s, ready to backtime the button (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Remove bars from the middle in one command
section: Cutting and fitting music to length (ffmpeg, pydub)
what: trim the two parts you keep and join them with a short equal-power crossfade
how: `ffmpeg -i song.wav -filter_complex "[0]atrim=0:8,asetpts=PTS-STARTPTS[a];[0]atrim=16:30,asetpts=PTS-STARTPTS[b];[a][b]acrossfade=d=0.05:c1=qsin:c2=qsin" short.wav` turned 30 s into 21.95 s (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Hard join with the concat filter
section: Cutting and fitting music to length (ffmpeg, pydub)
what: for audio-only segments set `v=0:a=1`; all segments must start at timestamp 0
how: `ffmpeg -i a.wav -i b.wav -filter_complex "[0][1]concat=n=2:v=0:a=1" ab.wav` gave 50.0 s from 30 + 20 s (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: End after whole bars with a fade
section: Cutting and fitting music to length (ffmpeg, pydub)
what: at 105 BPM a 4/4 bar is 240/105 = 2.2857 s, so 10 bars end at 22.857 s; fade inside the last bar
how: `ffmpeg -i song.wav -af "atrim=end=22.857,afade=t=out:st=20.571:d=2.286" out.wav` gave 22.857 s (tested here 2026-10-24)
refs: Wikipedia "Film score" (written click 60/bpm x beats), https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Film_score, checked 2026-10-24

name: Pad music to the exact film length
section: Cutting and fitting music to length (ffmpeg, pydub)
what: apad `whole_dur` sets a minimum total duration, adding silence only if needed
how: `ffmpeg -i song2.wav -af apad=whole_dur=25 out.wav` made a 20 s track exactly 25.0 s (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Strip silence before the first note
section: Cutting and fitting music to length (ffmpeg, pydub)
what: silenceremove with `start_periods=1` trims until non-silence; `start_silence` keeps that much silence
how: `silenceremove=start_periods=1:start_threshold=-50dB` cut 3.5 s of lead-in (23.5 to 20.0 s); adding `:start_silence=0.2` left 20.2 s (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Start a cue at a hit point
section: Cutting and fitting music to length (ffmpeg, pydub)
what: adelay with `all=1` delays every channel by the same milliseconds
how: `ffmpeg -i cue.wav -af adelay=delays=3500:all=1 cue_at_3500ms.wav` (20 s became 23.5 s) (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Music ends with the picture
section: Cutting and fitting music to length (ffmpeg, pydub)
what: `-shortest` stops when the shortest stream ends
how: `ffmpeg -i video.mp4 -i song.wav -map 0:v -map 1:a -c:v copy -af "afade=t=out:st=2:d=1" -shortest out.mp4` ended at the 3 s video length (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Millisecond slicing in pydub
section: Cutting and fitting music to length (ffmpeg, pydub)
what: AudioSegment slices in ms: `s[:5000]` first 5 s, `s[-5000:]` last 5 s, `s[::5000]` 5-second chunks
how: `list(AudioSegment.from_file('song.wav')[::5000])` gave 6 slices of a 30 s file (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Silence as a building block
section: Cutting and fitting music to length (ffmpeg, pydub)
what: `AudioSegment.silent(duration=ms)` makes silence to pad or space cues
how: `AudioSegment.silent(duration=1500)+cue` gave 21500 ms from a 20 s cue (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Measure a track's lead-in
section: Cutting and fitting music to length (ffmpeg, pydub)
what: `silence.detect_leading_silence` returns the ms before the first sound above the threshold
how: on 800 ms of silence + music it returned 790 (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Silent and sounding ranges in ms
section: Cutting and fitting music to length (ffmpeg, pydub)
what: `detect_silence` / `detect_nonsilent` return [start, end] lists for a minimum length and threshold
how: `silence.detect_silence(seg,min_silence_len=1000,silence_thresh=-50)` returned [[20000, 25000]] (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Split a medley at its gaps
section: Cutting and fitting music to length (ffmpeg, pydub)
what: `split_on_silence` cuts at silences and can keep a little silence on each piece
how: `silence.split_on_silence(seg,min_silence_len=1000,silence_thresh=-50,keep_silence=200)` split two tracks separated by 1.5 s gaps into 2 pieces (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Splice at the most similar waveform point
section: Cutting and fitting music to length (ffmpeg, pydub)
what: SoX `splice` cross-fades the join and compares waveforms to find the best joining point within an excess (default 5 ms) and leeway (default 5 ms)
how: needs sox (missing): `sox song.wav p1.wav trim 0 30.130; sox song.wav p2.wav trim 1:03.422; sox p1.wav p2.wav out.wav splice 30.130` (the manual's cut-a-verse example)

name: Radio-spot fitting is time-stretching
section: Cutting and fitting music to length (ffmpeg, pydub)
what: time stretching is used to fit radio commercials and TV ad audio into exactly 30 or 60 s, or longer material into a slot
how: stretch by source/target duration (see the atempo fit below) only when trimming bars can't hit the length
refs: Wikipedia "Audio time stretching and pitch scaling", https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Audio_time_stretching_and_pitch_scaling, checked 2026-10-24

name: Loop one bar a set number of times
what: aloop's `size` is in samples and `loop` is the number of extra repeats
how: a 4 s bar at 44.1 kHz is 176400 samples: `ffmpeg -i song.wav -af "atrim=start=0:end=4,asetpts=N/SR/TB,aloop=loop=3:size=176400" loop.wav` gave 16.0 s (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Endless loop cut to length
what: `loop=-1` loops forever; follow with atrim to stop it
how: `aloop=loop=-1:size=88200:start=44100,atrim=duration=10` gave 10.0 s of a 2 s segment starting at 1 s (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Loop from a time instead of a sample
what: aloop's `time` sets the loop start in seconds, used only when `start=-1`
how: `aloop=loop=2:size=88200:start=-1:time=3` repeated 2 s from 3 s twice (30 s became 34 s) (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Loop a whole file without re-encoding
what: `-stream_loop N` loops an input N times (-1 = infinite)
how: `ffmpeg -stream_loop 2 -i bed.wav -c copy bed3.wav` made 60 s from 20 s (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Loop the bed under any video length
what: infinite `-stream_loop` on the music input plus `-shortest`
how: `ffmpeg -i video.mp4 -stream_loop -1 -i bed.wav -map 0:v -map 1:a -c:v copy -shortest out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Crossfaded loop seams use constant-gain curves
what: SoX's splice table: for correlated audio (the same material) use constant-gain fades (t linear or h half-cosine); quarter-cosine (constant power) is for uncorrelated audio
how: `[0][1]acrossfade=d=0.2:c1=hsin:c2=hsin[a];[a][2]acrossfade=d=0.2:c1=hsin:c2=hsin` joined three 2 s copies into 5.6 s (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Repeat a segment in pydub
what: `segment * 3` repeats it
how: a 20 s bed `*3` gave 60000 ms (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Loop a pattern under a track until it ends
what: `overlay(..., loop=True)` repeats the overlaid sound from `position` to the end; the result keeps the base length
how: `base.overlay(pattern,loop=True)` stayed 30000 ms (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Play a pattern N times from a point
what: `overlay(..., times=N, position=ms)` repeats N times starting at position, still truncated to the base
how: `base.overlay(pattern,times=3,position=4000)` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: How the repo's generated bed loops
what: the media-use BGM engine generates one seed clip (at most about 28-30 s) and crossfade-loops it up to the target length, or trims down, to avoid per-segment seams
how: for a long film, loop one good clip instead of generating many

name: Two-track crossfade with exponential curves
what: acrossfade fades over the end of the first stream; the docs' first example uses `c1=exp:c2=exp`
how: `ffmpeg -i a.wav -i b.wav -filter_complex acrossfade=d=4:c1=exp:c2=exp ab.wav` gave 46 s from 30 + 20 s (4 s overlap) (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Fade out, then fade in, no overlap
what: `o=0` (overlap off) plays the faded end and the faded start back to back
how: `acrossfade=d=4:o=0:c1=exp:c2=exp` gave 50 s, the full 30 + 20 s (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Check the local ffmpeg before using new doc options
what: the online docs list acrossfade `n`/`inputs` for crossfading many inputs, but ffmpeg 6.1.1 here rejects it ("Option not found"); chain pairs instead
how: `ffmpeg -h filter=acrossfade` to see options; `[0][1]acrossfade=d=2[a];[a][2]acrossfade=d=2` joined three files to 62 s (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Crossfade length in samples
what: `nb_samples`/`ns` (default 44100) sets the crossfade when no duration is given
how: `acrossfade=ns=88200` overlapped 2 s at 44.1 kHz (30 + 20 s became 48 s) (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Keep the outgoing track at full level
what: curve `nofade` leaves that input as-is while the other fades
how: `acrossfade=d=3:c1=nofade:c2=tri` brings the new track in under an unchanged old one (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Constant power for different songs, constant gain for the same song
what: SoX's table: t (linear) and h (half-cosine) are constant-gain fades for correlated audio; q (quarter-cosine) is constant power for uncorrelated audio. Measured ffmpeg fade-outs at the midpoint: qsin 0.707 (-3.0 dB), hsin and tri 0.500 (-6.0 dB)
how: two different tracks: `c1=qsin:c2=qsin`; the same track to itself: `c1=hsin:c2=hsin` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Square-root curve is the other -3 dB fade
what: `squ` also sits at 0.707 at the midpoint but holds more at the end (0.866 / 0.707 / 0.500 at 25/50/75 %, vs qsin 0.924 / 0.707 / 0.383)
how: measured with `afade=t=out:st=0:d=1:curve=squ` on a constant signal (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Curves that hold the old track up
what: measured fade-out gain at the midpoint: log -0.5 dB, quatr -1.5 dB, cbr -2.0 dB, ipar -2.5 dB; they drop late
how: pick one for c1 when the outgoing music must stay present until the end of the crossfade, e.g. `c1=log:c2=qsin` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Curves that get the old track out fast
what: measured midpoint gain: exp -50 dB, quat -24 dB, cub -18 dB, qua and hsin2 -12 dB; the docs' acrossfade examples use exp
how: `c1=cub` clears space quickly for a new track's downbeat (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: S-shaped crossfades
what: desi (double-exponential sigmoid) and losi (logistic sigmoid) cross at 0.5 like linear but are flatter at both ends: 0.938/0.500/0.062 and 0.882/0.500/0.118 at 25/50/75 %, against tri 0.75/0.5/0.25
how: `acrossfade=d=2:c1=desi:c2=desi` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Dip the music instead of fading it out
what: afade's `silence` sets the final gain of a fade-out (default 0), `unity` the starting gain
how: `afade=t=out:st=5:d=1:silence=0.3` held the music at 0.30 of its level after 6 s (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Sample-counted fades
what: afade takes `start_sample`/`nb_samples` as well as times
how: `afade=t=in:ss=0:ns=4410` fades in over exactly 100 ms at 44.1 kHz (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Bass swap during a transition
what: Wikipedia's beatmatching notes a smoother transition when the low frequencies are taken out of one song while the other's are kept
how: high-pass the outgoing tail, then crossfade: `[0]atrim=0:26,asetpts=PTS-STARTPTS[a1];[0]atrim=26:30,asetpts=PTS-STARTPTS,highpass=f=200[a2];[a1][a2]concat=n=2:v=0:a=1[A];[A][1]acrossfade=d=4:c1=qsin:c2=qsin` (ran; listen-check by the owner) (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Match tempos before the overlap
what: beatmatching adjusts the incoming track's tempo so beats (and usually bars) coincide; mismatched BPMs make one song sound too fast or slow
how: `atempo=<target BPM>/<source BPM>`: a 126 BPM click with `atempo=120/126` then read the same as the 120 BPM click in librosa (117.45, its grid value) (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: pydub joins crossfade 100 ms by default
what: `append()` uses a 100 ms crossfade to avoid pops; `crossfade=0` or `a + b` joins with none
how: 30 s + 20 s gave 49900 ms with `append`, 45000 ms with `crossfade=5000`, 50000 ms with `+` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Crossfades in HyperFrames are two tracks
what: a crossfade is two clips on different tracks that overlap, each with a fade (`data-fade-in`, `data-fade-out` in seconds)
how: put the second `<audio>` on another `data-track-index` starting before the first ends, fade-out on the first and fade-in on the second

name: Join AI song parts at instrumental gaps
what: the website-promo pipeline joins separately generated song parts at instrumental gaps with 1.5 s acrossfades
how: `acrossfade=d=1.5` at a gap found in the parts' vocal timing

name: Mix in key
what: harmonic mixing matches keys to avoid dissonance: same key, relative keys, or keys in a dominant/subdominant relationship; the Camelot wheel is based on the circle of fifths
how: before a long musical crossfade, compare the two tracks' keys

name: Camelot codes: number and letter
what: each key gets a number (its place on a 12-step wheel) and a letter: A = minor, B = major
how: note each track's code next to its BPM in the edit notes

name: Safe Camelot moves
what: from 8A try 8A, 7A, 9A or 8B: same code, one step either way with the same letter, or the same number with the other letter
how: shortlist next tracks that way, then audition the actual overlap; key compatibility does not guarantee the blend

name: One step clockwise = up a fifth
what: moving 8B to 9B (C major to G major) shifts the key centre up a perfect fifth, the strongest interval connection; anticlockwise (9B to 8B) is a fourth, almost as strong
how: prefer these for a lift that still sounds connected

name: Relative major/minor swap changes mood, not notes
what: 8B to 8A (C major to A minor) uses the same notes; relative keys share a key signature and the minor tonic is three semitones below the major's
how: use the swap to go happy to sad (or back) at a story turn

name: Energy boost (+2) and Jaws (-5) moves
what: two steps up on the same side lifts energy (a whole-tone rise, sometimes a little clashy); the Jaws mix, 5 steps anticlockwise (one semitone up, e.g. 1A to 8A), is dissonant and only for deliberate surprise
how: use +2 for a final-chorus lift; test any Jaws move by ear first

name: Shift a track into a compatible key
what: DJ software can pitch-shift a track to a key compatible with the playing one
how: shift by the semitone difference with `rubberband=pitch=2^(n/12)` (see pitch skills below)
refs: Wikipedia "Audio time stretching and pitch scaling", https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Audio_time_stretching_and_pitch_scaling, checked 2026-10-24

name: Slow a track down, pitch kept
section: Time-stretch and retime without pitch change
what: atempo changes tempo in the 0.5-100 range
how: `ffmpeg -i song.wav -af atempo=0.8 slow.wav` turned 30.0 s into 37.49 s (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Above 2x, chain atempo
section: Time-stretch and retime without pitch change
what: atempo over 2 skips samples instead of blending them; chain instances to reach the product tempo
how: `atempo=sqrt(3),atempo=sqrt(3)` (both this and `atempo=3` gave about 10.0 s from 30 s; the docs offer the chain for when skipped samples are a concern) (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Fit a cue to an exact duration
section: Time-stretch and retime without pitch change
what: tempo factor = current length / wanted length
how: `ffmpeg -i song.wav -af atempo=30/27.5 fit.wav` gave 27.507 s from 30 s (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Change tempo at a set time
section: Time-stretch and retime without pitch change
what: asendcmd can send atempo a new `tempo` mid-file (the docs' example changes it at 4.0 s)
how: `ffmpeg -i song.wav -af "asendcmd=c='4.0 atempo tempo 1.5',atempo" out.wav` gave 21.31 s (4 s + 26 s/1.5) (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Rubber Band tempo in ffmpeg
section: Time-stretch and retime without pitch change
what: the rubberband filter (librubberband) sets a tempo scale factor (0.01-100 locally)
how: `ffmpeg -i song.wav -af rubberband=tempo=1.1 out.wav` gave 27.27 s from 30 s (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Rubber Band tempo change mid-file
section: Time-stretch and retime without pitch change
what: the filter accepts `tempo` and `pitch` commands
how: `ffmpeg -i song.wav -af "asendcmd=c='10.0 rubberband tempo 1.2',rubberband" out.wav` gave 26.68 s (10 s + 20 s/1.2) (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Drum-friendly Rubber Band settings
section: Time-stretch and retime without pitch change
what: the Rubber Band CLI's crispness level 6 equals no phase lamination + short window and "may be good for drums"; the ffmpeg filter exposes `phase=independent` and `window=short`
how: `rubberband=tempo=0.95:phase=independent:window=short` (the options ran here; the CLI hint is for the R2 engine) (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Piano-friendly Rubber Band settings
section: Time-stretch and retime without pitch change
what: crispness 1 equals soft detector + no lamination + long window, "for piano"
how: `rubberband=tempo=0.95:detector=soft:phase=independent:window=long` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Percussive transient detector
section: Time-stretch and retime without pitch change
what: `detector` can be compound (default), percussive or soft
how: `rubberband=tempo=1.05:detector=percussive` on a 16 s click gave 15.24 s (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Smooth transients for pads
section: Time-stretch and retime without pitch change
what: `transients` can be crisp (default), mixed or smooth; `smoothing=on` adds window presum and time-domain smoothing (CLI `--smoothing`)
how: `rubberband=tempo=0.9:transients=smooth` or `:smoothing=on` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Keep the stereo image locked
section: Time-stretch and retime without pitch change
what: `channels=together` processes channels together (default apart)
how: `rubberband=tempo=1.05:channels=together` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Stretch to an exact output length with the CLI
section: Time-stretch and retime without pitch change
what: Rubber Band's `-D X` stretches or squashes to make output X seconds long; `-T X:Y` changes tempo from X to Y BPM
how: needs rubberband CLI (missing): `rubberband -D 27.5 song.wav out.wav` or `rubberband -T 126:120 in.wav out.wav`

name: Warp music onto hit points with a time map
section: Time-stretch and retime without pitch change
what: `-M file` holds lines of "source-frame target-frame" pairs, fixing points inside the audio for a varying stretch; an overall -t/-T/-D is still required
how: needs rubberband CLI (missing): write sample pairs (beat sample -> hit sample) and run `rubberband -M map.txt -D <len> in.wav out.wav`

name: R3 "finer" engine
section: Time-stretch and retime without pitch change
what: `-3` selects the R3 engine, which "almost always produces better results than the R2 engine" at higher CPU load; `--centre-focus` preserves centre material in stereo
how: needs rubberband CLI (missing): `rubberband -3 --centre-focus -t 1.1 in.wav out.wav`

name: Rubber Band licence
section: Time-stretch and retime without pitch change
what: the library is GPL; distributing it inside a proprietary app needs a commercial licence
how: the commercial licence is needed only to distribute it in a proprietary application, so never bundle it into a closed product we hand over

name: Time-stretch in Python
section: Time-stretch and retime without pitch change
what: `librosa.effects.time_stretch(y, rate=)` speeds up for rate > 1; its docs point to pyrubberband for higher quality
how: `librosa.effects.time_stretch(y,rate=1.25)` turned 30 s into 24 s (librosa 1.0 warns that `hop_length`/`n_fft` are deprecated there) (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Align two performances of the same music
section: Time-stretch and retime without pitch change
what: chroma features + DTW give a warping path between versions played at different tempos
how: `D,wp=librosa.sequence.dtw(X=chroma1,Y=chroma2,metric='cosine')`; on a clip vs its 1.2x stretch the path slope was 0.826 (expected 0.833) (tested here 2026-10-24)
refs: librosa tutorial "Music Synchronization with Dynamic Time Warping", https://librosa.org/doc/latest/auto_tutorials/03-advanced/plot_music_sync.html, checked 2026-10-24

name: Non-uniform stretch along the DTW path
section: Time-stretch and retime without pitch change
what: the sync tutorial turns the path into a timing grid with `path_to_steps` and phase-vocodes the slow version onto it (some audible artifacts)
how: `steps=librosa.sequence.path_to_steps(wp); st=librosa.phase_vocoder(librosa.stft(x1,hop_length=1024),t_out=steps); librosa.istft(st,hop_length=1024,length=len(x2))` produced 8.33 s matching the target (tested here 2026-10-24)
refs: librosa tutorial "Music Synchronization with Dynamic Time Warping", https://librosa.org/doc/latest/auto_tutorials/03-advanced/plot_music_sync.html, checked 2026-10-24

name: Retime in HyperFrames without rendering audio
section: Time-stretch and retime without pitch change
what: `data-playback-rate` is a constant speed 0.1-10 with pitch preserved; a `rate` lane in `data-automation` makes a speed ramp
how: `<audio data-playback-rate="0.95" ...>`; give a video and its paired audio the same value

name: How far a stretch can go
section: Time-stretch and retime without pitch change
what: Corel VideoStudio's help: stretching an audio clip by 50-150 % leaves it undistorted, beyond that it may distort; Audacity's high-quality Change Tempo suits small to moderate changes only
how: if you need more than that, cut bars instead of stretching

name: Why stretched drums smear
section: Time-stretch and retime without pitch change
what: phase-vocoder stretching handles sinusoids well but early implementations smeared transients ("phasey"), and a residual smearing remains; time-domain SOLA fails when it mis-estimates the period of complex material like orchestral pieces
how: listen to drum hits and orchestral passages first after any stretch
refs: Wikipedia "Audio time stretching and pitch scaling", https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Audio_time_stretching_and_pitch_scaling, checked 2026-10-24

name: Extreme slow-down as a texture
section: Time-stretch and retime without pitch change
what: Paulstretch slows audio by extreme amounts without pitch change; a time resolution of 0.25 s is good for most music, over 2 s smears a song into a texture
how: needs Audacity Paulstretch (missing)

name: WSOLA tempo tuned for music
section: Time-stretch and retime without pitch change
what: SoX `tempo -m` optimises segment/search/overlap for music; default segment 82 ms suits small tempo changes, about 41 ms suits larger ones like 2x
how: needs sox (missing): `sox in.wav out.wav tempo -m 1.1`

name: Tape-speed change (pitch and tempo together)
section: Time-stretch and retime without pitch change
what: changing playback speed by sample-rate conversion scales pitch with speed (slower = lower). asetrate relabels the rate without touching samples
how: `ffmpeg -i song.wav -af asetrate=44100*0.9,aresample=44100 slow_low.wav` gave 33.33 s and a lower pitch (tested here 2026-10-24)
refs: Wikipedia "Audio time stretching and pitch scaling", https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Audio_time_stretching_and_pitch_scaling, checked 2026-10-24

name: Retime the MIDI, not the audio
section: Time-stretch and retime without pitch change
what: for our own MIDI-based tracks change the `set_tempo` meta message and re-render, so the notes are played at the new tempo instead of time-stretching audio
how: `for msg in track: if msg.type=='set_tempo': msg.tempo=mido.bpm2tempo(96)` took `romance-bollywood-72bpm.mid` from 21.667 s to 16.25 s, then `fluidsynth -ni -q -g 0.7 -r 48000 -F out.wav /usr/share/sounds/sf2/FluidR3_GM.sf2 out.mid` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Slow-downs by rate change lose clarity
section: Time-stretch and retime without pitch change
what: when resampling to a notably lower pitch, a higher-sample-rate source is preferred, because slowing playback reproduces a lower-resolution signal and reduces perceived clarity
how: for an `asetrate` slow-down start from the best source you have (e.g. a 48 kHz WAV, not a 22 kHz MP3)
refs: Wikipedia "Audio time stretching and pitch scaling", https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Audio_time_stretching_and_pitch_scaling, checked 2026-10-24

name: "Master tempo": match tempo, keep the key
section: Time-stretch and retime without pitch change
what: DJ software's master tempo / key adjust changes tempo while keeping pitch, unlike a turntable where 5% faster raises both pitch and tempo 5%
how: beatmatch with `atempo`/`rubberband=tempo` (pitch kept), not `asetrate` (pitch moves)

name: Pitch that changes over time
section: Time-stretch and retime without pitch change
what: Rubber Band's `--pitchmap` file lists input sample frames and semitone offsets (not cumulative); it implies realtime mode, so the output duration is not exact
how: needs rubberband CLI (missing): `rubberband --pitchmap map.txt in.wav out.wav` for a rising key-change effect

name: Semitones to a pitch ratio
what: an equal-tempered semitone is 2^(1/12), about 1.05946 (100 cents)
how: `pitch = 2^(n/12)`: +2 = 1.122462, -2 = 0.890899; `rubberband=pitch=1.122462` moved a 440 Hz tone to 494 Hz and `pitch=0.890899` to 392 Hz, length unchanged (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Keep a singer's timbre when shifting
what: Rubber Band formant preservation keeps the formant envelope so vocals keep their character; in ffmpeg it is `formant=preserved`
how: `ffmpeg -i song.wav -af rubberband=pitch=0.890899:formant=preserved out.wav` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Pitch quality mode
what: `pitchq` can be quality, speed (default) or consistency
how: `rubberband=pitch=1.059463:pitchq=quality` moved 440 Hz to 466 Hz (+1 semitone) (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Pitch shift with stock ffmpeg filters
what: transposition can be done by time-stretching and then resampling back to the original length; with ffmpeg: speed up by rate change, then atempo back
how: `asetrate=44100*1.122462,aresample=44100,atempo=1/1.122462` moved 440 Hz to 494 Hz and kept 4.0 s (3.996 s) (tested here 2026-10-24)
refs: Wikipedia "Audio time stretching and pitch scaling", https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Audio_time_stretching_and_pitch_scaling, checked 2026-10-24

name: Pitch shift in Python
what: `librosa.effects.pitch_shift(y, sr=, n_steps=)` shifts by (fractional) steps and keeps the length
how: `n_steps=-3` moved 440 Hz to 370 Hz, same length (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Quarter-tone or microtonal shifts
what: a step equals a semitone only with `bins_per_octave=12`; 24 gives quarter-tones
how: `librosa.effects.pitch_shift(y,sr=sr,n_steps=1,bins_per_octave=24)` moved 440 Hz to 453 Hz (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Cents for fine detune
what: a cent is 1/1200 of an octave (1/100 of a semitone)
how: ratio = 2^(cents/1200); librosa's `resolution=0.01` in tuning estimates means cents

name: Is the track tuned off A440?
what: `estimate_tuning` returns the deviation in fractions of a bin (-0.5 to 0.5); `tuning_to_A4`/`A4_to_tuning` convert to a reference pitch
how: the lofi clip read 0.01 bins; `librosa.A4_to_tuning(432)` = -0.318 and `librosa.tuning_to_A4(-0.32)` = 431.9 Hz (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Name the note being played or sung
what: pYIN estimates f0 with voicing; the docs recommend fmin C2 (~65 Hz) and fmax C7 (~2093 Hz)
how: `f,v,p=librosa.pyin(y,fmin=librosa.note_to_hz('C2'),fmax=librosa.note_to_hz('C7'),sr=sr); librosa.hz_to_note(np.nanmedian(f))` read B4 (493.9 Hz) on the shifted tone (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Note, MIDI and Hz conversions
what: `note_to_hz('A4')` = 440, `hz_to_note(261.63)` = C4, `midi_to_note(69)` = A4, `note_to_midi('C4')` = 60
how: use them to name keys and transpose amounts in edit notes (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Spell a key's notes
what: `key_to_notes('F:min')` lists the 12 pitch classes spelled for that key (C, D♭, D, E♭ ... B♭, B)
how: compare two tracks' key spellings before a crossfade (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Hindustani thaats for desi tracks
what: librosa lists the ten thaats (bilaval, khamaj, kafi, asavari, bhairavi, kalyan, marva, poorvi, todi, bhairav) and gives each one's scale degrees
how: `librosa.thaat_to_degrees('kafi')` = [0 2 3 5 7 9 10] (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Sa-Re-Ga names for pitches
what: `hz_to_svara_h` names frequencies as Hindustani svara relative to a given Sa

name: Carnatic melakarta list
what: `list_mela()` maps the 72 melakarta raga names to numbers (kanakangi 1, ratnangi 2, ganamurthi 3 ...)
how: `librosa.mela_to_degrees(n)` for a raga's degrees (list tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Chroma for harmony comparisons
what: `feature.chroma_cqt` gives 12 pitch-class energies per frame; the sync tutorial compares versions with it
how: `librosa.feature.chroma_cqt(y=y,sr=sr)` gave 12 x 1292 for 30 s (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: CQT resolution for pitch work
what: CQT defaults to 12 bins/octave from C1 over 7 octaves; for finer pitch use bins_per_octave=36 and raise n_bins with it (12*3*8 for 8 octaves)
how: `librosa.cqt(y=y,sr=sr,bins_per_octave=36,n_bins=36*8)`

name: Transpose our own MIDI before rendering
what: General MIDI reserves channel 10 for percussion (mido counts channels 0-15, so it is `channel==9`); shift every other note and re-render
how: `if msg.type in('note_on','note_off') and msg.channel!=9: msg.note=min(127,msg.note+2)` then FluidSynth; ran on the library MIDI (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Pitch shifting changes formants unless handled
what: time-domain pitch scaling of vocals distorts formants into a chipmunk-like effect; formant-preserving methods analyse and resynthesise
how: use `formant=preserved` for any vocal key change; plain `asetrate` tricks are for instrumentals
refs: Wikipedia "Audio time stretching and pitch scaling", https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Audio_time_stretching_and_pitch_scaling, checked 2026-10-24

name: Instrumental from a song with the local MDX model
what: audio-separator runs UVR/MDX/Demucs/Roformer models from the CLI; `--single_stem` writes only one stem and `--model_file_dir` points at models already on disk
how: `/home/user/tools/venv/bin/audio-separator vsong.wav --model_file_dir /home/user/tools/sep-models -m UVR-MDX-NET-Voc_FT.onnx --single_stem Instrumental --output_format WAV --output_dir sep` took 20 s for a 10 s clip (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Four stems with Demucs v4 through audio-separator
what: `-m htdemucs.yaml` gives Bass, Drums, Other and Vocals; the model (about 81 MB) downloads on first use
how: `audio-separator vsong.wav --model_file_dir <dir> -m htdemucs.yaml --output_format WAV --output_dir sep4` took 23 s for 10 s on this 4-core CPU (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Separated stems add back up to the mix
what: the four htdemucs stems summed with `amix=inputs=4:normalize=0` matched the input with a -33 dB residual (after resampling the 48 kHz input to the stems' 44.1 kHz)
how: `ffmpeg -i bass.wav -i other.wav -i vocals.wav -i drums.wav -filter_complex amix=inputs=4:normalize=0 sum.wav` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Stems come out at 44.1 kHz unless told
what: audio-separator's `--sample_rate` defaults to 44100, so a 48 kHz song gave 44.1 kHz stems
how: add `--sample_rate 48000` for video-rate stems; with `--output_format MP3 --output_bitrate 320k` it wrote a 48000 Hz, 320 kb/s MP3 (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Drumless (or vocal-less) version from stems
what: mix only the stems you want with amix and normalize off
how: `ffmpeg -i bass.wav -i other.wav -i vocals.wav -filter_complex amix=inputs=3:normalize=0 nodrums.wav` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Name the stem files yourself
what: `--custom_output_names` takes JSON mapping stem to file name
how: `--custom_output_names '{"Instrumental": "inst_mdx"}'` wrote `inst_mdx.wav` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Find the right model per stem
what: `-l --list_filter=<stem> --list_limit=N` lists models for a stem with SDR scores
how: for drums/bass the top picks were htdemucs_ft, hdemucs_mmi, htdemucs; guitar and piano only htdemucs_6s; instrumental BS-Roformer 317/368 and MelBand Inst V2 (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Piano and guitar stems are weak
what: Demucs' 6-source model adds guitar and piano; the README says guitar is okay but piano has a lot of bleeding and artifacts
how: `-m htdemucs_6s.yaml` only when you need those; check the piano stem by ear

name: Karaoke via preset, not via the filter
what: `--list_filter=karaoke` crashed in 0.47.1 (ValueError: empty list), but `--list_presets` lists a `karaoke` preset (3-model ensemble, avg_wave) for lead-vocal removal
how: `audio-separator song.wav --ensemble_preset karaoke` (preset list tested here 2026-10-24; separation not run)

name: Ensemble presets by goal
what: presets include instrumental_clean (minimal vocal bleed), instrumental_full, instrumental_balanced, instrumental_low_resource, vocal_balanced, vocal_clean, vocal_full and vocal_rvc, each 2 models with a set algorithm (uvr_max_spec, avg_fft, min_fft, max_fft, avg_wave)
how: `audio-separator --list_presets`, then `--ensemble_preset instrumental_clean` (list tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Your own ensemble
what: `-m` primary model plus `--extra_models`, combined with `--ensemble_algorithm` (avg_wave default, median/min/max wave or fft, uvr_max_spec, uvr_min_spec, ensemble_wav) and optional `--ensemble_weights`
how: `audio-separator a.wav -m model1.ckpt --extra_models model2.onnx --ensemble_algorithm max_fft`

name: Long files in chunks
what: `--chunk_duration` splits, separates and concatenates; chunks join without crossfade, so rare boundary artifacts are possible; 600 s is recommended for files over an hour
how: `audio-separator long.wav --chunk_duration 600`

name: Peak normalisation is on by default
what: `--normalization` sets the max peak for input and output (default 0.9); `--amplification` sets a minimum peak
how: remember stems are peak-normalised when comparing levels between runs

name: Separation quality/speed knobs
what: MDX: `--mdx_overlap` 0.001-0.999 (higher better, slower; default 0.25) and `--mdx_segment_size`; VR: `--vr_aggression` -100..100 (typically 5) and `--vr_window_size` 320 slower/better, 1024 faster; Demucs: `--demucs_shifts` (default 2) and `--demucs_overlap`
how: raise overlap/shifts only for the final pass on this CPU box

name: Pitch trick for deep or high vocals
what: `--mdxc_pitch_shift` shifts the audio by semitones while processing (Roformer/MDXC models) and "may improve output for deep/high vocals"
how: `--mdxc_pitch_shift 2` on a hard case

name: Demucs speed on CPU
what: the README says CPU processing takes roughly 1.5x the track duration and `htdemucs_ft` takes 4 times longer than htdemucs; `--shifts` multiplies time and is not advised without a GPU. Here htdemucs took 23 s for 10 s
how: use htdemucs for drafts; queue separations, never next to another heavy torch job (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Demucs two-stem mode is not faster
what: `--two-stems=vocals` (karaoke mode) mixes the other stems after a full separation, so it saves neither time nor memory; transformer models allow at most 7.8 s `--segment`
how: needs demucs CLI (missing; audio-separator covers the same models): `demucs --two-stems=vocals -d cpu song.mp3`

name: Clipping in separated stems
what: Demucs rescales each stem to avoid clipping, which can break relative volumes between stems; `--clip-mode clamp` hard-clips instead
how: needs demucs CLI (missing): `demucs --clip-mode clamp song.wav`, or lower the input level first

name: Quick drums vs. melody split with no model
what: HPSS separates harmonic and percussive parts with median filters and returns waveforms of the input length
how: `h,p=librosa.effects.hpss(y)` ran in seconds (rms 0.094 harmonic, 0.038 percussive vs 0.113 mix) (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Cleaner HPSS with a margin
what: a margin requires one filter to beat the other by that factor; noise and vocals then go to neither part (residual); the tutorial finds margins of 4 or more give strictly harmonic/percussive parts
how: `librosa.effects.hpss(y,margin=4)` left a residual of rms 0.060 (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Only the percussive part
what: `librosa.effects.percussive(y, margin=)` returns just the drums-like component (`harmonic` the rest)
how: `librosa.effects.percussive(y,margin=3)` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: REPET-SIM style repeating-background filter
what: nn_filter replaces each spectrogram column by aggregating its nearest neighbours; `aggregate=np.median` gives REPET-SIM de-noising (Rafii & Pardo, music/voice separation)
how: `S,ph=librosa.magphase(librosa.stft(y)); Sf=np.minimum(S,librosa.decompose.nn_filter(S,aggregate=np.median,metric='cosine',width=int(librosa.time_to_frames(2,sr=sr))))` ran (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Classic centre cancel ("invert and mix")
what: subtracting one channel from the other removes centre-panned audio, often the lead vocal, giving dual mono
how: `ffmpeg -i song.wav -af "pan=stereo|c0=c0-c1|c1=c1-c0" nocentre.wav`; on our wide AI song it removed only 1.8 dB of level, so check the result (tested here 2026-10-24)
refs: Audacity Manual "Vocal Reduction and Isolation", https://manual.audacityteam.org/man/vocal_reduction_and_isolation.html, checked 2026-10-24

name: Keep the bass when cancelling the centre
what: Audacity's vocal removal leaves frequencies below Low Cut (default 120 Hz; about 170 for female, 230 for children's voices) to keep bass and kick
how: `[0]asplit[a][b];[a]lowpass=f=120[lo];[b]highpass=f=120,pan=stereo|c0=c0-c1|c1=c1-c0[hi];[lo][hi]amix=inputs=2:normalize=0` (tested here 2026-10-24)
refs: Audacity Manual "Vocal Reduction and Isolation", https://manual.audacityteam.org/man/vocal_reduction_and_isolation.html, checked 2026-10-24

name: Check stereo correlation before trying centre tricks
what: Audacity's Analyze reports channel correlation and how likely centre removal is to work; ffmpeg's aphasemeter exports mean phase (-1 out of phase to 1 in phase)
how: `aphasemeter=video=0,ametadata=mode=print:key=lavfi.aphasemeter.phase:file=phase.txt` averaged 0.334 on our AI song, where centre cancel removed only 1.8 dB (tested here 2026-10-24)
refs: Audacity Manual "Vocal Reduction and Isolation", https://manual.audacityteam.org/man/vocal_reduction_and_isolation.html, checked 2026-10-24

name: Mid/side split for editing
what: stereotools `mode=lr>ms` converts L/R to mid/side; `mlev`/`slev` set the mid and side levels (0.015625-64)
how: `stereotools=mode=lr\>ms`; `stereotools=mlev=0.015625` leaves mostly side (L/R correlation went 0.972 to -0.967) (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Separate the singer before transcribing a song
what: Whisper misses whole sung stretches on a long song; separate vocals first (UVR-MDX-NET Voc FT, about 2 min for 200 s) and transcribe with `condition_on_previous_text=False`, then align lyric lines with a global in-order DP
how: see `library/templates/website-promo/dp_align.py`

name: A sung background stays "voice"
what: any vocal model keeps a song's singer as voice; only instrumental sound is removable when cleaning speech
how: if a client clip's background is a song with vocals, expect it to survive `clean_voice.py`
refs: repo: CLAUDE.md "Voice and songs with words"

name: Stems in post-production
what: a stem is a group of sources mixed to be handled downstream as one unit; film mixes keep dialogue, music and effects (D-M-E) separate so music can be changed to fit
how: deliver music on its own stem so it can be swapped later

name: Prefetch a separation model
what: `--download_model_only` downloads one model file without separating, so a later run can start immediately (or offline)
how: `audio-separator -m htdemucs.yaml --model_file_dir /home/user/tools/sep-models --download_model_only`

name: 3-4 frames is close enough
section: Hit points and scoring to picture
what: when syncing music to picture a leeway of 3-4 frames early or late is generally sufficiently accurate
how: at 30 fps that is about 100-133 ms; don't over-stretch music to hit closer than that

name: Written click: seconds per bar
section: Hit points and scoring to picture
what: W = (60/bpm) x beats-per-bar, rounded to 1/3 s in written clicks
how: 88 BPM in 4/4: 60/88 x 4 = 2.727 s, written as 4 beats in 2 2/3 s (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Which beat a sync point falls on
section: Hit points and scoring to picture
what: B = bpm x sp / 60 + 1 (sp = sync point in seconds)
how: at 88 BPM a hit at 33.7 s falls on beat 50.43, i.e. just after beat 50 (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Pick the tempo that lands a hit on a beat
section: Hit points and scoring to picture
what: rearranging the same formula: bpm = (B - 1) x 60 / sp
how: to put a reveal at 12.0 s on beat 17 (bar 5's downbeat in 4/4) use 80 BPM (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Frames per beat can be fractional
section: Hit points and scoring to picture
what: a beat lasts 60/bpm s (the written-click formula with one beat), so frames per beat = fps x 60 / BPM: 24 fps gives whole numbers at 72/90/120 BPM (20/16/12), 25 fps does not (20.833/16.667/12.5), 30 fps gives 25/20/15
how: at 25 fps place hits from the beat time (`round(t*fps)`) instead of adding a rounded frame count (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Fit one tempo to several hit points
section: Hit points and scoring to picture
what: Frans Absil's film-cue tempo tool takes event hit points and finds the best fixed tempo and beat fit (with the matching error), within a tempo range, for 24/25/30 fps or 50 ms timing
how: enter your cue's hit times at fransabsil.nl, then generate or choose music at that BPM

name: Clicks need a tempo map for expressive cues
section: Hit points and scoring to picture
what: a click track without a tempo map does not allow natural tempo shifts (fermata, accelerando, ritardando)
how: for an emotional cue, let it breathe (PLP or dynamic tempo, skills above) rather than forcing a grid

name: Mickey-mousing: use it on purpose
section: Hit points and scoring to picture
what: syncing music to every on-screen action is called Mickey Mousing; it is also used as a pejorative for being too simplistic and is associated with melodrama
how: it fits cartoon and game-style moments (where the article says it is common); in pieces for adults it can read as too simplistic, so sync only key hits there

name: Animate to pre-recorded music
section: Hit points and scoring to picture
what: animators time movement to pre-recorded music with an exposure sheet marking beats frame by frame
how: export beat frames (`round(beat_time*fps)`) from the beats JSON and key GSAP moves to them

name: Cutting picture to finished music is legitimate
section: Hit points and scoring to picture
what: some directors edit the film to the music (Baby Driver; Koyaanisqatsi to Philip Glass; E.T.'s finale re-edited to John Williams' cue)
how: for music-led reels lock the music edit first, then cut picture to it

name: Temp track = guide, not final
section: Hit points and scoring to picture
what: a temp track is existing music used during editing to show the tempo and mood wanted; it is usually replaced before release
how: if the owner's rough cut uses a copyrighted song as temp, replace it with CC0/own music of the same tempo before delivery

name: Count desi cycles, not just bars
section: Hit points and scoring to picture
what: Teental has 16 beats in four groups of 4 (sam on beat 1, khali on 9); Keherwa has 8 beats in two groups (sam 1, khali 5); the sam is the most emphasised beat where phrases resolve
how: for tabla-led music cut big moments on the sam: every 16 beats in teental, 8 in keherwa

name: Phrases can start before the downbeat
section: Hit points and scoring to picture
what: in Indian classical music a composition may be offset so the most accented word falls on the sam, or start with an anacrusis on the last beats of the previous cycle
how: when cutting a sung phrase, keep its pickup notes before the cycle's first beat instead of cutting exactly on the sam

name: Preview where a cue's hits will land before placing it
section: Placing music in HyperFrames and pydub
what: `hyperframes audio <file> --place-at <film s> --skip-file-seconds <s>` analyses a file not yet in the film as if placed there
how: `npx hyperframes audio cue.wav --place-at 5 --skip-file-seconds 2 --only onsets --json` returned placement {dataStart 5, mediaStart 2} and onsets in file seconds from 2 s, so film time = 5 + (t - 2) (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Start inside the file with data-media-start
section: Placing music in HyperFrames and pydub
what: the repo's riser crests 3.47 s into its file, so `data-media-start` is used to make that moment land on the hit; every `<audio>` also needs `data-duration` equal to the clip's real length
how: `<audio src="assets/music.mp3" data-start="0" data-media-start="12.5" data-duration="30" data-track-index="0">`

name: Overlapping music clips need their own lanes
section: Placing music in HyperFrames and pydub
what: overlapping clips need different `data-track-index` values or lint warns `duplicate_audio_track`
how: old cue on track 0, incoming cue on track 1 during the crossfade

name: Volume envelopes on the music clip
section: Placing music in HyperFrames and pydub
what: `data-automation` lanes target `volume`, `rate` or an effect parameter; `t` is seconds from the clip's start, and a lane holds its first value back to the clip start, so add an explicit full-level point at t 0
how: `data-automation='{"version":1,"lanes":[{"target":"volume","points":[{"t":0,"v":1},{"t":2.5,"v":0.35}]}]}'`; don't also tween volume with GSAP

name: Check the render, not the timeline
section: Placing music in HyperFrames and pydub
what: the sound guide says to run `npx hyperframes audio <video> --json` on the rendered file: sound present, hits where the picture hits, loudness in range, and to say it was measured, not heard
how: run it on every final render

name: Lower the bed under an overlay in one call
section: Placing music in HyperFrames and pydub
what: pydub's `overlay(..., gain_during_overlay=dB)` changes the base audio by that many dB while the overlaid sound plays
how: `base.overlay(sting,position=4000,gain_during_overlay=-8)` took that 2 s window from -21.1 to -29.1 dBFS (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Partial fade to a new level
section: Placing music in HyperFrames and pydub
what: `fade(to_gain=-6.0, start=ms, duration=ms)` fades from 0 to -6 dB and keeps everything after at -6 dB
how: `song.fade(to_gain=-6.0,start=7500,duration=1000)` read -25.0 dBFS after the fade vs -19.0 before (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Fade in/out and export at a bitrate
section: Placing music in HyperFrames and pydub
what: `fade_in(ms)` / `fade_out(ms)` then `export(..., format='mp3', bitrate='192k')`
how: `song.fade_in(2000).fade_out(3000).export('bed.mp3',format='mp3',bitrate='192k')` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: pydub gain past 0 dBFS clips
section: Placing music in HyperFrames and pydub
what: `segment + dB` / `apply_gain` changes level; a track peaking at -0.4 dBFS read max 0.0 dBFS after `+6`, i.e. clipped
how: check `seg.max_dBFS` before boosting (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Reverse a phrase into a hit
section: Placing music in HyperFrames and pydub
what: areverse plays a clip backwards and buffers the whole clip in memory, so trim first (the docs' example: `atrim=end=5,areverse`)
how: `ffmpeg -i song.wav -af "atrim=end=2,areverse" rev.wav`; pydub's `segment.reverse()` does the same (both tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Music at a quarter weight under a vocal
section: Placing music in HyperFrames and pydub
what: the amix docs' example mixes vocals and music with weights "1 0.25", normalize off, duration longest
how: `amix=inputs=2:duration=first:dropout_transition=0:weights=1 0.25:normalize=0` (with duration=first it kept the 30 s song length) (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Resample stems with soxr
section: Placing music in HyperFrames and pydub
what: aresample takes resampler options such as `resampler=soxr`
how: `ffmpeg -i in48k.wav -af aresample=44100:resampler=soxr out.wav` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Load only the part you need
section: Python audio utilities for music edits (librosa)
what: `librosa.load(path, sr=None, offset=, duration=, mono=False)` keeps native rate and stereo
how: `librosa.load('song.wav',sr=None,offset=10,duration=5,mono=False)` gave (2, 220500) at 44100 (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Duration without decoding
section: Python audio utilities for music edits (librosa)
what: `librosa.get_duration(path=...)`
how: returned 30.0 for the test clip (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Stream long songs in blocks
section: Python audio utilities for music edits (librosa)
what: `librosa.stream` yields fixed-size blocks of frames for long files; librosa 1.0 warns its default `sr` changes from None to 22050 in 1.1, so pass `sr` explicitly
how: `librosa.stream('song.wav',block_length=64,frame_length=2048,hop_length=512)` gave 41 blocks for 30 s (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Frames, samples and seconds
section: Python audio utilities for music edits (librosa)
what: `frames_to_time` / `time_to_frames` convert with the hop length (512 default at 22050 Hz)
how: `librosa.frames_to_time(beats,sr=sr)`; `librosa.time_to_frames(2,sr=sr)` for a 2 s width (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Re-order beats or bars
section: Python audio utilities for music edits (librosa)
what: `effects.remix(y, intervals)` rebuilds audio from (start, end) sample intervals, snapping to zero crossings when `align_zeros=True`; the docs reverse a song's beats
how: pass a numpy array: `iv=np.stack([b[:-1],b[1:]],1)[::-1]; librosa.effects.remix(y,iv)` worked, a Python list of tuples raised a numba TypingError here (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Test tones and sweeps
section: Python audio utilities for music edits (librosa)
what: `librosa.tone(f, sr=, duration=)` and `librosa.chirp(fmin=, fmax=, sr=, duration=)` make reference signals for checking pitch shifts
how: both gave 22050 samples for 1 s (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: librosa example tracks are not free to use
section: Python audio utilities for music edits (librosa)
what: the tutorials' example audio carries CC-BY-4.0, CC-BY-NC-4.0 and CC-BY-NC-SA-4.0 licences (trumpet, sweetwaltz, fishin)
how: use them only for testing code, never in an owner video (credit/non-commercial terms)

name: aubio tempo and beat
what: `aubio tempo <file>` gives the overall tempo in BPM; `aubio beat <file>` gives beat locations (buffer 1024, hop 512 by default)
how: needs aubio (missing): `aubio tempo song.wav`

name: aubio onsets with a minimum gap
what: `aubio onset` takes a novelty method (energy, hfc, complex, phase, specdiff, kl, mkl, specflux), a threshold, a silence floor (-70 dB) and `-M` minimum inter-onset interval
how: needs aubio (missing): `aubio onset song.wav -M 30ms` (the manual's example)

name: Slice a file at beats
what: `aubiocut -b -c` cuts the input into one file per beat (`-o` sets the folder); without `-b` it cuts at onsets with threshold `-t` (0.001-0.9, default 0.3; lower = more slices)
how: needs aubio (missing): `aubiocut -i loop.wav -b -c -o slices/`

name: Mark onsets audibly
what: `aubioonset -o out.wav` writes a copy with a wood-block-like sound at each onset; `-m` mixes the source in
how: needs aubio (missing): `aubioonset -i song.wav -o marked.wav -m`

name: HFC for percussive onsets
what: aubio's default onset method is hfc (high-frequency content), which the manual calls efficient at detecting percussive onsets
how: needs aubio (missing): `aubioonset -i drums.wav -O hfc`

name: What CC0 lets you do
what: the CC0 deed: the work is dedicated to the public domain; you can copy, modify, distribute and perform it, even commercially, without asking permission
how: a CC0 track can be cut, looped, stretched and re-keyed for a client video with no credit

name: CC0 still leaves other rights
what: patent, trademark, publicity and privacy rights are not affected, and you should not imply endorsement by the author
how: never present a CC0 artist as endorsing the client's brand

name: The CC0 waiver is irrevocable and covers advertising
what: the legal code waives all copyright and related rights permanently and irrevocably, for any purpose including commercial, advertising or promotional purposes
how: CC0 music is safe for promos like the FireCraft or client reels
refs: Creative Commons CC0 1.0 legal code, https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/zero/1.0/legalcode.en, checked 2026-10-24

name: Public Domain Mark is a label, not a waiver
what: PDM marks a work identified as free of known copyright; it may not be free in all jurisdictions and moral rights (e.g. to be identified as author) may persist in some
how: for PDM tracks keep the source page link as proof and credit the composer when convenient
refs: Creative Commons Public Domain Mark 1.0, https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/mark/1.0/, checked 2026-10-24

name: OpenGameArt licence meanings
what: OGA's FAQ: CC0 works may be used in any way without asking, crediting or notifying the artist; CC-BY / CC-BY-SA / OGA-BY require credit (and SA requires sharing alike)
how: keep only CC0 tracks (the owner's no-credit rule rules out CC-BY)

name: Several licences listed: follow one
what: on OGA, when an artist lists multiple licences you must follow only one of them
how: if CC0 is among them, use the track under CC0 and save the page as proof

name: A later licence change doesn't take your licence away
what: OGA: an artist may change licence terms at any time, but you are under no obligation because the licence you obtained it under is irrevocable
how: record the licence and date when downloading (as `library/music/cc0/README.md` does)

name: FMA "Public Domain" filter is not proof
what: the repo's FMA crawl found some uploaders mislabel commercial songs as PD, so each track page was opened and kept only if its licence link pointed to creativecommons.org/publicdomain with no CC BY link, from well-known CC0 artists
how: apply the same per-page check to any new FMA track

name: Field recordings are atmosphere
what: the CC0 desi field recordings (damal drumming, wedding music, men singing) contain crowds and voices: use them as atmosphere, not as a clean song
how: low under picture, not as the main bed

name: YouTube Audio Library facts
what: tracks there are copyright-safe and won't be Content ID-claimed; Creative Commons tracks need credit in the description (filter "Attribution required" / "Attribution not required"); YouTube is not responsible for "royalty-free" music from other channels or libraries
how: the owner's rule still asks for CC0/PD/own music, so ask before using even "attribution not required" Audio Library tracks

name: Own songs and instrumentals in one model load
what: `music_pack.py` runs ACE-Step 1.5 turbo once for a JSON list of {name, caption, lyrics ("[Instrumental]" for music only), lang, duration, bpm, seed} and writes 192k MP3s at -14 LUFS, skipping names already done
how: `cd /home/user/tools/ACE-Step-1.5 && ../venv/bin/python -u /home/user/new-startup/library/tools/music_pack.py SPEC.json OUTDIR` (only when the owner asks for our own music)

name: The recipe the owner loved
what: `ai_song.py` with seed 7, 80 BPM, 60 s and the caption "romantic hindi pop ballad, soft piano, acoustic guitar, strings, gentle tabla, rainy evening mood, warm male vocals, clear hindi lyrics"; run in the background with a per-minute status
how: reuse this style for new songs; result in `library/music/baarish-ki-pehli-shaam-ai-song.mp3`
refs: repo: CLAUDE.md "Voice and songs with words"

name: Keep each AI song generation short
what: a 47-line, 200 s generation skipped about half the lyrics; keep each part to about 16-19 lines (130-150 s) and join parts at an instrumental gap with a crossfade; parts in one process share one model load
how: `gen_parts.py` in the website-promo template

name: ACE-Step on this CPU
what: load the DiT with `quantization=int8_weight_only` (fp32 ran out of memory at VAE decode) and raise `ACESTEP_GENERATION_TIMEOUT`; a turbo 60 s song takes about 5 min
how: `music_pack.py` already sets both

name: ACE-Step "lego" did not add vocals here
what: the base model's lego task (vocals over an instrumental) returned a 0.97 copy of the input on CPU
how: make vocal songs with turbo text2music + lyrics instead

name: Melody by Magenta, arrangement by script
what: `magenta/melody.mjs` writes 12 Improv RNN takes over a chord progression (best first); `magenta/arrange.py` arranges a take for sitar, flute, piano, strings, bass, celesta and dholak-style percussion
how: serve the checkpoint with `python3 -m http.server 8766 --directory library/models/magenta/chord_pitches_improv`, then `node melody.mjs <url> out.json` and `python3 arrange.py out.json out.mid`

name: Render MIDI to a finished bed
what: FluidSynth with the GM SoundFont, then trim, fade and normalise in ffmpeg
how: `fluidsynth -ni -q -g 0.7 -r 48000 -F out.wav /usr/share/sounds/sf2/FluidR3_GM.sf2 out.mid` then `ffmpeg -i out.wav -af "atrim=0:21.6,afade=t=out:st=20.2:d=1.4,loudnorm=I=-16:TP=-1.5" bed.wav` (render tested here 2026-10-24)

name: FluidSynth renders a tail past the MIDI length
what: the library MIDI is 21.667 s long (mido `length`) but the render lasted 26.0 s; at 96 BPM, 16.25 s rendered to 20.58 s
how: always atrim + afade the render to the bar you want (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Dry render for later processing
what: FluidSynth `-R 0` turns reverb off, `-C 0` chorus off; `-T` sets file type, `-O` sample format (s16, s24, s32, float ...)
how: `fluidsynth -ni -q -R 0 -C 0 -g 0.7 -r 44100 -T wav -O s24 -F dry.wav FluidR3_GM.sf2 song.mid` gave 24-bit WAV (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: FluidSynth gain default is low
what: `-g` master gain range 0-10, default 0.2; the repo render uses 0.7
how: set `-g 0.7` and normalise afterwards rather than raising gain until it clips

name: MIDI tempo is microseconds per beat
what: MIDI stores tempo as microseconds per quarter note (default 500000 = 120 BPM in 4/4); `bpm2tempo`/`tempo2bpm` convert, and `tick2second`/`second2tick` convert ticks
how: `mido.bpm2tempo(96)` = 625000; `mido.second2tick(1.0,480,833333)` = 576 (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Read a MIDI file's length and tempo
what: `MidiFile(...).length` gives playback seconds for type 0/1 files (type 2 raises ValueError); tempo is in `set_tempo` meta messages
how: the library MIDI: type 1, 480 ticks per beat, 21.667 s, set_tempo 833333 = 72 BPM (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: More ticks per beat if rounding drifts
what: tick conversions round to integers; if rounding errors pile up, raise `ticks_per_beat` (typical 96-480)
how: `MidiFile(ticks_per_beat=960)` for new files that must hit exact frame times

name: Zero-install synth bed
what: `romance_synth.py` writes a 72 BPM, 6-bar romantic piano + strings bed with numpy only
how: `python3 library/tools/romance_synth.py out.wav` wrote 21.60 s in about 10 s (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Generated BGM tempo bands
what: the media-use Lyria recipe accepts `--bpm` (90-110 calm, 110-130 energetic), `--brightness`, `--density`, `--scale` and `--negative-prompt`; MusicGen ignores them, so put the mood in its prompt
how: only when that backend is available and the owner wants generated music

name: Vendor GSAP plugins from the npm tarball
what: every GSAP plugin (SplitText, ScrambleText, DrawSVG, MorphSVG, MotionPath, CustomEase, EasePack, Physics2D...) ships in the public `gsap` npm package next to the core, so the plugin build can match the vendored core exactly and never touch the CDN
how: `npm pack gsap@3.14.2 && tar xzf gsap-3.14.2.tgz` then copy `package/dist/SplitText.min.js` (etc.) into `assets/vendor/` beside `gsap-3.14.2.min.js` and load them with `<script src>` after the core (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Register every plugin once before building the timeline
what: plugins must be registered with `gsap.registerPlugin()`; registering twice does no harm
how: `gsap.registerPlugin(SplitText, DrawSVGPlugin, MorphSVGPlugin, MotionPathPlugin, ScrambleTextPlugin, CustomEase);` at the top of the scene script, then build `tl` and set `window.__timelines["main"]=tl` last; a 4 s test scene using all six passed `npx hyperframes check --json` with ok:true (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: EasePack is a separate file
what: `slow`, `rough` and `expoScale` are not in the core; they live in EasePack, while CustomEase, CustomBounce and CustomWiggle are separate files too (CustomBounce/Wiggle also need CustomEase)
how: copy `EasePack.min.js` (and `CustomEase.min.js` before `CustomBounce.min.js`/`CustomWiggle.min.js`) into `assets/vendor/`; `gsap.registerPlugin(EasePack, CustomEase, CustomBounce, CustomWiggle)` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Snapshot plugin scenes, don't trust the code
what: SplitText masks, DrawSVG, MorphSVG, MotionPath and ScrambleText all rendered correctly in HyperFrames snapshots of a seeked paused timeline
how: `npx hyperframes snapshot --at 0.3,1.0,2.2,3.9` then open `.hyperframes/artifacts/snapshots/<id>/contact-sheet.jpg` and check each effect at mid-move and at rest (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Prove seek-safety of a tween
what: HyperFrames seeks frames out of order, so a tween must give the same value whichever way the playhead arrives; GSAP timelines did (seek 1.5 -> 0.25 -> 1.5 returned identical values)
how: `tl.seek(1.5); a=o.x; tl.seek(0.25); tl.seek(1.5); console.assert(a===o.x)` in a headless page (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Random-based plugins are not seed-stable
what: ScrambleTextPlugin and the `rough` ease use `Math.random` (two RoughEase creations gave 0.321 vs 0.268 at the same progress), so each page load (preview, each render worker) can differ; HyperFrames wants seeded randomness
how: for frame-exact scrambles use the registry `scramble-reveal`/`matrix-decode` (fixed-seed tables) or set `rough({randomize:false})`; `grep -c Math.random dist/ScrambleTextPlugin.js` showed 3 uses (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Default ease is power1.out
