refs: libass wiki: ASS File Format Guide, https://github.com/libass/libass/wiki/ASS-File-Format-Guide, checked 2026-10-24

name: Layers decide what sits on top
what: lower `Layer` values are drawn behind higher ones; a Layer 1 yellow "TOP" drew over a larger Layer 0 "BOTTOM"
how: box/drawing events on Layer 0, text on Layer 1 (tested here 2026-10-24)
refs: libass wiki: ASS File Format Guide, https://github.com/libass/libass/wiki/ASS-File-Format-Guide, checked 2026-10-24

name: Overlapping lines stack themselves
what: two unpositioned events in the same style that overlap in time were stacked (the later one above), not drawn over each other; events on different Layers never count as colliding
how: to keep two speakers apart use `\an1`/`\an3` or `\pos`, otherwise let libass stack them (tested here 2026-10-24)
refs: libass wiki: ASS File Format Guide, https://github.com/libass/libass/wiki/ASS-File-Format-Guide, checked 2026-10-24

name: Comment lines and inline comments
what: `Comment:` events are never rendered (frame identical to the bare video); unknown text inside `{}` is silently ignored, so `{note}` works as an inline comment
how: keep alternate takes as `Comment:` lines in the master ASS (tested here 2026-10-24)
refs: libass wiki: ASS File Format Guide, https://github.com/libass/libass/wiki/ASS-File-Format-Guide, checked 2026-10-24
Aegisub manual: ASS Override Tags, https://aegisub.org/docs/latest/ass_tags/, checked 2026-10-24

name: Name field = speaker label for you, not the viewer
what: the `Name` field is free metadata for who speaks and does not affect rendering
how: fill Name with the speaker so a script can colour or position by speaker later
refs: libass wiki: ASS File Format Guide, https://github.com/libass/libass/wiki/ASS-File-Format-Guide, checked 2026-10-24

name: Built-in ticker and credit roll
what: the Effect field `Banner;delay` scrolls text sideways (lower delay = faster) and `Scroll up;y1;y2;delay` rolls it up between two y limits
how: `Dialogue: 0,0:00:00.00,0:00:03.00,Default,,0,0,0,Scroll up;40;320;10,Credits roll up` (tested here 2026-10-24)
refs: libass wiki: ASS File Format Guide, https://github.com/libass/libass/wiki/ASS-File-Format-Guide, checked 2026-10-24

name: Don't use the VSFilter fadeaway effect argument or \fe
what: the optional `fadeaway` effect parameter is not supported by libass and must not be used; `\fe` must not be used at all
how: do fades with `\fad`, and fonts by name, never by encoding
refs: libass wiki: ASS File Format Guide, https://github.com/libass/libass/wiki/ASS-File-Format-Guide, checked 2026-10-24

name: Three kinds of line break
section: ASS override tags for caption styling
what: `\N` always breaks, `\n` breaks only in wrap mode 2 (otherwise a space), `\h` is a non-breaking space that also isn't trimmed at line ends
how: `Mr.\hSmith` kept "Mr. Smith" together when the line wrapped (tested here 2026-10-24)
refs: Aegisub manual: ASS Override Tags, https://aegisub.org/docs/latest/ass_tags/, checked 2026-10-24

name: Line-level vs text-level tags
section: ASS override tags for caption styling
what: `\pos`, `\move`, `\clip`, `\iclip`, `\org`, `\fade`, `\fad` set properties of the whole line and should appear once (and `\pos`/`\move`, `\clip`/`\iclip`, `\fad`/`\fade` exclude each other); all other tags change the text after them
how: put one positioning tag at the start: `{\an5\pos(540,1180)}`
refs: Aegisub manual: ASS Override Tags, https://aegisub.org/docs/latest/ass_tags/, checked 2026-10-24

name: Separate X and Y outline
section: ASS override tags for caption styling
what: `\xbord`/`\ybord` set border width per axis (a later `\bord` overrides both); useful to correct borders on anamorphic renders
how: `{\xbord4\ybord2}`
refs: Aegisub manual: ASS Override Tags, https://aegisub.org/docs/latest/ass_tags/, checked 2026-10-24

name: Shadow up-left with negative offsets
section: ASS override tags for caption styling
what: `\shad` can't be negative, but `\xshad`/`\yshad` can, putting the shadow above/left of the text
how: `{\xshad-4\yshad-4\4c&H0000FF&\4a&H00&}` drew a red shadow up-left (tested here 2026-10-24)
refs: Aegisub manual: ASS Override Tags, https://aegisub.org/docs/latest/ass_tags/, checked 2026-10-24

name: Glow outline with \blur
section: ASS override tags for caption styling
what: `\blur` softens the border (or the fill if there is no border) with a Gaussian kernel; use it instead of `\be`, which does not scale with resolution
how: `{\bord6\blur6\3c&H00D7FF&}` gave a soft gold glow (tested here 2026-10-24)
refs: Aegisub manual: ASS Override Tags, https://aegisub.org/docs/latest/ass_tags/, checked 2026-10-24
Aegisub manual: Resolution and Matrix, https://aegisub.org/docs/latest/resolution_and_matrix/, checked 2026-10-24

name: Animate size with \fscx/\fscy, not \fs
section: ASS override tags for caption styling
what: `\fs` is integer and goes through font hinting, so animating it jumps; `\fscx`/`\fscy` scale after hinting and should be used inside `\t`
how: `{\t(0,200,\fscx120\fscy120)}` instead of `{\t(\fs60)}`
refs: Aegisub manual: ASS Override Tags, https://aegisub.org/docs/latest/ass_tags/, checked 2026-10-24

name: Font weight numbers
section: ASS override tags for caption styling
what: `\b<weight>` takes 100-900 (400 normal, 700 bold), but most fonts only have one or two weights
how: `{\b900}` only helps with a font that ships a Black weight
refs: Aegisub manual: ASS Override Tags, https://aegisub.org/docs/latest/ass_tags/, checked 2026-10-24

name: Letter spacing
section: ASS override tags for caption styling
what: `\fsp` adds spacing in script pixels, can be negative or fractional
how: `{\fsp6}SPACED OUT` (tested here 2026-10-24) (not on Urdu/Hindi, see 2797)
refs: Aegisub manual: ASS Override Tags, https://aegisub.org/docs/latest/ass_tags/, checked 2026-10-24

name: Shear for a speed look
section: ASS override tags for caption styling
what: `\fax`/`\fay` shear the text; values outside -2..2 rarely look right
how: `{\fax-0.3}` gave a forward-leaning line (tested here 2026-10-24)
refs: Aegisub manual: ASS Override Tags, https://aegisub.org/docs/latest/ass_tags/, checked 2026-10-24

name: Colours are BGR
section: ASS override tags for caption styling
what: `\1c` fill, `\2c` karaoke pre-highlight, `\3c` border, `\4c` shadow, written `&HBBGGRR&` (opposite of HTML)
how: HTML #FFD700 gold is `\1c&H00D7FF&` (tested here 2026-10-24)
refs: Aegisub manual: ASS Override Tags, https://aegisub.org/docs/latest/ass_tags/, checked 2026-10-24

name: Outline-only (hollow) text
section: ASS override tags for caption styling
what: `\1a&HFF&` makes the fill invisible and leaves border and shadow
how: `{\1a&HFF&\bord2}OUTLINE ONLY` (tested here 2026-10-24)
refs: Aegisub manual: ASS Override Tags, https://aegisub.org/docs/latest/ass_tags/, checked 2026-10-24

name: Numpad alignment and its anchor
section: ASS override tags for caption styling
what: `\an1..9` follows the numeric keypad (1 bottom-left, 5 centre, 8 top-centre) and is also the anchor point for `\pos` and rotation
how: to centre a caption on a point use `{\an5\pos(540,1180)}` (tested here 2026-10-24)
refs: Aegisub manual: ASS Override Tags, https://aegisub.org/docs/latest/ass_tags/, checked 2026-10-24

name: Slide in with \move and times
section: ASS override tags for caption styling
what: `\move(x1,y1,x2,y2,t1,t2)` holds at the start until t1 ms, moves at constant speed to t2, then holds; one move per line and no easing
how: `{\move(100,300,540,300,500,1500)}` was still at 0.2 s and 0.4 s and moved by 1.0 s (tested here 2026-10-24)
refs: Aegisub manual: ASS Override Tags, https://aegisub.org/docs/latest/ass_tags/, checked 2026-10-24

name: Fade inside the line's time
section: ASS override tags for caption styling
what: `\fad(in,out)` in ms uses the line's own start/end, so fade-in + fade-out must not exceed the duration
how: `{\fad(150,150)}` on a 1.2 s caption (tested with `\fad(1000,500)` here 2026-10-24)
refs: Aegisub manual: ASS Override Tags, https://aegisub.org/docs/latest/ass_tags/, checked 2026-10-24

name: Five-part fade
section: ASS override tags for caption styling
what: `\fade(a1,a2,a3,t1,t2,t3,t4)` with decimal alpha 0-255 and ms times, e.g. fade in, hold, fade to half
refs: Aegisub manual: ASS Override Tags, https://aegisub.org/docs/latest/ass_tags/, checked 2026-10-24

name: Eased transforms
section: ASS override tags for caption styling
what: `\t(t1,t2,accel,tags)`: accel 1 is linear, below 1 starts fast and ends slow, above 1 starts slow
how: `{\t(0,250,0.5,\fscx100\fscy100)}` for an ease-out settle
refs: Aegisub manual: ASS Override Tags, https://aegisub.org/docs/latest/ass_tags/, checked 2026-10-24

name: Pop-in word
section: ASS override tags for caption styling
what: the manual's example grows text from 0 to 100% scale with `\t`; add a small overshoot with a second `\t`
refs: Aegisub manual: ASS Override Tags, https://aegisub.org/docs/latest/ass_tags/, checked 2026-10-24

name: Wipe-on reveal with an animated clip
section: ASS override tags for caption styling
what: only rectangular `\clip` can be animated with `\t`; a clip growing from width 0 to full reveals the line left to right
refs: Aegisub manual: ASS Override Tags, https://aegisub.org/docs/latest/ass_tags/, checked 2026-10-24

name: Hide part of a line with \iclip
section: ASS override tags for caption styling
what: `\iclip` hides what is inside its rectangle (e.g. where text would cover a logo); vector clips work too but can't be animated
how: `{\iclip(0,0,320,360)}` hid the left half (tested here 2026-10-24)
refs: Aegisub manual: ASS Override Tags, https://aegisub.org/docs/latest/ass_tags/, checked 2026-10-24

name: Rounded caption pill from a drawing
section: ASS override tags for caption styling
what: `\p1` turns text into drawing commands (`m`, `l`, `b` Bézier) filled with the primary colour; put the pill on Layer 0 and the text on Layer 1 at the same `\pos`. Coordinates starting at 0 placed correctly; a drawing with negative coordinates landed off-centre
refs: Aegisub manual: ASS Override Tags, https://aegisub.org/docs/latest/ass_tags/, checked 2026-10-24

name: Jump bounce via a far rotation origin
section: ASS override tags for caption styling
what: the manual notes that an `\org` placed far away turns small `\frz` rotations into near-straight up/down moves
refs: Aegisub manual: ASS Override Tags, https://aegisub.org/docs/latest/ass_tags/, checked 2026-10-24

name: Reset mid-line with \r
section: ASS override tags for caption styling
what: `\r` returns to the line's style and `\rStyle` switches to another style for the rest of the line
how: `{\c&H0000FF&\bord5}Red {\r}normal {\rKara}kara` (tested here 2026-10-24)
refs: Aegisub manual: ASS Override Tags, https://aegisub.org/docs/latest/ass_tags/, checked 2026-10-24

name: \kf sweeps, \k jumps, \ko outlines
section: Karaoke and word-by-word highlight in ASS
what: `\k` switches a syllable from secondary to primary colour at its start, `\K`/`\kf` sweep left to right over the syllable's duration, `\ko` also hides the outline until the syllable starts; durations are centiseconds
how: `{\k50}Har {\kf80}lafz {\ko60}chamakta {\k60}hai` with PrimaryColour yellow and SecondaryColour white showed "lafz" half-filled at 0.9 s (tested here 2026-10-24)
refs: Aegisub manual: ASS Override Tags, https://aegisub.org/docs/latest/ass_tags/, checked 2026-10-24

name: The not-yet-sung colour is SecondaryColour
section: Karaoke and word-by-word highlight in ASS
what: `\2c`/`\2a` are only used as karaoke pre-highlight; set the style's Secondary to the "waiting" colour and Primary to the "sung" colour
how: `Style: K,...,&H0000FFFF,&H00FFFFFF,...` = sung yellow, waiting white (tested here 2026-10-24)
refs: Aegisub manual: Editing styles, https://aegisub.org/docs/latest/styles/, checked 2026-10-24

name: \kt for gaps between sung words
section: Karaoke and word-by-word highlight in ASS
what: `\kt` sets the next syllable's start relative to the line start, so pauses don't need dummy syllables; supported in libass since 0.17.0 (this box has 0.17.1)
how: `{\kt0\k20}One {\kt150\k30}Two` lit "Two" only after 1.5 s (tested here 2026-10-24)
refs: libass wiki: ASS File Format Guide, https://github.com/libass/libass/wiki/ASS-File-Format-Guide, checked 2026-10-24

name: Karaoke ASS straight from Whisper words
section: Karaoke and word-by-word highlight in ASS
what: make one event per 4 words and give each word `\kf` = (next word start − this word start) × 100 so the fill follows the speech
how: Python over `result["segments"][i]["words"]`: `"{\\kf%d}%s" % (round((nxt-w["start"])*100), w["word"].strip())`; burned with `ass=` the fill sat on "fellow" at 1.3 s in the JFK test clip (tested here 2026-10-24)
refs: Aegisub manual: ASS Override Tags, https://aegisub.org/docs/latest/ass_tags/, checked 2026-10-24

name: BorderStyle 3 = a box per line in OutlineColour
section: libass-only extensions (fine for burn-in, not for shared softsubs)
what: with BorderStyle 3 each line got its own opaque rectangle, coloured by OutlineColour (`\3c`), with `Outline` as padding
how: `Style: Box3,...,&H00FF0000 (Outline),...,3,6,0,...` gave blue per-line boxes (tested here 2026-10-24)
refs: libass wiki: Libass' ASS Extensions, https://github.com/libass/libass/wiki/Libass'-ASS-Extensions, checked 2026-10-24

name: BorderStyle 4 = one box for the whole event
section: libass-only extensions (fine for burn-in, not for shared softsubs)
what: libass-only: the shadow becomes a single background box for the event, coloured by `\4c`/`\4a` (BackColour), padding set by `\shad`, and the normal outline is kept; VSFilter draws it as BorderStyle 1
how: `Style: Box4,...,BackColour &H00FF0000,...,4,2,6,...` gave one rectangle behind both lines (tested here 2026-10-24)
refs: libass wiki: Libass' ASS Extensions, https://github.com/libass/libass/wiki/Libass'-ASS-Extensions, checked 2026-10-24

name: Kerning: yes
section: libass-only extensions (fine for burn-in, not for shared softsubs)
what: a `[Script Info]` header that turns on kerning in libass (VSFilter ignores it); safe for plain dialogue
how: add `Kerning: yes`; "AVATAR WAVE To" rendered differently with it (tested here 2026-10-24)
refs: libass wiki: Libass' ASS Extensions, https://github.com/libass/libass/wiki/Libass'-ASS-Extensions, checked 2026-10-24

name: Language header for local glyph forms
section: libass-only extensions (fine for burn-in, not for shared softsubs)
what: `Language: xx` (ISO 639-1 two-letter codes only) enables language-specific character variants in libass
how: `Language: ur` for Urdu files, `Language: hi` for Hindi (rendered fine here 2026-10-24) (tested here 2026-10-24)
refs: libass wiki: Libass' ASS Extensions, https://github.com/libass/libass/wiki/Libass'-ASS-Extensions, checked 2026-10-24

name: Literal curly braces
section: libass-only extensions (fine for burn-in, not for shared softsubs)
what: in libass `\{` and `\}` print braces; in VSFilter the same text can vanish, so add an empty `{}` after escaped opening braces if the file may travel
how: `Literal \{braces\} here` rendered "Literal {braces} here" (tested here 2026-10-24)
refs: libass wiki: Libass' ASS Extensions, https://github.com/libass/libass/wiki/Libass'-ASS-Extensions, checked 2026-10-24

name: Nastaliq needs complex shaping
section: Urdu, Arabic and other RTL captions
what: Noto Nastaliq Urdu rendered as empty boxes with `shaping=simple` and as correct joined Nastaliq with `complex`/`auto` in the `ass` filter
how: `-vf "ass=ur.ass:fontsdir=fonts:shaping=complex"` (tested here 2026-10-24, frames inspected)

name: Get a free Nastaliq font
section: Urdu, Arabic and other RTL captions
what: Noto Nastaliq Urdu is OFL-licensed in google/fonts (`ofl/notonastaliqurdu`, variable weight, Regular to Bold); Noto Naskh Arabic and Noto Sans Devanagari are in the same repo
how: `curl -LO "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/google/fonts/main/ofl/notonastaliqurdu/NotoNastaliqUrdu%5Bwght%5D.ttf"` (+ OFL.txt) and point `fontsdir` at it (downloaded and used here 2026-10-24) (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Nastaliq reads small: size it up
section: Urdu, Arabic and other RTL captions
what: at the same Fontsize 40 the words "پاکستان کیپشن / دوسری لائن" measured 60 px wide in Noto Nastaliq Urdu against 106 px in Noto Naskh Arabic, with a similar block height (70 vs 59 px)
how: give Nastaliq styles a larger Fontsize than the Naskh/Latin styles and size it by checking a rendered frame (tested here 2026-10-24, measured with numpy)

name: Mixed Urdu + English comes out scrambled by default
section: Urdu, Arabic and other RTL captions
what: with the standard `Encoding 1` libass laid "میں نے FireCraft پر 25 ہارٹس جیتے!" out left-to-right, putting the words in the wrong order
how: always check a frame when Urdu lines contain English names or numbers (tested here 2026-10-24, frame inspected)
refs: libass wiki: Libass' ASS Extensions, https://github.com/libass/libass/wiki/Libass'-ASS-Extensions, checked 2026-10-24

name: Encoding=-1 auto-detects RTL in libass
section: Urdu, Arabic and other RTL captions
what: libass-only: `Encoding -1` (style or `\fe`) detects the base direction and bidi-reorders the line; the mixed line rendered in correct RTL order. Use it only for lightly styled dialogue, never if VSFilter might play the file
how: `Style: UrduRTL,Noto Nastaliq Urdu,...,-1` (last field) (tested here 2026-10-24)
refs: libass wiki: Libass' ASS Extensions, https://github.com/libass/libass/wiki/Libass'-ASS-Extensions, checked 2026-10-24

name: Portable fix: Unicode isolates
section: Urdu, Arabic and other RTL captions
what: wrapping the whole line in RLI…PDI (U+2067…U+2069) and each Latin/number run in LRI…PDI (U+2066…U+2069) gave the correct order with ordinary `Encoding 1`

name: An RLM alone did not fix it
section: Urdu, Arabic and other RTL captions
what: prefixing the line with U+200F RIGHT-TO-LEFT MARK left the mixed line in the wrong order in libass
how: use isolates (2841) or Encoding -1 (2840), not a single RLM (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Know the bidi control characters
section: Urdu, Arabic and other RTL captions
what: LRI U+2066, RLI U+2067, FSI U+2068 (direction from first strong character), PDI U+2069 ends an isolate; LRM U+200E, RLM U+200F and ALM U+061C are invisible strong characters with local effect
how: keep a table of these in caption scripts; FSI is handy when a name's script is unknown

name: In HTML captions use markup, not control characters
section: Urdu, Arabic and other RTL captions
what: UAX #9 says markup should be used where available: `dir="rtl"` / CSS `direction:rtl; unicode-bidi:isolate` is the equivalent of RLI…PDI
how:
in HyperFrames caption groups write `
…
` and wrap English names in `` or `dir="ltr"` spans

name: WebVTT direction escapes
section: Urdu, Arabic and other RTL captions
what: cue text may use `‎` and `‏` (also `&`, `<`, `>`, ` `); `&` and `<` must be escaped in cues
how: in a `.vtt` write `‏` before a line that starts with an English word inside Urdu text

name: WebVTT `align:start` follows the text direction
section: Urdu, Arabic and other RTL captions
what: start alignment is the left of the cue box for LTR text and the right for RTL text, so a translated cue stays under the same speaker
how: use `align:start`/`end` rather than `left`/`right` in multilingual VTT

name: Check a font really covers Urdu
section: Urdu, Arabic and other RTL captions
what: fontconfig lists the languages a font file supports; Noto Nastaliq Urdu reported `ur`, `ps-pk`, `pa-pk`, `fa`
how: `fc-scan --format '%{lang}\n' NotoNastaliqUrdu.ttf | tr '|' '\n' | grep -x ur` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Arabic (MSA) Netflix rules: no italics
section: Urdu, Arabic and other RTL captions
what: the Netflix Arabic guide bans italics entirely
how: in Urdu/Arabic styles keep `Italic 0` and mark narration or song with other cues (e.g. quotes, brackets)

name: Arabic dual speakers: hyphen + space
section: Urdu, Arabic and other RTL captions
what: unlike English/Hindi (hyphen, no space), Arabic uses a hyphen followed by a space, one speaker per line
how: `- نعم`/`- لا` on two lines

name: Arabic punctuation rules
section: Urdu, Arabic and other RTL captions
what: no space before commas, question or exclamation marks; never combine `?!`/`!?`; don't replace a repeated conjunction with a comma
how: QC Arabic-script lines with a regex for `\s[،؟!,?]` and `[?؟]!|![?؟]`

name: Tanween placement for line height
section: Urdu, Arabic and other RTL captions
what: Netflix puts tanween on the letter before the alef because tall line heights otherwise make marks overlap
how: follow it in Arabic captions, and check two-line Nastaliq/Naskh events for mark collisions on a frame

name: Arabic reading speed
section: Urdu, Arabic and other RTL captions
what: 20 characters/second for adult programmes and 17 for children's; SDH may go to 23 and 20
how: run the CPS check (2884) with `max_cps=20` on Arabic-script files

name: Arabic line shape
section: Urdu, Arabic and other RTL captions
what: max two lines, keep to one line where possible, and avoid a single word alone on the second line (shorten or break earlier)
how: in QC flag two-line events whose second line has one word

name: Arabic numbers
section: Urdu, Arabic and other RTL captions
what: 1-10 written as words (except times and dates), above 10 as numerals; thousands with a comma (1,234) but no comma in years (1940)
how: apply the same pattern to Urdu captions for consistency

name: Devanagari conjuncts need complex shaping
what: with `shaping=simple` "नमस्ते … क्षत्रिय श्री" showed visible halants and split conjuncts; `complex` joined them (क्ष, त्र, श्री)
how: `-vf "ass=hi.ass:fontsdir=fonts:shaping=complex"` and look at one frame before rendering the whole video (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Library Devanagari fonts work through `ass`
what: Kalam and Rozha One from library/fonts rendered correct conjuncts with the `ass` filter but broken ones through `subtitles` (same font)
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf "ass=hi.ass:fontsdir=/home/user/new-startup/library/fonts" out.mp4` with `Fontname Kalam` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Hindi reading speed is higher than English
what: Netflix Hindi: up to 22 characters/second (adult) and 18 (children); Hindi SDH up to 25 and 20
how: QC Devanagari files with `max_cps=22` (2884)

name: Hindi caption font spec
what: proportional sans-serif (Mangal as placeholder), white, sized so 42 characters fit across the screen
how: Noto Sans Devanagari in white at a size where a 42-character line fits inside the safe area

name: No italics in Hindi
what: use quotation marks for album, book, film and programme titles instead
how: `आज मैं थिएटर में "हैमिल्टन" देखने गया था।`

name: Hindi ellipsis rules
what: use the single character … (U+2026); no ellipsis when a sentence simply runs over two subtitles; use one for a pause of 2 s or more or an abrupt interruption, and at the start of the next subtitle when the sentence continues after such a pause
how: replace `...` with `…` in QC (2884)

name: Hindi dual speakers
what: hyphen without a space, one speaker per line, each line a complete sentence

name: Hindi numbers and money
what: 1-10 in words, 11+ as numerals; ordinals 1st-9th in words, 10th+ as numeral + वीं; decades "20 का दशक"; currency names transliterated, no symbols (10 डॉलर)
how: write "50,000 रुपये"-style amounts, never "₹" or "$"

name: Hindi spacing and quotes
what: no space between text and a following punctuation mark; double quotes for quotations, single inside; direct speech introduced by a comma
how: QC regex `\s[।?!,]` on Hindi lines

name: Bindu for chandrabindu is allowed
what: Netflix Hindi permits bindu in place of chandrabindu
how: if a font or keyboard makes ँ awkward, ं is acceptable

name: Romanized Hindi forced narratives
what: Netflix uses Romanized Hindi FNs, but not over English dialogue or Devanagari on-screen text, and skips everyday Urdu words (Akhbar, Waqt, Shukriya, Mehfooz…); plot-relevant Urdu shayari does get them
how: for the owner's Roman Urdu captions, keep common Urdu words as-is and translate/transliterate only lines a Hindi-speaking viewer wouldn't follow

name: English words inside Hindi lines
what: in Hindi SDH, English words in a mostly Hindi line need no language label but are transliterated with correct spelling (अरे, वेरी सॉरी)
how: keep this rule for Hinglish captions written in Devanagari

name: Hindi song lines
what: only ? and ! at line ends (no commas or full stops); SDH lyrics get ♪ at start and end with a space either side; duet lines each get their own ♪
how: `♪ लग जा गले ♪`

name: Hindi SDH labels
what: square brackets for speaker IDs and sounds, [आदमी]/[औरत] before a name is known, numbered IDs restart each scene, and onomatopoeia preferred ([धमाका!] over [बड़ा विस्फोट])
how: keep a glossary of Hindi/Urdu sound labels for client SDH jobs

name: Word timestamps from Whisper
what: `word_timestamps=True` adds a `words` list to every segment with `word`, `start`, `end` and `probability`
how: `/home/user/tools/venv/bin/python -c "import whisper; r=whisper.load_model('small').transcribe('a.wav', word_timestamps=True, fp16=False)"` → `r["segments"][0]["words"][0]` = `{'word': ' And', 'start': 0.0, 'end': 0.52, 'probability': 0.76}` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Flag low-confidence words for a human check
what: each word carries `probability`; in the JFK test "my" scored 0.52 while "fellow" scored 0.995
how: list words with `probability < 0.6` and re-listen to those spots before burning captions (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Built-in underline-per-word SRT/VTT
what: `highlight_words` (needs word timestamps) writes one cue per word with that word wrapped in `<u>`
how: `whisper.utils.get_writer("srt", outdir)(r, "a.wav", {"highlight_words": True, "max_line_width": None, "max_line_count": None, "max_words_per_line": None})`; CLI `--word_timestamps True --highlight_words True` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Line width and line count from Whisper
what: `max_line_width` breaks lines at N characters and `max_line_count` caps lines per cue (both need word timestamps)
how: writer options `{"max_line_width": 42, "max_line_count": 2}` (CLI `--max_line_width 42 --max_line_count 2`) split the 10 s JFK sentence into a 2-line cue and a 1-line cue (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Whisper's line limits don't limit duration
what: that 2-line cue lasted 9.06 s, past Netflix's 7 s maximum, so always run a duration/CPS check after the writer
how: run the QC script (2884) on every Whisper SRT (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Short social cues from Whisper
what: `max_words_per_line` (no effect when `max_line_width` is set) makes each cue N words
how: `{"max_words_per_line": 3}` gave cues "And so my" / "fellow Americans, ask" / "not what your" (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: All output formats at once
what: the CLI writes txt, vtt, srt, tsv and json (`--output_format all` is the default); TSV times are integer milliseconds
how: writers `get_writer(fmt, outdir)` for each of `srt vtt tsv txt json` (TSV row `0 10340 And so my…`) (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Urdu and Hindi are Whisper languages
what: the tokenizer maps `ur` → urdu and `hi` → hindi; pass the code so detection doesn't guess
how: `--language ur` / `transcribe(..., language="ur")` (`whisper.tokenizer.LANGUAGES["ur"]` = "urdu") (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: English subtitles from foreign speech
what: `--task translate` does X→English recognition instead of transcription
how: `transcribe(audio, task="translate", fp16=False)` ran here (on English audio it returned the English text) (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Steer spelling and punctuation with initial_prompt
what: `initial_prompt` is text given as a prompt for the first window (`carry_initial_prompt` repeats it for every window). With `initial_prompt="Ask not."` the JFK line came back with an extra full stop and capital ("…do for you. Ask what…")
how: pass names and style, e.g. `initial_prompt="FireCraft SMP, lifesteal, Season 2."` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Skip hallucinations over silence
what: `hallucination_silence_threshold` (needs word timestamps) skips silent periods longer than N seconds when a possible hallucination is detected
how: `transcribe(audio, word_timestamps=True, hallucination_silence_threshold=2.0)` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Transcribe a time range from Python (clip_timestamps)
what: `clip_timestamps` takes start,end,... pairs in seconds
how: `transcribe(audio, clip_timestamps=[0, 4.0])` returned one segment 0-4 s "And so my fellow Americans, ask..." (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Punctuation sticks to words
what: with word timestamps, `prepend_punctuations` (default `"'“¿([{-`) merge with the next word and `append_punctuations` (default `"'.。,，!！?？:：”)]}、`) with the previous one, so "Americans," is one word
how: strip punctuation yourself before upper-casing single-word captions if you don't want commas on screen (tested here 2026-10-24, observed in JSON)

name: Whisper result straight into pysubs2
what: `pysubs2.load_from_whisper(result)` builds an SSAFile from a Whisper result dict or segment list
how: `subs = pysubs2.load_from_whisper(r); subs.save("jfk.ass")` (one event 0-10340 ms here) (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: WebVTT karaoke from Whisper words
what: WebVTT timestamp tags inside a cue (`When the moon <00:17.500>hits your eye`) mark when each part becomes active; players can style `:past`/`:future`
how: generator writes `And <00:00.520>so <00:00.860>my …` per 5-word cue; ffmpeg read the file (and dropped the tags when converting) (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: One QC pass for every caption file
what: check per cue: characters/second, duration (min 5/6 s, max 7 s), line length (42), line count (2) and "..." instead of …
how: `qc(subs)` in Python over `pysubs2` events using `len(e.plaintext.replace("\n",""))/duration`; on a test file it flagged `cps 94.5`, `short 0.55`, `cpl 52`, `three dots` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Close small gaps to exactly 2 frames
what: Netflix: gaps should be 2 frames or at least half a second; extend the previous out-time to two frames before the next in-time
how: `if 0 <= b.start - a.end < 500: a.end = b.start - round(2000/fps)` turned a 100 ms gap into 83 ms at 24 fps (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Replace three dots with the ellipsis character
what: Netflix English and Hindi both require the single U+2026 character
how: `e.text = e.text.replace("...", "…")` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Look at frames, not just the file
what: render one PNG per caption style at a time when text is on screen and inspect it; that is how the Urdu tofu, broken conjuncts and scrambled RTL order above were caught
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -ss 1 -vf "ass=caps.ass:fontsdir=fonts" -frames:v 1 check.png` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Hormozi-style recipe as vendors describe it
section: Social caption styles (vendor descriptions, built in ASS)
what: Kapwing: ALL-CAPS, key word in each phrase highlighted in colour, captions in the lower-middle, timed to speech rhythm rather than full sentences; SendShort says Montserrat Black 900 with bold colours and rotation/size effects
how: one event per spoken word, the active word coloured `\1c&H00D7FF&` (gold), others white, `\pos(540,1190)` on 1080x1920 (generator tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Hormozi font history per Submagic
section: Social caption styles (vendor descriptions, built in ASS)
what: Submagic lists an older style (TheBoldFont, uppercase, shadow, no stroke) and a newer one (uppercase, slight shadow, yellow stroke, pop-in from bottom to top), with 4-6 words over 2 lines and keywords made bigger by splitting the caption at that word
how: pop-in = `{\fscx80\fscy80\t(0,80,\fscx100\fscy100)}` on the first word of each group (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: MrBeast-style per Submagic
section: Social caption styles (vendor descriptions, built in ASS)
what: Submagic says the font is Komika (free alternatives Bangers, Obelix Pro; one of its FAQs instead names CCSignLanguage), black-and-white text with a heavy stroke and shadow, keywords in green, about 2 words per line
how: 2-word events, `\1c&H00FF00&` on the keyword; with library Anton at 96 px it fit 1080 wide (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Measure the widest group before rendering
section: Social caption styles (vendor descriptions, built in ASS)
what: with `WrapStyle: 2` (no wrap) three upper-case words at 90 px DejaVu Sans Bold overflowed a 1080 px frame; two words at 80 px fit
how: render the frame of the longest group (`-ss <time> -frames:v 1`) and lower words per group or font size until it fits (tested here 2026-10-24)
refs: Aegisub manual: ASS Override Tags, https://aegisub.org/docs/latest/ass_tags/, checked 2026-10-24

name: Accessible boxed captions
section: Social caption styles (vendor descriptions, built in ASS)
what: DCMP prefers white, medium-weight, sans-serif, proportionally spaced text with a drop or rim shadow and a translucent box (clearer on light backgrounds)
how: white non-bold style with `BorderStyle 4` and a semi-transparent BackColour such as `&H80000000` (libass box, 2832)

name: BBC-style background per line
section: Social caption styles (vendor descriptions, built in ASS)
what: BBC: background width calculated per line, height = line height with no gaps between lines, extended 0.5 em each side
how: ASS `BorderStyle 3` boxes are per line (2831); `Outline` sets the box padding; check the padding on a rendered frame

name: VTT file skeleton
what: optional BOM, `WEBVTT` (+ optional text after a space), a blank line, then optional STYLE/REGION/NOTE blocks, then cues; MIME `text/vtt`, UTF-8. A blank line inside a cue ends it
how: never leave an empty line between a cue's timing and its text when writing VTT by script

name: VTT timestamps
what: `mm:ss.ttt` or `hh:mm:ss.ttt` (hours may exceed two digits); start times must not go backwards; cues may overlap except in chapter tracks
how: use `.` before milliseconds (SRT uses `,`) when converting by hand

name: Position a VTT cue
what: cue settings `line` (number or %; `line:0` top, `line:-1` bottom), `position` (%), `size` (% width), `align` (start/center/end), `vertical` (rl/lr); lowercase, each once
how: `00:05.000 --> 00:10.000 line:0 position:20% size:60% align:start` puts a caption top-left to clear a lower third

name: Roll-up regions
what: a REGION block (`id`, `width`, `lines`, `regionanchor`, `viewportanchor`, `scroll:up`) makes cues scroll up inside a box; the spec's example gives two speakers their own 3-line region on each side
how: `REGION` / `id:fred` / `width:40%` / `lines:3` / `regionanchor:0%,100%` / `viewportanchor:10%,90%` / `scroll:up`, then `region:fred` on cues

name: Speaker and language tags
what: `<v Bob>` marks a voice, `<lang en-GB>` a language, `<c.class>` a class, plus `<i> <b> <u> <ruby>/<rt>`; STYLE blocks can match them with `::cue(v[voice="Bob"])` or `::cue(:lang(ur))`
how: in a web player give each speaker a colour with `::cue(v[voice="Ali"]) { color: yellow; }`

name: What ::cue can style
what: only colour, opacity, visibility, text-decoration, text-shadow, background, outline, font, line-height, white-space, ruby-position and text-combine-upright properties; backgrounds apply per cue
how: a readable web caption: `::cue { color: white; background-color: rgb(0 0 0 / 60%); }`

name: STYLE blocks go before the first cue
what: STYLE and REGION blocks must come before any cue; NOTE blocks can appear anywhere after the header
how: remember ffmpeg 6.1.1 drops every cue of a styled VTT (2737), so keep a STYLE-free copy for ffmpeg work

name: FCC accuracy
section: Accessibility law and standards (what "good captions" means)
what: captions must match the spoken words (and lyrics) in order, without substituting proper names or paraphrasing unless time forces it, with correct spelling, punctuation, tense and numbers; intentional slang/grammar errors are mirrored; speaker IDs, music, sound effects and audience reaction are included
how: caption Whisper output verbatim, then fix names by hand rather than rewording

name: FCC synchronicity
section: Accessibility law and standards (what "good captions" means)
what: captions begin when the speech or sound begins, end about when it ends, and stay up long enough to be read
how: in-times from Whisper word starts, out-times checked by the QC pass (2884)

name: FCC completeness
section: Accessibility law and standards (what "good captions" means)
what: captioning runs from the beginning to the end of the programme
how: caption the outro/CTA too, not just the talking part

name: FCC placement
section: Accessibility law and standards (what "good captions" means)
what: captions must not block faces, featured text, graphics or credits, must be legibly sized, must not overlap each other, and must not run off the screen edge
how: move a caption to the top (`{\an8}`) while a lower third or on-screen text is up

name: WCAG 1.2.2: captions for prerecorded video (Level A)
section: Accessibility law and standards (what "good captions" means)
what: captions include dialogue, who is speaking and meaningful non-speech sounds; open (always visible) captions are a sufficient technique (G93)
how: burned-in captions count for web accessibility if they also carry speaker IDs and sound cues

name: WCAG failure F8
section: Accessibility law and standards (what "good captions" means)
what: captions that omit some dialogue or important sound effects fail 1.2.2
how: compare caption word count with the Whisper transcript before delivery

name: Describe music, not just "music"
section: Accessibility law and standards (what "good captions" means)
what: WCAG's orchestra example identifies non-vocal music by title, movement and composer and adds a mood line between ♪
how: `[Orchestral Suite No. 3 in D major, Air]` / `♪ Calm melody with a slow tempo ♪` style labels

name: Mixed case, caps for shouting
what: mixed case is preferred for readability; capitals are used for screaming or shouting
how: don't upper-case long accessible captions; keep ALL-CAPS for short social styles only

name: DCMP duration limits
what: captions at least 40 frames (1 second 10 frames) and at most 6 seconds (background-music notes excepted)
how: QC with `min_s=1.33, max_s=6.0` for educational clients (2884)

name: DCMP placement
what: bottom two lines, left-aligned multi-line captions where possible, moved to the top if they'd cover names, faces, mouths or essential graphics; no more than two lines preferred; keep inside margins so characters and descenders aren't cut
how: ASS `Alignment 1`/`\an1` with MarginL for left-aligned blocks, `\an7` when moved up

name: Place captions under the speaker
what: dialogue goes under its speaker unless graphics interfere; an off-screen speaker's caption goes far left or right toward their position; a moving speaker keeps one placement
how: two simultaneous speakers as `{\an1}` and `{\an3}` events (rendered side by side here) (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: DCMP presentation rate by level
what: lower-level educational media at most 130 wpm, middle-level 140, upper-level 160, counting every word including speaker IDs and sound labels
how: words-per-minute = words / duration × 60 per caption in the QC script

name: Borrow 15 frames
what: DCMP reaches the target rate partly by starting or ending a caption up to 15 frames before or after its audio, which it says is hardly noticeable
how: before editing words, extend in/out times by up to 0.5 s at 30 fps where there is room

name: DCMP line division
what: break where speech pauses; don't separate a modifier from its word, don't split a prepositional phrase, don't end a line on a conjunction, and don't start a new sentence on the same line unless both are 1-2-word related sentences
how: put manual `\N` breaks in ASS (`\q2`) rather than trusting auto-wrap

name: DCMP sound effects
what: in brackets, lower case, naming the source unless it's clearly on screen ([coins jangling]); an onomatopoeia goes on the line under the described sound ([rain falling] / pitter-patter)
how: keep a per-project list of sound labels in that form

name: DCMP background music
what: describe essential music in brackets (italic if off-screen) with performer/title when possible and objective mood words; non-essential music gets a ♪ in the upper right, never at the expense of dialogue; music under 5 seconds isn't captioned
how: a `{\an9}♪` event for background music in ASS

name: DCMP lyrics
what: lyrics verbatim, introduced by artist and title in brackets if the rate permits; ♪ at the start and end of each caption, ♪♪ at the end of the song's last line, with spaces inside the notes
how: `♪ And I can't wait to get\Non the road again ♪♪`

name: DCMP speaker names
what: when placement can't show who speaks, put the known name in parentheses on its own line; don't name someone before they are introduced; otherwise identify by what a hearing viewer knows, in inclusive language
how: `(Ahmed)\NWelcome back!`

name: BBC line length by platform
what: broadcast Teletext allows 37 fixed-width characters; online, the line is limited by width: 68% of a 16:9 frame, 90% of 4:3, 1:1 and 9:16; 37 characters in a 75%-wide 16:9 region correspond to about 25 in a 90%-wide 9:16 region
how: for vertical reels plan about 25 characters per line

name: Lines per subtitle by aspect
what: up to two lines for 16:9, 4:3 and 1:1; up to three lines for 9:16 vertical video
how: allow a third line only in portrait styles

name: Minimum time per word
what: at the recommended 160-180 wpm, aim for about 0.3 s per word (1.2 s for a 4-word subtitle), as a guide rather than a crude rule
how: QC warns when `duration < 0.3 × words`

name: Sync limits
what: when the speaker is in shot, don't anticipate speech by more than 1.5 s or hang on more than 1.5 s after it stops; never appear more than 2 s after the words; don't pre-empt a dramatic sound such as a bang
how: check `start - first_word_start` and `end - last_word_end` per cue against ±1.5 s

name: Lips moving = text on screen
what: a subtitle or label should be on screen whenever someone's lips are moving, even if that breaks timing conventions for slow speakers
how: don't leave caption gaps during long slow words; extend the cue

name: Avoid straddling cuts
what: a subtitle should not start mid-shot one and end mid-shot two; split or delay it, or merge two short shots' speech so it ends on the second cut
how: use scdet cut times (2779) to split cues at cuts

name: Speaker colours
what: in priority white, yellow (#FFFF00), cyan (#00FFFF), green (#00FF00), all on black; a speaker keeps one colour; the narrator is yellow by convention; mixed-colour speech in one subtitle runs on without new lines
how: ASS `\1c&H00FFFF&` (yellow) / `&HFFFF00&` (cyan) / `&H00FF00&` (green) per speaker

name: Colour as a floater
what: with many minor characters green may be reused for several who never appear together; white can be any number of speakers
how: assign yellow/cyan to the two main speakers and green to minor ones

name: Off-screen speech
what: single quotes mark an out-of-vision speaker (e.g. phone) when colour can't; labels in white caps only if it's unclear who speaks or more than four speakers share colours; simultaneous speech gets a white label like TOGETHER:
how: `'I'm outside.'` for a voice on the phone

name: Caption size for landscape and vertical
what: author font size to fit a line height of 7-8% of the active video height for 16:9, 4:3 and 1:1, and 3.9-4.5% for 9:16
how: 1080p landscape line height 76-86 px; 1080x1920 vertical 75-86 px (4.5% × 1920 = 86)

name: Author in a wide font
what: use a wide font (Reith Sans, Verdana, Tiresias) when authoring so a narrower presentation font never reflows lines; players may shrink (multipliers 0.6-0.8 on most screens, x1 on small phones) but never enlarge
how: when sizing soft-sub lines, test with a wide font such as DejaVu Sans

name: BBC safe positioning
what: 16:9 landscape: keep subtitles inside the central 90% vertically and 75% horizontally; 9:16: central 75% vertically and 90% horizontally; 4:3 and 1:1: central 90% both ways
how: for 1080x1920 keep captions between y 240 and y 1680 and x 54-1026

name: Vertical video: a little higher
what: in 9:16 it is common to place subtitles a bit higher but still in the lower third, since faces sit in the top half
how: vertical ASS style with `Alignment 2` and `MarginV 600` on PlayRes 1080x1920 (rendered here) (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Move vertically for graphics, horizontally for people
what: vertical displacement avoids on-screen captions/graphics; horizontal displacement indicates speakers or avoids a mouth when moving up would cover a face
how: lower third up → `\an8`; face above the lower third → shift sideways with `\an1`/`\an3`

name: Prepared vs live alignment
what: prepared subtitles are centre-aligned in a centred region; live (cued or cumulative) subtitles are normally left-aligned
how: keep edited reels centred

name: Sarcasm, incredulity and stress
what: sarcasm: `Charming(!)`; sarcastic question `(?)`; incredulous question `?!`; stressed words in caps used sparingly; shouting in caps
how: apply in English captions instead of extra styling

name: Whispered speech
what: a `WHISPERS:` label is most effective; when time is short put the words in brackets; for long whispers label the first subtitle only
how: `WHISPERS:\NDon't let him near you.`

name: BBC sound-effect labels
what: white caps, own line, placed left unless the sound clearly comes from the right; describe sounds not actions (GUNFIRE, not THEY SHOOT EACH OTHER); subject + active verb (FLOORBOARDS CREAK); don't label what can be subtitled
how: `{\an1}DOOR SLAMS`

name: BBC music labels
what: source music in caps (POP MUSIC ON RADIO); identifiable incidental music as `MUSIC: "Title"` (title in mixed case); unknown mood music only labelled when needed for the plot (EERIE MUSIC)
how: use these as text events in `\an8` while dialogue runs

name: BBC song lyrics
what: every song subtitle starts with # (♫ allowed online) and the last has # at both ends; well-known lyrics are never edited; song lines are centred and follow the song's pace; `..` at the start if the song is joined mid-way, `...` at the end if it continues
how: `♫ ..Now I need a place to hide away`

name: No emoji notes
what: emoji such as 🎵 (U+1F3B5) must not be used; use ♫ (U+266B)
how: `text.replace("\U0001F3B5", "♫")` in caption scripts

name: Cumulative subtitles
what: two or three parts appearing at different times with one out-time; for punchlines, quiz answers, backing singers or delayed responses; max three lines, not at a shot change, not over mouths
how: in ASS, a second event starting later at `\an2` with `MarginV` raised by one line height, same end time

name: Bleeped words
what: write BLEEP in caps, in a contrasting colour, without an exclamation mark
how: `{\1c&H00FFFF&}BLEEP{\r}`

name: Children's subtitles: keep timings even
what: avoid jumping between inconsistent timings (e.g. a 6 s then an 8 s two-liner of similar difficulty) and give more time when visuals matter
how: for kids' content compare neighbouring cue durations in QC

name: Netflix duration window
section: Netflix timing and SDH rules (beyond CPL/CPS)
what: minimum 5/6 second per event (20 frames at 24 fps), maximum 7 seconds
how: QC with `min_s=5/6, max_s=7.0` (2884)

name: "Half a second" scales with frame rate, the 2-frame gap doesn't
section: Netflix timing and SDH rules (beyond CPL/CPS)
what: the timing rules are written for 24 fps (12 frames); at 30 fps half a second is 15 frames, at 60 fps 30 frames, but the minimum gap stays 2 frames at every rate
how: in scripts use `half = 0.5` s and `gap = 2/fps`

name: Don't chain past half a second of hang
section: Netflix timing and SDH rules (beyond CPL/CPS)
what: Netflix: if an out-time was already extended half a second beyond the end of the audio, don't extend it further to close a gap; re-segment, merge, or leave a gap of half a second or more (at 24 fps no 3-11 frame gaps may remain)
how: in the gap closer (2885) skip cues where `a.end - last_word_end >= 0.5` and flag them for merging

name: Pull the in-time back onto the cut
section: Netflix timing and SDH rules (beyond CPL/CPS)
what: if dialogue starts on a shot change or within half a second after it, the in-time goes on the first frame of the new shot (Netflix allows bringing in-times forward to sync with cuts)
how: with scdet cut times (2779): `if 0 <= start - cut < 0.5: start = cut`

name: Dialogue that crosses a cut
section: Netflix timing and SDH rules (beyond CPL/CPS)
what: a subtitle may cross a shot change only if the dialogue does; then its in-time must be at least half a second before the cut (or moved to the first frame after it), and its out-time either 2 frames before the cut or at least half a second after
how: move an in-time that lands less than half a second before a cut either onto the cut or to 0.5 s before it

name: Reserve 20 frames for tiny lines
section: Netflix timing and SDH rules (beyond CPL/CPS)
what: no subtitle shorter than 20 frames, and that minimum is for one- or two-word lines; extend longer subtitles where possible
how: QC warning when a cue has > 2 words and lasts < 1 s

name: Borrow time across neighbours
section: Netflix timing and SDH rules (beyond CPL/CPS)
what: when reading speeds are uneven, merge with the previous or next subtitle to even out the rhythm, then re-time to shot and audio without spoiling punchlines
how: merge two short cues whose combined CPS is under the limit

name: Time on-screen-text translations to the text
section: Netflix timing and SDH rules (beyond CPL/CPS)
what: forced narratives for on-screen text mimic its timing; for text that fades, set in/out halfway through the fade
how: for a promo's title card, start the Urdu translation cue at the middle of the card's fade-in

name: Forced narratives in English: ALL CAPS, never mixed with dialogue
section: Netflix timing and SDH rules (beyond CPL/CPS)
what: FNs for on-screen text are in caps (sentence case for long passages), never in the same subtitle as dialogue, and redundant FNs are deleted; an FN interrupting dialogue gets ellipses either side
how: `I don't think we should…` / `NO TRESPASSING` / `…go any further.`

name: Positioning and on-screen text
section: Netflix timing and SDH rules (beyond CPL/CPS)
what: subtitles are centre-justified at the top or bottom; avoid overlapping on-screen text, and if text is at both top and bottom choose the easier-to-read place
how: `{\an8}` for the events that overlap a lower-third card

name: SDH labels in US English
section: Netflix timing and SDH rules (beyond CPL/CPS)
what: brackets, all lower case except proper nouns, describe sounds not visuals, [man]/[woman] or [male voice] before a name is known, numbers for repeated IDs, and never italicise IDs or effects even in italic narration
how: `-[Kimmy] Are you coming?` / `-[Titus] In a minute.`

name: Interruptions vs trail-offs
section: Netflix timing and SDH rules (beyond CPL/CPS)
what: two hyphens for an abrupt interruption by an action, sound or other speaker (`-What are you--`), an ellipsis for a trail-off or change of thought by the same speaker; no ellipsis when a sentence just continues into the next subtitle
how: QC that `--` only appears at line ends

name: English lyric formatting
section: Netflix timing and SDH rules (beyond CPL/CPS)
what: italicise sung lyrics, ♪ at the start and end of each lyric subtitle with spaces, a capital at the start of every line, and only ? or ! at line ends; song titles in quotes, e.g. ["Forever Your Girl" playing]
how: `{\i1}♪ Line one\NLine two ♪{\i0}`

name: English punctuation preferences
section: Netflix timing and SDH rules (beyond CPL/CPS)
what: no double spaces, no en or em dashes, avoid colons and semicolons, prefer "okay" over "OK", interrobang as `?!`
how: QC regexes for `  `, `[–—]`, `\bOK\b` on English files

name: Censored audio
section: Netflix timing and SDH rules (beyond CPL/CPS)
what: dialogue is never censored unless the audio itself is dipped or bleeped; then use one asterisk per letter and only audible letters (f***, ****)
how: match the bleep in the captions of client cuts that have it

name: Promos and social cuts may read faster
section: Netflix timing and SDH rules (beyond CPL/CPS)
what: Netflix's marketing-asset guide allows reading speed above the normal limits to keep meaning and audio alignment (social viewers tolerate dense, fast subtitles), forbids condensing punchlines/taglines/iconic lines, and says not to condense if the full line fits in the safe area
how: for the owner's promos keep near-verbatim captions and only split them

name: Marketing subs live at the bottom, inside the safe area
section: Netflix timing and SDH rules (beyond CPL/CPS)
what: for marketing assets subtitles are not placed at the top (they get repositioned to the bottom), translations must stay fully inside the prescribed safe area, and song lyrics are left out unless instructed
how: keep promo captions in one bottom band and skip lyric captions on music beds

name: EBU R 95 safe areas
section: Netflix timing and SDH rules (beyond CPL/CPS)
what: all graphics inside the Graphics Safe Area (5% in from top, bottom and each side) and essential action inside the Action Safe Area (3.5%)
how: on 1920x1080 keep captions at least 96 px from the sides and 54 px from top/bottom (5% of each dimension)

name: Pick the screen colour from the subject, not habit
section: Shooting green screen so it keys (photography rules)
what: the most important factor for a key is colour separation between subject and screen: use blue when the subject is mostly green (plants, a green costume), green otherwise. Bright green is less likely in foregrounds and digital cameras and lossy codecs keep the most detail in the green channel
how: before the shoot list the wardrobe/prop colours; if any is green, book a blue screen and key it later with `chromakey` on the sampled blue.

name: Two characters, two screens
section: Shooting green screen so it keys (photography rules)
what: when two subjects need opposite screen colours (a red-blue costume and an all-green costume), shoot each against the screen that is far from its colours and composite both later (Spider-Man was shot on green, the Green Goblin on blue)
how: shoot separate passes and stack them in ffmpeg with two keyed `overlay` layers or two HyperFrames video layers.

name: Blue for night scenes
section: Shooting green screen so it keys (photography rules)
what: blue is still the better screen when green spill would look wrong, for example a night scene, or when a costume or prop is green
how: for a night composite ask for a blue screen and key with `chromakey`/`hsvkey` on the blue.

name: Screen dress code
section: Shooting green screen so it keys (photography rules)
what: nothing on the subject may match the backing colour, or that part is keyed out (presenters 'disappear' into the key); also check glasses and watches for green reflections
how: send the owner/client a one-line brief: 'no green clothes, jewellery or props; remove shiny watches'.

name: Simple silhouettes key cleanly
section: Shooting green screen so it keys (photography rules)
what: frizzy hair and fine detail may not resolve, and partly transparent costume parts cause problems, so a fairly simple outline gives a clean division
how: prefer tied-back hair and solid fabric for a key you will pull with ffmpeg; budget `rembg` alpha matting or a softer `blend` for hair.

name: Matte screen material
section: Shooting green screen so it keys (photography rules)
what: shiny surfaces reflect the lights as pale hot areas and dark patches; a matte surface diffuses light and gives a narrow colour range. Non-reflective fabric or vinyl avoids hot spots
how: reject shiny paper or glossy paint as a backdrop for owner shoots.

name: Taut, clean, wrinkle-free screen
section: Shooting green screen so it keys (photography rules)
what: wrinkles and folds cast shadows; dirty marks also stay in the key. Stretch fabric tight on all sides
how: check the first frame at 100% before recording; a shadowed fold shows up as a separate colour when you sample it with `crop=...,scale=1:1`.

name: Two-stop value difference
section: Shooting green screen so it keys (photography rules)
what: for the cleanest key create a value difference between subject and screen, for example the screen two stops brighter than the subject or the other way round
how: ask the shooter to meter screen and face separately and keep the two-stop gap.

name: Expose the screen bright and saturated
section: Shooting green screen so it keys (photography rules)
what: under- or over-exposing the backing lowers its saturation, and underexposed video is noisy; the screen must be bright enough for a bright, saturated colour, and too dark or blown out gives no clean key
how: check the sampled screen colour: a dull, grey sample means the exposure is off.

name: Soft lights at 45 degrees on the screen
section: Shooting green screen so it keys (photography rules)
what: light the screen with at least two diffused lights a few feet away (out of shot) at about 45 degrees; uncovered lights give harsh falloff. Check where the two beams overlap for hot spots
how: softboxes or diffusion gel in front of LED panels; keep fabric away from hot tungsten lamps.

name: Same lights, same settings, same colour temperature
section: Shooting green screen so it keys (photography rules)
what: screen lights should be the same make and model with the same settings, and every light on the screen should share one colour temperature (3200K tungsten or about 5600K daylight LEDs, not mixed), with camera white balance matched
how: mixed lamps make the green shift across the screen, which shows as two different sampled colours.

name: Light the subject for the target scene
section: Shooting green screen so it keys (photography rules)
what: light the subject for where they are meant to be, not where they are: blue light for a night scene, beach light for a beach. Lighting in both scenes must match: overcast skies are easier to match, direct sun must match in direction and colour
how: pick the background plate first, then brief the subject lighting from it.

name: Magenta-gel the backlight
section: Shooting green screen so it keys (photography rules)
what: a backlight separates the subject from the screen, and gelling it with minus-green (magenta) counters green spill on hair and shoulders
how: add a magenta-gelled rim light behind the subject.

name: Bigger, farther screen against spill
section: Shooting green screen so it keys (photography rules)
what: the screen scatters its own colour onto the set (spill); a larger screen placed far from the actors avoids it
how: if spill remains, plan `despill` in post.

name: Defocus the screen slightly
section: Shooting green screen so it keys (photography rules)
what: keeping the screen a little out of focus evens out marks and shadows on it
how: use a wider aperture so the backdrop is soft while the subject stays sharp.

name: Shutter for keying
section: Shooting green screen so it keys (photography rules)
what: a fast shutter cuts motion blur and helps with flyaway hair (Artlist); 1/48 at 24 fps is the cinematic default (Finchley). A faster shutter needs exposure rebalanced
how: for fast action ask for a faster shutter; for talking heads keep the 180-degree default.

name: Shoot at the highest resolution
section: Shooting green screen so it keys (photography rules)
what: more recorded detail keys more accurately, and spare resolution lets you crop and reframe as an emergency fix when the key fails near the frame edge
how: shoot 4K for a 1080p delivery when a key is planned.

name: Match depth of field to the plate
section: Shooting green screen so it keys (photography rules)
what: the depth of field of the screen shot should match the background, which can mean a larger depth of field than usual
how: if the plate is deep-focus, stop down on the subject; if the plate is soft, blur it with `gblur` before the `overlay`.

name: Rehearse for shadows and test-key on set
section: Shooting green screen so it keys (photography rules)
what: do a dry run of the whole move to catch shadows and green flashes, and test-key a sample clip before the full shoot
how: pull a 5 s test clip and key it here with `chromakey` the same day.

name: Tracking markers for a moving camera
section: Shooting green screen so it keys (photography rules)
what: tape crosses, a painted grid or tennis balls on the screen give the software points to compute the camera move so the background matches perspective and motion
how: put markers on the screen (not the subject) and remove them later with the garbage matte or keyer.

name: Keep a real shadow on purpose
section: Shooting green screen so it keys (photography rules)
what: shadowed areas of the screen can be replaced with a darker version of the new background so the subject seems to cast a shadow
how: needs a soft matte where the shadow is: use `blend` in `chromakey` and check the shadow region in the alpha.

name: Shoot a clean plate
section: Shooting green screen so it keys (photography rules)
what: capturing the background without actors first lets you cancel it per pixel (a difference matte), but objects similar to the background vanish and camera noise or small changes leave background behind
how: record 3 s of empty set from the locked camera before the take; use it with the difference-key skills below.

name: Reflective props pick up the screen
section: Shooting green screen so it keys (photography rules)
what: green or blue screens caused problems on reflective armour and gave no interactive light (one reason The Mandalorian used LED walls); green screen stays the practical choice for most shoots
how: cover or dull reflective props, or plan to roto and grade them.

name: Sample the real screen colour
what: key on the colour the camera recorded, not on pure 0x00FF00: average a patch of clean screen and print its RGB
how: `ffmpeg -v error -i green.png -vf "crop=40:40:0:0,scale=1:1:flags=area" -f rawvideo -pix_fmt rgb24 - | od -An -tu1` printed `0 175 62` for a 0x00b140 screen with noise (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: chromakey output carries alpha
what: the chromakey output stream is yuva420p, so it can go straight into `overlay`, `alphaextract` or an alpha codec
how: `ffprobe -v error -f lavfi -i "movie=green.mp4,chromakey=0x00b140:0.1" -show_entries stream=pix_fmt -of csv=p=0` printed `yuva420p` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: chromakey on exact YUV values
what: with `yuv=1` the colour is read as YUV hex, so you can pass exact Y/U/V values from a scope; colour names like green no longer make sense then
how: `chromakey=color=0x8C2C24:similarity=0.1:yuv=1,format=yuva420p` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Doc example: key over a black plate
what: the ffmpeg docs overlay a green-screen video on a black background with `chromakey=0x70de77:0.1:0.2`; give the lavfi colour source a duration so the job ends
how: `ffmpeg -f lavfi -i color=c=black:s=320x180:d=2 -i green.mp4 -shortest -filter_complex "[1:v]chromakey=0x70de77:0.1:0.2[ckout];[0:v][ckout]overlay[out]" -map "[out]" out.mkv` (without `:d=` on the colour source the run did not end here) (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Animate key settings with sendcmd
what: chromakey (and colorkey, hsvkey, lumakey, despill, backgroundkey) accept their options as commands, so similarity can change at a given time when the light changes mid-shot
how: `-vf "sendcmd=c='1.0 chromakey similarity 0.3',chromakey=0x00b140:0.1:0.05,format=yuva420p"` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: colorkey defaults to black
what: colorkey's default colour is black, so it can drop a dark background from stock elements shot on black
how: `colorkey=color=black:similarity=0.1:blend=0.3,format=rgba` on a glow-on-black clip (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: lumakey a black background
what: threshold=0 keys the darks, the job for elements shot on black (explosions, smoke, debris); for things that emit light, a Screen or Add blend usually looks better than a key
how: `lumakey=threshold=0:tolerance=0.05:softness=0.2` then `overlay` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: backgroundkey for a static background
what: backgroundkey turns a static background into transparency (threshold for scene-change detection, default 0.08; similarity 0.1; blend 0); it exists in this ffmpeg 6.1
how: `-vf "backgroundkey=threshold=0.08:similarity=0.1:blend=0.05,format=yuva420p" -c:v png -f nut out.nut` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Keep one colour: chromahold/colorhold/hsvhold
what: the hold filters remove colour from everything except one colour (chromahold in YUV, colorhold in RGB, hsvhold by HSV range); `blend` 0 makes pixels fully grey or not at all
how: `chromahold=color=red:similarity=0.2:blend=0.1`, `colorhold=color=0xff0000:similarity=0.3:blend=0.1`, `hsvhold=hue=0:sat=0.8:val=0.8:similarity=0.3:blend=0.1` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: despill a blue screen
what: for blue screen set type=blue and blue=-1 (green scale back to 0)
how: `despill=type=blue:blue=-1:green=0` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: What the spillmap mix means
what: in the Natron Despill (same parameter set, after Steve Wright's unspill) mix 0 limits green by blue, 0.5 by the average of red and blue, 1 by red; expand lowers the subtracted values to remove leftover spill
how: try `despill=type=green:mix=0` and `mix=1` against the default 0.5 on a skin close-up (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Despill brightness and colour push
what: despill can add red/blue into the spill area and set its brightness while trying to keep colours, instead of only removing green
how: `despill=type=green:brightness=0.3:red=0.2` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Look at the spillmap
what: with alpha=1 despill writes the generated spillmap into alpha, which shows where spill is being removed
how: `-vf "format=rgba,despill=type=green:alpha=1,alphaextract"` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Average-limit despill by expression
what: Blender's Color Spill 'Average' limit uses the average of the other two channels as the limit for the spill channel; in ffmpeg that is g = min(g, (r+b)/2)
how: `-vf "format=gbrp,geq=r='r(X,Y)':g='min(g(X,Y),(r(X,Y)+b(X,Y))/2)':b='b(X,Y)'"` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: The simplest spill fix
what: Wikipedia gives a very simple spill function g(r,g,b) = (r, min(g,b), b), close to analogue/film screen pulling
how: `-vf "format=gbrp,geq=r='r(X,Y)':g='min(g(X,Y),b(X,Y))':b='b(X,Y)'"` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Colour-difference key by expression
what: the simplest green-screen alpha is f = A(r+b) - Bg with A and B user constants defaulting to 1; modern keyers use nested surfaces in RGB space
how: alpha from geq: `format=rgba,geq=r='r(X,Y)':g='g(X,Y)':b='b(X,Y)':a='clip(255*((r(X,Y)+b(X,Y))-g(X,Y))/255*4,0,255)'` (the *4 is a gain to taste) (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: PIK / IBK key formula in numpy
what: PIK's green key is alpha = 0 if (Ag - Ar*rw - Ab*gbw) < 0 else 1 - (Ag - Ar*rw - Ab*gbw)/(Bg - Br*rw - Bb*gbw), A = (denoised) foreground, B = screen colour or clean plate, weights default 0.5; screen subtraction removes (1-alpha) x screen colour
how: implement on a float RGB frame with Bc = mean of a clean screen patch, then `fg - (1-alpha)*Bc` for the despilled fill (/home/user/tools/venv/bin/python, numpy) (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Lower a weight to fix a discoloured edge
what: in PIK/IBK a discoloured edge after screen subtraction is not spill but a matte that is too strong; lower the weight of that colour (red edge: lower red weight)
how: in the numpy PIK, drop rw from 0.5 to 0.3 and compare the edge.

name: Clean-plate keying for uneven screens
what: IBK/PIK use an image of the screen (clean plate, or one generated by IBKColor/PIKColor) instead of one picked colour, which gives good results on uneven blue/green screens
how: use a shot clean plate (or `tmedian` over a long empty stretch) as B in the numpy PIK formula, per pixel instead of one colour.

name: Key a denoised copy, keep the original colour
what: feed a denoised or pre-blurred copy to the keyer to pull the matte, and use the original for colour (PIK's PFg input; Keylight's Screen PreBlur for grainy footage)
how: `[0:v]split[o][k];[k]hqdn3d=4:3:6:4,chromakey=0x00b140:0.12:0.05,format=yuva444p,alphaextract[m];[o][m]alphamerge` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Screen balance starting points
what: Keylight's Screen Balance: blue screens tend to work best around 0.95, green around 0.5; if not, try 0.05, 0.5 and 0.95
how: there is no balance option in ffmpeg's keyers; in the numpy colour-difference key, vary the red/blue weights the same way.

name: Multi-pass keying
what: shots that one key can't handle are keyed in several passes on different parts and combined (Keylight Intermediate Result, Natron 'Add to Inside Mask')
how: two chromakeys on two sampled screen colours, mattes combined with the darker (more transparent) value: `[0:v]split=3[o][a][b];[a]chromakey=0x00b140:0.10:0.02,format=yuva444p,alphaextract[m1];[b]chromakey=0x00c060:0.10:0.02,format=yuva444p,alphaextract[m2];[m1][m2]blend=all_mode=darken[m];[o][m]alphamerge` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Uneven screen: sample several screen colours
what: Blender's Keying Screen builds a gradient plate from colours sampled at tracks across the screen so each area keys against its own shade, instead of widening tolerance (which also eats the foreground)
how: sample 3-4 patches with the crop+scale=1:1 command; if they differ a lot, use multi-pass keys or the clean-plate PIK formula.

name: Black and white clip on the matte
what: Keylight Clip Black/White (Blender Black/White Level) set where the matte becomes fully transparent/opaque; keep black as low and white as high as possible, too aggressive gives hard edges
how: `alphaextract,lut=y='clip((val-40)*255/(215-40),0,255)'` then `alphamerge` back (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Matte monitor view
what: a matte monitor stretches alpha values strictly between 0 and 1 toward 0.5 so near-0/near-1 values become visible; for viewing only
how: `chromakey=0x00b140:0.15:0.3,format=yuva444p,alphaextract,lut=y='if(eq(val,0)+eq(val,255),val,128+(val-128)*0.5)'` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Check the key on white and on black
what: inspect a matte over both a light and a dark temporary plate before styling; reject missing hair/fingers, halos and thick outlines
how: `[1:v][0:v]overlay[w];[2:v][0:v]overlay[k];[w][k]hstack` with color=white and color=black plates (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Checkerboard behind a cutout
what: a checkerboard plate makes transparent areas obvious in a still
how: `-f lavfi -i "nullsrc=s=320x180,geq=lum='if(eq(mod(floor(X/16)+floor(Y/16),2),0),200,120)':cb=128:cr=128" -i cut.png -filter_complex "[0:v][1:v]overlay"` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Measure how much is keyed
what: average alpha per frame is a quick number for a key that changes over time (light change, subject leaving)
how: `chromakey=...,format=yuva444p,alphaextract,signalstats,metadata=print:key=lavfi.signalstats.YAVG:file=alpha_avg.txt` printed YAVG=41.59 on frame 0 (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: alphaextract needs an alpha format first
what: chromakey output fed straight into alphaextract failed here ('could not choose their formats'); insert `format=yuva444p` before it
how: `chromakey=0x00b140:0.12:0.08,format=yuva444p,alphaextract` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Carry alpha as fill + matte videos
what: alphaextract + alphamerge exist to carry alpha through formats without an alpha channel: write the fill and the grey matte as two ordinary files
how: `[0:v]chromakey=0x00b140:0.12:0.08,format=yuva444p,split[a][b];[a]alphaextract[m];[b]format=yuv420p[c]` -> `-map "[c]" fill.mp4 -map "[m]" -pix_fmt yuv420p matte.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: mergeplanes as a second way to attach alpha
what: mergeplanes maps planes from up to four inputs; the doc's example merges a yuv444p stream and a grey stream into yuva444p
how: `[0:v]format=yuv444p[c];[1:v]format=gray[m];[c][m]mergeplanes=0x00010210:yuva444p` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: maskedmerge composites with a third-stream matte
what: maskedmerge takes the first stream where the mask is 0, the second where it is max (255 at 8-bit) and mixes in between; all three must share size and format
how: `[a][b][m]maskedmerge` with all three converted to yuv444p (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Shrink a matte (choke)
what: erosion replaces each pixel with the local 3x3 minimum, so repeated passes pull the matte edge inward; follow with a small blur to soften
how: `alphaextract,erosion,erosion,gblur=sigma=1.5` then `alphamerge` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Grow a matte
what: dilation replaces each pixel with the local 3x3 maximum, pushing the matte outward (Blender's Dilate is the same idea for including more edge)
how: `alphaextract,dilation` then `alphamerge` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Open/close a matte with a structuring element
what: morpho applies erode, dilate, open, close, gradient, tophat or blackhat with a structure from a second input, and is the fast option when speed matters
how: `[a][s]morpho=mode=open:structure=first` with a 5x5 white `color` source as the structure (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Despot a matte
what: Keylight's despot removes isolated black specks in a white matte (and white in black); a median filter on the matte does a similar cleanup
how: `alphaextract,median=radius=2` then `alphamerge` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: inflate/deflate for gentle edge changes
what: inflate averages only higher neighbours, deflate only lower ones (3x3), softer than dilation/erosion
how: `format=gray,inflate,deflate` on a matte image (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Binary matte with the threshold filter
what: threshold takes four streams (input, threshold, min, max) and picks min below the threshold and max above; colour sources make binary, inverted, truncate and to-zero variants
how: `[a][t][lo][hi]threshold` with color=gray, color=black, color=white plates (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Hysteresis for robust edge masks
what: hysteresis grows the first stream into the second by connected components, so strong pixels pull in connected weak ones
how: strong = `lut=y='if(gt(val,240),255,0)'`, weak = `lut=y='if(gt(val,60),255,0)'`, then `[strong][weak]hysteresis=threshold=128` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Garbage matte with a box
what: an outside/garbage matte always removes rigs and stands from the output, and in Natron/Keylight it wins over the inside mask
how: `alphaextract,drawbox=x=0:y=0:w=40:h=180:color=black:t=fill` then `alphamerge` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Core matte by lighten blend
what: a core/holdout matte marks areas that are definitely foreground and is merged with the key, fixing parts that keyed through
how: combine with the lighter value: `[k][core]blend=all_mode=lighten[m]` where core is a white box on black (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Edge size vs tolerance
what: Blender's Keying node: small edge Size with large Tolerance gives a sharp matte but may lose stray hairs; large Size with small Tolerance keeps edge detail but may halo. Start with edges before feathering
how: see the edges of a matte with `format=gray,edgedetect=low=0.1:high=0.3` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Difference key from a clean plate
what: a difference key compares the shot with a background-only plate; Natron outputs |A-B| to alpha after offset and gain, Blender uses tolerance and falloff
how: `[x][c]blend=all_mode=difference,extractplanes=y,lut=y='clip(val*8,0,255)'[m];[o][m]alphamerge` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: maskedthreshold to pick changed pixels
what: maskedthreshold returns the first stream where |A-B| <= threshold and the second elsewhere, a quick changed/unchanged split against a clean plate
how: `[a][b]maskedthreshold=threshold=12` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Motion mask with tblend + maskfun
what: maskfun is meant for motion masks after tblend: low/high thresholds binarise, and `sum` fills the whole frame with `fill` when the frame average is too high (a scene change)
how: `format=gray,tblend=all_mode=difference,maskfun=low=10:high=10:fill=0:sum=200` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Channel key
what: Blender's Channel Key separates by one channel's level (useful for bright explosions on dark backgrounds); start by pulling the channel
how: `format=gbrp,extractplanes=g` then threshold or lut it (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Distance key in RGB or CbCr
what: Blender's Distance Key sets alpha by the 3D distance from the key colour; in YCbCr only Cb and Cr count. It works for any single background colour, not only green
how: ffmpeg's colorkey (RGB distance) and chromakey (YUV) are the matching tools.

name: HSV tolerance per axis
what: Blender's Color Key has separate hue, saturation and value tolerances; the saturation one helps avoid removing desaturated areas such as skin
how: in ffmpeg set `sat` in hsvkey near the screen's saturation and raise similarity slowly.

name: Natron Keyer piecewise ramp
what: Natron's Keyer maps the foreground key to transparency with four points: 0 below A, linear A-B, 1 between B and C, linear C-D, 0 above D; luminance mode is the tool for masking a sky
how: reproduce a soft luma window with `lut=y=` ramps on the luma matte.

name: The over formula
what: straight over: alpha_o = a_a + a_b(1-a_a), C_o = (C_a a_a + C_b a_b (1-a_a))/alpha_o; premultiplied over: C_o = C_a + C_b(1-a_a)
how: checked numerically in numpy: both forms give (0.1, 0.45, 0.4) for green@0.5 over opaque blue-grey (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Why premultiply
what: premultiplied alpha blends, interpolates and filters correctly; filtering straight alpha leaks RGB from fully transparent areas into borders. Porter-Duff ops are simple only in premultiplied form
how: premultiply before blurring or scaling a cutout, unpremultiply before colour work.

name: premultiply / unpremultiply in ffmpeg
what: premultiply applies the alpha premultiply using the first plane of a second stream, or the frame's own alpha with inplace=1; unpremultiply reverses it
how: `chromakey=...,format=yuva444p,premultiply=inplace=1` and `format=yuva444p,unpremultiply=inplace=1` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Tell overlay the alpha is premultiplied
what: overlay has an `alpha` option, straight or premultiplied (default straight in this 6.1 build; newer docs add auto)
how: `[fg]` premultiplied, then `[0:v][fg]overlay=alpha=premultiplied:format=yuv444` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Overlay in 4:4:4 for clean edges
what: overlay's output format defaults to yuv420; format=yuv444 (or rgb/gbrp/auto) avoids subsampling the composite inside the filter
how: `[0:v][fg]overlay=format=yuv444[v]` then `-pix_fmt yuv420p` for delivery (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Emission with no occlusion
what: premultiplied alpha can hold additive pixels (flame, glitter) next to normal ones, written as RGB with alpha 0; straight alpha cannot represent that
how: for fire overlays use an additive blend (`blend=all_mode=addition`) instead of an alpha cutout.

name: Porter-Duff operators
what: over A+B(1-a), under, in Ab, mask Ba, out A(1-b), stencil B(1-a), atop Ab+B(1-a), xor A(1-b)+B(1-a); 'in' and 'out' act like clipping with the second image's alpha
how: over = ffmpeg overlay; in/out = alphamerge with a matte or its `negate`.

name: Disjoint and conjoint over
what: Disjoint over assumes the background was held out by the foreground (cleaner edges with many layers); conjoint assumes they overlap. Formulas: conjoint A+B(1-a)/b, A if a>b; disjoint A+B(1-a)/b, A+B if a+b<1
how: use these terms when stacking several cutouts that share edges.

name: RGB-only inputs are opaque
