section: Slow motion quality: interpolation and blending
what: `mb_size` (4-16, default 16) is the macroblock size and `search_param` (default 32) the search range; smaller blocks follow small moving parts, a smaller search range suits slow motion between frames. `vsbmc=1` uses smaller blocks at object boundaries so they blur less
how: `-vf minterpolate=fps=60:mi_mode=mci:mb_size=8:search_param=16` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Scene-cut protection in minterpolate
section: Slow motion quality: interpolation and blending
what: at a scene change motion vectors point in random directions, so `scd=fdiff` replaces interpolated frames there with duplicates when the frame difference passes `scd_threshold` (default 10); lower the threshold if a cut inside the clip still morphs
how: `-vf minterpolate=fps=60:mi_mode=mci:scd=fdiff:scd_threshold=5` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Exact NTSC rates in minterpolate
section: Slow motion quality: interpolation and blending
what: `fps` accepts a rational like 60000/1001, so a 29.97 source can be doubled without drift
how: `-vf minterpolate=fps=60000/1001:mi_mode=mci` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Only analyse the part you use
section: Slow motion quality: interpolation and blending
what: Final Cut analyses only the media between the clip's start and end points for optical flow; in ffmpeg put `-ss`/`-t` on the input before minterpolate so the slow filter only sees the used seconds
how: `ffmpeg -ss S -t T -i in.mp4 -vf minterpolate=... out.mp4` (the CLAUDE.md slow-mo recipe already uses this form)

name: framerate filter: cheap blended rate change
section: Slow motion quality: interpolation and blending
what: `framerate` builds new frames as a linear interpolation of two frames inside the interp_start..interp_end window (0-255, defaults 15 and 240) and has its own scene detection (`scene`, default 8.2). It is not for interlaced media (deinterlace first)
how: `-vf framerate=fps=60`; `-vf framerate=fps=50:interp_start=64:interp_end=192:scene=20` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Turn off framerate's scene detection
section: Slow motion quality: interpolation and blending
what: the `scene_change_detect` flag is on by default; set `flags=0` on a single continuous shot where false cuts would leave duplicate frames
how: `-vf framerate=fps=60:flags=0` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: See the motion vectors before interpolating
section: Slow motion quality: interpolation and blending
what: `mestimate` exports block motion vectors as side data; `codecview` can draw them, showing where the motion is too big or chaotic for clean interpolation
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf mestimate=method=epzs:mb_size=16:search_param=7,codecview=mv=pf -frames:v 5 mv.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: ML frame interpolation (RIFE)
section: Slow motion quality: interpolation and blending
what: Practical-RIFE interpolates with `inference_video.py --multi=2` (or 4) on a video, `--img=input/` on numbered PNGs, `--scale=0.5` (or `--UHD`) for 4K, `--fps` to force the output rate; the README recommends model 4.25 for most scenes, needs Python <= 3.11, MIT licence. It is the open stand-in for Final Cut's Best (Machine Learning)
how: needs Practical-RIFE + a model download (missing)

name: Average frames for a motion-blur or long-exposure look
section: Slow motion quality: interpolation and blending
what: `tmix` mixes successive frames; the docs' example averages 7 frames with equal weights. Moving parts smear, static parts stay sharp
how: `-vf tmix=frames=7:weights="1 1 1 1 1 1 1"` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Weighted trails with tmix
section: Slow motion quality: interpolation and blending
what: each frame gets its own weight (space separated; missing ones reuse the last) and the sum is normalised unless `scale` is set. Rising weights favour one end of the window; check by eye which end, since the docs only define the weights
how: `-vf tmix=frames=5:weights="1 2 3 4 5"` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Show only what moves
section: Slow motion quality: interpolation and blending
what: the docs' temporal-difference example `weights="-1 2 -1":scale=1` keeps only temporal differences: a quick way to see which areas move (to place a reframe or check that a "static" shot is static)
how: `-vf tmix=frames=3:weights="-1 2 -1":scale=1` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Blend-then-drop time-lapse
section: Slow motion quality: interpolation and blending
what: instead of dropping frames (choppy), average every 10 frames and keep one of each 10, then retime to 30 fps; motion between kept frames becomes blur
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf "tmix=frames=10,framestep=10,setpts=N/(30*TB)" -r 30 -an lapse.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24; how it looks not judged)

name: Two-frame blend with tblend
section: Slow motion quality: interpolation and blending
what: tblend blends each frame with the previous one using any blend mode; `all_mode=average` is a 2-frame mix, `difference` shows change between frames
how: `-vf tblend=all_mode=average`; `-vf tblend=all_mode=difference` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Check for high-frame-rate sources first
section: Slow motion quality: interpolation and blending
what: Final Cut marks clips recorded at 95 fps or more as high frame rate, and iPhone Slo-mo records up to 240 fps; such clips give real slow motion without interpolation. Read the true rate before choosing a method
how: `ffprobe -v error -select_streams v:0 -show_entries stream=r_frame_rate,avg_frame_rate -of csv=p=0 in.mp4`

name: Conform a high-fps clip so every frame plays
section: Slow motion quality: interpolation and blending
what: Final Cut's Automatic Speed plays every frame of, say, 120 fps footage at the project's 30 fps, so nothing is skipped or duplicated. In ffmpeg renumber the timestamps at the project rate: a 2 s 60 fps clip became 4 s with all 120 frames
how: `ffmpeg -i hfr.mp4 -vf "setpts=N/(30*TB)" -r 30 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24: 120 frames, 4.0 s)

name: Or scale the input timestamps with -itsscale
section: Slow motion quality: interpolation and blending
what: `-itsscale` rescales input timestamps by a factor before decoding filters; 2 on a 60 fps clip, output at 30 fps, also gave 4 s with 120 frames. Audio would need its own tempo change
how: `ffmpeg -itsscale 2 -i hfr.mp4 -an -r 30 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: setpts knows time, frame number and timebase
section: Speed changes, ramps and time remap in ffmpeg
what: the expression can use T (current time in s), N (frame count), PTS, STARTPTS, TB (timebase), FRAME_RATE (constant-rate video only), PREV_INPTS/PREV_OUTPTS and the eval functions (if, lt, between, clip, st/ld). That is enough to write a whole speed curve in one filter
how: see 3503

name: One-expression speed ramp
section: Speed changes, ramps and time remap in ffmpeg
what: keep the first second at normal speed, then play the rest at half speed: output time = T before 1 s, 1+(T-1)*2 after. A 3 s clip came out 5 s long. Add `fps=30` after it so the output is constant-rate (frames are duplicated where it slows; interpolate first if that stutters)
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf "setpts='if(lt(T,1),PTS,(1+(T-1)*2)/TB)',fps=30" -an ramp.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24: 5.0 s)

name: Speed segments like Final Cut's Blade Speed
section: Speed changes, ramps and time remap in ffmpeg
what: Final Cut builds variable speed from "speed segments", each with its own constant speed (its Speed Ramp preset splits a range into four). In ffmpeg: split, trim each segment, give each its own setpts factor and concat. 1 s at 1x + 1 s at 0.5x + 1 s at 2x gave 3.5 s
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -filter_complex "[0:v]split=3[a][b][c];[a]trim=0:1,setpts=PTS-STARTPTS[v1];[b]trim=1:2,setpts=2*(PTS-STARTPTS)[v2];[c]trim=2:3,setpts=0.5*(PTS-STARTPTS)[v3];[v1][v2][v3]concat=n=3:v=1:a=0,fps=30[v]" -map "[v]" seg.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24: 3.5 s)

name: Speed segments with their sound
section: Speed changes, ramps and time remap in ffmpeg
what: give each audio segment the inverse tempo with atempo and concat video and audio together (v=1:a=1), so sound stays in sync per segment
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -filter_complex "[0:v]trim=0:1,setpts=PTS-STARTPTS[v1];[0:a]atrim=0:1,asetpts=PTS-STARTPTS[a1];[0:v]trim=1:2,setpts=2*(PTS-STARTPTS)[v2];[0:a]atrim=1:2,asetpts=PTS-STARTPTS,atempo=0.5[a2];[v1][a1][v2][a2]concat=n=2:v=1:a=1[v][a]" -map "[v]" -map "[a]" out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Ramp duration = ramp feel
section: Speed changes, ramps and time remap in ffmpeg
what: in Final Cut a speed transition between segments makes the change gradual; the shorter the transition, the faster the speed ramps; there is no smooth transition between a forward and a reverse segment. In ffmpeg build the ramp from several short in-between segments (e.g. 1x → 0.75x → 0.5x) instead of one jump
how: extend the 3504 graph with more trim/setpts pairs (tested here 2026-10-24 with three segments)

name: atempo above 2x skips samples
section: Speed changes, ramps and time remap in ffmpeg
what: atempo accepts 0.5-100, but above 2 it skips samples instead of blending them; for a clean 3x chain two instances of sqrt(3)
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -af "atempo=sqrt(3),atempo=sqrt(3)" -vf setpts=PTS/3 out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24: 1.07 s from 3 s)

name: rubberband for slowed sound
section: Speed changes, ramps and time remap in ffmpeg
what: the rubberband filter (librubberband, present in this build) time-stretches with controls for transients (crisp/mixed/smooth), window (standard/short/long), phase and pitch quality; tempo also works as a command. Compare it with atempo on a slow-mo voice
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vn -af rubberband=tempo=0.5:transients=smooth:window=long out.wav` (tested here 2026-10-24: 3 s → 6.04 s)

name: Let the pitch move with the speed (tape effect)
section: Speed changes, ramps and time remap in ffmpeg
what: Final Cut preserves pitch by default and lets you turn Preserve Pitch off to accentuate a retime. In ffmpeg, asetrate changes speed and pitch together (like a tape), then aresample restores the sample rate; 2x halved a 3 s file to 1.5 s
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vn -af asetrate=44100*2,aresample=44100 chip.wav` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: trim does not reset timestamps
section: Speed changes, ramps and time remap in ffmpeg
what: trim keeps the original timestamps (the docs say so), so a clip trimmed from 1 s still starts at 1.0 s and players or concat may show a gap. Add setpts=PTS-STARTPTS (and asetpts for audio) after it
how: `-vf trim=start=1,setpts=PTS-STARTPTS -af atrim=start=1,asetpts=PTS-STARTPTS` (tested here 2026-10-24: without the setpts the mkv start_time was 1.000000)

name: Trim by frame number
section: Speed changes, ramps and time remap in ffmpeg
what: `start_frame`/`end_frame` count frames that pass through the filter instead of reading timestamps: exact for "frames 15 to 44"
how: `-vf trim=start_frame=15:end_frame=45,setpts=PTS-STARTPTS` (tested here 2026-10-24: 30 frames)

name: Several trim limits are OR, not AND
section: Speed changes, ramps and time remap in ffmpeg
what: with more than one start/end option, trim keeps every frame that matches at least one of them; to require all at once, chain two trim filters
how: `trim=start=2,trim=end_frame=200` instead of one trim with both

name: fps rounding mode
section: Speed changes, ramps and time remap in ffmpeg
what: the fps filter drops or duplicates frames to reach a constant rate; `round` picks zero, inf, down, up or near (default). Keep the same mode across clips so conversions line up
how: `-vf fps=fps=24:round=down` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Pad a late video start with fps start_time
section: Speed changes, ramps and time remap in ffmpeg
what: `start_time=0` makes fps assume the first frame belongs at 0 s, padding the beginning with copies of the first frame (e.g. video starting after the audio) or trimming negative-time frames
how: `-vf fps=fps=30:start_time=0` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Keep the last frame when converting rate
section: Speed changes, ramps and time remap in ffmpeg
what: `eof_action=pass` passes the last frame through if the input duration has not been reached; a 3 s 30 fps clip at 24 fps gave 72 frames, 3.0 s
how: `-vf fps=fps=24:eof_action=pass` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Named rates in fps
section: Speed changes, ramps and time remap in ffmpeg
what: fps accepts source_fps, ntsc (30000/1001), pal (25), film (24) and ntsc_film (24000/1001) as constants
how: `-vf fps=fps=ntsc_film` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: -fps_mode decides what the muxer does with timing
section: Speed changes, ramps and time remap in ffmpeg
what: passthrough passes each frame with its demuxer timestamp, cfr duplicates/drops to a constant rate, vfr passes frames through (dropping same-timestamp ones). After dropping duplicates, vfr kept the original timing (75 frames, 2.97 s)
how: `ffmpeg -i dup.mp4 -vf mpdecimate -fps_mode vfr -an out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Keep one frame in N with framestep
section: Speed changes, ramps and time remap in ffmpeg
what: `framestep=step=N` selects one frame every N; renumber at the target rate for a time-lapse (3 s at step 4 → 0.77 s). select with `not(mod(n,5))` does the same with more conditions available
how: `-vf "framestep=step=4,setpts=N/(30*TB)" -r 30`; `-vf "select='not(mod(n,5))',setpts=N/(30*TB)"` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Jump cuts instead of fast motion
section: Speed changes, ramps and time remap in ffmpeg
what: Final Cut's "Jump Cut at Markers" compresses time by skipping 3-30 frames at each marker rather than playing fast. In ffmpeg drop a frame range from video and the same time from audio with select/aselect
how: `-vf "select='not(between(n,30,59))',setpts=N/FRAME_RATE/TB" -af "aselect='not(between(t,1,2))',asetpts=N/SR/TB"` (tested here 2026-10-24: 3 s → 2.02 s)

name: Stutter or drop frames in a pattern
section: Speed changes, ramps and time remap in ffmpeg
what: shuffleframes maps input frames to output slots per group; `0 2 1` swaps frames 2 and 3 of every three, `-1` drops a slot (so `0 -1` keeps every other frame). Use for deliberate stutter or step-printing looks
how: `-vf "shuffleframes=0 2 1"`; `-vf "shuffleframes=0 -1"` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Repeat a short chunk for a stutter loop
section: Speed changes, ramps and time remap in ffmpeg
what: loop repeats `size` frames starting at `start` `loop` times; the docs' example loops the first 10 frames 5 times. Renumber timestamps after it
how: `-vf loop=loop=5:size=10:start=0,setpts=N/FRAME_RATE/TB` (tested here 2026-10-24: 3 s → 4.67 s)

name: Hold the first frame before the action starts
section: Speed changes, ramps and time remap in ffmpeg
what: tpad with `start_mode=clone` adds copies of the first frame before the clip (start_duration in seconds), a pre-roll hold for a title to land on
how: `-vf tpad=start_duration=1:start_mode=clone` (tested here 2026-10-24: 3 s → 4 s)

name: Replace a frame range with one frame from another input
section: Speed changes, ramps and time remap in ffmpeg
what: freezeframes freezes frames first..last using frame `replace` from the second input (e.g. a clean frame over a glitch or blink)
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -i in.mp4 -filter_complex "[0:v][1:v]freezeframes=first=30:last=60:replace=30" -an out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Instant replay
section: Speed changes, ramps and time remap in ffmpeg
what: Final Cut's Instant Replay appends a duplicate of the selected range and plays it at the chosen speed. In ffmpeg split the range, slow the copy, concat
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -filter_complex "[0:v]trim=1:2,setpts=PTS-STARTPTS,split[a][b];[b]setpts=2*PTS[s];[a][s]concat=n=2:v=1:a=0,fps=30" -an replay.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Rewind effect
section: Speed changes, ramps and time remap in ffmpeg
what: Final Cut's Rewind duplicates the range, plays the copy backwards at 1x, 2x or 4x, then plays the range forward again. In ffmpeg: three copies, the middle one reversed and sped up
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -filter_complex "[0:v]trim=1:2,setpts=PTS-STARTPTS,split=3[a][b][c];[b]reverse,setpts=0.5*PTS[r];[a][r][c]concat=n=3:v=1:a=0" -an rewind.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Stream-copy segments split only at keyframes
section: Speed changes, ramps and time remap in ffmpeg
what: to reverse a long clip in pieces, `-f segment -c copy` cuts only on keyframes, so a short phone clip may come out as one piece; re-encode with forced keyframes (or use trim) when you need exact pieces
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -f segment -segment_time 1 -reset_timestamps 1 -c copy sg%02d.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24: one segment only, keyframe interval longer than the clip)

name: Drop near-duplicate frames (screen recordings, static stretches)
section: Speed changes, ramps and time remap in ffmpeg
what: mpdecimate drops frames whose 8x8 blocks differ less than hi (768 = 64*12) and where no more than frac (0.33) of blocks exceed lo (320); `max`/`keep` limit consecutive drops. Renumbering afterwards compresses static stretches (a 25-in-30 clip went from 3 s to 2.5 s); keep `-fps_mode vfr` instead to keep real timing
how: `-vf mpdecimate=hi=768:lo=320:frac=0.33,setpts=N/FRAME_RATE/TB` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Remove one duplicate in every N frames
section: Speed changes, ramps and time remap in ffmpeg
what: decimate drops one frame per `cycle`; a 25 fps clip stored as 30 fps with duplicates came back to 25 fps with cycle=6. (mpdecimate `mode=1` from the online docs does not exist in 6.1.)
how: `-vf decimate=cycle=6` (tested here 2026-10-24: r_frame_rate 25/1)

name: 24p to 30 with a pulldown pattern
section: Speed changes, ramps and time remap in ffmpeg
what: telecine applies a pulldown pattern; 23 is classic 24p→30i, 2332 is listed as preferred, 222222222223 is "Euro pulldown" for 24p→25i. 1 s of 24p became 30 frames. Undo such material with dejudder (cycle 4 for 24→30, 5 for 25→30, 20 mixed)
how: `-vf telecine=pattern=23`; `-vf dejudder=cycle=4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Find frozen stretches after retiming
section: Speed changes, ramps and time remap in ffmpeg
what: freezedetect logs where the picture does not change for at least `d` seconds within noise `n`; useful to confirm a hold is as long as planned, or that a ramp did not freeze by mistake
how: `ffmpeg -i out.mp4 -vf freezedetect=n=-60dB:d=1 -map 0:v -f null -` (tested here 2026-10-24: reported freeze_duration 2.03333 on a 2 s hold)

name: Pick the frame rate before anything else
section: Speed changes, ramps and time remap in ffmpeg
what: Final Cut's guide says the most important early decision is the project frame rate: format and size are easy to change later, but changing the rate can shift every edit point. Decide 30 (or 25/24) before cutting on beats
how: probe the main source, then set `fps` once for every clip

name: Find the action peak for a ramp from optical flow
section: Speed changes, ramps and time remap in ffmpeg
what: OpenCV's DIS optical flow gives a per-frame motion size; the frame with the most motion is a candidate for the slowest point of a ramp
how: `/home/user/tools/venv/bin/python -I motion_peak.py in.mp4` using `cv2.DISOpticalFlow.create(cv2.DISOPTICAL_FLOW_PRESET_FAST)` and the mean flow length per frame (tested here 2026-10-24: printed the peak frame and time)

name: HyperFrames can't play media backwards
section: Reverse, holds and timing in HyperFrames and GSAP
what: `data-playback-rate` and the `rate` automation lane take 0.1-10, so reverse, rewind and boomerang must be rendered in ffmpeg first and placed as their own clip
how: render with `reverse` (see 3526), then `<video src="rewind.mp4" data-duration=...>`

name: Constant speed in HyperFrames keeps pitch
section: Reverse, holds and timing in HyperFrames and GSAP
what: `data-playback-rate` on the media gives a constant speed change (0.1-10) with pitch-preserved sound; use it for a plain 1.5x setup shot instead of re-encoding
how: `<video ... data-playback-rate="1.5">`

name: Slow the whole GSAP animation with timeScale
section: Reverse, holds and timing in HyperFrames and GSAP
what: timeScale 0.5 plays a timeline at half speed (a 2 s timeline takes 4 s), -1 plays it backwards; duration() still reports 2, so place later beats by real time
how: `tl.timeScale(0.5)` (tested here 2026-10-24 in node with gsap 3.14.2: duration() 2)

name: Replay a stretch of animation with tweenFromTo
section: Reverse, holds and timing in HyperFrames and GSAP
what: `tl.tweenFromTo(1, 3, {duration: 1})` creates a tween that scrubs the timeline's playhead from 1 s to 3 s (here at 2x), which is a time remap for motion graphics; it pauses the timeline first
how: `master.add(tl.tweenFromTo(1, 3, {duration: 1}))` (tested here 2026-10-24: half-way the timeline time was 2)

name: SlowMo ease for fly-through text
section: Reverse, holds and timing in HyperFrames and GSAP
what: SlowMo decelerates, moves linearly for a chosen share (linearRatio), then accelerates: zoom text in, keep it moving slowly long enough to read, zoom out, without the velocity jumps of three chained tweens. It lives in EasePack (not GSAP core; the repo vendors only core)
how: copy `EasePack.min.js` from the gsap 3.14.2 npm package to assets/vendor, `gsap.registerPlugin(EasePack)`, `ease: "slow(0.5, 0.8)"` (tested here 2026-10-24 in node)

name: Custom speed curves with CustomEase
section: Reverse, holds and timing in HyperFrames and GSAP
what: CustomEase turns an SVG path drawn in the Ease Visualizer into an ease, e.g. a camera move that rushes, hangs, then settles
how: `CustomEase.create("hop", "M0,0 C...")` then `ease: "hop"` (needs CustomEase.min.js beside gsap in assets/vendor)

name: cropdetect's default rounding cuts into the picture
section: Find the real picture: borders and embedded video
what: cropdetect rounds width/height to a multiple of `round` (default 16) and centres the offset; on a 640x270 picture inside 640x360 the default reported 640:256:0:52 (14 lines lost), while `round=2` reported the exact 640:270:0:44. Use round=2 and then decide
how: `ffmpeg -i bars.mp4 -vf cropdetect=limit=24:round=2:skip=2 -f null -` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: cropdetect threshold as a fraction
section: Find the real picture: borders and embedded video
what: `limit` is the highest value still counted as black (0-255 for 8-bit, default 24); a value between 0.0 and 1.0 is scaled to the bit depth, so the same number works for 10-bit sources
how: `-vf cropdetect=limit=0.1:round=16` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Reset cropdetect when a logo or title fools it
section: Find the real picture: borders and embedded video
what: by default cropdetect returns the largest area seen during playback; `reset` (reset_count) restarts detection after N frames, which helps when channel logos or a title card distort the area
how: `-vf cropdetect=reset=30` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Ignore stray bright pixels with max_outliers
section: Find the real picture: borders and embedded video
what: the 6.1 build has a `max_outliers` option ("threshold count of outliers"); with round=2 and max_outliers=5 it still found 640:270:0:44 on the test clip
how: `-vf cropdetect=round=2:max_outliers=5` (tested here 2026-10-24); see `ffmpeg -h filter=cropdetect`

name: Find a video playing inside a video (screen, TV, phone)
section: Find the real picture: borders and embedded video
what: `mode=mvedges` finds the playing area from motion vectors plus edge pixels, using decoder vectors (`-flags2 +export_mvs`) or vectors from mestimate. On the synthetic test the mestimate route gave 640:272:0:44 and the export_mvs route 544:272:8:44, so check the numbers on a frame
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf mestimate,cropdetect=mode=mvedges,metadata=mode=print -f null -` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: bbox: per-frame box of non-black pixels
section: Find the real picture: borders and embedded video
what: bbox prints the bounding box of luma above min_val (default 16) for each frame, including a ready crop= and drawbox= string
how: `ffmpeg -i bars.mp4 -vf bbox=min_val=20 -frames:v 1 -f null -` (tested here 2026-10-24: printed crop=640:272:0:44)

name: Remove borders before any auto-reframe
section: Find the real picture: borders and embedded video
what: AutoFlip runs a BorderDetectionCalculator (borders and background colour) before cropping, so letterbox bars don't count as content. Do the same: cropdetect, crop, then reframe
how: `ffmpeg -i bars.mp4 -vf crop=640:270:0:44 out.mp4` after 3540 (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Clean dirty edges without changing the size
section: Find the real picture: borders and embedded video
what: fillborders repaints N pixels at each edge (smear, mirror, fixed, reflect, wrap, fade, margins) instead of cropping, keeping the frame size a codec-friendly number
how: `-vf fillborders=left=20:right=20:mode=mirror`; `-vf fillborders=top=30:bottom=30:mode=fade:color=black` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: crop x/y are per frame, w/h are not
section: Crop windows that move: pans, punch-ins, virtual camera
what: crop evaluates x and y for every frame (they can use t and n) but w/h only at configuration or on a command; so a pan is a crop, a zoom needs scale or zoompan
how: pan: `-vf "crop=ih*9/16:ih:'(iw-ow)*t/2':0,scale=1080:1920"` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Ease a crop pan with a cosine
section: Crop windows that move: pans, punch-ins, virtual camera
what: 0.5-0.5*cos(PI*p) goes from 0 to 1 with slow start and end; put it in crop's x for an eased 2 s pan across a 16:9 frame

name: lerp, clip and st/ld for camera curves
section: Crop windows that move: pans, punch-ins, virtual camera
what: the expression evaluator has lerp(x,y,z), clip(), and ten store/load slots, so a smoothstep pan fits in one option: store p, then 640*p*p*(3-2p). lerp exists in 6.1 here

name: Handheld drift from the docs' "trembling" crop
section: Crop windows that move: pans, punch-ins, virtual camera
what: the crop docs give a trembling effect, a half-size window moved by sin(n/10) and sin(n/7), and an erratic camera driven by sin(t*10), sin(t*13); scale the amplitude down for a gentle handheld float on a locked-off shot
how: `-vf "crop=in_w/2:in_h/2:(in_w-out_w)/2+((in_w-out_w)/2)*sin(n/10):(in_h-out_h)/2+((in_h-out_h)/2)*sin(n/7)"` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Animate crop position between two times with sendcmd
section: Crop windows that move: pans, punch-ins, virtual camera
what: sendcmd with the `[expr]` flag evaluates the argument per frame; TI is the 0-1 position inside the command interval, so `0.5-1.5 [expr] crop x 320*TI` slides the window across 1 s
how: `-vf "sendcmd=c='0.5-1.5 [expr] crop x 320*TI',crop=w=640:h=360:x=0:y=180"` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Don't change crop size by command in 6.1
section: Crop windows that move: pans, punch-ins, virtual camera
what: the docs list w/h as crop commands, but sending `crop w` and `crop h` mid-stream crashed ffmpeg 6.1 here (exit 139). Change size with scale `eval=frame` or zoompan instead, and only send x/y to crop
how: see 3554 (crash observed here 2026-10-24)

name: Smooth zoom on video with scale eval=frame
section: Crop windows that move: pans, punch-ins, virtual camera
what: scale re-evaluates w/h every frame with `eval=frame` (t and n become available); scale up gradually, then crop back to the frame size for a push-in. Keep the width even with trunc(.../2)*2

name: zoompan on video: d=1 and in_time
section: Crop windows that move: pans, punch-ins, virtual camera
what: with video input set d=1 (one output frame per input frame) and drive zoom by in_time; the docs' example zooms 2x into the centre for the first second only
how: `-vf "zoompan=z='if(between(in_time,0,1),2,1)':d=1:x='iw/2-(iw/zoom/2)':y='ih/2-(ih/zoom/2)':s=1280x720:fps=30"` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Always set zoompan's s and fps
section: Crop windows that move: pans, punch-ins, virtual camera
what: zoompan defaults to s=hd720 and fps=25, so a 1080p 30 fps job silently comes out 1280x720 at 25 fps unless you set both
how: add `:s=1920x1080:fps=30` (or your size/rate) to every zoompan (tested here 2026-10-24 with s=1280x720:fps=30)

name: Timed punch-in framed on the eyes line
section: Crop windows that move: pans, punch-ins, virtual camera
what: a zoompan punch that switches at a time and anchors the crop on the upper third instead of the centre (y term uses ih/3)
how: `-vf "zoompan=z='if(gte(in_time,1),1.25,1)':d=1:x='iw/2-(iw/zoom/2)':y='ih/3-(ih/zoom/3)':s=1280x720:fps=30"` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Slow creep-in on moving footage
section: Crop windows that move: pans, punch-ins, virtual camera
what: the same zoompan with a zoom that grows with in_time gives a continuous push on video (not just stills)
how: `-vf "zoompan=z='1+0.1*in_time/2':d=1:x='iw/2-(iw/zoom/2)':y='ih/2-(ih/zoom/2)':s=1280x720:fps=30"` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: zoompan without the pause
section: Crop windows that move: pans, punch-ins, virtual camera
what: the docs give a "without pausing" form that continues from the previous zoom with max(zoom,pzoom) and d=1, and a form that pans toward a spot while zooming (x+1/a, y+1 until zoom reaches 1.5)
how: `-vf "zoompan=z='min(max(zoom,pzoom)+0.0015,1.5)':d=1:x='iw/2-(iw/zoom/2)':y='ih/2-(ih/zoom/2)':s=1280x720"`; `zoompan=z='min(zoom+0.0015,1.5)':d=90:x='if(gte(zoom,1.5),x,x+1/a)':y='if(gte(zoom,1.5),y,y+1)':s=640x360` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Continuous pan across a big still with scroll
section: Crop windows that move: pans, punch-ins, virtual camera
what: scroll moves the picture at a constant speed (h/v from -1 to 1, start at hpos/vpos 0-1) and wraps around; good for a slow pan over a panorama or a credits plate
how: `ffmpeg -i pano.png -vf "loop=loop=89:size=1,scroll=h=0.01" -frames:v 90 -r 30 scroll.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Fix keystone on a filmed screen or board
section: Crop windows that move: pans, punch-ins, virtual camera
what: perspective moves four corner points (x0..y3: top-left, top-right, bottom-left, bottom-right); with sense=source those points go to the output corners, which straightens a monitor or whiteboard filmed at an angle. cubic interpolation is available
how: `-vf perspective=x0=40:y0=20:x1=600:y1=0:x2=0:y2=360:x3=640:y3=340:interpolation=cubic` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Fake a camera tilt with perspective sense=destination
section: Crop windows that move: pans, punch-ins, virtual camera
what: sense=destination sends the source corners to the given points instead; with eval=frame the points can move over time
how: `-vf "perspective=sense=destination:x0=0:y0=0:x1=W:y1=40:x2=0:y2=H:x3=W:y3=H-40:eval=init"` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Straighten wide-angle barrel distortion
section: Crop windows that move: pans, punch-ins, virtual camera
what: lenscorrection uses k1 (quadratic) and k2 (fourth-power) coefficients in [-1,1] around cx/cy; the docs suggest OpenCV's calibration sample to measure them, or trial and error. Default interpolation is nearest, so ask for bilinear
how: `-vf lenscorrection=k1=-0.2:k2=-0.02:i=bilinear` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Pull a normal shot out of 360 footage
section: 360 and fisheye: a virtual camera inside the sphere
what: v360 with output=flat renders a rectilinear view; yaw/pitch/roll aim the virtual camera (degrees) and h_fov/v_fov set its lens
how: `-vf v360=input=e:output=flat:h_fov=90:v_fov=59:w=640:h=360:yaw=30:pitch=-10` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: A vertical 9:16 view from 360
section: 360 and fisheye: a virtual camera inside the sphere
what: give v360 a tall output size and a tall field of view; lanczos interpolation needs more memory (the docs warn that complex methods use much more)
how: `-vf v360=e:flat:h_fov=60:v_fov=100:w=576:h=1024:interp=lanczos` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Pan inside 360 over time
section: 360 and fisheye: a virtual camera inside the sphere
what: v360 supports a subset of options as commands; yaw sent with sendcmd at 1 s turned the view here. For a smooth pan, send it with `[expr]` and TI like 3552
how: `-vf "sendcmd=c='1.0 v360 yaw 90',v360=e:flat:h_fov=90:v_fov=59:w=640:h=360"` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Flatten a fisheye clip
section: 360 and fisheye: a virtual camera inside the sphere
what: v360 reads fisheye (and dual fisheye) input with ih_fov/iv_fov for the lens and writes flat output with its own h_fov/v_fov
how: `-vf v360=input=fisheye:output=flat:ih_fov=180:iv_fov=180:h_fov=100:v_fov=70` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Animate 360 orientation only for flat deliverables
section: 360 and fisheye: a virtual camera inside the sphere
what: Final Cut reorients 360 clips with Tilt (X), Pan (Y) and Roll (Z) and notes that keyframed "camera moves" may not suit a 360 deliverable because the viewer navigates it; it suggests animating a 360 clip inside a rectilinear project instead. So: keep 360 exports static, animate yaw/pitch only when rendering flat

name: Gentle Dutch-angle sway
what: rotate's angle is an expression evaluated per frame; the docs' oscillation A*sin(2*PI/T*t) with a small A gives a slow sway
how: `-vf "rotate='0.05*sin(2*PI/1.5*t)':c=black"` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Rotate without cutting corners, keep sizes even
what: rotw(a)/roth(a) give the size that fully contains the rotated frame; for libx264 4:2:0 round them to even numbers or the encoder refuses (an odd 255x255 failed here)
how: `-vf "rotate=PI/12:ow='trunc(rotw(PI/12)/2)*2':oh='trunc(roth(PI/12)/2)*2'"` (tested here 2026-10-24: 710x512)

name: Spin with no background showing
what: the docs' "no background ever shown" form shrinks the output to min(iw,ih)/sqrt(2) and sets c=none; again make the size even
how: `-vf "rotate=2*PI*t/3:ow='trunc(min(iw,ih)/sqrt(2)/2)*2':oh=ow:c=none"` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Level a slightly tilted horizon
what: rotate by the tilt (negative = counter-clockwise), scale up a little and crop back so the black corners leave the frame; check the corners in a snapshot and raise the scale if any show
how: `-vf "rotate=-2*PI/180:bilinear=1,scale=iw*1.07:-2,crop=640:360"` (tested here 2026-10-24; corner coverage not measured)

name: Use transpose names, not numbers
what: transpose's numeric values are deprecated; use cclock_flip, clock, cclock, clock_flip. clock turned 640x360 into 360x640
how: `-vf transpose=clock` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Rotate only the clips that need it
what: `passthrough=portrait` skips the transposition when the input is already portrait (height >= width), so one command can run over a mixed folder
how: `-vf transpose=dir=clock:passthrough=portrait` (tested here 2026-10-24: a 360x640 input stayed 360x640)

name: 180 degrees = hflip plus vflip
what: for an upside-down clip, chain hflip and vflip (no resize, no interpolation)
how: `-vf hflip,vflip` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Read a phone clip's rotation before touching it
what: rotation lives in the display matrix side data, not in width/height; ffprobe shows it
how: `ffprobe -v error -select_streams v:0 -show_entries stream=width,height:stream_side_data=rotation,displaymatrix -of default=nw=1 in.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24: 640x360 with rotation=90)

name: Fix a wrong rotation tag without re-encoding
what: `-display_rotation` (an input option, degrees counter-clockwise) overrides the file's rotation; with `-c copy` it is written into the output. 0 removed a bad 90-degree tag here
how: `ffmpeg -display_rotation 0 -i in.mp4 -c copy out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24: rotation -0.00)

name: Mirror by metadata only
what: `-display_hflip` / `-display_vflip` set a flip in the display matrix (applied after any -display_rotation), so a selfie can be un-mirrored with stream copy
how: `ffmpeg -display_hflip -i in.mp4 -c copy out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24: displaymatrix with -65536 in the first cell)

name: ffmpeg auto-rotates when decoding; -noautorotate stops it
what: autorotate is on by default, so a rotated clip decodes upright (360x640 here); with `-noautorotate` you get the stored 640x360 frames, e.g. to fix rotation yourself
how: `ffmpeg -noautorotate -i in.mp4 -frames:v 1 raw.png` vs `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -frames:v 1 upright.png` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Re-encoding bakes the rotation in
what: when transcoding with autorotate on, the rotation is applied in the filter stage and the output has upright pixels and no rotation tag (360x640, no rotation entry here), so later tools no longer depend on reading the tag
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -c:v libx264 -crf 18 -c:a copy upright.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: OpenCV rotates too, and reports clockwise
what: cv2.VideoCapture honours rotation by default (CAP_PROP_ORIENTATION_AUTO); a file tagged 90 by ffmpeg's counter-clockwise -display_rotation read back as CAP_PROP_ORIENTATION_META 270 and came out 640 rows tall. Set auto to 0 to get stored frames
how: `cap.set(cv2.CAP_PROP_ORIENTATION_AUTO, 0)` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Odd crop widths leave non-square pixels
section: Aspect ratio, pixel shape and conforming
what: crop=ih*9/16 on 720p asks for 405 px, the encoder gets 404, and scaling that to 1080x1920 keeps the display aspect by setting SAR 404:405; rounding the crop to even alone still gave 404:405. Add setsar=1 after the scale
how: `-vf "crop=ih*9/16:ih,scale=1080:1920,setsar=1"` (tested here 2026-10-24: 1080x1920, SAR 1:1)

name: force_divisible_by may bend the aspect slightly
section: Aspect ratio, pixel shape and conforming
what: with force_original_aspect_ratio, force_divisible_by=2 makes both sides even; the docs say the aspect may be slightly modified, and here a 405x720 box gave 404x228 with SAR 304:303. Add setsar=1 or pad if exact pixels matter
how: `-vf scale=405:720:force_original_aspect_ratio=decrease:force_divisible_by=2` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Make pixels square in 6.1 without reset_sar
section: Aspect ratio, pixel shape and conforming
what: the online docs' `reset_sar` option is not in 6.1 (Option not found here); use the docs' other recipe, scale to trunc(ih*dar) wide and setsar=1
how: `-vf "scale='trunc(ih*dar/2)*2':ih,setsar=1/1"` (tested here 2026-10-24: a 320x360 SAR 2:1 clip became 640x360 SAR 1:1)

name: crop keep_aspect makes anamorphic output
section: Aspect ratio, pixel shape and conforming
what: crop's keep_aspect=1 keeps the input display aspect by changing the sample aspect; a 320x360 crop of a 16:9 clip came out SAR 2:1, i.e. stretched pixels. Leave it off for social video
how: `-vf crop=320:360:keep_aspect=1` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: exact=1 for odd crop offsets
section: Aspect ratio, pixel shape and conforming
what: on subsampled formats crop rounds w/h/x/y down to valid values unless exact=1; with 4:4:4 the exact 201x113 crop was kept
how: `-vf "crop=201:113:11:7:exact=1,format=yuv444p" -c:v libx264` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: setdar changes the label, not the pixels
section: Aspect ratio, pixel shape and conforming
what: setdar sets the display aspect by changing SAR (DAR = W/H x SAR); pixel dimensions stay, and later filters may change it again. 640x360 with setdar 4/3 became SAR 3:4
how: `-vf setdar=dar=4/3` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Pad to an aspect ratio directly
section: Aspect ratio, pixel shape and conforming
what: pad has an `aspect` option ("pad to aspect instead of a resolution"); with x/y -1 the input is centred. 640x360 padded to aspect 9/16 became 640x1138
how: `-vf "pad=aspect=9/16:x=-1:y=-1"` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Pad anamorphic sources with sar in the formula
section: Aspect ratio, pixel shape and conforming
what: the docs' 16:9 pad needs `/sar` for anamorphic input (X = output_dar / sar), or the padded frame has the wrong shape
how: `-vf "pad='ih*16/9/sar':ih:(ow-iw)/2:(oh-ih)/2"` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Square canvas from any clip
section: Aspect ratio, pixel shape and conforming
what: pad to max(iw,ih) in both directions with the clip centred
how: `-vf "pad='max(iw\,ih)':ow:(ow-iw)/2:(oh-ih)/2"` (tested here 2026-10-24: 640x640)

name: Fit, Fill or None
section: Aspect ratio, pixel shape and conforming
what: Final Cut's Spatial Conform offers Fit (whole picture, bars where shapes differ), Fill (fills the frame, crops the long side) and None (native size: cropped if larger, surrounded by black if smaller). ffmpeg: Fit = scale decrease + pad; Fill = scale increase + crop; None = pad only
how: Fit `-vf "scale=1080:1920:force_original_aspect_ratio=decrease,pad=1080:1920:-1:-1,setsar=1"`; None `-vf "pad=1080:1920:-1:-1"` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Size an inset from the main video (6.1)
section: Aspect ratio, pixel shape and conforming
what: the current docs size one input from a reference with `scale=rw:rh` (their "scale2ref" example), but that form is not in 6.1 (it failed here); 6.1 still ships the separate scale2ref filter, which outputs the scaled clip and the reference
how: `-filter_complex "[1:v][0:v]scale2ref=w=iw/4:h=ow/mdar[s][m];[m][s]overlay=20:20"` (tested here 2026-10-24; options from `ffmpeg -h filter=scale2ref`)

name: 4:5 and 1:1 crops from 16:9
section: Aspect ratio, pixel shape and conforming
what: a full-height 4:5 window from 1280x720 is 576 px wide (45% of the width), a 1:1 window 720 px (56%); scale to 1080x1350 or 1080x1080 and set square pixels
how: `-vf "crop='trunc(ih*4/5/2)*2':ih,scale=1080:1350,setsar=1"`; `-vf "crop=ih:ih,scale=1080:1080,setsar=1"` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Make the vertical version a separate render
section: Aspect ratio, pixel shape and conforming
what: Final Cut makes square or vertical versions by duplicating the project with a new Video Format and Smart Conform, which analyses each clip for faces or other areas of interest and reframes it; you then fine-tune Position. Keep the 16:9 master untouched and render each ratio from it
how: one ffmpeg/HyperFrames render per ratio from the same master

name: Draw an EBU R 95 safe-area review overlay
what: EBU R 95 puts essential action inside an action-safe area 3.5% in from each edge and graphics inside a graphics-safe area 5% in, and asks that the image centre keeps its position through all processing. Draw both as a review overlay (never in the export)
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf "drawbox=x=iw*0.035:y=ih*0.035:w=iw*0.93:h=ih*0.93:color=yellow:t=2,drawbox=x=iw*0.05:y=ih*0.05:w=iw*0.9:h=ih*0.9:color=red:t=2" -frames:v 1 safe.png` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Final Cut's title-safe and action-safe
what: Final Cut defines title-safe as the inner 80% and action-safe as 90% of the image, and supports custom alpha PNG overlays (e.g. a 2.35:1 letterbox matte or social frame) that appear only in the viewer. Same idea here: a guide image overlaid only on review snapshots
how: `-vf "drawbox=x=iw*0.05:y=ih*0.05:w=iw*0.9:h=ih*0.9:color=green:t=2,drawbox=x=iw*0.1:y=ih*0.1:w=iw*0.8:h=ih*0.8:color=cyan:t=2"` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Check a 2.35:1 framing with a matte
what: Final Cut recommends a letterbox overlay to reframe for a wider release ratio because you can reposition and scale under it without changing the frame. For a check render, draw the bars; the bar height is (ih - iw/2.35)/2
how: `-vf "drawbox=x=0:y=0:w=iw:h=(ih-iw/2.35)/2:color=black:t=fill,drawbox=x=0:y=ih-(ih-iw/2.35)/2:w=iw:h=(ih-iw/2.35)/2:color=black:t=fill"` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Meta Reels ad margins in pixels
what: Meta's Reels ad safe zone keeps the top 14%, bottom 35% and 6% on each side clear; on 1080x1920 that is 269 px, 672 px and 65 px, leaving 950x979 px. Ads with a disclaimer keep the bottom 40% clear. Draw it as a review mask
how: `ffmpeg -f lavfi -i color=gray:s=1080x1920 -vf "drawbox=x=0:y=0:w=iw:h=ih*0.14:color=red@0.4:t=fill,drawbox=x=0:y=ih*0.65:w=iw:h=ih*0.35:color=red@0.4:t=fill,drawbox=x=0:y=0:w=iw*0.06:h=ih:color=red@0.4:t=fill,drawbox=x=iw*0.94:y=0:w=iw*0.06:h=ih:color=red@0.4:t=fill" -frames:v 1 -update 1 meta_safe.png` (tested here 2026-10-24)
refs: Inrō Reels Safe Zone Checker, https://www.inro.social/tools/instagram-reels-safe-zone-checker, checked 2026-10-24

name: Organic Reels have no official safe zone
what: the 14/35/6 margins are Meta's for ads only; Inrō found no equivalent published for organic Reels, and the 4:5 feed-preview and 3:4 profile-grid crops are community-measured, not Meta's. Treat organic numbers as estimates and keep key text well inside
how: use the ad margins as a conservative guide (3598)
refs: Inrō Reels Safe Zone Checker, https://www.inro.social/tools/instagram-reels-safe-zone-checker, checked 2026-10-24

name: Centre-square method for one creative everywhere
what: Billo recommends keeping headline, logo and CTA inside a centred 1080x1080 square on a 1080x1920 canvas so the message survives Feed, Stories and Reels crops; it also notes taller 20:9 phones and advises pulling key elements toward the centre instead of designing edge to edge
how: `ffmpeg -f lavfi -i color=gray:s=1080x1920 -vf "drawbox=x=0:y=(ih-iw)/2:w=iw:h=iw:color=yellow:t=6" -frames:v 1 -update 1 centre_sq.png` as a guide (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: TikTok ad frame minimums and safe-zone files
what: per the TikTok Ads Manager specs summarised by Relevant Audience: In-Feed ads take 9:16 at 540x960 or more (recommended), 16:9 at 960x540+, 1:1 at 640x640+, up to 500 MB; TikTok gives no fixed pixel safe zone but publishes downloadable safe-zone overlay files, because the area depends on ratio and caption length. Export at 1080x1920 rather than the minimum
how: overlay the downloaded safe-zone PNG on review snapshots only

name: YouTube's 16:9 ladder and no 5K
what: YouTube's help lists the 16:9 encode sizes (7680x4320, 3840x2160, 2560x1440, 1920x1080, 1280x720, 854x480, 640x360, 426x240) and says it started removing playback support for resolutions between 4K and 8K in 2022 (e.g. 5K). Deliver on the ladder
how: `scale=1920:1080` / `scale=3840:2160` for exports

name: Shorts: vertical, up to 3 minutes
what: YouTube Help says Shorts tools make videos up to 3 minutes long, vertical videos from a computer or phone can be uploaded as Shorts, and notes a maximum resolution of 1080p for Short uploads. Export Shorts at 1080x1920
how: `scale=1080:1920` with setsar=1

name: Face detection in OpenCV 5 = YuNet (FaceDetectorYN)
section: Auto-reframe with face and object tracking (OpenCV, AutoFlip ideas)
what: the OpenCV 5.0.0 in the venv has no `cv2.CascadeClassifier` (and no cv2.data Haar files) but has `cv2.FaceDetectorYN`; the YuNet ONNX model (MIT, opencv_zoo) found the face in OpenCV's sample photo with score 0.92
how: `d = cv2.FaceDetectorYN.create("face_detection_yunet_2026may.onnx", "", (w, h), 0.6, 0.3, 5000); _, faces = d.detect(frame)` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Use the 2026may YuNet file with OpenCV 5
section: Auto-reframe with face and object tracking (OpenCV, AutoFlip ideas)
what: the README says `face_detection_yunet_2026may.onnx` has dynamic input dims and suits OpenCV 5's ONNX Runtime engine, while the 2023mar file has a fixed input shape (fine on OpenCV 4 DNN). Both worked on a still here; prefer 2026may for video of any size. The files are Git LFS: fetch them from media.githubusercontent.com, not github.com/raw
how: `curl -sL -o yunet.onnx https://media.githubusercontent.com/media/opencv/opencv_zoo/main/models/face_detection_yunet/face_detection_yunet_2026may.onnx` (tested here 2026-10-24, 229,738 bytes)

name: YuNet sees faces of about 10x10 to 300x300 px
section: Auto-reframe with face and object tracking (OpenCV, AutoFlip ideas)
what: the model was trained for that face size range, so on a 4K close-up downscale the frame before detecting (and scale the box back), and on a wide shot don't downscale too far
how: `small = cv2.resize(frame, None, fx=0.25, fy=0.25)`, detect, multiply the box by 4

name: What YuNet returns
section: Auto-reframe with face and object tracking (OpenCV, AutoFlip ideas)
what: each row has 15 values: box x, y, w, h; right eye, left eye, nose tip, right and left mouth corners (x, y each); score last. The eyes give a better vertical anchor for headroom than the box centre
how: `x, y, w, h = faces[i, :4]; eyes_y = (faces[i, 5] + faces[i, 7]) / 2; score = faces[i, 14]` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Detect at a low rate, crop at full rate
section: Auto-reframe with face and object tracking (OpenCV, AutoFlip ideas)
what: AutoFlip scales frames to 480 px wide and thins the stream to one frame per 200,000 µs (5 fps) for face and object detection, while cropping the full-rate video. Doing the same keeps a Python reframe fast on CPU
how: in the loop run `detect()` only when `n % 6 == 0` at 30 fps and reuse the last centre between detections (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Hold still or follow: AutoFlip's 50% rule
section: Auto-reframe with face and object tracking (OpenCV, AutoFlip ideas)
what: per scene, AutoFlip keeps the crop steady if all focus objects stay within `motion_stabilization_threshold_percent` of the frame (0.5 = 960 px of 1920) and only tracks when they range wider. A static crop looks shot on purpose; tracking a talker who barely moves looks nervous
how: `if xs.max() - xs.min() <= 0.5 * W: path = full(xs.mean())` else smooth and track (tested here 2026-10-24: the panning test clip chose "track", x 0-237)

name: Snap a steady crop to the centre when it's close
section: Auto-reframe with face and object tracking (OpenCV, AutoFlip ideas)
what: when AutoFlip decides on a stable view and that view is within `snap_center_max_distance_percent` of the frame centre, it locks to the exact centre; useful when the operator already centred the subject or centred titles and logos are expected
how: after choosing a stable x, `if abs(x_c - W/2) < snap * W: x_c = W/2`

name: Reframe shot by shot
section: Auto-reframe with face and object tracking (OpenCV, AutoFlip ideas)
what: AutoFlip finds shot boundaries (ShotBoundaryCalculator) and makes its crop decision per scene, so the window never glides across a cut. Split the clip at cuts first and run the face/crop pass on each shot
how: cut at scene changes (e.g. `select='gt(scene,0.4)'` to list them, see catalogue scene-detection skills), then one crop path per shot

name: Priority when several things compete
section: Auto-reframe with face and object tracking (OpenCV, AutoFlip ideas)
what: AutoFlip's default fusion scores rank face core landmarks highest (0.85-0.9), then all face landmarks and full faces (0.8-0.85), humans (0.75-0.8), pets and cars (0.7-0.75), generic objects (0.1-0.2). Follow the same order when choosing what a vertical crop keeps
how: weight detections by type before averaging the target x

name: When the must-keep subjects don't fit, pad
section: Auto-reframe with face and object tracking (OpenCV, AutoFlip ideas)
what: features marked `is_required` are hard constraints; if they are too spread out to fit the target ratio, AutoFlip applies a padding effect (its defaults: blur_cv_size 200, overlay_opacity 0.6) to cover as much salient content as possible. Two people far apart: fit both with a blurred fill instead of cropping one out
how: switch that shot to the catalogue's blurred-fill command (skills #168/#493)

name: AutoFlip itself is legacy: copy the ideas, not the build
section: Auto-reframe with face and object tracking (OpenCV, AutoFlip ideas)
what: Google ended support for this MediaPipe legacy solution on 1 March 2023, and its docs say it only works with OpenCV 3 and builds with bazel; this box has OpenCV 5. Re-implement its rules (3608-3613) in a small Python script
how: see 3615

name: Face-tracked 9:16 crop path written as sendcmd
section: Auto-reframe with face and object tracking (OpenCV, AutoFlip ideas)
what: detect every 6th frame with YuNet, keep the best-score face's centre, apply the 50% hold-or-track rule, smooth with a one-second moving average, clamp to the frame, and write one `T crop x X;` line per frame; ffmpeg's crop applies it. On the test clip a face was found in 9 of 9 sampled output frames
how: Python writes `face.cmd` (`f"{i/fps:.4f} crop x {int(v)};"`), then `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf "sendcmd=f=face.cmd,crop=w=202:h=360:x=0:y=0,scale=1080:1920,setsar=1" out.mp4` (w = even ih*9/16) (tested here 2026-10-24 without setsar; see 3582)

name: Track a non-face subject with TrackerMIL
section: Auto-reframe with face and object tracking (OpenCV, AutoFlip ideas)
what: this OpenCV 5 build has TrackerMIL (no CSRT/KCF; Nano and Vit need extra models); init it with a box on the first frame and update per frame to get the subject's box for a product or pet reframe
how: `tr = cv2.TrackerMIL.create(); tr.init(frame, (x, y, w, h)); ok, box = tr.update(next_frame)` (tested here 2026-10-24: returned an updated box every frame; tracking quality not judged)

name: Tune YuNet's thresholds
section: Auto-reframe with face and object tracking (OpenCV, AutoFlip ideas)
what: `FaceDetectorYN.create(model, "", size, score_threshold, nms_threshold, top_k)`: boxes scoring below score_threshold are dropped, boxes overlapping more than nms_threshold (IoU) are suppressed, and top_k boxes are kept before NMS. Raise the score threshold if posters or crowd faces pull the crop; call `setInputSize((w, h))` if you resize frames
how: `cv2.FaceDetectorYN.create(model, "", (w, h), 0.6, 0.3, 5000)` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: MediaPipe Face Detector for video (not installed)
section: Auto-reframe with face and object tracking (OpenCV, AutoFlip ideas)
what: in VIDEO mode it tracks between frames instead of running the model on every frame and needs a timestamp per frame (`detect_for_video(image, ms)`); options min_detection_confidence (default 0.5) and min_suppression_threshold (0.3); it returns the box plus eyes, nose tip, mouth and both ear tragions
how: needs `pip install mediapipe` and a face_detector .task model (missing)

name: List the ready-made camera moves first
what: the registry's camera tag lists dolly zoom, rack focus, camera shake, cursor zoom follow, drift hold, pan stations, pull-back reveal, push-in, scroll camera story, UI focus zoom and yt-camera-move, among others. Check it before hand-tweening a move
how: `npx hyperframes catalog --tag camera --json` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Dolly zoom (Vertigo) needs depth
what: `camera-dolly-zoom` moves the camera while solving the field of view every frame from d * tan(FOV/2) = const, so the subject keeps its size while the background rushes or collapses; the subject sits on z = 0 and the content behind must sit at two or more depths, or the move shows nothing
how: `npx hyperframes add camera-dolly-zoom`, then put layers at different translateZ (catalog listing tested here 2026-10-24)
refs: repo: HyperFrames registry catalog, `npx hyperframes catalog --tag camera --json`

name: Seek-safe procedural camera shake
what: the `camera-shake` component gives handheld, telephoto and rig shake for any wrapper from nine measured profiles with per-lens projection, closed-form and seek-safe, an alternative to a hand-written yoyo shake
how: `npx hyperframes add camera-shake` on the clip wrapper (catalog listing tested here 2026-10-24)
refs: repo: HyperFrames registry catalog, `npx hyperframes catalog --tag camera --json`

name: Auto-zoom for screen recordings
what: `cursor-zoom-follow` pushes in toward each upcoming click, trails the cursor on a spring, marks clicks with a press and ring, and eases back to full screen as the cursor leaves; `ui-focus-zoom` zooms and pans to an anchored region on a cue and holds it
how: `npx hyperframes add cursor-zoom-follow` / `ui-focus-zoom` (catalog listing tested here 2026-10-24)
refs: repo: HyperFrames registry catalog, `npx hyperframes catalog --tag camera --json`

name: Push-in and pull-back as components
what: `push-in` gives a headline focus through one slow continuous camera push and a gentle fade; `pull-back-reveal` holds a tight detail, then one decelerating pull-back reveals the headline and cards that recontextualise it
how: `npx hyperframes add push-in` / `pull-back-reveal` (catalog listing tested here 2026-10-24)
refs: repo: HyperFrames registry catalog, `npx hyperframes catalog --tag camera --json`

name: Lateral pans with stops
what: `pan-stations` moves the camera sideways across a row of labelled stations with a steady dwell at each; `scroll-camera-story` runs a tall scene past the camera top to bottom with parallax layers and decelerates into a held final section
how: `npx hyperframes add pan-stations` / `scroll-camera-story` (catalog listing tested here 2026-10-24)
refs: repo: HyperFrames registry catalog, `npx hyperframes catalog --tag camera --json`

name: Keep a held frame alive
what: `drift-hold` keeps a centred card subtly alive with loop-exact rotation, scale breathing and a slow light sweep, for holds that would otherwise look frozen
how: `npx hyperframes add drift-hold` (catalog listing tested here 2026-10-24)
refs: repo: HyperFrames registry catalog, `npx hyperframes catalog --tag camera --json`

name: Zoom, slide and tilt-pan helpers for footage
what: `yt-camera-move` gives dynamic zoom, slide and 3D tilt-pan helpers for any wrapper (video, include, card) with cubic-easing defaults and an edge-defocus pulse overlay
how: `npx hyperframes add yt-camera-move`, apply to the wrapper around the `<video>` (catalog listing tested here 2026-10-24)
refs: repo: HyperFrames registry catalog, `npx hyperframes catalog --tag camera --json`

name: Portrait footage in a 16:9 frame, three fills
what: `yt-vertical-fill` fills the sides of a widescreen frame around portrait media with a blurred scale, a mirror or a copy, plus grid texture and foreground contrast lift; its note says to keep live footage in the host (images inside the block)
how: `npx hyperframes add yt-vertical-fill` (catalog query "vertical reframe" tested here 2026-10-24)
refs: repo: HyperFrames registry catalog, `npx hyperframes catalog --query "vertical reframe" --json`

name: Music-led ramp, freeze and cut in one block
what: `beat-freeze-cut` is a beat-driven speed ramp, freeze-frame hit and hard-cut sequence for music promos and montages; `whip-pan-cut` whips scene A off with capped directional blur while scene B enters at matched velocity on a speed-ramp profile with a decelerating catch
how: `npx hyperframes add beat-freeze-cut` / `whip-pan-cut` (catalog query "speed ramp" tested here 2026-10-24)
refs: repo: HyperFrames registry catalog, `npx hyperframes catalog --query "speed ramp" --json`

name: Speed-dependent motion trails
what: `echo-smear` records each element's real trajectory and trails time-offset copies in proportion to its speed (brightest-pixel combine), so fast moves smear and slow ones stay sharp: a frame-blend look for animated elements
how: `npx hyperframes add echo-smear` (catalog query "speed ramp" tested here 2026-10-24)
refs: repo: HyperFrames registry catalog, `npx hyperframes catalog --query "speed ramp" --json`

name: Zoom into a card, or out to a grid
what: `parallax-zoom` scales a centre card up to fill the frame while its siblings parallax outward; `parallax-unzoom` is the reverse reveal into a grid
how: `npx hyperframes add parallax-zoom` / `parallax-unzoom` (catalog query "zoom" tested here 2026-10-24)
refs: repo: HyperFrames registry catalog, `npx hyperframes catalog --query "zoom" --json`

name: Rack focus between two depths
what: `focus-rack` shifts focus once between two cards at different apparent depths with blur, dimming, scale and parallax; `rack-focus` (WebGL) pulls focus with aperture bokeh and needs content at two clearly separated depths
how: `npx hyperframes add focus-rack` (catalog listing tested here 2026-10-24)
refs: repo: HyperFrames registry catalog, `npx hyperframes catalog --tag camera --json`

name: Even-looking zooms with ExpoScaleEase
section: Checking camera moves in HyperFrames and GSAP
what: a scale tween with linear ease seems to change speed (each step is a smaller relative change); `expoScale(start, end)` bends the curve to compensate. Measured here: 1→2 with expoScale gave scales 1, 1.189, 1.414, 1.682, 2 (a constant 1.189x per quarter), linear gave ratios 1.25 → 1.14. Pass the real start and end scale (non-zero)
how: `gsap.to(wrap, {scale: 1.24, duration: 3.3, ease: "expoScale(1.12, 1.24)"})` with EasePack registered (tested here 2026-10-24 in node, gsap 3.14.2)

name: expoScale can bend another ease
section: Checking camera moves in HyperFrames and GSAP
what: a third parameter applies the compensation to an ease such as power2.inOut, so a punch-in can still ease in and out. Here 1→2 with power2.inOut sampled 1, 1.044, 1.414, 1.915, 2
how: `ease: "expoScale(1, 2, power2.inOut)"` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Draw the camera path before rendering
section: Checking camera moves in HyperFrames and GSAP
what: `npx hyperframes keyframes --shot motion.png --selector '#id'` draws the real element's samples and motion path (9 samples, `--samples N`, `--angle` for 3D), so a wandering reframe or overshoot shows before a render
how: `npx hyperframes keyframes --json --selector '#wrap'` then `--shot`

name: Assert the subject stays in frame
section: Checking camera moves in HyperFrames and GSAP
what: a `<name>.motion.json` next to the composition lets `check` verify intent on the seeked timeline, e.g. `{"kind": "staysInFrame", "selector": ".card"}` fails as `motion_off_frame` when a punch-in or pan pushes it out
how: add the assertions file, run `npx hyperframes check`

name: Match speeds across a camera handoff
section: Checking camera moves in HyperFrames and GSAP
what: a "jump at a cut" usually means the outgoing and incoming states differ at the seam, and an ease that looks off at a handoff means speeds don't match: mirror the ease (power3.in out, power3.out in). Snapshot just before and after the seam
how: `npx hyperframes snapshot --at <t-0.04>,<t+0.04>`

name: Slow down without changing the clip length
what: Final Cut can apply a speed change without rippling: a slowed clip keeps its length and simply shows a shorter piece of the action (a 50% throw-and-catch ends before the catch). In ffmpeg slow first, then trim back to the slot
how: `-vf "setpts=2*PTS,trim=duration=3"` (tested here 2026-10-24: 2.97 s out of a 3 s slot)

name: Contact sheet of a reframe to check it in one image
what: select every 15th frame, shrink and tile them side by side; one PNG shows whether the face stays in the 9:16 window through the clip (look at it with the Read tool)
how: `ffmpeg -i out916.mp4 -vf "select='not(mod(n,15))',scale=180:-2,tile=6x1" -frames:v 1 -update 1 sheet.png` (tested here 2026-10-24: 1080x320)

name: Preview the crop window on the 16:9 source
what: draw the planned 9:16 window as a moving box over the original before cropping; drawbox takes expressions, so the same x formula as the crop can drive it
how: `-vf "drawbox=x='(iw-404)*t/2':y=0:w=404:h=ih:color=yellow:t=4"` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Concatenated input: count frames in both stabilization passes
what: the vid.stab README warns that `-f concat` input can present irregular timestamps; before blaming the stabilizer, check that both passes see the same frame count
how: `ffprobe -v error -count_frames -select_streams v:0 -show_entries stream=nb_read_frames -of csv=p=0 joined.mp4` before each pass (tested here 2026-10-24 on a single clip: 90)

name: Several stills, one zoompan
what: when zoompan gets several images in a row, `d` is the number of output frames per image and `in`/`on` count input and output frames, so one filter can push in on the first image and pull out on the next
how: `ffmpeg -i a.png -i b.png -filter_complex "[0:v][1:v]concat=n=2:v=1,zoompan=z='if(eq(in,0),min(zoom+0.002,1.3),max(1.3-on*0.002,1))':d=60:s=640x360:fps=30" out.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24: 120 frames, 4 s)

name: Timing wobble from setpts
what: the setpts docs give a jittered fixed rate `1/(25*TB)*(N+0.05*sin(N*2*PI/25))` and a random jitter `PTS+randomi(0,-100\,100)`; with fps after it this gives an uneven, hand-cranked cadence

name: Place a flat clip into a 360 frame with transparency
what: v360 from `flat` to `e` with `alpha_mask=1` marks unmapped pixels fully transparent, so the flat shot can be laid over a 360 background
how: `-vf v360=input=flat:output=e:ih_fov=90:iv_fov=60:alpha_mask=1,format=yuva420p -frames:v 1 v360a.png` (tested here 2026-10-24: rgba PNG)

name: Tweening timeScale ramps a whole animation
what: the GSAP docs say you can tween a timeline's timeScale to slow it down or speed it up gradually (a speed ramp for motion graphics). HyperFrames seeks timelines rather than playing them, so check the result with snapshots before relying on it in a render
how: `gsap.to(tl, {timeScale: 0.25, duration: 1})`

name: Save the Cat beats as runtime percentages
section: Feature-film beat sheets scaled to video length
what: Blake Snyder's 15-beat sheet gives page numbers for a ~110-page script (Opening Image p1, Theme Stated p5, Catalyst p12, Break into Two p25, B Story p30, Midpoint p55, All Is Lost p75, Break into Three p85, Final Image p110); treat them as fractions of runtime to place beats in any length of video
how: `python3 -c "L=90;[print(n,round(L*p/110,1)) for n,p in [('catalyst',12),('break2',25),('bstory',30),('midpoint',55),('allislost',75),('break3',85),('final',110)]]"` prints the second for each beat; put scene boundaries / markers there (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Opening Image sets tone, mood, type and scope
section: Feature-film beat sheets scaled to video length
what: the very first visual should tell the viewer what kind of film this is (The Matrix opens on a blinking command-line cursor)
how: choose the frame at 0 s for tone, not just for information; with HyperFrames it is also the thumbnail, so check it with `npx hyperframes snapshot --at 0`

name: Final Image mirrors the Opening Image
section: Feature-film beat sheets scaled to video length
what: end on a shot that echoes the first one so the change in between is visible
how: export the first frame `ffmpeg -ss 0 -i edit.mp4 -frames:v 1 first.png` and reframe/re-shoot or pick a matching last shot with the same composition, grab the last frame with `ffmpeg -sseof -0.1 -i edit.mp4 -frames:v 1 last.png` and compare them side by side (`ffmpeg -i first.png -i last.png -filter_complex hstack pair.png`) (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Theme Stated in passing by a secondary character
section: Feature-film beat sheets scaled to video length
what: around 5/110 of the runtime someone other than the hero says the theme offhand, in a line the hero doesn't yet grasp ("you need to unplug for a while")
how: find an offhand line from a side person that names the theme and place it near 5/110 (~4.5%) of runtime

name: Set-up shows "things that need fixing"
section: Feature-film beat sheets scaled to video length
what: the first ~10% shows the hero's world before the change and what is missing or broken in it (flaws, needs, wishes; Snyder calls six an arbitrary number); all main characters are introduced or hinted at
how: list what is missing or broken in the subject's world and show it in the first ~10% (p1-10), before the catalyst

name: Debate beat before committing
section: Feature-film beat sheets scaled to video length
what: after the Catalyst the hero doubts or refuses (Snyder p12-25; Campbell's "refusal of the call"), which makes the later decision weigh more
how: keep the doubt/refusal moment between the catalyst (~11%) and the decision (~23%) instead of jumping straight to action

name: Break into Two is a choice, not an accident
section: Feature-film beat sheets scaled to video length
what: the hero chooses to go on the adventure (Neo takes the red pill); that choice officially starts the plot
how: make the decision itself visible on screen at ~23% (25/110) of runtime

name: B Story as a breather that carries the theme
section: Feature-film beat sheets scaled to video length
what: just after Break into Two a second strand (often a relationship) starts; Snyder says it gives the audience a breather and carries the theme
how: start the second strand near 30/110 (~27%) of runtime, right after Break into Two

name: Fun and Games = the promise of the premise
section: Feature-film beat sheets scaled to video length
what: the first half of act two (p30-55) is "the promise of the premise", the fun heart of the movie, less concerned with forward progress and often lighter in tone
how: give ~27-50% of runtime (p30-55) to the fun core of the premise, after the set-up and before stakes rise

name: Midpoint false victory or false defeat
section: Feature-film beat sheets scaled to video length
what: at the middle the stakes rise through an apparent win or loss; the All Is Lost beat often inverts it (Wikipedia's example: a false-defeat midpoint pairs with a false-victory All Is Lost)
how: decide which one your midpoint (50%, 55/110) is, then make the ~68% beat (75/110) the opposite

name: All Is Lost carries a "whiff of death"
section: Feature-film beat sheets scaled to video length
what: the lowest point often includes something that suggests death (a mentor dies, a hint of an end)
how: at ~68% of runtime (75/110), place the moment that suggests an ending or a loss before the comeback

name: Dark Night of the Soul, then Break into Three
section: Feature-film beat sheets scaled to video length
what: after the low, a stretch of hopelessness, then the A and B stories intertwine to give the solution (p75-85)
how: after the low point, bring back the B-story person/element as the trigger for the final act

name: Finale deals with obstacles in ascending order
section: Feature-film beat sheets scaled to video length
what: the hero applies what was learned and the bad guys are dealt with from least to most important; succeeding is not enough, the world must change
how: order the climax montage so the biggest win/reveal comes last

name: "Save the cat" moment to make the hero likeable
section: Feature-film beat sheets scaled to video length
what: early on, the hero does something that makes the audience like them and want them to win (Aladdin shares stolen food with hungry kids)
how: find a likeable action of the subject in the footage and place it early, before the viewer is asked to root for them

name: "Pope in the Pool" exposition
section: Feature-film beat sheets scaled to video length
what: Snyder's trick for delivering exposition without boring the audience: put something entertaining on screen while the information is told
how: lay exposition over something entertaining on screen rather than over a plain shot

name: The Board: four rows of scene cards
section: Feature-film beat sheets scaled to video length
what: plan the story on a board with four rows (Act One, first half of Act Two, second half of Act Two, Act Three), one index card per scene with its emotional change and conflict, colour-coded by character/storyline
how: before cutting, write four lists (one per row) of scene notes in the scratchpad, each with its emotional change and conflict

name: Logline test before the edit
section: Feature-film beat sheets scaled to video length
what: Snyder wants a one-or-two-sentence logline (irony, a compelling mental picture, audience and cost, a killer title) written before the script; pitch it and adjust
how: write the video's logline at the top of the edit notes and pitch it before building the timeline

name: Pick a story type, not a surface genre
section: Feature-film beat sheets scaled to video length
what: Snyder sorts films into types like Monster in the House, Golden Fleece, Out of the Bottle, Dude with a Problem, Rites of Passage, Buddy Love, Whydunit, Fool Triumphant, Institutionalized, Superhero, and says to study films of the same type
how: name the story type of the piece and watch a few films of that same type before structuring, as Snyder advises

name: Beat sheet is a guide, not a formula
section: Feature-film beat sheets scaled to video length
what: critics say strict adherence to Snyder's beats and page counts makes films feel formulaic; some strong films hit the beats out of order and out of proportion
how: use the percentages as a check after a rough cut, not as fixed cut points

name: Hero's journey in three movements
section: Other story structures (and when to pick them)
what: Campbell's 17 stages group into Departure, Initiation and Return: called from the ordinary world, helped by a mentor, crossing into a special world of trials, the central crisis ("ordeal"), a reward, then the road back home with something that benefits others; not every story uses every stage, or in that order
how: sort selects into three bins (Departure, Initiation, Return) before ordering them

name: Vogler's 12-stage writer's version
section: Other story structures (and when to pick them)
what: Christopher Vogler's adaptation for screenwriters: Ordinary World, Call to Adventure, Refusal, Meeting the Mentor, Crossing the First Threshold, Tests/Allies/Enemies, the Inmost Cave, the Ordeal, Reward, the Road Back, the Resurrection, Return with the Elixir
how: use it as a checklist on a rough cut: which of the 12 is missing or too short?

name: Kishōtenketsu for conflict-free stories
section: Other story structures (and when to pick them)
what: four parts: ki (introduction), shō (development, no major change yet), ten (twist: the unexpected turn and biggest change), ketsu (conclusion); it doesn't need conflict, though it can contain it
how: split the material into four parts and keep the biggest change for part 3

name: Hold the key element back until "ten"
section: Other story structures (and when to pick them)
what: kishōtenketsu deliberately withholds a major story element until the third of four parts, and the twist can even change the genre of the piece
how: don't show the reveal in parts 1-2; keep it for part 3 of 4

name: Ketsu ends quickly, may call back
section: Other story structures (and when to pick them)
what: in the form's essay use the conclusion should be quick and not linger, and a writer can set up a callback to the beginning
how: keep the last part short, optionally with a callback to the opening

name: Pose a dramatic question at the first plot point
section: Other story structures (and when to pick them)
what: in three-act structure the end of act one raises a question ("Will X disable the bomb?") that only the climax answers
how: write the dramatic question in one line; raise it at the end of act one and answer it in the climax

name: Second plot point turns into act three
section: Other story structures (and when to pick them)
what: act two ends at a second plot point; the third act brings the problem to a boil, forces a confrontation and reaches the climax, which answers the dramatic question
how: mark the second plot point at the end of the middle block, then let act three force the confrontation

name: Freytag's five parts
section: Other story structures (and when to pick them)
what: Gustav Freytag (Die Technik des Dramas, 1863) outlined Introduction, Rise, Climax, Return or Fall, and Catastrophe, the basis of later three- and five-act forms
how: lay out sections as the five parts when the story falls after its peak

name: Two-act shape: complication and unbinding
section: Other story structures (and when to pick them)
what: Aristotle argued for a two-part plot, desis (binding/complication) and lysis (unbinding/dénouement), split by a reversal (peripeteia); the "beginning, middle, end" three-act form is falsely attributed to him
how: build two halves (complication, unbinding) with the reversal at the join

name: Dan Harmon's Story Circle (8 steps)
section: Other story structures (and when to pick them)
what: You (comfort zone), Need, Go (unfamiliar situation), Search (adapt), Find (get what they wanted), Take (pay a price), Return, Change; a simplified, character-focused hero's journey that ends back where it started, changed
how: label selects with the 8 step names and check each step is present

name: Story Circle low point is the false win
section: Other story structures (and when to pick them)
what: "Find" sits at the bottom of the circle: the hero gets what they wanted but must pay for it in "Take", so the mid-story victory is a false win
how: follow the mid-story success with its cost (Take) before the Return

name: The last step is what the hero does with the win
section: Other story structures (and when to pick them)
what: "Change" is not the victory itself but the choice the changed character now makes; "Return" can be to a routine or community, not a place
how: end on what the changed subject now does, not on the victory itself

name: Seven-point structure, planned backwards
section: Other story structures (and when to pick them)
what: Dan Wells's Hook, Plot Turn 1, Pinch 1, Midpoint, Pinch 2, Plot Turn 2, Resolution; plan the resolution first, make the hook its opposite, then the midpoint, then turns and pinches
how: decide the resolution first, then make the hook its opposite

name: Pinch points apply pressure
section: Other story structures (and when to pick them)
what: pinches push the character into action (Pinch 1: the antagonistic force appears; Pinch 2: pressure until it looks lost, often loss of a mentor)
how: place Pinch 1 after Plot Turn 1 and Pinch 2 after the midpoint

name: Midpoint: from reaction to action
section: Other story structures (and when to pick them)
what: in seven-point structure the first half is the character reacting, the second half acting on purpose; the midpoint is the decision that flips it, and Plot Turn 2 is acted on by free will where Plot Turn 1 was forced
how: show the subject reacting before the midpoint and acting by choice after it

name: Story Spine as an 8-line outline
section: Other story structures (and when to pick them)
what: Kenn Adams's prompts: Once upon a time… Every day… But one day… Because of that… Because of that… Because of that… Until finally… And ever since then…
how: fill the 8 sentences for the video before cutting

name: Scene = goal, conflict, disaster
what: Dwight Swain defined a scene as an effort to reach a goal despite opposition, built as goal → conflict → disaster
how: for each scene in the timeline write its goal, conflict and disaster

name: Sequel = reaction, dilemma, decision
what: Swain's linking unit: the character reacts to the disaster, faces a dilemma and decides, which becomes the next goal; it also "controls tempo"
how: after a scene's disaster, keep the reaction, dilemma and decision beats that lead to the next goal

name: Pace with the scene-to-sequel ratio
what: Swain: the author controls pacing with the proportion of scene to sequel; more scene = faster, more sequel = more reflection and believability
how: change the proportion of scene to sequel material to change the pace

name: Enter the scene as late as possible
what: skip arrivals, small talk and set-up; open just before the point of the scene (the couple already seated, then the news)
how: cut as much as possible from the head of each scene and check it still works

name: Leave on the line plus one reaction
what: end the scene on its key line, give a quick look at the listener's reaction, and cut away instead of playing out the argument we've heard before
how: cut the tail after the key line and a quick reaction shot

name: Slow scene openings need a reason
what: a slow build works only if an element justifies it (Deemer's example: the husband loads a gun before lunch, so every delay adds tension)
how: keep a long lead-in only when an element (like the gun) justifies the pacing

name: Hold longer for a breather at act starts
what: exceptions to "in late, out early" work at the start or end of an act or sequence, to give the audience a breather before rebuilding tension; make such holds interesting
how: allow longer holds at act/sequence starts or ends, and make them interesting

name: Content first, then form
what: Dmytryk's first rule: substance before technique; technical skill counts for nothing if the film has little to do with humanity
