how: judge the content of the cut before working on its form

name: First viewing should be emotional, not critical
what: a film's first viewing should evoke an emotional reaction, not a critical one
how: watch the cut straight through once for emotional reaction before critiquing it

name: Cut primarily for the picture
what: except some musical sequences, images drive the edit and the soundtrack accompanies, because hearing is continuous while viewing is not
how: choose cut points by the picture, except in musical sequences

name: When unsure of the frame, cut long
what: Dmytryk: undecided about the exact frame, cut long rather than short; the first instinct is usually right, and re-lengthening clipped shots makes jumpy viewing
how: when in doubt leave the cut longer and trim later

name: Cut at the centre of the movement
what: cutting too early makes the next shot feel nonsensical, too late tries patience; the precise point is near the dead centre of the action (the moment a seated man touches the bench)
how: step through the motion and place the cut near its centre (e.g. the contact frame)

name: Fresh beats stale: pad at the head of the new shot
what: if extra frames are needed between actions, add them at the beginning of the incoming shot (the viewer reads a new setting) rather than lingering on an emptied outgoing frame
how: don't linger after a subject exits; any extra frames go at the head of the next shot

name: Begin and end scenes on continuing action
what: never start on an actor preparing to act; start as they walk in, pick up a phone, wash dishes, and end with them leaving or slamming the phone down, so the scene feels like a fragment of continuing life
how: trim heads and tails so each scene starts and ends on action

name: Cut for values, not matches
what: when the strongest emotional take doesn't match in continuity, use it anyway; the audience follows the emotional flow and ignores the mismatch. Fallbacks: cut to a close-up to hide unwanted movement, or blow up a weak shot
how: pick takes by dramatic value; hide a mismatch with a close-up or a blow-up

name: Look-off to POV: eyes settle + 3-4 frames
what: the viewer accepts a look only once the actor's eyes focus off-screen; find the frame where the eyes freeze, add 3-4 frames, then cut to the POV, which lasts only as long as it takes to read
how: at 30 fps that is 0.10-0.13 s after the eyes settle: `python3 -c "print([round(f/30,3) for f in (3,4)])"` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Text inserts: favour the slow reader
what: an insert's length depends on how easily it reads; for text favour the slow reader, and a repeat of an earlier shot can be shorter than a new one
how: time text inserts for a slow reader; make repeats shorter

name: Cut to the listener before the sentence ends
what: the sense of a sentence is clear before it finishes (subject and predicate come first), so listeners react early; cut on the reaction rather than the words where you can
how: cut to the listener's reaction before the speaker's sentence ends

name: Reaction shot = first frame of the reaction + 3-4
what: find the first frame where the reaction starts and add 3-4 frames before cutting in; a brief freeze on the start of a "frozen" reaction is an option
how: at 30 fps start the reaction clip 0.10-0.13 s before the visible change

name: Judge action only with sound in; slow the cut for music
what: withhold judgement on an action scene until sound effects are laid in; a music score increases apparent pace, so the editor will probably want to decrease the cutting pace
how: lay SFX before judging an action cut; with score under it, consider decreasing the cutting pace

name: No audience cutaways in action
what: cutting to onlookers is generally unwise because the viewer doesn't want to be shown a model of how to react
how: avoid audience cutaways inside action scenes

name: Suspense: never let a shot be analysed
what: mood is everything; a suspense shot must never stay on so long that the audience can analyse it, and should never be repeated
how: in suspense passages, cut before a shot can be analysed and don't repeat shots

name: Find script beats in the actors' eyes
what: Norman Hollyn: the beats (where characters change) show in what the actors do with their eyes; change pacing, shot size, music or sound around those moments
how: mark where the eyes change, and change pacing/shot size/music/sound around those moments

name: Keep the great moment even if the cut is rough
what: Tim Squyres: if an actor gives a striking moment, use it; nobody cares if the head turn doesn't match
how: keep the striking moment even if the matching cut is imperfect

name: Collision (Eisenstein) vs linkage (Pudovkin)
section: Editing theory: montage and its schools
what: Eisenstein: montage is an idea arising from the collision of independent shots (meaning multiplies); Pudovkin: images build on one another by addition
how: decide whether a sequence should work by collision of opposed shots or by adding shot on shot

name: Intellectual montage by juxtaposition
section: Editing theory: montage and its schools
what: Strike intercuts violence on workers with a cow being slaughtered, so the pairing produces revulsion and an idea neither shot has alone
how: intercut the action with an image that carries the idea you want the pairing to produce

name: Choose a dominant stimulus for a sequence
section: Editing theory: montage and its schools
what: Eisenstein's "dominant" is the element (movement, light, timing…) that governs a sequence, with secondary elements supporting it; Vertov built one sequence on circular motion
how: pick one dominant element for the sequence and select shots that share it

name: Montage vs continuity: pick the contract
section: Editing theory: montage and its schools
what: continuity editing serves a predetermined narrative and keeps space logical (180° rule); montage makes meaning from associations and may break space on purpose (Man with a Movie Camera)
how: decide per section whether it follows continuity or montage

name: Pudovkin's theme from many angles
section: Editing theory: montage and its schools
what: Pudovkin starts from a theme and shows the phenomenon from different angles and distances so the viewer gets both the overview and the detail (his street-demonstration example: roof view plus readable banners)
how: show the key event from several angles and distances

name: Pudovkin's five relational edits
section: Editing theory: montage and its schools
what: contrast (opposed scenes compared), parallelism (jump times/places), symbolism (an object stands for an idea), simultaneity (two places at once), leitmotif (a repeated motif tied to a person or idea)
how: label each transition in the edit with one of the five; if none applies, ask why the cut is there

name: Kuleshov through music
section: Editing theory: montage and its schools
what: Baranowski & Hecht intercut faces with neutral scenes under happy, sad or no music and found the music significantly changed how the faces were judged
how: test a reaction shot under two music beds (`ffmpeg -i face.mp4 -i bed.mp3 -map 0:v -map 1:a -shortest -c:v copy test.mp4`) and choose the bed that makes the face read right (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Hitchcock's "pure editing" demo
section: Editing theory: montage and its schools
what: the same smiling face reads as a kind old man after a woman with a baby and as a "dirty old man" after a woman in a bikini
how: put the shot that gives the face its meaning directly before the reaction

name: Montage sequence to compress time
section: Editing theory: montage and its schools
what: British/American "montage sequence": many short shots (once with dissolves, split screens, superimpositions and music) to show long time passing (Rocky's training weeks, Ferris Bueller's hours)
how: compress a long stretch into a sequence of short shots with music

name: Training-montage conventions
section: Editing theory: montage and its schools
what: build-up where the hero faces failing to train, then a serious solo regimen in short cuts, an inspirational (often fast rock) song as the only sound, weeks pass in minutes, hero ready for the big task; it is also a cliché, often parodied
how: let the song be the only sound and end with the hero ready for the task

name: Newsreel and railroad montage devices
section: Editing theory: montage and its schools
what: classic devices: presses rolling and headlines zooming at the screen (Citizen Kane), or engines racing at camera and destination signs filling the screen
how: for a news beat, use presses and headlines zooming onto the screen

name: Script the montage yourself (Don Siegel)
section: Editing theory: montage and its schools
what: Siegel, head of Warner's montage department, turned the script's one-line montage description into his own five-page script instead of throwing stock shots together, and matched the director's style
how: write your own detailed script for a montage before pulling clips

name: Edit standing, write lying down (Murch)
section: Editing theory: montage and its schools
what: Walter Murch edits standing (like conductors, surgeons and cooks) and writes lying down to separate his editing mind from his creating mind
how: keep writing (planning) sessions and cutting sessions separate

name: Editing as steering the audience's thoughts
section: Editing theory: montage and its schools
what: Murch's In the Blink of an Eye treats editing as anticipating and controlling the audience's thoughts and puts emotion above technicalities
how: at each cut ask "what is the viewer thinking right now, and what should they think next?"
refs: Wikipedia "In the Blink of an Eye", https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_the_Blink_of_an_Eye_(Murch_book), checked 2026-10-24

name: Pick a Nichols mode as the film's dominant
what: Bill Nichols's six modes: poetic, expository, observational, participatory, reflexive, performative; modes overlap and one usually functions as the dominant without dictating every choice
how: name the dominant mode in the edit notes before structuring, then let other modes appear where needed
refs: IDA review of Introduction to Documentary, https://www.documentary.org/node/34718, checked 2026-10-24

name: Poetic mode: associations over continuity
what: poetic documentaries favour mood and tone, leave characters and events undeveloped, and edit by "associations and patterns that involve temporal rhythms and spatial juxtapositions"; continuity hardly matters (Ivens's Regen links unrelated shots of a rain shower)
how: cut by rhythm and visual rhyme instead of chronology for a mood piece

name: Expository mode: evidentiary editing
what: narration carries the argument, and images "illustrate, illuminate, evoke, or act in counterpoint to what is said"; viewers read the images as evidence for the commentary
how: write/record the narration first, then pick each image as proof or counterpoint of its line

name: Observational mode bylaws
what: pure observational documentaries use no music, no interviews, no staged scenes and no narration, with long takes and few cuts (fly on the wall)
how: for an observational piece, drop the music bed and the voice-over and keep takes long

name: Participatory mode: keep the filmmaker's voice in
what: the interaction between filmmaker and subject is on screen; at its simplest the filmmaker's voice is heard in the film (Rouch's Chronicle of a Summer; Errol Morris's Interrotron lets subjects talk to the director while looking into the lens)
how: leave the interviewer's questions in the cut when the exchange itself is the story

name: Reflexive mode: show the making
what: reflexive films expose their own construction (Vertov shows footage being shot and edited) and use re-enactment (Morris's The Thin Blue Line), which purists of vérité frown on
how: if you include re-enactments, make them read as re-enactments rather than real footage

name: Performative mode: subjective truth
what: like participatory, but builds truths significant to the filmmaker personally; suits personal stories told without arguing their validity, and allows more visual abstraction
how: for a first-person piece, let the narrator's own perspective lead and allow freer, abstract visuals

name: Vérité vs direct cinema
what: direct cinema aims for the subject and audience to forget the camera (observational, fly on the wall); cinéma vérité acknowledges the camera and the filmmaker may provoke or set up situations as a catalyst (Perrault asked old people to fish for whale)
how: decide which contract you keep: hide the crew entirely, or keep moments where subjects react to the camera

name: Nichols's four "legs" of documentary
what: Nichols names display/documentation, poetic experimentation, narrative storytelling and rhetorical oratory as the four legs a documentary stands on
how: check a doc cut for all four: real record, a poetic passage, a story line and an argument
refs: IDA review of Introduction to Documentary, https://www.documentary.org/node/34718, checked 2026-10-24

name: Screen hours of interviews at 2x-3x
what: Noam Kroll: watch every frame first, but at 2x (sometimes 3x) playback when there are many hours; a clip that jumps out at 2x is good
how: make a fast review copy `ffmpeg -i interview.mp4 -vf setpts=0.5*PTS -af atempo=2.0 -c:v libx264 -preset ultrafast -crf 30 review2x.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Watch everything once before pulling selects
what: Kroll: a full pass without pulling clips, then a second pass to pull selects; Andy Grieve also watches everything first and can't cut and screen at the same time
how: first pass = notes only; second pass = mark in/out of selects

name: Ruthless selects for short pieces
what: for a 2-3 minute promo "99.9%" of the interview isn't used; if a clip doesn't immediately grab you, stand out or add new insight, leave it
how: keep only clips that pass that test into the selects timeline

name: Look for intro, closing and throughline bites
what: Kroll's second selects pass keeps only a great introductory statement, a great closing statement, and concise explanations of the throughline; these make up "90%" of a short edit
how: tag selects INTRO / CLOSE / THROUGHLINE and drop wordy ones that would need many frankenbites

name: Group selects into beginning, middle, end
what: loosely sort selects into the three sections (or by day for a week-in-the-life), then cut from the over-full sections
how: three marker colours or three sub-timelines; trim the section with the most material first

name: Pick the best intro bite and let it choose the next
what: start the timeline with the very best intro clip; that choice dictates which clip comes next, and so on to the end
how: build the sequence one bite at a time from the top, never filling the middle first

name: Music, breathing pauses and B-roll come last
what: Kroll: after the bite order is set, drop in music, add pauses for breathing room and lay B-roll for each talking point; this should be the shortest phase
how: only start the `voice_over_music.py` / B-roll pass after the bite order is final
refs: repo: CLAUDE.md "Voice and songs with words"

name: Timestamped transcript for every interview
what: Todd Boruff has each interview transcribed with question breaks and a timestamp about every 60 s, then highlights candidate bites; automatic transcripts struggle with names and jargon
how: transcribe with the repo's Whisper install (word timings) and check names by hand

name: Keep the paper edit loose
what: how bites look on paper doesn't always match how they're said on video; the stringout reveals energy, stumbles and expressions that change a bite
how: after the paper order, listen to each bite in place before committing to it

name: Build "modules" (Andy Grieve)
what: cut each interview to its best parts (removing questions and dead air), organise by character and subject, and build little self-contained modules (a couple of minutes, ten minutes) that you later piece into the film
how: make one short sequence per topic first; assemble the film from those sequences

name: Interviews first, archive later
what: Grieve watches interviews first because they show which archival footage to look for and which characters share experiences to intercut; he only goes into archival once the story is known
how: lock the interview story line before searching B-roll/archive

name: Talking heads as characters, not experts
what: Grieve wants interviewees to feel like live characters driving the story, not experts "sitting in a chair", so he lets stories come from their experiences
how: prefer bites where people recount what happened to them over bites that explain

name: Never fake cause and effect
what: Grieve accepts shaping for emotion or arc but never wants to create a false sense of cause and effect; documentaries pursue truth
how: when reordering bites, check you haven't made one event appear to cause another that it didn't

name: Pace a story by where it lands
what: a story that seems like an opener may end up later in the film, and then needs different pacing and different archival because its function has changed
how: after moving a section, re-pace it and re-pick its B-roll for its new role

name: Searchable locators at each bite
what: Grieve's assistant puts a locator at the head (and sometimes middle) of each select with its first words or key words, so bites can be searched
how: name each select clip or marker with its first few words (e.g. from Whisper text)

name: Re-screen raw interviews near the end
what: late in the edit Grieve passes back through all the raw interviews for anything missed or anything that now means something different in context
how: schedule a final raw-interview pass before picture lock

name: Time-of-day map for all-archival stories
what: for an all-archival film about one day (the OJ Simpson chase), Grieve mapped a 24-hour timeline of the best footage on layers to see what overlapped
how: for multi-source event footage, place clips on a timeline by real clock time (creation time from `ffprobe -v error -show_entries format_tags=creation_time clip.mp4`) before story-cutting (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Stack alternatives on tracks
what: Grieve keeps options for a shot stacked on different tracks while debating them
how: in a HyperFrames scene keep the alternate clip as a second element with `visibility:hidden` until chosen

name: Frankenbite: know the line
what: Manfred Becker's term for re-ordering key elements or single words of a statement to create a confession or argument the original didn't contain; he studied the ethical dilemmas of 75 editors over it
how: in documentary/testimonial work avoid joins that change what the person meant; Kroll also advises against bites that need many frankenbites

name: B-roll after the interview, shot to support it
what: in ENG and documentary, B-roll is often shot after the main interview to supply scenes for what was said; types include inserts, FX shots, establishing shots, stock footage and pickups, usually laid under the continuing primary audio
how: list each talking point and the B-roll type that will cover it; keep the interview audio running under it

name: Two deliverables: highlight reel and full film
what: wedding editors usually cut a short highlight reel for sharing online and a full-length film that shows the day as it happened; some couples only want the highlight
how: build the full chronological timeline first, then derive the highlight from it

name: Highlight out of order, full film in order
what: don't show everything in order in the highlight; weave clips in the most engaging way and save the chronology for the full-length film
how: reorder freely in the highlight; keep the long cut chronological

name: Open the highlight with a speech or the vows
what: one of the most frequent openings uses a speech or the vows to introduce the couple, then shows the rest of the day (Joe Simon's reels use the father of the bride)
how: lay one speech line over the first shots, then cut the day around it

name: Five-act highlight: opening, build, ceremony, resolution, closing
what: RoughCut's arc for a ~7-minute highlight: Opening 0:00-1:00 (one universal emotional line over atmospheric B-roll), Build 1:00-3:00 (speeches telling the love story), Ceremony/Climax 3:00-5:00 (best vow lines, rings, kiss; music peaks), Resolution 5:00-6:30 (exhale, recessional, a light toast line), Closing 6:30-7:00 (one final line, the couple walking away, music fades, black)
how: scale the act boundaries to the target length: `python3 -c "L=180;[print(n,round(L*t/420)) for n,t in [('build',60),('ceremony',180),('resolution',300),('closing',390)]]"` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Don't open on the vows or a joke
what: in RoughCut's arc the opening should be short and evocative; starting with the vows, a joke or a long speech clip doesn't work
how: save the vows for the climax section and keep the opening to one line

name: Build section: 2-3 speakers, specific stories
what: introduce the couple through other people's eyes (parents, best man, maid of honour); more than 2-3 speakers or generic praise without a specific story weakens it; let each moment breathe
how: choose at most three speakers for the build and pick bites that tell an anecdote

name: Let the ceremony own the climax
what: use the most honest, personal vow lines, don't rush them, and don't cut the vows with speech audio
how: no speech bites inside the ceremony section; the music peak sits here

name: Resolution must exhale
what: after the peak, give release (warmth, joy, humour fits here); trying to match the climax's energy doesn't work
how: follow the vows with the recessional and a light line, at lower intensity

name: End on one strong line, never logistics
what: the last thing heard defines how the audience feels; 1-2 sentences max, not one more toast or "please proceed to the cocktail hour"
how: pick the closing bite separately and test the ending without it to see if it's earning its place

name: 8-15 soundbites for a 7-minute highlight
what: RoughCut's biggest-mistake warning: too much; a 7-minute highlight should carry 8-15 soundbites, not 30, and any clip whose removal doesn't hurt the story should go
how: count the bites on the timeline; above ~15 for 7 min, cut

name: Score bites by emotion, sync to music last
what: transcribe everything, score bites by emotional weight not information, find 2-3 candidates per section, check each bite flows into the next, and only then adjust trims to the music
how: pick words first; snap their placement to bar lines only in the final pass

name: Swap a great bite for a better transition
what: if two great clips feel jarring back-to-back, swap one for a slightly weaker clip that transitions better
how: play each bite join aloud; replace the bite, not the transition effect, when it jars

name: Two-song highlight
what: PremiumBeat's standard: a slow, steady song for the intro and ceremony, then a fast dance track for the reception footage; music for online reels must be licensed
how: pick both tracks from the repo's CC0 library per the owner's no-credit rule

name: Highlight under ten minutes, best of the best
what: keep the highlight short and tight, well under 10 minutes; full ceremony and speeches belong in the full film
how: if the highlight passes 10 min, move whole speeches to the long cut

name: Journalistic vs cinematic vs concept style
what: journalistic (documentary) wedding videos keep segments in the order they occurred; cinematic ones add slow motion, transitions, saturated colour, creative angles and dramatic music; concept videos are scripted with pre-wedding shoots and interviews
how: agree the style with the client before cutting; it decides ordering and effects

name: Event recap: theme decided before the event
what: RainFocus: identify the recap's theme and purpose while the event is being planned, know who should watch it and what they should do after, and tell the videographer the channels in advance (that shapes length and structure)
how: write the recap's one-line theme, audience and channel before the shoot

name: Recap length: sources differ
what: Canon says few recap videos run more than about a minute; RainFocus advises two to four minutes with a single song
how: cut a ~60 s social recap and, if the client wants it, a 2-4 min version on one track

name: Recap story: who, what, when, where, why — told chronologically
what: Canon: find the event's purpose, then generally tell it in order as it unfolded, with evocative visuals, brief interviews of organisers and participants, and sparing text overlays to fill gaps
how: order selects by clock time (`ffprobe -v error -show_entries format_tags=creation_time clip.mp4`) and drop in 2-3 short interview bites

name: No voice-over narration on recaps
what: Canon advises avoiding voice-over narration (clichéd) and using explanatory text with the interviews instead
how: carry information in short on-screen text, not a narrator

name: Put the key moment on the song's high point
what: RainFocus: tempo and beats speak louder than words; place an important moment at the high point of the song, and keep quotes short and memorable
how: find the track's peak (e.g. with `npx hyperframes audio <file>`) and align the event's biggest moment to it

name: Smiles, VIPs and behind-the-scenes
what: RainFocus: film attendees smiling and laughing, make sure VIPs are captured, and include behind-the-scenes footage of the people who made the event for context
how: check the selects contain each of the three kinds before cutting

name: Proof all text and add the logo
what: misspelled names and typos distract; the viewer should be able to tell whose event it is from the logo
how: spell-check every caption/name card against the client's list; place the logo at least once

name: Recap ends on a CTA
what: Canon: identify a strong brand-relevant call to action, often an invitation to share memories with a hashtag or to register for the next event
how: end card with the hashtag or next-event date

name: Trailer skeleton: cold open, three acts, button
what: Derek Lieu's breakdown (via Jonny Elwyn) of most modern trailers: Cold Open, Act 1 (introduction), Act 2 (escalation), Act 3 (climax), then the Button
how: mark the five sections on the timeline before choosing shots

name: Reach act two about a minute in
what: Chris St. Pierre (Harry Potter, Gravity trailers): Act One sets the world and characters, Act Two presents the conflict and antagonists, and you typically want to be in act two by about a minute in
how: for a ~2:30 trailer, check the conflict starts near 1:00

name: Act three is "montage land"
what: once the story is out of the way, cut a montage of images to music with cool lines sprinkled in until the main title
how: after the conflict is set, switch to bar-driven montage cutting up to the title card

name: Logo/graphic after the cold open
what: the intriguing open is usually followed by a logo or graphic (often the studio logos, or a "This Summer" / "From Director X" card) to separate it from what follows
how: place the brand/server logo card right after the cold open

name: Story cards carry the copy
what: copy cards like "This summer," "get ready," "to rumble!" run through the trailer; trailers also include studio logos, date and pedigree cards
how: split the slogan over several cards placed through the trailer

name: End on the tag line (before or after the title)
what: have one last dramatic line before the title, or a cool moment after it (the button), sometimes both; the goal is a takeaway line the audience remembers
how: reserve the best line for just before or after the title card

name: Trailer prep: transcribe and build select reels
what: transcribe the whole film, cut a master dialogue reel with pauses removed, then duplicate it into topic reels (jokes, mystery, scary, exciting); do the same for visuals (wides, emotional shots, character shots, head-turns)
how: keep one master dialogue timeline and derive category timelines from copies of it

name: Bites can be out of film order, but must make sense
what: in the paper cut the order of lines need not follow the film, only make sense in the trailer's order
how: write the bite order on paper and read it aloud as a story

name: Build the audio shell first
what: cut in music cues and dialogue and make it sound good before any visuals; place dialogue before musical downbeats, not on them, and let lyrics play between lines
how: in HyperFrames lay out `<audio>` lanes first (different `data-track-index` per overlapping clip), then add video

name: Music builds through two or three cues
what: the music should build in intensity across the trailer, sometimes via 2-3 cues: minimal open, a melody by act one, more intensity in act two, the big chorus in act three
how: order the CC0 cues from sparse to full and change cue at act boundaries

name: Cause-and-effect shot flow
what: think cause and effect: a character fires a gun, cut to an explosion; on a downbeat it hits harder than mid-phrase
how: pair "action" and "result" shots across a cut that lands on a beat

name: Vary focal length; sprinkle wides for scope
what: head shot after head shot is visually stale; wide shots give scope, place and production value
how: alternate close and wide selects

name: Cut the music out to land a joke
what: the Masterclass trailer Elwyn breaks down cuts the track out to emphasise a joke or a point of surprise; the break also lets the music restart or change track
how: drop the music to silence for the punchline, then bring in the next cue

name: Title cards arrive with a sound
what: each title (and cut to black) in that trailer comes in with a cymbal riser, a slam or a whoosh, adding energy
how: give every card a riser/impact from `library/` SFX, timed so the hit lands on the card
refs: repo: CLAUDE.md "HyperFrames learnings" (riser crest at 3.47 s)

name: Short cold open vs long cold open
what: Elwyn's comparison: Joker's cold open is about 9 s (a question and a look), Hobbs & Shaw's runs about 45 s of jokes and punches; Joker sells the world and arc while being less explicit on plot
how: keep the cold open short when selling mood; don't spell out the whole plot

name: Social trailer: title card before 5 s, watchable on mute
what: Noam Kroll opened his social trailer aggressively instead of easing in, put a title card before the 5-second mark, and made it fully watchable with sound off (subtitles or title cards)
how: first card by 5 s, and captions/cards for every line

name: Micro-teaser / bumper at the head
what: since the mid-to-late 2010s many trailers start with a 5-10 s preview ("micro-teaser" or "bumper") of the trailer itself so viewers don't skip on streaming sites
how: put a 5-10 s preview of the trailer's moments at the very start

name: Comedy trailers: neater, shorter, faster
what: Tony Zhou (via Elwyn): the UK Ghostbusters trailer, cut from the same footage, was funnier than the US one; the editor is responsible for the jokes, and good trailers do everything the movie does "neater, shorter and faster"
how: time joke setups/punches frame by frame and compare two cuts of the same joke

name: Colour-code shots by actor
what: colour-coding trailer shots by actor lets you see at a glance how much screen time each has when feedback asks for more of someone
how: in the edit list, tag every shot with the person in it and count per person

name: Bookend and intercut, not linear chunks
what: StudioBinder: trailers needn't be a linear edit of scenes; try bookending and intercutting, while keeping an abridged three-act shape
how: open and close on the same moment and intercut two storylines in the middle

name: Game trailers: say if it's cinematic or gameplay
what: cinematic game trailers are CGI made apart from the engine; gameplay ("in-engine") trailers imply real footage, and trailers that showed features or graphics the game didn't ship (Cyberpunk 2077, Aliens: Colonial Marines) drew criticism
how: in a gameplay trailer show only what the real game/server actually does

name: Lay a full-song "bed" performance shot first
what: JG Harding (Sound On Sound): sync one of the best whole-song performance shots (e.g. a wide of the band) on the bottom track as a bed, then layer performance takes over it, keeping the parts you like; the bed is something to cut back to (only 10 frames of his remained)
how: put the full-length wide take as the lowest video layer for the song's whole duration, then add cut sections above it

name: Take one bar of the best part of each clip
what: use only the key part of a clip (e.g. one bar of a 10-second pan, picked for a lens flare or a great expression) so the edit becomes a "best-of" from start to finish; more takes give more serendipitous moments
how: bar length = 240/BPM s for 4/4 (`python3 -c "print(240/120)"` → 2.0 s at 120 BPM); trim each clip to its best bar (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Beat cuts with occasional 2-beat and 2-bar cuts
what: for 4/4 performance pieces, sticking to the beat with occasional two-beat and two-bar cuts keeps it from becoming monotonous (Harding's rule of thumb)
how: mostly one-bar shots, with a few half-bar and two-bar shots mixed in

name: Slow songs: cut slightly off the bar
what: the Fever Ray video mostly cuts slightly off the start of bars, with many shots about three and a half bars long; cutting out of sync with the main musical events shifts focus to the shot content
how: for a slow track, hold shots for several bars and place cuts a little after bar starts

name: Every shot moves, even in a slow edit
what: in Glasvegas's slow video every shot has some motion (pan, track or handheld at similar speed), and still frames contain movement
how: if a shot is locked off, add a slow scale/position tween on its wrapper so nothing sits dead
refs: repo: CLAUDE.md "Editing a phone video" step 5

name: Software zoom on locked-off shots
what: Harding: scale up a tripod shot and pan a little or zoom in a few percent; keeping the viewer's interest matters more than a few pixels of sharpness
how: `ffmpeg -i still.mp4 -vf "scale=iw*1.05:-2,crop=iw/1.05:ih/1.05" -c:a copy zoom5.mp4` for a fixed 5% punch-in (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Cut between wide and intimate close shots
what: a static point of view reduces involvement and often happens in amateur videos; cut in and out between wider shots and close-ups
how: alternate shot sizes through each section of the song

name: Name every clip before cutting
what: descriptive names like "Band: SOLO 2 (good)" instead of "MOV_4578", sorted into bins, save time when you need "just one more nice shot" late in the edit
how: rename source clips by content before building the timeline

name: Echo instruments and riffs with a repeated visual
what: Videomaker: whenever an instrument or riff recurs, reinforce it with the same effect or a related visual; mirror verse/chorus/bridge structure with corresponding visual patterns
how: assign one visual treatment per recurring riff and reuse it each time the riff returns

name: Tap markers in real time
what: most editors let you add a marker with one keystroke during playback: play the song, tap the beat, then refine marker positions and snap clips to them
how: needs an NLE with live markers (missing; e.g. Kdenlive, GPL-3.0): play the song tapping markers, refine them, snap cuts to them

name: Fade picture or a credit card with the song's fade
what: when a song fades out, fade the picture to black with it or fade in a graphic with the artist's name and contact
how: `ffmpeg -i mv.mp4 -vf "fade=t=out:st=8:d=2" -c:a copy out.mp4` matching the fade start/length to the song's fade (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Establish a look and stick with it
what: try wild ideas, but once the video's look is established keep it throughout, building variations off it rather than switching to something entirely different
how: pick one grade/treatment for the whole video; vary only within it

name: The visual story may contradict the lyrics
what: use the video to emphasise the song's story; sometimes the visual narrative works best in contradiction to the lyrical story
how: decide up front whether visuals follow or counter the lyrics

name: Audio-reactive effects from the waveform
what: the waveform is data: tools such as Trapcode Sound Keys or Boris Beat Reactor, or After Effects audio-to-keyframes with expressions, link effect values to amplitude
how: in ffmpeg, `showwaves`/`showfreqs` draw audio-driven visuals that can be overlaid (`ffmpeg -i song.mp3 -filter_complex "showwaves=s=640x120:mode=cline" -t 3 waves.mp4`) (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Give the eye time after a big brightness change
what: PremiumBeat: cutting between dark and light rooms needs time for the eyes to adjust, and the viewer must understand the new scene before the next cut
how: in fast montages, hold the first shot after a dark→bright change a little longer

name: Hook, body, close for short ads
what: TikTok's ad guidance recommends a three-part structure: a hook, a body that highlights the unique selling points, and a close with a clear CTA that tells the audience what to think, feel or do
how: split the ad timeline into three labelled blocks before choosing shots

name: Proposition in 3 s, hook within 6 s
what: TikTok: introduce the content proposition in the first 3 seconds for recall, and prioritise the hook in the first 6 seconds (it cites 90% of ad recall impact captured in the first six seconds)
how: make sure the product/offer is named or shown before 3.0 s

name: Show the product on screen in the body
what: TikTok reports that ads showing the product on screen drive higher brand affinity and recall ("additive branding cues" through the body)
how: keep the product/logo visible in several body shots, not only in the end card

name: CTA cards instead of interrupting
what: TikTok recommends closing with CTA cards rather than interrupting the content
how: add an end-card overlay with the action over the last shot instead of cutting to a separate slate

name: Ad text at 5-10 words per second
what: TikTok suggests displaying 5-10 words per second when using text overlays
how: check each card: words ÷ seconds on screen should be ≤ 10 (`python3 -c "w=12;s=1.5;print(w/s)"` → 8.0) (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Native, not over-polished
what: TikTok advises a DIY, not overly polished style that fits user-generated content, featuring creators, employees or customers
how: feature real creators, employees or customers and keep a DIY look

name: Before-After-Bridge (BAB)
what: show the current painful state (Before), the desired state (After), then the product as the Bridge, then a CTA; Benly's 30 s blocks: Before 0-8 s, After 8-20 s, Bridge 20-27 s, CTA 27-30 s; suits visible transformations and can use split screen
how: `ffmpeg -i before.mp4 -i after.mp4 -filter_complex hstack ba.mp4` for a side-by-side Before/After beat (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: UGC testimonial flow
what: Benly's 30 s structure: personal hook 0-4 s (start mid-story), problem/context 4-12 s, discovery of the product 12-22 s ("then someone told me about…"), result/proof 22-27 s, direct recommendation 27-30 s
how: order a creator's talking-to-camera bites in these five slots

name: Product-demo structure
what: lead with the most impressive capability (0-5 s), walk through it solving a real task (5-18 s), show what's different (18-24 s), then social proof + CTA (24-30 s); Benly places it mid-to-bottom funnel, for viewers who already know they need a solution
how: open on the "wow" feature shot, then screen recording/close-ups of the task

name: Combine frameworks across one ad
what: Benly notes common combinations: PAS for the first 15 s then a product demo, or BAB for emotion then social proof from the UGC format, with smooth transitions
how: plan two blocks with a clear hand-off line between them

name: Agitate with vivid consequences
what: in PAS the agitation moves from factual to emotional: specific stories of the problem interfering with lives; then present the solution with benefits over features (Dan Kennedy called PAS "the most reliable copywriting formula for sales ever invented")
how: in the agitate block use shots of the consequence, not the product

name: AIDA's original seller steps
what: E. St. Elmo Lewis's model; the original selling stages were: secure attention, hold attention through interest, arouse desire, create confidence and belief, secure decision and action, create satisfaction
how: check a promo has a "confidence/belief" beat (proof) between desire and the CTA

name: AIDA is a poor predictor, use loosely
what: empirical studies found AIDA and other hierarchy models poor predictors of actual consumer behaviour, and they ignore post-purchase effects
how: treat AIDA as a script checklist, not a guarantee

name: StoryBrand: customer is the hero, brand is the guide
what: Donald Miller's SB7: a Character (the customer) with a Problem meets a Guide who gives a Plan and Calls them to Action, helping them avoid Failure and end in Success; the brand is Yoda, not Luke
how: cast the customer/player as the on-screen hero and the brand as the helper

name: Three problem layers
what: SB7: external (the tangible thing), internal (how it makes them feel), philosophical (why it's wrong they have it); most brands only sell the external one
how: give the problem block one line or shot per layer

name: Guide = empathy + authority
what: the brand earns the guide role by showing it understands the problem (empathy) and can solve it (authority), without taking the spotlight
how: one empathy line, then one proof of competence (result, credential)

name: 3-4 step plan plus direct and transitional CTAs
what: give a simple plan of three or four steps, a direct CTA (buy, book) and a transitional one (free guide, webinar) for people not ready; spell out failure and success stakes
how: end card with the main action plus one low-commitment action

name: "If you confuse, you lose"
what: Miller's rule: clarity beats clever; marketing should be understood, not impressive
how: after a rough cut, have someone say in one sentence what is offered; if they can't, simplify

name: Explainer formula with 90 s time budget
what: Levitate: Hook 0-5 s, Problem 5-20 s, Solution 20-50 s (no feature list yet), How It Works 50-80 s (two or three steps), Social Proof 80-90 s (one proof point), CTA in the last 10 s; a 60 s version compresses hook, problem and solution
how: scale the block edges: `python3 -c "L=60;[print(n,round(L*t/90,1)) for n,t in [('problem',5),('solution',20),('how',50),('proof',80)]]"` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Biteable's 60 s skeleton
what: Hook 0-8 s, Problem 8-20 s, Solution 20-45 s (with "here's how it works: step one, two, three"), CTA 45-60 s; about 150 words for 60 s, solution gets the most time
how: count script words before recording (`wc -w script.txt`) and aim near 150 per minute (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Two-column script: audio left, visuals right
what: professional explainer scripts pair each voice-over line with what the viewer sees; write the visual column after the audio is approved
how: keep a two-column table (line | shot) in the scratchpad and build scenes row by row

name: One idea, one audience, one CTA
what: a strong explainer has one core idea, one target audience and one call to action; everything else belongs in a different video
how: strike any scene that serves a second audience or second ask

name: Read the script aloud with a timer
what: read at natural pace; if you're rushing, cut the script, not the pace (conversational VO lands around 125-150 words per minute)
how: `python3 -c "w=210;print(round(w/140*60),'s')"` estimates runtime at 140 wpm, then time a real read (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Open in the viewer's world, not the company's
what: start with a pain point or a question the audience already asks; nobody cares about the founding story in the first five seconds
how: first line of VO = the viewer's problem; brand name comes later

name: Specific numbers, not "saves time"
what: replace vague benefits with concrete outcomes ("cuts reporting from three hours to twenty minutes"), pulled from real data
how: every benefit line in the VO should contain a concrete, true number or result from the client

name: Adapt the hook to the use case
what: Biteable: product explainer hooks on the task the buyer dreads; new-hire training on a day-one confusion; internal announcements on what's changing and why now; sales follow-ups on the prospect's goal
how: pick the hook angle from the video's use, keep the four-part body

name: Give each vlog a repeatable story template
what: Fstoppers: successful vloggers often follow traditional storytelling principles; pick a template borrowed from favourite vloggers (e.g. open on a time-lapse, or on a sneak peek of something later in the episode) so you know what to film and where it goes
how: fix the episode's opening type and section order before shooting

name: Sneak-peek opening
what: start the episode with a short preview of something that happens later
how: copy the strongest later moment to 0 s: `ffmpeg -ss 40 -t 3 -i vlog.mp4 -c:v libx264 -c:a aac peek.mp4`, then place it before the start (cut command tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Don't spoon-feed: cut what the viewer can assume
what: skip the wake-up-to-arrival details; Neistat often cuts mid-sentence, which shortens, speeds up and lets viewers feel they worked something out (Abrams's "mystery box")
how: remove transitional routine footage and test whether the story still reads

name: Don't get attached to your own footage
what: great montage shots are often on screen for only a second; lingering because you shot it kills an upbeat edit
how: in self-shot montages, trim every shot to its best second first

name: "Neistat cut-off"
what: Sven Pape's breakdown: cut abruptly to a new scene in the middle of a sentence or thought
how: end the clip on a word mid-sentence and start the next scene's audio immediately

name: Continuous thought across locations
what: start a story in one location and finish it in one or more others, stringing small pieces together
how: split one spoken thought across clips from different places, keeping the sentence continuous

name: Associative cut
what: cut in small bits of referential content (often clips from films) to comment on what's said
how: use only licensed/CC0 reference clips per the owner's rules

name: Task-progress montage on sped-up footage
what: rapid cuts showing one task progressing, usually on footage that's already sped up
how: speed the task clip first (`ffmpeg -i task.mp4 -vf setpts=PTS/4 -an fast.mp4`), then cut it into short pieces (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: In-camera transitions
what: putting the camera down/picking it up, a "lens slap", or pushing the camera closer to the face to intensify a moment (an in-camera "edit")
how: when filming yourself, cover scene changes with a hand over the lens and cut inside it

name: Show the end result first
what: before the hook, show a ~5-second clip of the finished result so viewers know it's what they searched for
how: put a 3-5 s clip of the final output at 0 s, then the hook

name: Hook = prerequisite + specific promise
what: after the result preview, state the prerequisite level and a specific promise of what the viewer will be able to do
how: one line each, in about 15 s total, no channel intro animation

name: Steps first, theory after each step
what: put explanations in short callouts after the step they explain ("the reason this works is…"), not as preamble
how: move any theory segment to right after the step it explains

name: Number every step, aloud and on screen
what: numbered steps signal progress and create rewatch points
how: say "Step 3: …" and show a "Step 3" card at the same moment

name: Address the common failure point
what: find the 1-2 steps where viewers hit errors and add "if you see this error, here's the fix"
how: insert a short troubleshooting aside at that step

name: End with recap + the next logical step
what: one-sentence recap, then the specific next problem the viewer will have and where it's solved
how: close on the recap line, then point to the follow-up video

name: Tell first, then show silently
what: Georgia Tech Library: if the viewer must pay attention to something, don't speak while showing it; tell them first, then show
how: leave a narration gap over the key screen action

name: No cursor-waving; annotate in the edit
what: don't move the cursor around for emphasis; add animation or annotation during editing instead
how: draw a highlight box over the target, e.g. `ffmpeg -i rec.mp4 -vf "drawbox=x=100:y=80:w=200:h=60:color=yellow@0.8:t=4:enable='between(t,1,2)'" hl.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Speed up loading; use a still if nothing moves
what: speed up or slow down a browser load in the edit; if no movement is needed, use a static screenshot instead of a recording
how: freeze a frame for a still segment: `ffmpeg -ss 1 -i rec.mp4 -frames:v 1 shot.png` then `ffmpeg -loop 1 -t 3 -i shot.png -pix_fmt yuv420p still.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Change the visual at each new point
what: use visuals for pacing: change the visual each time a new point is introduced, to cue that something new is being said
how: align a visual change to the start of every new script point

name: Clean screen before recording
what: simplify the screen: no extra browser tabs, clean desktop
how: record with a fresh browser profile / single tab

name: Action needs stakes before choreography
what: Eddie Hamilton (Kingsman, Mission: Impossible): the trick to great action is being invested in the outcome — caring about the characters and knowing what happens if the protagonist succeeds or fails; choreography, then sound and music, come after
how: before the action section, make sure a line or shot has stated what's at stake

name: Cut to faces for the human stakes
what: reaction close-ups during action (pain after a punch, fear in a skid) remind us of human stakes; Frame.io's case study is Hamilton's bathroom fight in Mission: Impossible – Fallout
how: include faces reacting through the action, not only the moves

name: Mix long shots with one-second hits
what: in Haywire (no music) shots up to ten seconds long sit among one-second cuts of punches and kicks, which sell the speed and violence
how: let the fight breathe in longer shots and cut short only on the impacts

name: Establish geography, then keep it
what: map the space early (John Wick 2's garage wide at 0:07), never lose the viewer's orientation, and after a deliberate surprise cut straight back to re-orient; Hamilton adds very wide shots into action for the same reason
how: open each action section with a wide that shows where everyone is; re-show it after any disorienting moment

name: Action sequence as a mini-story
what: the best sequences work standalone with a beginning, middle and end (a character wants something and overcomes obstacles); in Wonder Woman's Veld sequence each section opens with an obstacle and every cut shows it being overcome
how: split the sequence into sub-goals (each: obstacle, then overcoming it) and drop shots that don't advance one

name: Let a shot show a complete action
what: over-cutting makes action indecipherable (Taken 3's single fence hop in 14 cuts); Atomic Blonde keeps three full actions in one short shot
how: don't split one movement across several cuts; keep each action whole in a shot

name: Start a scene from the wide, ignoring the script
what: Hamilton watches a wide shot first to get the story of the scene as shot (the script is a working document), then quickly throws the scene together before refining
how: first assembly of any scene = the wide/master, then layer coverage

name: Previs the complex sequence before shooting
what: Hamilton built Kingsman 2's opening from stunt videos, pencil storyboards and borrowed clips, with sound effects, music and his own voice reading lines, so the director could approve it before filming
how: for a planned HyperFrames/voxel sequence, cut an animatic from sketches + temp audio first

name: Peaks and troughs over the whole film
what: Hamilton aims for a "rollercoaster" with the right amount of excitement, character, humour and breathing space, and may trim a sequence by ~10 s months later
how: review the whole video's energy curve and give each peak a quieter trough around it

name: Quick cuts for urgency, held shots for dread
section: Pacing per genre: horror and suspense
what: Videomaker: a fast succession of short clips disorients and feels urgent (best with lots of action and several perspectives); a shot held longer than expected creates discomfort and anticipation that should pay off in a reveal
how: hold only inside a sequence that already has tension, then deliver the reveal

name: The false scare in steps
section: Pacing per genre: horror and suspense
what: isolated protagonist with limited vision; their anxiety shows; the antagonist is revealed to us (blocking or POV) and hidden again; tension rises (music or slow push-in); a false reveal with a quick move and exaggerated sound; relief; the guard drops; a moment's hesitation and the real reveal
how: lay out the beats on the timeline in this order before fine-cutting

name: Hold the peak a beat longer
section: Pacing per genre: horror and suspense
what: at the tension peak, don't release yet; let it simmer a beat longer than the audience expects, then hit the scare
how: after building tension, add a few extra frames before the scare and compare both versions

name: The Lewton bus
section: Pacing per genre: horror and suspense
what: Cat People (1942): gradual buildup, then a sudden shock through misdirection and a sharp sonic jolt (an explosive bus entrance), not a monster
how: end a dread build on a harmless loud event with a sharp sound

name: Lull with a steady sound, not only silence
section: Pacing per genre: horror and suspense
what: absolute silence isn't necessary: a low drone or soft repetitive sound (ticking clock, babbling brook, cicadas, the shower water in Psycho) lulls the audience before the jolt
how: run a steady ambience bed under the build and cut it dead at the scare

name: Flip the sound hierarchy
section: Pacing per genre: horror and suspense
what: in horror the usual dialogue-first mix goes out the door: what a sound reveals takes priority, so a faint drip of water can become the dominant element
how: for a horror beat, raise a small diegetic sound above the dialogue level

name: Pick the take that reveals the threat
section: Pacing per genre: horror and suspense
what: horror blocking often lets the audience see what the protagonist can't (the monster in the window); choose the take where the threat is visible, which needs knowing the director's intent
how: check every take of a reveal shot frame by frame for the visible threat

name: Scare when the guard is down
section: Pacing per genre: horror and suspense
what: The Exorcist's demon flash appears during a medical exam, not a "scary" scene; The Descent's creature appears in the camera flash's light, not the dark
how: place a scare in a calm moment or a bright frame

name: Ration jump scares; keep a backup scare
section: Pacing per genre: horror and suspense
what: overusing jump scares makes them predictable; Jaws holds back the primary scare and substitutes a secondary one (Ben Gardner's boat)
how: count jump scares; replace one with held tension

name: Testimonial arc: who, challenge, solution, results, recommendation
what: Origin Films: the customer introduces themselves, explains the challenge before, how the business came in, measurable results, then a genuine recommendation; the customer, not the company, is the hero
how: order interview bites into those five slots

name: Specific answers beat generic praise
what: "we were losing qualified leads because our website wasn't converting" beats "we needed help"; avoid scripted lines like "they're the best company ever"
how: pick the bite with concrete detail even if it's less polished

name: Keep the human imperfections
what: slight pauses, smiles and laughter make testimonials feel human; memorable moments often happen between prepared answers
how: don't tighten every pause in a testimonial; keep the laugh between answers

name: Prepare questions, not scripts
what: use interview questions about challenges, why they chose you, the experience and the results, rather than scripted responses
how: give the client a question list, not lines

name: Testimonial length 60 s-3 min
what: Origin Films says most high-performing testimonial videos run between 60 seconds and 3 minutes
how: cut a 60 s version first, a longer one only if there's material

name: Short film rules of thumb
section: Short films and general structure discipline
what: Tom Barrance: grab attention from the start, keep the story moving, include only what tells the story, keep it simple (one story, one or two places, one or two characters), show don't tell, let the audience imagine
how: check the cut against each rule; cut a location or character if it breaks "one or two"

name: Very short films can skip three acts
section: Short films and general structure discipline
what: a very short movie can rely on an unusual approach, or show a small slice of life the viewer understands is part of a longer story
how: for sub-minute pieces, cut a single slice of life instead of forcing setup/confrontation/resolution

name: Be wary of twist-only shorts
section: Short films and general structure discipline
what: a twist can work, but not on its own; the story must be interesting all the way through, not just at the end
how: watch the short with the twist removed; if the rest is dull, rework it

name: Open online shorts with intrigue
section: Short films and general structure discipline
what: online you have a few seconds: use striking camerawork, evocative music/sound, show something intriguing before revealing what it is, or make it obvious the story is about interesting people/places/things
how: open on a detail or partial view and reveal its context a few shots later

name: Retell a known story differently
section: Short films and general structure discipline
what: change the point of view (Red Riding Hood from the wolf's side), the form (Goldilocks as a news story), the period/place, or add a character from another genre
how: for a promo, retell a familiar story beat as a different form (e.g. news report)

name: "Spine and nine"
section: Short films and general structure discipline
what: Jonny Elwyn's director lays the film out as Part 1, Part 2, Part 3 title cards on the timeline, each holding three short, simple ideas (nine in total), before any B-roll, sound design or titles
how: make three placeholder cards and place three bites under each before decorating

name: Shuffle: an opener may be an ender
section: Short films and general structure discipline
what: a line chosen to set context at the start often "feels like" a Part 3 ending thought because of how it was said or what it's next to
how: try each strong bite in the last section before settling its position

name: Remove repeated ideas; split conjoined ones
section: Short films and general structure discipline
what: bites that seem to expand a point often just repeat it (cut one); a long "single" thought may hold two different ideas — keep the right one
how: write each bite's idea in a few words; delete duplicates and split doubles

name: Give the cut a haircut (2:30 → 90 s?)
section: Short films and general structure discipline
what: ask whether a cut that works at 2:30 would be more digestible at 90 s; come back next day or watch with someone for fresh eyes
how: make a 90 s alternative before delivery and compare

name: Send the client a shorter first cut
section: Short films and general structure discipline
what: it's easier to add material back than to take it out once the client has seen it ("The mind cannot absorb what the butt cannot endure" — Steve Audette)
how: deliver the tight version first; keep the trims ready to restore

name: Turn a top moment into the next video
what: YouTube recommends expanding the content from your top moments into new uploads
how: list the top moments of the last 5 videos, pick the subject that repeats, and brief the next edit around it

name: A spike can mean confusion
what: spikes mark rewatched/shared parts, but the same page says a spike can mean the content was unclear and viewers had to rewatch
how: at each spike check: is it a highlight (keep, reuse) or a fast/unclear moment (slow it, add a caption or a zoom)?

name: Key moments need 60 s and 100 views
what: moments are only highlighted if detected, on videos at least 60 seconds long with at least 100 views; retention data takes 1-2 days to process
how: don't judge a fresh upload's retention on day 0; check again after 48 h; Shorts under 60 s won't show key moments

name: Typical retention = your last 10 similar videos
what: the retention chart can be compared with "typical retention" of your 10 latest videos of similar length, a fairer yardstick than all of YouTube
how: compare a new edit style against typical retention, not against a viral outlier

name: Split retention by viewer segment
what: the Segments drop-down compares new vs returning viewers, subscribers vs non-subscribers, and organic vs paid traffic (skippable ads, display ads)
how: compare the curves; if non-subscribers drop off early while subscribers stay, test an intro that explains the setup for newcomers

name: Detailed activity: absolute starts and stops
what: the detailed activity report shows the absolute number of views per segment and how many viewers started and stopped watching at each moment; a segment can exceed the total views because one viewer rewatches
how: use it to find the exact second people stop, then look at that frame (`ffmpeg -ss T -i master.mp4 -frames:v 1 stop.png`)

name: What counts as an impression
section: YouTube analytics metrics (CTR, AVD, APV, views)
what: a thumbnail impression counts only when shown for more than 1 second with at least 50% visible, on Home, Search, feeds, Up Next and playlists; NOT on external sites, mobile web, YouTube Kids, cards/end screens inside the player, or notifications
how: when most traffic is external or from end screens, judge the video by views/AVD, not by CTR

name: Normal CTR range is 2-10%
section: YouTube analytics metrics (CTR, AVD, APV, views)
what: YouTube states half of all channels and videos have an impressions CTR between 2% and 10%; new channels or videos under 100 views can swing wider
how: don't panic at 3%; compare CTR between your own videos over the long term with their traffic sources

name: Don't read CTR too early or too finely
section: YouTube analytics metrics (CTR, AVD, APV, views)
what: YouTube advises against deciding before a substantial number of impressions, reacting to small CTR changes that aren't statistically significant, or checking right after upload
how: wait for a substantial number of impressions (YouTube gives no number) before changing a title/thumbnail

name: Falling CTR with rising impressions is success
section: YouTube analytics metrics (CTR, AVD, APV, views)
what: YouTube's example: 10,000 early impressions at 9% CTR, a week later 100,000 impressions at 3.5% CTR; the drop means the video reached a broader, less familiar audience
how: always read CTR next to the impressions count for the same period

name: CTR differs by surface
section: YouTube analytics metrics (CTR, AVD, APV, views)
what: search viewers have high intent so search CTR runs higher with fewer impressions; the Homepage gives many impressions at lower CTR because viewers are browsing
how: in Advanced mode break CTR down by traffic source before comparing two videos

name: Niche-topic impression ceiling
section: YouTube analytics metrics (CTR, AVD, APV, views)
what: even excellent CTR and AVD can plateau when the topic is hyper-specific (the pool of interested viewers runs out) or very crowded (competing with established channels)
how: for a FireCraft-only topic expect a ceiling; widen the angle (a general Minecraft hook) when you want reach

name: Early CTR is inflated by core fans
section: YouTube analytics metrics (CTR, AVD, APV, views)
what: CTR in the first hours comes from the most loyal audience; it often drops when YouTube pushes the video wider
how: don't call a title a winner from first-hour CTR; compare at the same lifespan (7 days)

name: Views can exceed impressions
section: YouTube analytics metrics (CTR, AVD, APV, views)
what: with lots of outside traffic (links, embeds) views can be higher than impressions, and CTR is not views divided by impressions because some views don't come from counted impressions
how: never compute CTR yourself from the totals; read the Studio figure

name: Views counted at play start (from Aug 24 2026)
section: YouTube analytics metrics (CTR, AVD, APV, views)
what: since 24 Aug 2026 a view counts the moment a video starts to play on Shorts, long videos and live; YPP earnings still use engaged views/engaged watch hours and eligibility qualified views
how: compare pre- and post-August view counts with care; judge edits by engaged views and retention instead

name: AVD and APV only count viewers who stayed
section: YouTube analytics metrics (CTR, AVD, APV, views)
what: average view duration (minutes) and average percentage viewed are calculated from engaged views (those who stayed past the initial seconds) and their watch time
how: AVD leaves out viewers who left in the initial seconds, so read engaged views / "stayed to watch" next to AVD

name: Engaged views exclude loops
section: YouTube analytics metrics (CTR, AVD, APV, views)
what: engaged views count viewers who stayed past the initial seconds, not including any loops; "Stayed to watch" is the percentage of times viewers stayed past the initial seconds of a Short
how: for a Short, the edit's first seconds decide "stayed to watch"; loops raise views but not engaged views

name: Low-quality playbacks are discarded
section: YouTube analytics metrics (CTR, AVD, APV, views)
what: YouTube may slow, freeze or change counts and discard low-quality playbacks, e.g. watching the same video on several devices or in several tabs
how: don't ask friends/family to replay a video in loops; counts can take several days to settle

name: When an ad view counts
section: YouTube analytics metrics (CTR, AVD, APV, views)
what: skippable in-stream: full watch of an 11-30 s ad or 30 s of a longer one (or interaction); in-feed: click to play or 10 s of a >10 s ad; Shorts ads: a click or 10 s
how: when promoting a FireCraft trailer as an ad, put the server name and hook inside the first 10 s

name: Unique reach vs co-viewed views
section: YouTube analytics metrics (CTR, AVD, APV, views)
what: unique reach estimates individual people (3 people at one TV = 1 view but +3 reach); Views (Co-viewed) counts everyone watching together
how: use unique reach to compare TV-heavy content honestly

name: Know the traffic source names
what: Browse features (Home, subscriptions, Watch Later), Suggested videos (next to/after videos AND description links), Shorts feed, YouTube search, Channel pages, Playlists, End screens, Video cards, Notifications (belled subscribers separate), Sound pages, Remixed video, External, Direct or unknown
how: read "How viewers find this video" first, then decide: search-led → fix title words, suggested-led → match neighbour videos

name: Mine the YouTube search terms card
what: the Reach tab's "YouTube search terms" report lists what viewers typed to find the video
how: reuse the top 2-3 terms verbatim in the next title, description first line and spoken intro

name: Use "Content suggesting this video"
what: this report shows which videos viewers were watching when yours was suggested
how: study those neighbour videos' length, pacing and packaging; make a follow-up in the same lane

name: Sound pages bring Shorts traffic
what: "Sound pages" is traffic from the shared-audio results page in the Shorts player; "Remixed video" is traffic from remixes of your content
how: check these two sources in the Shorts traffic report regularly

name: End screen element click rate
what: the Engagement tab of a single video reports how often viewers clicked each end screen element
how: if one element gets almost no clicks, swap it for a "best for viewer" video or a playlist on the next upload

name: Subscribers by content type
what: the Content tab "Subscribers" report shows subscribers gained from videos, Shorts, live, posts and others (search, channel page)
how: put more edit effort into the format that converts best

name: Viewers across formats
what: this Content tab report shows the overlap of viewers watching videos, Shorts and live
how: if Shorts viewers rarely watch your long videos, don't count on crossover: promote the long videos on their own

name: New, casual and regular viewers
what: new = first watch in the period (also private browsing, cleared history, >1 year away); casual = at least monthly for 1-5 months of the past year; regular = at least monthly for over 6 months. Segments do not affect reach or monetization
how: read them in Audience tab to see if a video grew the core or only brought strangers

name: Regular viewers under 1% is normal
what: YouTube says regular viewers can be as low as <1%, common for new channels, trending videos and Shorts-heavy channels
how: don't treat it as a failure signal; track its trend instead

name: Grow regulars with consistency
what: channels gaining casual/regular viewers usually upload consistent topics or a familiar format, keep consistent hosts, and run popular series
how: keep one host (the default blocky host skin), one intro style and a series name across FireCraft videos

name: How-to videos draw one-time viewers
what: YouTube notes "how-to" channels see many new viewers who may not return after getting the answer
how: for tutorial edits add a next-step hook ("part 2: ...") and an end-screen playlist to turn answers into return visits

name: Monthly audience beats subscriber count
what: monthly audience = unique viewers in the last 28 days, recalculated daily; it is a truer active-audience size than subscribers
how: report monthly audience to the owner, not subs, when judging a season's videos

name: Subscribers watch about twice as much
what: YouTube says subscribers have been shown to watch twice as much video as non-subscribers
how: compare the "Watch time from subscribers" report; videos with a low subscriber share are reaching new people

name: Average views per viewer
what: in Advanced mode "SEE MORE", "Average views per viewer" shows how many of your videos a unique viewer watches
how: a rising value after a series launch means the series is binge-able

name: Schedule by "When your viewers are on YouTube"
what: this Audience report shows when viewers are online in the last 28 days; YouTube suggests it for scheduling Premieres and live streams
how: set the Premiere/publish time inside the darkest band of that chart

name: Check the device type split
what: the Device type report shows the share of watch time on mobile, computer, TV and tablet, also per content type
how: if TV watch time is high, check the edit's small text in a full-frame snapshot; if mobile dominates, check it at phone size

name: Find topics from "What your audience watches"
what: shows other videos/Shorts/live/podcasts your viewers watched outside your channel in the past 7 days; "Channels your audience watches" (28 days) suggests collaborators
how: take topic and title ideas from it; pitch collabs to channels in that list

name: Formats your viewers watch
what: shows whether your audience watches more videos, Shorts or live over 28 days
how: use it to decide whether a promo should be cut as a Short, a long video, or both

name: Group videos by editing style
what: Advanced mode groups hold up to 500 videos; YouTube's own example groups videos with a new editing style and compares their retention against the old style
how: Analytics > Advanced mode > channel name > Groups > Create new group "new-cut-style"; then Add comparison against the old group

name: Compare videos at the same lifespan
what: compare videos over their first 24 hours, 7 days or 28 days so old and new uploads are judged fairly (e.g. first 7 days CTR for a new thumbnail style)
how: Advanced mode > Add comparison > lifespan option

name: Top vs bottom video in one series
what: YouTube suggests comparing the best and worst video of the same series on CTR, retention and traffic sources to see what made the difference
how: do it regularly per series; note the edit difference in library/research

name: Group by length
what: the Advanced-mode tips page suggests grouping all videos under 5 minutes against those over 10 minutes
how: use it to choose the target length of the next promo instead of guessing

name: Special reports: first 24 hours and retention rate
what: Advanced mode's top navigation has special reports for age/gender, retention rate, first 24 hours of video performance and real-time
how: open "first 24 hours" the day after a launch video goes live

name: Export analytics (500-row limit)
what: "Export current view" downloads the current report; downloads are capped at 500 rows (the YouTube Reporting API gives more); up to 50 saved reports
how: export the retention/traffic view to CSV, keep it in the scratchpad (it is channel data, not for the repo) and read it with Python csv

name: Filter by content type and external traffic
what: Advanced mode filters include content type (to isolate Shorts), traffic source (e.g. external) and a title filter
how: filter traffic source = External to see which video brings Discord/website visitors best

name: Over 1 minute + a claim: sources disagree
section: YouTube Shorts rules that shape the edit
what: the three-minute-Shorts page says a Short longer than one minute with an active copyright claim of any type is blocked globally (not playable, recommended or monetized), while the "Create YouTube Shorts" page now says such Shorts will no longer be automatically blocked and may remain playable; the monetization page still lists them as blocked and ineligible
how: play safe: keep any Short with third-party music under 60 s, or use library/music CC0 tracks; check `ffprobe -v error -show_entries format=duration -of csv=p=0 short.mp4` before upload (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Shorts Audio Library songs: up to 90 s
section: YouTube Shorts rules that shape the edit
what: in a 3-minute Short most Shorts-library songs can run up to 90 s, some only 60 or 30 s; royalty-free YouTube Audio Library music won't get a Content ID claim
how: for a 2-3 min Short, plan the music bed in sections (≤90 s per library song) or use our own CC0 track for the full length

name: Keep it long-form with a wide frame
section: YouTube Shorts rules that shape the edit
what: YouTube says to stop a video being classified as a Short, use a wider aspect ratio such as 16:9; square or vertical up to 3 min becomes a Short
how: a 1:1 teaser under 3 min WILL be a Short; render 16:9 (1920x1080) if it must live on the watch page

name: Old vertical uploads stay long-form
section: YouTube Shorts rules that shape the edit
what: vertical/square videos uploaded before 15 Oct 2024 (Official Artist Channels: before 8 Dec 2025) remain long-form videos
how: to turn an old vertical clip into a Short, re-cut and upload it as new content rather than expecting it to move

name: Use the Shorts visual guides for overlays
section: YouTube Shorts rules that shape the edit
what: in the YouTube app editor, moving text or stickers shows guides where the like button, comments and description appear; white lines mark a non-safe area near the edges
how: after rendering, open the Short in the app's text tool once to check our burned-in captions don't sit under those guides

name: Align tool for match transitions
section: YouTube Shorts rules that shape the edit
what: Shorts' Align shows a transparent overlay of the last captured frame so the next clip lines up for a seamless transition
how: in our pipeline do the same: export the last frame (`ffmpeg -sseof -0.04 -i a.mp4 -frames:v 1 last.png`) and overlay it at 50% in the next shot's preview

name: Speed range 0.3x-3x
section: YouTube Shorts rules that shape the edit
what: the Shorts camera Speed tool offers 0.3x to 3x, suggested for slow-mo trick shots and sped-up action
how: our equivalent is ffmpeg `setpts` (with minterpolate for slow-mo, see CLAUDE.md recipe)

name: Sync to beat for photo/video montages
section: YouTube Shorts rules that shape the edit
what: select at least two photos/videos and Shorts auto-syncs them to music; you can change the track or skip
how: offline we cut on bars instead (CLAUDE.md: pick a BPM, cut every bar); use the app feature only for quick phone-made Shorts

name: Poll sticker: 2 options, stays open
section: YouTube Shorts rules that shape the edit
what: a poll sticker gives 2 options, stays open while the Short is published, viewers can change votes; not on unlisted/private Shorts
how: end a FireCraft Short with a question ("Kaun jeetega?") and add the poll in the app after upload

name: Quiz sticker
section: YouTube Shorts rules that shape the edit
what: question up to 3 lines, two answers up to 2 lines each; the first option is the correct one by default; if the video already shows the question, leave the field blank
how: burn the question into the end of the Short and add only the answer options as a quiz sticker (the question field can stay blank)

name: Q&A and "Add yours" stickers
section: YouTube Shorts rules that shape the edit
what: Q&A answers become public comments; "Add yours" lets viewers respond with their own Short to a prompt
how: use "Add yours" for community challenges (e.g. "apna best PvP clip dikhao") to spread the prompt through other channels

name: Reply to comments with a Short
section: YouTube Shorts rules that shape the edit
what: a Short made as a reply notifies the commenter and appears under the original comment
how: turn the best question in comments into an answer Short

name: Text keeps viewers with you through fast edits
section: YouTube Shorts rules that shape the edit
what: YouTube's Shorts tips say on-screen text guides viewers and keeps context through fast edits, can carry calls to action, explain a joke or introduce you
how: in HyperFrames time each caption to the clip it explains; drag start/stop like the Shorts timeline

name: Filters stack
section: YouTube Shorts rules that shape the edit
what: a filter chosen while editing a Short is layered on top of one chosen while recording
how: when the owner records with a Shorts filter, don't add our grade on top without checking a frame first (`npx hyperframes grade-compare`)

name: Volume mix in the Shorts editor
section: YouTube Shorts rules that shape the edit
what: Volume balances music, original audio and voiceover
how: if the owner adds app music over our render, ask them to lower the app music so our voice stays on top (our render already holds the mix)

name: Post a test Short first
section: YouTube Shorts rules that shape the edit
what: YouTube suggests uploading a test Short (private/unlisted) to learn the steps, then keep a posting schedule you can maintain
how: upload the render as private once, check crop/safe zones on a phone, then publish

name: Remixes credit you back
section: YouTube Shorts rules that shape the edit
