name: Vimeo H.264 tops out at 4K
what: Vimeo notes H.264 only supports up to 4K there; HEVC supports up to 8K
how: use HEVC for 8K Vimeo uploads.

name: Vimeo HDR needs PQ/HLG, 10-bit
what: Vimeo HDR: only PQ or HLG transfer, 10-bit or more; for PQ include SMPTE 2086 mastering display and CEA 861.3 light level metadata

name: X: recommended video
what: X recommends H.264 High profile, 30 or 60 fps, 1280x720 / 720x1280 / 720x720, min 5,000 kbps video and 128 kbps AAC-LC audio
how: `ffmpeg -y -i in.mp4 -vf scale=1280:720,format=yuv420p -r 30 -c:v libx264 -profile:v high -b:v 5000k -maxrate 5000k -bufsize 10000k -c:a aac -b:a 128k -movflags +faststart x_post.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: X: hard limits
what: X video: <= 60 fps, 32x32 to 1280x1024, aspect 1:3 to 3:1, square pixels, YUV 4:2:0 only, no open GOP, progressive
how: `ffmpeg -y -i in.mp4 -vf setsar=1,format=yuv420p -c:v libx264 -flags +cgop -c:a aac x_safe.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: X: size and duration caps
what: default accounts: Post video 0.5 s-20 min, 8 GB; DM video 0.5-140 s, 512 MB. Premium: Post 125 min, 16 GB; DM 10 min, 1 GB

name: X: animated GIF limits
what: X GIFs: <= 15 MB, <= 1280x1080, <= 350 frames, <= 300 million pixels (w x h x frames)
how: check before upload: `ffprobe -v error -count_frames -select_streams v:0 -show_entries stream=width,height,nb_read_frames -of csv=p=0 anim.gif` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: X: 1080p playback needs a subscription
what: subscribed users can upload 1080p and get 1080p playback; unsubscribed users get 720p

name: Telegram bots: 50 MB video
what: Bot API sendVideo, sendAnimation and sendDocument take files up to 50 MB; bots download up to 20 MB; a local Bot API server allows uploads to 2000 MB
how: pick CRF/bitrate so the file fits; -fs only stops writing at the limit (it cuts the end), so use it as a last safety net: `ffmpeg -y -i in.mp4 -c:v libx264 -crf 26 -c:a aac -b:a 96k -fs 49000000 -movflags +faststart tg_bot.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Telegram supports_streaming
what: sendVideo has supports_streaming=True for videos suitable for streaming; Telegram clients support MPEG4 video, other formats go as Document
how: make it streamable (faststart MP4): `ffmpeg -y -i in.mp4 -c copy -movflags +faststart tg_stream.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Telegram animation = silent H.264
what: sendAnimation takes GIF or H.264/MPEG-4 AVC video without sound
how: `ffmpeg -y -i in.mp4 -an -c:v libx264 -pix_fmt yuv420p -movflags +faststart tg_anim.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Telegram users: 2 GB, 4 GB Premium
what: Telegram users can send files up to 2 GB each, 4 GB with Premium

name: Two-pass GIF: palettegen then paletteuse
section: GIF, WebP, APNG and image sequences
what: make one global palette from the whole clip, then map with it; scale with lanczos and reduce fps
how: `ffmpeg -y -i in.mp4 -vf "fps=15,scale=320:-1:flags=lanczos,palettegen" palette.png && ffmpeg -y -i in.mp4 -i palette.png -lavfi "fps=15,scale=320:-1:flags=lanczos[x];[x][1:v]paletteuse" anim.gif` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Seek before -i for GIF slices
section: GIF, WebP, APNG and image sequences
what: put -ss and -t before -i in both passes, or palettegen sees only one frame
how: `ffmpeg -y -ss 0.5 -t 1 -i in.mp4 -vf "fps=15,scale=320:-1:flags=lanczos,palettegen" pal2.png && ffmpeg -y -ss 0.5 -t 1 -i in.mp4 -i pal2.png -lavfi "fps=15,scale=320:-1:flags=lanczos[x];[x][1:v]paletteuse" slice.gif` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: stats_mode=diff for moving subjects
section: GIF, WebP, APNG and image sequences
what: palettegen stats_mode diff counts only changed pixels, giving the moving part more colours over a static background; single makes a new histogram each frame
how: `ffmpeg -y -i in.mp4 -vf "fps=15,scale=320:-1,palettegen=stats_mode=diff" pald.png` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Dither choice for GIF size
section: GIF, WebP, APNG and image sequences
what: bayer is the only predictable dither (bayer_scale 0-5, default 2); error diffusion (floyd_steinberg, sierra2, sierra2_4a default) looks better but compresses worse; dither=none is smallest
how: `ffmpeg -y -i in.mp4 -i palette.png -lavfi "fps=15,scale=320:-1[x];[x][1:v]paletteuse=dither=bayer:bayer_scale=3" bayer.gif` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: diff_mode=rectangle for static backgrounds
section: GIF, WebP, APNG and image sequences
what: paletteuse diff_mode rectangle reprocesses only the changing rectangle, limiting dither noise to the moving area
how: `ffmpeg -y -i in.mp4 -i palette.png -lavfi "fps=15,scale=320:-1[x];[x][1:v]paletteuse=diff_mode=rectangle" rect.gif` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Fewer palette colours
section: GIF, WebP, APNG and image sequences
what: palettegen max_colors sets the colour count (palette still has 256 entries)
how: `ffmpeg -y -i in.mp4 -vf "fps=10,scale=240:-1,palettegen=max_colors=64" pal64.png` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: GIF transparency detection
section: GIF, WebP, APNG and image sequences
what: gifflags transdiff (default on) detects unchanged pixels between frames; turn it off only for heavy motion or colour changes
how: `ffmpeg -y -i in.mp4 -vf scale=200:-1 -gifflags -transdiff notrans.gif` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: GIF loop count and end pause
section: GIF, WebP, APNG and image sequences
what: gif muxer -loop (0 infinite default, -1 none) and -final_delay in centiseconds; frame delay can't be under 1 cs
how: `ffmpeg -y -i anim.gif -loop 0 -final_delay 100 pause.gif` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Frames as separate GIF files
section: GIF, WebP, APNG and image sequences
what: to write one GIF per frame force the image2 muxer
how: `ffmpeg -y -i in.mp4 -frames:v 3 -c:v gif -f image2 gifs/out%d.gif` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Animated WebP
section: GIF, WebP, APNG and image sequences
what: libwebp_anim with -loop 0 (webp muxer, 0 = infinite) and -quality 0-100
how: `ffmpeg -y -i in.mp4 -vf fps=15,scale=320:-1 -c:v libwebp_anim -quality 75 -loop 0 anim.webp` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: WebP presets
section: GIF, WebP, APNG and image sequences
what: libwebp -preset: none, default, picture, photo, drawing, icon, text; -compression_level 0-6 (default 4)
how: `ffmpeg -y -i cover.jpg -c:v libwebp -preset photo -quality 80 -compression_level 6 cover.webp` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Lossless WebP
section: GIF, WebP, APNG and image sequences
what: -lossless 1 gives lossless WebP (RGB); alpha works in both modes
how: `ffmpeg -y -i frames/img_0001.png -c:v libwebp -lossless 1 ll.webp` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: APNG with loops and end delay
section: GIF, WebP, APNG and image sequences
what: apng muxer: -plays (0 infinite, 1 no loop) and -final_delay seconds
how: `ffmpeg -y -i in.mp4 -t 1 -vf fps=10,scale=200:-1 -plays 0 -final_delay 0.5 anim.apng` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: APNG beats GIF on colour
section: GIF, WebP, APNG and image sequences
what: APNG supports many colour depths while animated GIF is 8-bit indexed only; browsers: Chrome 59, Firefox 3, Safari 8, Edge 12

name: Image sequence with zero-padded names
section: GIF, WebP, APNG and image sequences
what: image2 pattern %04d pads numbers; -start_number sets the first
how: `ffmpeg -y -i in.mp4 -start_number 0 seq/frame_%04d.png && ls seq | head -1` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: One still per second
section: GIF, WebP, APNG and image sequences
what: -fps_mode cfr -r 1 writes one image per second
how: `ffmpeg -y -i in.mp4 -fps_mode cfr -r 1 stills/img-%03d.jpeg` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Name frames by PTS
section: GIF, WebP, APNG and image sequences
what: -frame_pts 1 puts the timestamp in the file name (use with -copyts)
how: `ffmpeg -y -i in.mp4 -copyts -frame_pts 1 -frames:v 3 pts/%d.png && ls pts` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Overwrite one thumbnail
section: GIF, WebP, APNG and image sequences
what: -update 1 keeps writing the same file name
how: `ffmpeg -y -i in.mp4 -r 1 -update 1 latest.jpg` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Encode an image sequence to video
section: GIF, WebP, APNG and image sequences
what: read a numbered sequence with -framerate and -i pattern
how: `ffmpeg -y -framerate 30 -i frames/img_%04d.png -c:v libx264 -pix_fmt yuv420p -crf 18 fromseq.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Lossless 16-bit TIFF/PNG sequence
section: GIF, WebP, APNG and image sequences
what: image2 picks the PNG encoder from the extension; rgb48be keeps 16 bits per channel
how: `ffmpeg -y -i in10.mkv -pix_fmt rgb48be seq16/f_%04d.png` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Decoded-content hash with -f hash
what: the hash muxer hashes all decoded frames (SHA-256 default; MD5, CRC32, adler32...), ignoring timestamps: proves two files decode to the same picture/sound
how: `ffmpeg -v error -i in.mp4 -f hash -hash md5 -` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Per-stream hash
what: streamhash prints one hash per stream, so audio and video can be checked separately
how: `ffmpeg -v error -i in.mp4 -map 0 -f streamhash -hash sha256 -` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Frame-by-frame MD5
what: framemd5 writes an MD5 per packet with dts/pts/duration/size, to find the first differing frame
how: `ffmpeg -v error -y -i in.mp4 -f framemd5 frames.md5 && head -12 frames.md5 | tail -2` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Per-frame SHA-256
what: framehash defaults to SHA-256 per packet
how: `ffmpeg -v error -y -i in.mp4 -f framehash -hash sha256 fh.txt` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Compare stream-copied packets
what: with -c copy, framemd5 hashes the coded packets, so a remux can be checked against the original. Here a remux with use_editlist 0 shifted every timestamp but kept every hash, so compare the stream index + hash columns only
how: `ffmpeg -v error -y -i in.mp4 -c copy -f framemd5 a.md5 && ffmpeg -v error -y -i yt.mp4 -c copy -f framemd5 b.md5 && diff <(grep -v '^#' a.md5 | cut -d, -f1,6 | sort) <(grep -v '^#' b.md5 | cut -d, -f1,6 | sort) && echo SAME` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Lossless round-trip proof
what: encode FFV1/lossless and compare the decoded hash with the source's
how: `ffmpeg -v error -i in10.mkv -f hash -hash md5 - > s.txt && ffmpeg -v error -y -i in10.mkv -c:v ffv1 -level 3 rt.mkv && ffmpeg -v error -i rt.mkv -f hash -hash md5 - > r.txt && cmp s.txt r.txt && echo LOSSLESS` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Quick CRC
what: the crc muxer prints one Adler-32 over all decoded frames; framecrc one per packet
how: `ffmpeg -v error -i in.mp4 -f crc -` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Decode test with -f null
what: the null muxer writes nothing: decode a file fully to find errors (add -benchmark for speed)
how: `ffmpeg -v error -benchmark -i in.mp4 -f null -` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Whole-file checksum list for deliveries
what: a sha256sum manifest next to the files lets the client verify the transfer
how: `sha256sum in.mp4 in.wav > SHA256SUMS && sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Count keyframe spacing
what: list keyframe packet times to check GOP length matches the spec
how: `ffprobe -v error -select_streams v:0 -show_entries packet=pts_time,flags -of csv=p=0 fixedgop.mp4 | grep K | head -3` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Check faststart (moov before mdat)
what: trace the top-level atoms: moov must come before mdat for progressive playback
how: `ffprobe -v trace -i yt.mp4 2>&1 | grep -oE "type:'(moov|mdat)'" | head -2` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Confirm profile, level, pix_fmt
what: read profile, level, pix_fmt and B-frames before sending to a platform
how: `ffprobe -v error -select_streams v:0 -show_entries stream=codec_name,profile,level,pix_fmt,has_b_frames,r_frame_rate -of default=nw=1 l41.mp4` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Bit-exact output for reproducible files
what: -bitexact enables bitexact mode for muxers/encoders (no version strings), so reruns can be byte-compared
how: `ffmpeg -y -i in.wav -c:a pcm_s16le -bitexact -fflags +bitexact be1.wav && ffmpeg -y -i in.wav -c:a pcm_s16le -bitexact -fflags +bitexact be2.wav && cmp be1.wav be2.wav && echo IDENTICAL` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: MPEG-TS service names
what: mpegts metadata service_provider/service_name (defaults FFmpeg / Service01) plus service_id, PIDs
how: `ffmpeg -y -i in.mp4 -c copy -mpegts_service_id 0x0101 -mpegts_pmt_start_pid 0x1500 -mpegts_start_pid 0x150 -metadata service_provider=FireCraft -metadata service_name=Promo bc.ts` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Constant muxrate TS
what: -muxrate sets a constant TS mux rate (default VBR); PCR every 20 ms in CBR
how: `ffmpeg -y -i in.mp4 -c:v libx264 -x264-params nal-hrd=cbr -b:v 1M -minrate 1M -maxrate 1M -bufsize 1M -c:a mp2 -b:a 192k -muxrate 2M cbrmux.ts` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: DVB System B flag
what: mpegts_flags system_b conforms to DVB instead of ATSC; resend_headers re-emits PAT/PMT
how: `ffmpeg -y -i in.mp4 -c copy -mpegts_flags system_b+resend_headers dvb.ts` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: M2TS mode
what: mpegts_m2ts_mode 1 writes Blu-ray style m2ts (fixed PIDs)
how: `ffmpeg -y -i in.mp4 -c:v copy -c:a ac3 -mpegts_m2ts_mode 1 out.m2ts` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: MXF wrapping
what: ffmpeg has mxf, mxf_d10 and mxf_opatom muxers
how: `ffmpeg -y -i in.mp4 -c:v mpeg2video -b:v 10M -c:a pcm_s16le -ar 48000 out.mxf` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Matroska for archive masters
what: FFV1 in Matroska is the LoC Preferred archive pairing; Matroska can carry almost any codec
how: `ffmpeg -y -i in10.mkv -i in.wav -map 0:v -map 1:a -c:v ffv1 -level 3 -g 1 -slicecrc 1 -c:a flac master.mkv` (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Keep the full-res frames for final grade
what: the VFX wiki: compressed clips are for reviews; final reviews and grades use the full-resolution frames
how: archive the image sequence or lossless master, not only the H.264.

name: Pick the naming convention before the shoot
what: Frame.io: decide it before a single shot is recorded; a camera name like `WB2A2468.MOV` says nothing, while `20181004-wfg-filenaming-camA-01-001-4k30.mov` gives date (YYYYMMDD), project ID, scene, camera, shot, take and format
how: agree one pattern per job (e.g. `YYYYMMDD-<proj>-<cam>-<shot>-<take>-<res><fps>`) and write it in the job's notes before ingest; apply it to every render too.

name: Two naming flavours: narrative vs series
what: Frame.io's examples: narrative `20180606-wfg-camB-roll03-shot05-take002-4k30.mov`, broadcast `20180215-wfg-s02-ep04-bts-1080p60.mov` (season/episode/subject instead of scene/take)
how: client reels and FireCraft episodes are series-like (`sNN-epNN-<subject>`); one-off films use roll/shot/take.

name: Unique names stop offload overwrites
what: a convention that forbids duplicate file names makes it much harder to overwrite footage during camera offloads, and every team (DIT, editorial, VFX) must use the same date format
how: before merging cards, `find card -type f -printf '%f\n' | sort | uniq -d` must print nothing; it printed `A001_Clip001.mov` when two cards held that name. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Numbered top-level folders
what: bins grouped into sequences, audio, footage, graphics and misc, numbered (`00_Sequences`, `10_Audio`, `20_Footage`, `30_Graphics`, `40_Misc`) only so alphabetical sorting keeps that order
how: `mkdir -p proj/{00_Sequences,10_Audio/{Music,SFX,VO},20_Footage,30_Graphics,40_Misc}`; `ls proj` lists 00_Sequences first. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Audio bins by type and shoot day
what: inside the audio category: music, SFX, VO and on-location audio per shoot day ("Day 1 Audio", usually with the date)
how: `10_Audio/{Music,SFX,VO,Location/20261024}`; library tracks stay in `library/music` and are only referenced.

name: One folder per camera card (A001, B002 ...)
what: give every camera a letter and count its cards in shooting order (A001-A005, B001-B002, C001-C004) so `/A003/Clip001.mov` and `/F002/Clip001.mov` stay distinguishable even when clip names collide
how: `mkdir -p OCN/<date>/{A001,B001}` and copy each card into its own folder untouched.
refs: Frame.io Workflow Guide, "Pitfalls of an offline workflow", https://workflow.frame.io/guide/offline-workflow-pitfalls, checked 2026-10-24

name: ISO-8601 date folders above the cards
what: Freethink's layout: `Original Digital Negatives/20180723/{A001,B001,...}` plus `20180723_Sound`, so the file system lists days chronologically and a director can say "the shot from Tuesday"
refs: Frame.io Workflow Guide, "Pitfalls of an offline workflow", https://workflow.frame.io/guide/offline-workflow-pitfalls, checked 2026-10-24

name: Prefix repeating prosumer clip names with the card
what: DSLRs, GoPros and drones restart numbering every card, so one day can hold ten `C0001` files; Resolve relinks largely by file name, so rename every clip to be unique
how: `for d in card/*/; do r=$(basename "$d"); for f in "$d"*.mov; do b=$(basename "$f"); echo "$f,$d${r}_$b" >> rename_log.csv; mv "$f" "$d${r}_$b"; done; done` gave `A001/A001_Clip001.mov`, `F002/F002_Clip001.mov`. (tested here 2026-10-24)
refs: Frame.io Workflow Guide, "Pitfalls of an offline workflow", https://workflow.frame.io/guide/offline-workflow-pitfalls, checked 2026-10-24

name: Log the original camera name before any rename
what: renaming clips and losing the original camera file names "can be a disaster" for conform; copy the OCF names into another column first
how: keep the `old,new` `rename_log.csv` written by the rename loop next to the media and hand it over with the project. (tested here 2026-10-24)
refs: Frame.io Workflow Guide, "The most common conform issues", https://workflow.frame.io/guide/common-conform-issues, checked 2026-10-24

name: Rename clips from their recording date
what: exiftool can rename by writing FileName from CreateDate with a date format; `%%-c` adds a copy number if the name exists and `%%e` keeps the extension
how: `exiftool '-FileName<CreateDate' -d '%Y%m%d_%H%M%S%%-c.%%e' dir` renamed a clip stamped 2018-10-04 09:30 to `20181004_093000.mp4`. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Sort a dump into date folders without moving originals
what: `-o .` with `-Directory<CreateDate -d %Y/%m/%d` copies instead of moving
how: `exiftool -o . '-Directory<CreateDate' -d '%Y/%m/%d' dir` put `x.mp4` into `2018/10/04/x.mp4` and left the original. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Keep the whole card structure, sidecars included
what: some technical metadata lives in camera-specific XML sidecar files next to the media, which is why the entire card structure must be kept before importing
how: copy the card root folder (`cp -r card/. dest/` or rsync), never just the `.MP4` files.

name: Folder plan that tells people where new files go
what: a hierarchy should lead to existing files, show where new files belong, and scale from the first 100 shots to the last 100,000 VFX, colour and sound files
how: create `50_Renders/{draft,review,final}` and `60_Exports` at the start instead of dropping renders into the footage tree.

name: Shared bins for series-wide elements
what: productions keep openers and graphics packages in a shared project every episode editor opens
how: in this repo the shared project is `library/` (fonts, blocks, music, SFX); reference it from each job instead of copying into the job.

name: Back up the card before anything else
what: the first thing after a card leaves the camera is a backup in multiple places; keep the original camera files ("camera negative") even after later conversions
how: copy the card to two different drives before transcoding or renaming anything, and never delete the OCN after making proxies.
refs: Frame.io Workflow Guide, ch.02 "Prep", https://workflow.frame.io/guide/, checked 2026-10-24

name: Source checksum, copy, destination checksum, compare
what: checksum software reads the file (source checksum), copies it, reads the copy (destination checksum) and compares; one changed bit gives a different sum
how: `cd card && find . -type f -exec sha256sum {} + > ../card.sha256`, copy, then `cd ../bk && sha256sum -c ../card.sha256` printed OK for every file. (tested here 2026-10-24)
refs: Frame.io Workflow Guide, "Checksums and Robust Backup", https://workflow.frame.io/guide/checksums-backups, checked 2026-10-24

name: A single changed byte fails verification
what: the reason checksums are used: they detect a problem as it happens
how: after appending one byte to a copied clip, `sha256sum -c --quiet ../card.sha256` printed `FAILED` for that file and nothing for the others. (tested here 2026-10-24)
refs: Frame.io Workflow Guide, "Checksums and Robust Backup", https://workflow.frame.io/guide/checksums-backups, checked 2026-10-24

name: Choosing the checksum algorithm
what: MD5 is popular in video for speed and cross-platform support but old; xxHash, SHA-2 or SHA-3 are newer choices. DPC: MD5 is sufficient against accidental damage; stronger algorithms matter when you must resist deliberate tampering or need legal weight
how: `sha256sum` (coreutils, installed) for manifests; `md5sum` when the other side only speaks MD5.
refs: Frame.io Workflow Guide, "Checksums and Robust Backup", https://workflow.frame.io/guide/checksums-backups, checked 2026-10-24
Digital Preservation Coalition Handbook, "Fixity and checksums", https://www.dpconline.org/handbook/technical-solutions-and-tools/fixity-and-checksums, checked 2026-10-24

name: Checksum shelf drives at creation and re-check later
what: a drive stored a long time can lose bits; make checksums at the start so you can check later. DPC suggests checking tape about yearly and hard drives about every six months ("data scrubbing")
how: store `card.sha256` on the drive and in the job notes; on each check run `sha256sum -c --quiet` and replace failed files from another copy.
refs: Frame.io Workflow Guide, "Checksums and Robust Backup", https://workflow.frame.io/guide/checksums-backups, checked 2026-10-24
Digital Preservation Coalition Handbook, "Fixity and checksums", https://www.dpconline.org/handbook/technical-solutions-and-tools/fixity-and-checksums, checked 2026-10-24

name: New checksum after a deliberate change
what: migrating or transcoding changes the checksum, so a new reference must be made for the new file
how: regenerate the manifest after every transcode or rewrap and keep the old one with the original.
refs: Digital Preservation Coalition Handbook, "Fixity and checksums", https://www.dpconline.org/handbook/technical-solutions-and-tools/fixity-and-checksums, checked 2026-10-24

name: Every file needs a second copy, even tiny ones
what: rule 1: at least one extra copy of every file, from the hero shot to metadata files for the credits
how: back up the whole job folder (logs, `.otio`, CSVs, fonts), not only the media.
refs: Frame.io Workflow Guide, "Checksums and Robust Backup", https://workflow.frame.io/guide/checksums-backups, checked 2026-10-24

name: A backup must not be connected to the original
what: rule 2: a copy on the same computer or network can be lost to the same virus or bug
how: a second folder inside this cloud container is not a backup; one copy must live off this machine.
refs: Frame.io Workflow Guide, "Checksums and Robust Backup", https://workflow.frame.io/guide/checksums-backups, checked 2026-10-24

name: Off-site copy
what: rule 3: keep backups in a different physical location; Backblaze's 3-2-1 says one of three copies off-site, ideally miles away
how: cloud storage or a drive kept at another address counts; two drives on one desk do not.
refs: Frame.io Workflow Guide, "Checksums and Robust Backup", https://workflow.frame.io/guide/checksums-backups, checked 2026-10-24

name: No RAID 0 for backups
what: rule 4: RAID 0 has no redundancy, one failed disk loses everything, making it less stable than a single drive; use reliable, durable storage
how: keep backup copies on single drives or redundant arrays, never on a striped RAID 0.
refs: Frame.io Workflow Guide, "Checksums and Robust Backup", https://workflow.frame.io/guide/checksums-backups, checked 2026-10-24

name: Write down where every backup is
what: rule 5: without a record of where backups are and what they are called, they practically do not exist; rule 6: at least one complete backup must be reachable fast
how: keep a `BACKUPS.md` per job (drive name, path, date, checksum file) in the job notes.
refs: Frame.io Workflow Guide, "Checksums and Robust Backup", https://workflow.frame.io/guide/checksums-backups, checked 2026-10-24

name: 3-2-1-1-0 for ransomware
what: add one offline/air-gapped or immutable copy, and zero errors: monitor backups and run regular restore tests
how: keep one drive unplugged, and once a month restore one random clip and `sha256sum -c` it.

name: 4-3-2 when a recovery firm holds data
what: four copies, three locations (yours, a provider's, a cloud), two of them off-site
how: reserve it for high-value archives and name it as the upgrade path when a client asks about safety.

name: Sync by content, not date
what: rsync's default quick check compares size and modification time; `-c` compares a checksum for each same-size file (much more disk I/O)
how: `rsync -a --checksum card/ backup/`, then a second `rsync -a --checksum --itemize-changes card/ backup/` printed 0 lines (nothing differs). (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Dry-run before syncing
what: `-n` does a trial run; with `-i` its itemised output matches the real run; always dry-run before `--delete`
how: `rsync -an --itemize-changes card/ backup/` listed `>f+++++++++ A001/note.txt` and copied nothing. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Daily snapshots that cost no space for unchanged clips
what: `--link-dest=DIR` hard-links files unchanged since DIR
how: `rsync -a card/ snap/day1/` then `rsync -a --link-dest=../day1 card/ snap/day2/`; `stat -c %h` on an unchanged clip showed 2 links. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Keep overwritten versions on sync
what: `--backup-dir=DIR` (implies `--backup`) stores replaced files in DIR; a relative path is relative to the destination, so start it with `../`
how: `rsync -a --backup --backup-dir=../old_$(date +%Y%m%d) card/ rs1/` kept the old `note.txt` in `old_20261024/A001/`. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Resume big transfers
what: rsync deletes a partly transferred file on interruption unless `--partial` keeps it; `--partial-dir=DIR` keeps it in DIR and creates DIR if missing
how: `rsync -a --partial-dir=.rsync-partial card/ pd/` copied the card tree normally. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Copy only one file type, keep the folders
what: the man page's filter idiom: `--include='*/' --include='*.pdf' --exclude='*'` with `-m` to prune empty folders
how: `rsync -avm --include='*/' --include='*.mov' --exclude='*' src/ movonly/` copied the .mov files and skipped a `notes.txt`. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Git is not a backup and has hard size limits
what: GitHub warns above 50 MiB, blocks files over 100 MiB (Git LFS needed), recommends repos under 1 GB (<5 GB strongly) and says Git is not designed as a backup tool
how: media and weights stay out of this repo (owner rule); only small reusable assets go to `library/`.
refs: GitHub Docs, "About large files on GitHub", https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/working-with-files/managing-large-files/about-large-files-on-github, checked 2026-10-24

name: ProRes 422 Proxy with ffmpeg
section: Proxies, optimised media and mezzanine files
what: Frame.io names ProRes 422 Proxy as one of two good offline formats
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf scale=iw/2:ih/2 -c:v prores_ks -profile:v proxy -c:a pcm_s16le px.mov` → ffprobe `prores,Proxy,320,180`. (tested here 2026-10-24)
refs: Frame.io Workflow Guide, "Pitfalls of an offline workflow", https://workflow.frame.io/guide/offline-workflow-pitfalls, checked 2026-10-24

name: Proxy codec: intra-frame and low bitrate
section: Proxies, optimised media and mezzanine files
what: avoid long-GOP (temporal) compression and use a low bitrate; ProRes and DNxHD/HR are the common, nearly interchangeable choices, Cineform a third
how: pick ProRes 422 Proxy or DNxHR LB, never H.264, for editing proxies.
refs: Frame.io Workflow Guide, "How to Choose a Proxy Codec", https://workflow.frame.io/guide/proxy-codecs, checked 2026-10-24

name: DNxHR LB with ffmpeg
section: Proxies, optimised media and mezzanine files
what: the other recommended offline format, easy to create cross-platform
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf scale=1280:720 -c:v dnxhd -profile:v dnxhr_lb -pix_fmt yuv422p -c:a pcm_s16le lb.mov` → ffprobe `dnxhd,DNXHR LB`. (tested here 2026-10-24)
refs: Frame.io Workflow Guide, "Pitfalls of an offline workflow", https://workflow.frame.io/guide/offline-workflow-pitfalls, checked 2026-10-24
Frame.io Workflow Guide, "How to Choose a Proxy Codec", https://workflow.frame.io/guide/proxy-codecs, checked 2026-10-24

name: Size proxies from the storage maths
section: Proxies, optimised media and mezzanine files
what: start with the smallest ProRes/DNx flavour at capture resolution and multiply its GB/hr by your hours of footage; if it doesn't fit (or the machine is weak) step the resolution down
how: `ffprobe -v error -show_entries format=bit_rate -of csv=p=0 px.mov` gave 2681245 bit/s → ×3600/8 ≈ 1.21 GB per hour of that proxy. (tested here 2026-10-24)
refs: Frame.io Workflow Guide, "How to Choose a Proxy Codec", https://workflow.frame.io/guide/proxy-codecs, checked 2026-10-24

name: "Half" resolution is a quarter of the pixels
section: Proxies, optimised media and mezzanine files
what: Resolve's Half/Quarter fractions refer to one dimension, so Half = (1/2)² = 1/4 of the pixels
how: `scale=iw/2:ih/2` turned 640x360 into 320x180 (1/4 of the pixels). (tested here 2026-10-24)
refs: Frame.io Workflow Guide, "DaVinci Resolve Proxy Workflow", https://workflow.frame.io/guide/resolve-proxies, checked 2026-10-24

name: Only shrink clips bigger than the timeline
section: Proxies, optimised media and mezzanine files
what: Resolve's "Choose automatically" downsizes only media larger than the timeline (8K→quarter, 4K→half in a 1080 project) and leaves 1080 and smaller at source size
how: `scale=w=min(iw\,1920):h=-2` caps width; tested with a 320 cap: a 640-wide clip became 320, a 320-wide clip stayed 320. (tested here 2026-10-24)
refs: Blackmagic, DaVinci Resolve 19.1 Reference Manual ch.8 "Improving Performance, Proxies, and the Render Cache", https://documents.blackmagicdesign.com/UserManuals/DaVinci_Resolve_19_Reference_Manual.pdf, checked 2026-10-24

name: Proxies must carry the source timecode
section: Proxies, optimised media and mezzanine files
what: timecode is "the glue" of offline/online; proxies whose timecode matches the camera originals let apps switch back and forth
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -c:v prores_ks -profile:v proxy -timecode 01:00:00:00 tc.mov` wrote a `tmcd` track reading 01:00:00:00, and transcoding that MOV kept 01:00:00:00. (tested here 2026-10-24)
refs: Frame.io Workflow Guide, "Pitfalls of an offline workflow", https://workflow.frame.io/guide/offline-workflow-pitfalls, checked 2026-10-24

name: Rewrap production audio losslessly into proxies
section: Proxies, optimised media and mezzanine files
what: don't transcode the interleaved WAV to AAC; rewrapping keeps every ISO track and saves hunting the field-recorder files later
how: `ffmpeg -i pic.mp4 -i prod.wav -map 0:v -map 1:a -c:v prores_ks -profile:v proxy -c:a copy synced.mov` kept `pcm_s24le, 2 ch`. (tested here 2026-10-24)
refs: Frame.io Workflow Guide, "Pitfalls of an offline workflow", https://workflow.frame.io/guide/offline-workflow-pitfalls, checked 2026-10-24

name: Bake the LUT into proxies only
section: Proxies, optimised media and mezzanine files
what: pre-baking the camera LUT into proxies spares the editor LUT management and CPU, but only if you go back to the camera originals later
how: `ffmpeg -i log.mov -vf "lut3d=file=show.cube,scale=iw/2:-2" -c:v prores_ks -profile:v proxy px.mov` (ran with an identity cube). (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Mezzanine: never bake the LUT
section: Proxies, optimised media and mezzanine files
what: a mezzanine file replaces the originals, so baking a LUT would throw away the log latitude; apply the LUT as an effect instead
how: transcode log footage to the mezzanine codec untouched and add `lut3d` only at render.

name: Mezzanine codec at least as good as capture
section: Proxies, optimised media and mezzanine files
what: match chroma and bit depth (4:2:0 8-bit source needs at least 4:2:0 8-bit) and raise the bitrate a lot when leaving long-GOP; for 100 Mbps H.264 use ProRes 422 or 422 HQ
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -c:v prores_ks -profile:v hq -an mez.mov` → profile `HQ`. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Mezzanine for mixed frame rates and sizes
section: Proxies, optimised media and mezzanine files
what: with many frame rates/sizes, or third-party sync tools that complicate relinking, a mezzanine workflow avoids proxy relink headaches
how: for mixed phone clips, transcode everything once to one mezzanine spec and edit those.

name: Proxy tree mirrors the original tree
section: Proxies, optimised media and mezzanine files
what: OCN and proxy folder structures should be identical
how: copy only the directory tree with rsync's include/exclude pair: `rsync -a --include='*/' --exclude='*' card/ PROXY/` created `PROXY/A001`, `PROXY/F002` with no files. (tested here 2026-10-24)
refs: Frame.io Workflow Guide, "Pitfalls of an offline workflow", https://workflow.frame.io/guide/offline-workflow-pitfalls, checked 2026-10-24

name: Batch proxies into the mirrored tree
section: Proxies, optimised media and mezzanine files
how: `for f in $(find card -name '*.mov'); do o=PROXY/${f#card/}; ffmpeg -nostdin -n -i "$f" -vf scale=iw/2:-2 -c:v prores_ks -profile:v proxy -c:a pcm_s16le "$o"; done` wrote `PROXY/A001/A001_Clip001.mov` and `PROXY/F002/F002_Clip001.mov`. (tested here 2026-10-24)
refs: Frame.io Workflow Guide, "Pitfalls of an offline workflow", https://workflow.frame.io/guide/offline-workflow-pitfalls, checked 2026-10-24

name: Proxy format for sending vs for speed
section: Proxies, optimised media and mezzanine files
what: Resolve: for faster playback while keeping quality use ProRes 422 HQ or DNxHR HQ; to send media over the internet use ProRes Proxy or even H.264/H.265 to keep files small
how: choose by purpose: `-profile:v hq` locally, `libx264` for a remote editor's preview set.
refs: Blackmagic, DaVinci Resolve 19.1 Reference Manual ch.8 "Improving Performance, Proxies, and the Render Cache", https://documents.blackmagicdesign.com/UserManuals/DaVinci_Resolve_19_Reference_Manual.pdf, checked 2026-10-24

name: Optimised media that keeps alpha and overshoots
section: Proxies, optimised media and mezzanine files
what: Resolve preserves alpha only in Uncompressed 10-bit/16-bit float, ProRes 4444/4444 XQ and DNxHR 444; to avoid clipping super-whites use 16-bit float or ProRes 4444/XQ (also for HDR)
how: for alpha graphics proxies `ffmpeg -f lavfi -i "color=red@0.5:s=320x180:d=1,format=rgba" -c:v prores_ks -profile:v 4444 -pix_fmt yuva444p10le a.mov` → ffprobe `4444,yuva444p12le`. (tested here 2026-10-24)
refs: Blackmagic, DaVinci Resolve 19.1 Reference Manual ch.8 "Improving Performance, Proxies, and the Render Cache", https://documents.blackmagicdesign.com/UserManuals/DaVinci_Resolve_19_Reference_Manual.pdf, checked 2026-10-24

name: Two dailies sets in one pass
section: Proxies, optimised media and mezzanine files
what: DITs often make an editorial codec set plus an H.264 set for producers
how: one ffmpeg command with two outputs: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -map 0:v -c:v prores_ks -profile:v proxy -s 320x180 ed.mov -map 0 -c:v libx264 -preset ultrafast -c:a aac rev.mp4` made both. (tested here 2026-10-24)
refs: Frame.io Workflow Guide, ch.02 "Prep", https://workflow.frame.io/guide/, checked 2026-10-24

name: Use licensed ProRes for paid deliverables
section: Proxies, optimised media and mezzanine files
what: Frame.io: unlicensed ProRes encoders in some software transcoders have no quality control and may fail QC; use licensed implementations for professional deliverables
how: ffmpeg's `prores_ks` is fine for our proxies/mezzanine; if a client's QC demands licensed ProRes, say so rather than promising it.

name: Transcoding never improves quality
section: Proxies, optimised media and mezzanine files
what: an intermediate codec cannot make images better, only worse if chosen badly; don't transcode when the camera codec is already edit-friendly (e.g. Canon XF 50 Mb 4:2:2)
how: check with ffprobe first; if the source is already intra-frame and editable, edit it directly.
refs: Frame.io Workflow Guide, "The most common conform issues", https://workflow.frame.io/guide/common-conform-issues, checked 2026-10-24

name: Lock picture before conform
section: Picture lock, conform and hand-off packages
what: after a conform, a "simple" shot swap costs the colourist, VFX artist, sound editor and sound designer extra work each; Van Hurkman calls locking "a scheduling milestone"
how: tag the locked HyperFrames project (`git tag -a v010-lock -m "picture lock"`) and route later change requests through a written change list.
refs: Frame.io Workflow Guide, "Pitfalls of an offline workflow", https://workflow.frame.io/guide/offline-workflow-pitfalls, checked 2026-10-24
Pro Git, "2.6 Git Basics - Tagging", https://git-scm.com/book/en/v2/Git-Basics-Tagging, checked 2026-10-24

name: Name versions by edit stage
section: Picture lock, conform and hand-off packages
what: assembly (often over twice the final length, close to script), rough cut, optional first/fine cut, director's/producer's cut, picture lock
how: use the stage in render names (`proj_v003_rough.mp4`, `proj_v007_fine.mp4`) so a client knows what kind of feedback fits.
refs: Frame.io Workflow Guide, "Stages of the editing process", https://workflow.frame.io/guide/editing-stages, checked 2026-10-24

name: Show clients a polished cut, not the assembly
section: Picture lock, conform and hand-off packages
what: film producers see past a rough cut's flaws; a marketing client may not, so wait for a more polished version before asking for feedback
how: send the first client link at fine-cut stage with temp music and graphics in place.
refs: Frame.io Workflow Guide, "Stages of the editing process", https://workflow.frame.io/guide/editing-stages, checked 2026-10-24

name: Include the project file in every turnover
section: Picture lock, conform and hand-off packages
what: online facilities need the `.prproj`/`.avb` (the most complete history) to fall back on when an EDL/XML/AAF is missing something
how: our equivalent: hand over the HyperFrames project folder (or `.otio`) plus any EDL/XML, never the list alone.
refs: Frame.io Workflow Guide, "The most common conform issues", https://workflow.frame.io/guide/common-conform-issues, checked 2026-10-24

name: One "final" sequence only
section: Picture lock, conform and hand-off packages
what: several sequences called "final", "final approved revised" confuse the conform; put exactly one sequence in a final bin
how: one `FINAL/` folder holding one render and one timeline file; older ones move to `50_Renders/archive`.
refs: Frame.io Workflow Guide, "The most common conform issues", https://workflow.frame.io/guide/common-conform-issues, checked 2026-10-24

name: Intra-frame reference movie for conform
section: Picture lock, conform and hand-off packages
what: H.264 reference QuickTimes are often unfriendly to conform/grading tools because of inter-frame compression; send ProRes or DNxHD
how: `ffmpeg -i final.mp4 -c:v prores_ks -profile:v proxy -c:a pcm_s16le reference.mov`.
refs: Frame.io Workflow Guide, "The most common conform issues", https://workflow.frame.io/guide/common-conform-issues, checked 2026-10-24

name: Use long-name EDLs
section: Picture lock, conform and hand-off packages
what: the CMX3600 template truncates source names to 8 characters; export with Avid File32/File129 or Premiere's "32-character name" option
how: OTIO's cmx_3600 writer also truncates reels (see the EDL section) — check the reel column before sending.
refs: Frame.io Workflow Guide, "The most common conform issues", https://workflow.frame.io/guide/common-conform-issues, checked 2026-10-24

name: Ship LUTs and CDLs with the turnover
section: Picture lock, conform and hand-off packages
what: include show LUTs, scene LUTs or CDLs so the conform editor can set up the colour project
how: copy the `.cube` files into the hand-off folder with a CSV saying which clip uses which.
refs: Frame.io Workflow Guide, "The most common conform issues", https://workflow.frame.io/guide/common-conform-issues, checked 2026-10-24

name: Prepare a flattened file for colour
section: Picture lock, conform and hand-off packages
what: remove temp colour, put titles/graphics on a separate layer, include an A-mode EDL to notch the file, add outgoing/incoming shots with handles for dissolves and separate layers for composites at the end, list fonts, include full-resolution stills
how: render a textless version (titles hidden) plus a separate graphics pass with alpha (`render --format mov`).
refs: Frame.io Workflow Guide, "The most common conform issues", https://workflow.frame.io/guide/common-conform-issues, checked 2026-10-24

name: Subtitles won't survive the conform
section: Picture lock, conform and hand-off packages
what: captions typed in the NLE may not translate to the finishing platform and may have to be recreated; discuss early
how: deliver captions as a separate `.srt` (Whisper writer) instead of baking them into the master.
refs: Frame.io Workflow Guide, "The most common conform issues", https://workflow.frame.io/guide/common-conform-issues, checked 2026-10-24

name: No "giant shovel" data dumps
section: Picture lock, conform and hand-off packages
what: online editors don't know the footage; organise the OCFs and trim unused takes on large handoffs
how: hand over only the cut's media plus handles, in the folder/naming scheme above.
refs: Frame.io Workflow Guide, "The most common conform issues", https://workflow.frame.io/guide/common-conform-issues, checked 2026-10-24

name: Stringout of treated shots
section: Picture lock, conform and hand-off packages
what: many editors string out, at the end of the timeline, the untouched originals of shots that got speed changes or plugins, so the clean shot is at hand later
how: append the raw source ranges after the end card in a separate "alts" render.

name: Annotated tags for every sent version
what: annotated tags store tagger, date and message; lightweight tags are just a pointer
how: `git tag -a v001-rough -m "Rough cut sent to client 2026-10-24"`; `git show v001-rough` shows the Tagger line. (tested here 2026-10-24)
refs: Pro Git, "2.6 Git Basics - Tagging", https://git-scm.com/book/en/v2/Git-Basics-Tagging, checked 2026-10-24

name: List versions with their notes
how: `git tag -n1` printed each tag with the first line of its message (`v002-fine  Fine cut`). (tested here 2026-10-24)
refs: Pro Git, "2.6 Git Basics - Tagging", https://git-scm.com/book/en/v2/Git-Basics-Tagging, checked 2026-10-24

name: What changed between two versions
how: `git diff --stat v001-rough v002-fine` listed `index.html` as changed; for pictures use `npx hyperframes compare` on the two checkouts. (tested here 2026-10-24)
refs: Pro Git, "2.6 Git Basics - Tagging", https://git-scm.com/book/en/v2/Git-Basics-Tagging, checked 2026-10-24

name: Alternate ending without disturbing the main cut
what: `git worktree add -d <path>` makes a throwaway worktree with a detached HEAD at the current commit; remove it with `git worktree remove`
how: `git worktree add -d ../alt-ending` then `git worktree remove ../alt-ending`; `git worktree list` was back to one entry. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Large reusable assets via Git LFS
what: `git lfs track <pattern>` writes the pattern to `.gitattributes`; `--dry-run` shows what it would do
how: `git lfs track "*.wav"` wrote `*.wav filter=lfs diff=lfs merge=lfs -text`; `git check-attr -a song.wav` reported `filter: lfs`. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Ignore media formats as a safety net
what: this repo's `.gitignore` blocks common video/photo formats
how:
`printf "*.mp4
*.mov
*.jpg
" > .gitignore`; `git status --porcelain --ignored` listed `!! a.mp4`. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Content metadata doesn't travel with the file
what: it lives in the NLE project or a MAM, so copying media loses the logging; every re-encode changes creation date, size and codec
how: keep logs as CSV next to the media and copy dates back after transcodes (`-tagsFromFile`, below).

name: Three kinds of metadata
what: technical (from the file/camera), content (logs, keywords, transcripts; may cover only part of a clip) and distribution (rights/IDs such as EIDR)
how: technical from ffprobe/exiftool, content in our CSV logs, distribution in the delivery sheet.

name: Dump everything, duplicates included
what: `-a -u -g1` prints all tags incl. duplicates and unknown, grouped; `-ee3 -api RequestAll=3` extracts absolutely everything
how: `exiftool -a -u -g1 clip.mp4`; GPS from an ffmpeg `location` tag showed as `[UserData] LocationInformation` plus Composite GPS tags. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Tab-separated media log for a folder
what: `-T` prints one row per file
how: `exiftool -T -FileName -Duration -ImageSize -VideoFrameRate -CreateDate -ext mp4 . > log.tsv` gave one line per clip. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: CSV in, CSV out
what: `-csv` exports (first column SourceFile) and `-csv=FILE` imports tag values back
how: `exiftool -csv -FileName -Duration -ImageSize -ext mp4 . > meta.csv`. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: JSON with raw numbers for scripts
what: `-j` JSON, `-n` disables print conversion
how: `exiftool -j -n -Duration -ImageWidth -ImageHeight a.mp4` → `"Duration": 3, "ImageWidth": 640`. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Only process files that match a condition
what: `-if EXPR`; exit status is 2 when all files fail the condition
how: `exiftool -if '$ImageHeight >= 360' -p '$FileName $ImageSize' -ext mp4 .` listed only the 640x360 clips; with an impossible condition the exit code was 2. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: QuickTime dates: UTC vs local
what: the spec says integer QuickTime dates are UTC but cameras often store local time, so exiftool assumes no zone unless `-api QuickTimeUTC` is set, which converts to local time
how: a clip stamped 07:30Z read `07:30:00` plain, `07:30:00+00:00` with the option, and `12:30:00+05:00` with `TZ=Asia/Karachi`. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Fix a wrong camera clock
what: date shifts with `+=`/`-=` (e.g. `-AllDates+=1:30`, or `'0:0:0 1:30:0'`)
how: `exiftool -overwrite_original "-CreateDate+=0:0:0 1:30:0" clip.mp4` moved 10:00:00 to 11:30:00. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: File date from the recording date
what: `'-FileModifyDate<CreateDate'` copies metadata time to the file system date
how: after it, `exiftool -FileModifyDate` showed the clip's 2026:10:01 11:30:00. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Video tags go to QuickTime and XMP
what: when writing video files exiftool creates both QuickTime and XMP tags unless a group is given
how: `exiftool -overwrite_original -Title="Boss reel v003" t1.mp4` wrote `[ItemList] Title` and `[XMP-dc] Title`. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Restore dates after a transcode
what: `-tagsFromFile SRC -TAG` copies chosen tags from the original
how: a proxy made with `-map_metadata -1` had no CreateDate; `exiftool -overwrite_original -tagsFromFile geo.mp4 -CreateDate px.mp4` brought back 2026:10:20. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Description from the file name
what: advanced formatting with a substitution strips the extension
how: `exiftool -overwrite_original '-Description<${FileName;s/\.[^.]*$//}' t2.mp4` set Description `t2`. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Keep the file's modified time when tagging
what: `-P` preserves the modification date/time
how: a clip touched to 2020-01-01 still showed 2020-01-01 after `exiftool -P -overwrite_original -Title=x`. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Recursive by extension, one line per file
what: `-r` recurses, `-ext` filters, `-p` formats each line
how: `exiftool -r -ext mp4 -p '$Directory/$FileName $Duration' ..` listed every MP4 below with its duration. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Values only for scripts
what: `-s3` (or `-s -s -s`) prints values without tag names
how: `exiftool -s -s -s -Duration a.mp4` printed just `3.00 s`. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Strip location before sharing (MP4 from ffmpeg)
what: `-gps:all=` changed nothing on an ffmpeg-tagged MP4 ("0 image files updated"); the position sat in `UserData:LocationInformation`
how: `exiftool -overwrite_original -UserData:LocationInformation= clip.mp4` removed it (no GPS/location tags left). (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Without -overwrite_original you get a backup
what: by default exiftool keeps the original as `FILE_original`; `-overwrite_original` doesn't
how: use `-overwrite_original` only on copies; on originals keep the `_original` until checked. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Sidecar XMP from a clip
what: `-o %d%f.xmp` creates XMP files from a file's metadata
how: `exiftool -o %d%f.xmp a.mp4` wrote `a.xmp` next to the clip. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Embedded GPS tracks from drones/dashcams
what: `-ee3 -p '$gpslatitude, $gpslongitude, $gpstimestamp'` extracts all GPS positions from a video (documented example: AVCHD)
how: run it before deciding which drone shots to strip; our test clips had no track.

name: Keep global metadata with -map_metadata 0
what: ffmpeg 6.1 here dropped `creation_time` on a plain `-c copy` remux and on a re-encode (location stayed); adding `-map_metadata 0` kept it
how: `ffmpeg -i geo.mp4 -c copy -map_metadata 0 k2.mp4` → `creation_time=2026-10-20T07:30:00Z`. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Delete one key with an empty value
what: `-metadata key=` deletes metadata
how: `ffmpeg -i geo.mp4 -c copy -map_metadata 0 -metadata location= -metadata location-eng= g5.mp4` removed the GPS location and kept the date. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Edit metadata as a text file
what: the `ffmetadata` muxer exports metadata to a `;FFMETADATA1` file; feed it back with `-map_metadata 1`
how: `ffmpeg -i a.mp4 -f ffmetadata m.txt`, add `title=Edited title`, then `ffmpeg -i a.mp4 -i m.txt -map 0 -map_metadata 1 -c copy out.mp4`. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Custom keys in MP4 need use_metadata_tags
what: the mov/mp4 muxer flag `use_metadata_tags` writes an mdta atom
how: `-movflags use_metadata_tags -metadata shot_id=A001_C003 -metadata take=2` kept both keys; without the flag `shot_id` was dropped. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Set the recording timestamp
what: `-timestamp date` sets the container's recording time
how: `ffmpeg -i a.mp4 -c copy -timestamp "2026-10-24T12:00:00" ts.mp4` → `creation_time=2026-10-24...`. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Read timecode where ffprobe puts it
what: MOV timecode is in the tmcd stream tags (`TAG:timecode`), MPEG-1/2 in the video stream, DV/GXF/AVI in the format tags
how: `ffprobe -v error -show_entries stream=codec_tag_string:stream_tags=timecode -of csv=p=0 tc.mov` printed `tmcd,01:00:00:00`. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: One-line spec per file into a CSV log
what: `-show_entries` picks fields, the csv writer with `p=0` drops the section name
how: `for f in *.mp4 *.mov; do printf "%s," "$f"; ffprobe -v error -select_streams v:0 -show_entries stream=codec_name,width,height,r_frame_rate:format=duration -of csv=p=0:s=, "$f" | paste -sd, ; done > media_log.csv` → `t.mp4,h264,640,360,30/1,3.000000`. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: JSON for scripts, jq to read it
how: `ffprobe -v error -show_entries format=duration,size:stream=index,codec_type,codec_name -of json t.mp4 | jq -r '.streams[] | "\(.index) \(.codec_type) \(.codec_name)"'` printed `1 audio aac`. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Shell variables straight from ffprobe
what: the flat writer's output is shell-escaped so it can be embedded in sh scripts (with an alphanumeric or underscore separator)
how: `eval $(ffprobe -v error -select_streams v:0 -show_entries stream=width,height -of flat=s=_ t.mp4); echo $streams_stream_0_width` → 640. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Exact frame count vs fast packet count
what: `-count_frames` decodes and reports `nb_read_frames`; `-count_packets` reports `nb_read_packets` without decoding
how: both gave 90 on a 3 s 30 fps clip; use packets for quick checks, frames when VFR or damage is suspected. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Read only part of a long file
what: `-read_intervals START%END`, `+` for relative, `#N` for N packets; ffprobe seeks to the interval start
how: `ffprobe -v error -select_streams v:0 -read_intervals "1%+#3" -show_entries packet=pts_time -of csv=p=0 t.mp4` returned 3 packets, starting from the keyframe at 0 (decode order: 0, 0.1, 0.033). (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Keyframe map before a stream-copy cut
how: `ffprobe -v error -select_streams v:0 -skip_frame nokey -show_entries frame=pts_time -of csv=p=0 in.mp4` lists only keyframe times; `-show_entries packet=pts_time,flags` marks them `K`. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Human-readable durations and sizes
what: `-sexagesimal` prints HH:MM:SS.micro; `-pretty` adds units and prefixes
how: `ffprobe -v error -sexagesimal -show_entries format=duration -of default=nw=1:nk=1 cuts.mp4` → `0:00:03.000000`; `-pretty` gave `size=62.769531 Kibyte`. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Find broken files in a batch
what: `-show_error` prints an ERROR section; ffprobe exits 1 on a damaged file
how: a truncated MP4 gave `[ERROR] ... Invalid data found when processing input` and `rc=1`; in a loop, log names with rc≠0. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Write the probe to a file
what: `-o` writes ffprobe's output to a file instead of stdout
how: `ffprobe -v error -o probe.json -of json -show_format t.mp4 && jq .format.format_name probe.json`. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Spot frame-time gaps
how: `ffprobe -v error -select_streams v -show_entries frame=pts_time -of csv=p=0 t.mp4 | awk 'NR>1{d=$1-p; if(d>m)m=d} {p=$1} END{print "max_gap", m}'` → `max_gap 0.033334` (a clean 30 fps file); large gaps reveal dropped or VFR frames. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Shot table from detected cuts
how: `ffmpeg -i cuts.mp4 -vf "scdet=t=10,metadata=print:key=lavfi.scd.time:file=cuts.txt" -f null -`, pull the times, then awk them into `shot,start,end,dur` rows; the 3-shot test gave 3 rows of 1.000 s. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Rate and describe clips, then filter
what: editors tag/rate/colour clips and sift by rating, duration and description ("great interior")
how: a `clip,in,out,rating,desc` CSV and `awk -F, 'NR>1 && $4==3 && $5 ~ /interior/ {print $1, $3-$2}' log.csv | sort -k2 -n -r` returned the longest great interior first. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Tag ranges, not whole clips
what: content metadata is most valuable on a time range ("good" part of a 3-minute take) rather than the whole file; searching tags replaces bins, subclips, stringouts and selects ("4 Rachel best couch")
how: one CSV row per tagged range with a `tags` column; `grep -i 'rachel' log.csv | grep best`.

name: Dialogue stringout: every take of one line back to back
what: lets a director compare takes of a line instantly in the session
how: from a `line,file,in,out` CSV, build `-ss in -to out -i file` inputs and a `concat` filter for one line id; two ranges (1.0 s + 0.8 s) gave a 1.8 s `L1_stringout.mp4`. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Trim slates but not the performance
what: in a dailies stringout cut clearly unusable heads/tails (slate in shot, operator panning to the boom) but leave room; the moments after the slate can hold the performance
how: set log in-points just after the slate leaves frame, not at "action".

name: Watch each camera angle separately at stringout stage
what: multicam helps syncing, but laying out each camera one at a time gives real knowledge of the material
how: make one stringout per camera letter (A, B, C) from the shot log.

name: Slated alternates at the end
what: alt shots for other outlets (clean versions, framing variants) go at the end of the master as a stringout, each with a slate like "Alternate for Closeup on X at Timecode Y"
how: `ffmpeg -f lavfi -i color=black:s=640x360:d=2:r=30 -vf "drawtext=text='ALT for CU on X at 01\:00\:10\:00':fontcolor=white:fontsize=28:x=(w-text_w)/2:y=(h-text_h)/2" slate.mp4`, then concat slate + alt. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: VFX handoff with neighbours and handles
what: include the shot before and after the VFX shot, the whole scene at low resolution for reference, and handles as the house asks
how: cut `[in-handle, out+handle]` of the VFX shot plus the adjacent shots into a `vfx_<shot>/` folder.

name: Field notes drive documentary stringouts
what: when not everything can be watched, field producers' timed notes decide which footage gets strung out
how: turn notes into `file,start,end,note` rows and build stringouts from those ranges first.

name: Frankenbite on consonants, not vowels
what: avoid tonal shifts; cut on s, th, hard k/t; drop the line or re-record if it can't sound natural
how: take word boundaries from Whisper `--word_timestamps True` JSON, choose joins that fall on those consonants, and look at the join with `showwavespic` of a 1 s window (`ffmpeg -ss 1 -t 1 -i in.mp4 -filter_complex showwavespic=s=400x80 -frames:v 1 w.png` ran).

name: Fewer frames than cells
what: `nb_frames` limits how many frames fill the grid (doc example `tile=3x2:nb_frames=5:padding=7:margin=2`)
how: ran on a 9 s clip with one frame per second selected. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Mosaic of scene starts
what: the select docs' example: `select='gt(scene\,0.4)',scale=160:120,tile`; scene values 0.3-0.5 are "generally a sane choice"
how: on a 9-shot test, `select=gt(scene\,0.4),scale=160:90,tile` produced a 960x450 sheet (default 6x5). (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Minimum spacing between picks
what: `select='isnan(prev_selected_t)+gte(t-prev_selected_t\,10)'` keeps frames at least 10 s apart
how: with 2 s on a 9 s clip, showinfo listed 5 frames (0, 2, 4, 6, 8). (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: One still per second with numbered names
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -fps_mode cfr -r 1 img-%03d.jpeg` (doc example) wrote 9+ stills for a 9 s clip. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Time code on every tile
what: drawtext's `%{pts:hms}` expands to HH:MM:SS.mmm
how: `select=not(mod(n\,30)),scale=320:-2,drawtext=text='%{pts\:hms}':x=5:y=5:fontsize=18:fontcolor=white:box=1:boxcolor=black@0.6,tile=3x3` stamped 00:00:00.000 … 00:00:08.000 on the sheet. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Multi-page sheets
what: without `-frames:v 1`, tile writes one image per filled grid
how: `select=not(mod(n\,30)),scale=160:-2,tile=3x1` with `sheet_%02d.png` wrote 3 pages for 9 selected frames. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Waveform strip for an audio log
what: `showwavespic` renders the whole waveform as one picture
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -filter_complex "showwavespic=s=800x120:split_channels=0" -frames:v 1 wave.png` → 800x120; silent gaps show as flat lines. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Same frame from two versions side by side
how: `[0:v]select=eq(n\,45),scale=320:180,setpts=PTS-STARTPTS[a];[1:v]select=eq(n\,45),scale=320:180,setpts=PTS-STARTPTS[b];[a][b]hstack` with `-frames:v 1` → 640x180 still. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Cut times with select + showinfo
section: Scene and event detection with ffmpeg
how: `ffmpeg -v info -i cuts.mp4 -vf "select=gt(scene\,0.4),showinfo" -f null - 2>&1 | grep -o "pts_time:[0-9.]*"` → `pts_time:1`, `pts_time:2` (showinfo logs at info level, so not with `-v error`). (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Scene times with ffprobe alone
section: Scene and event detection with ffmpeg
what: the lavfi input device reads a filtergraph's output, so ffprobe can probe a `movie=...,select` graph
how: `ffprobe -v error -f lavfi "movie=cuts.mp4,select=gt(scene\,0.4)" -show_entries frame=pts_time -of csv=p=0` printed 1.0 and 2.0. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Keyframes on scene cuts (ffmpeg 7+)
section: Scene and event detection with ffmpeg
what: `-force_key_frames scd_metadata` forces a keyframe where scdet set `lavfi.scd.time`; don't put frame-duplicating filters after scdet
how: ffmpeg 6.1 here rejected it ("Invalid keyframe time: scd_metadata"); on 6.1 pass the detected times instead: `-force_key_frames 1,2`. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Is this the same footage?
section: Scene and event detection with ffmpeg
what: the signature filter computes MPEG-7 video signatures; with `nb_inputs=2:detectmode=full` it reports whether two videos match
how: comparing a clip with its re-encoded 320x180 copy logged `matching of video 0 at 2.366667 and 1 at 2.366667, 90 frames` and `whole video matching`. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Shot list straight from the segmenter
section: Scene and event detection with ffmpeg
what: segment's `segment_list` with `.csv` writes `file,start,end` rows
how: `ffmpeg -i cuts.mp4 -force_key_frames 1,2 -c:v libx264 -c:a aac -f segment -segment_times 1,2 -segment_list shots.csv -reset_timestamps 1 shot_%02d.mp4`. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Add segment_time_delta when forcing keyframes
section: Scene and event detection with ffmpeg
what: forced keyframes can land just before the requested time due to rounding; the doc suggests `segment_time_delta` = 1/(2*fps)
how: without it the split at 1 s was missed (2 segments: 0-2.07, 2.07-3.07); with `-segment_time_delta 0.0167` all 3 segments were written. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Rejoin split shots with the generated ffconcat
section: Scene and event detection with ffmpeg
what: `segment_list` ending `.ffconcat` writes a concat-demuxer script
how: `-segment_list shots.ffconcat`, then `ffmpeg -f concat -safe 0 -i shots.ffconcat -c copy rejoin.mp4`. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Verify a cut with three frames
section: Scene and event detection with ffmpeg
what: Resolve's Scene Detect shows the last outgoing frame and the first two incoming frames: a real cut has a clearly different left frame and two similar right frames
how: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf "select=between(n\,29\,31),scale=160:-2,tile=3x1" -fps_mode passthrough -frames:v 1 cut30.png` for a cut at frame 30. (tested here 2026-10-24)
refs: Blackmagic, DaVinci Resolve 19.1 Reference Manual ch.23 "Using Scene Detection", https://documents.blackmagicdesign.com/UserManuals/DaVinci_Resolve_19_Reference_Manual.pdf, checked 2026-10-24

name: Dissolves look like a cluster of candidates
section: Scene and event detection with ffmpeg
what: dissolves are not detected as single cuts and show as a triangular cluster; Resolve's Prune keeps only the highest-probability cut in a range
how: from a `time score` list, keep only the max score inside any 0.5 s window with awk (tested on a fade: one cut kept). (tested here 2026-10-24)
refs: Blackmagic, DaVinci Resolve 19.1 Reference Manual ch.23 "Using Scene Detection", https://documents.blackmagicdesign.com/UserManuals/DaVinci_Resolve_19_Reference_Manual.pdf, checked 2026-10-24

name: Which detector
what: `detect-adaptive` or `detect-content` for fast cuts, `detect-threshold` for fades in/out
how: `scenedetect -i cuts9.mp4 detect-content list-scenes -n` printed a 9-scene table and the comma-separated cut list. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Adaptive detector for camera motion
what: two-pass: content scores then a rolling average (`--threshold` 3.0, `--min-content-val` 15, `--frame-window` 2), which reduces false cuts from camera movement
how: `scenedetect -i in.mp4 -o out detect-adaptive list-scenes` wrote `in-Scenes.csv`. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Content detector tuning
what: score 0-255 per frame from hue, saturation, luma and edges (`-w` weights, default 1 1 1 0); default threshold 27, lower = more sensitive; `-l` = luma only for greyscale
how: start at 27 and adjust after reading the stats file (next skill).

name: Stats file for threshold tuning
what: `-s stats.csv` writes per-frame metrics (`content_val` etc.)
how: `scenedetect -i cuts9.mp4 -s stats.csv detect-content` → first row has `content_val`. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Fades: threshold detector
what: detects fade-out/in by average pixel value (`-t` default 12) and places the cut between them; `--fade-bias` -100..100 skews it
how: on a 2 s fade-out + 2 s fade-in clip, `detect-threshold` put the cut at 2.000 s (2 scenes). (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Hash and histogram detectors
what: `detect-hash` (perceptual hash, threshold 0.395) and `detect-hist` (YUV histogram, threshold 0.05) as alternatives for fast cuts
how: both found the same 9 scenes on the test clip. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Minimum scene length
what: `-m` (default 0.6 s) merges short scenes with neighbours; `--drop-short-scenes` drops them instead
how: on 9 one-second shots, `scenedetect -i cuts9.mp4 -m 2s detect-content list-scenes -n` merged everything into 1 scene, so keep `-m` below your shortest real shot. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Scene-detect only a time window
what: `time --start/--end/--duration` (seconds, frames or timecode)
how: `scenedetect -i cuts9.mp4 time --start 3s --end 6s detect-content list-scenes -n` listed 3 scenes, 3.0-6.0 s. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Clean CSV
what: `list-scenes --skip-cuts` drops the cut-list first row for RFC 4180 CSV
how: the CSV then starts with `Scene Number,...`. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Stills per scene
what: `save-images -n N` (default 3; with 1 it takes the midpoint), `-W/-H` size, `--png/--webp`
how: `scenedetect -i cuts9.mp4 -o out detect-content save-images -n 1 -W 160` wrote 9 images. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: HTML review page
what: `save-html` uses the preceding `save-images` result
how: `... list-scenes save-images -n 1 save-html` wrote `cuts9-Scenes.html`. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Split into shot files
what: `split-video` re-encodes with ffmpeg (`-crf` default 22, `--preset` veryfast, `-hq` = crf 17 slow); `--copy` is faster but not frame-accurate
how: `scenedetect -i cuts9.mp4 -o out detect-content split-video` wrote 9 MP4s. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Cuts to an editor: EDL, OTIO, FCP XML
what: `save-edl` (CMX 3600, reel default AX, `--start-timecode`), `save-otio`, `save-fcp --format fcpx|fcp7`
how: `... detect-content save-edl save-otio save-fcp` wrote `.edl`, `.otio`, `.xml`; `--format fcp7` gave xmeml. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Keyframes on the cuts for x264
what: `save-qp` writes a QP file of I-frames for x264/x265 `--qpfile`
how: `scenedetect -i cuts9.mp4 -o out detect-content save-qp` wrote lines like `30 I -1`. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Re-use an edited scene list
what: `load-scenes -i scenes.csv` skips detection and uses the CSV's start column
how: fix false cuts in the CSV, then `scenedetect -i in.mp4 load-scenes -i in-Scenes.csv list-scenes -n` (printed "Loaded 9 scenes"); add `split-video` to cut. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Python: detect() returns timecode pairs
what: `detect(path, ContentDetector())` returns (start, end) FrameTimecode pairs; `start_in_scene=True` returns one scene when no cut is found
how: on 9 shots: `len(s)=9`, `s[1][0].get_seconds()=1.0`, `s[-1][1].get_frames()=270`; a cut-less clip gave 0 scenes, 1 with `start_in_scene=True`. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Several files as one stream
what: `detect()` accepts a list of paths and treats them as one continuous video
how: `detect(["cuts.mp4","cuts.mp4"], ContentDetector())` → 6 scenes. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Write EDL/FCP from Python
what: `write_scene_list_edl(path, scenes, title, reel, start_timecode)`; `write_scene_list_fcp7` needs `source_duration` or NLEs play the clip frozen
how: use these after filtering scenes in Python instead of the CLI.

name: Its EDL may not round-trip
what: OTIO's cmx_3600 reader raised `EDLParseError: Unknown event type` on PySceneDetect 0.7.2's EDL (`001  AX V     C ...`)
how: to move cuts into OTIO use `save-otio`, which `otiotool --list-clips` read fine. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Silence report to a file
section: Silence detection and cutting with ffmpeg
what: `ametadata=mode=print:file=` (doc example)
how: `-af "silencedetect=n=-50dB:d=0.5,ametadata=mode=print:file=sil.txt"` wrote `lavfi.silence_start` lines. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: silenceremove keeps stop_duration of each gap
section: Silence detection and cutting with ffmpeg
what: `stop_duration` is how much silence must exist before audio stops being copied, so that much stays
how: `silenceremove=stop_periods=-1:stop_duration=1:stop_threshold=-90dB` turned a 6 s file with a 2 s gap into 5.04 s; adding `stop_silence=0.5` gave 5.54 s. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Cut picture and sound at the same silences
section: Silence detection and cutting with ffmpeg
how: turn silencedetect start/end pairs into a keep expression `between(t,0,2.01985)+gte(t,4.01665)`, write `select='EXPR',setpts=N/FRAME_RATE/TB` and `aselect='EXPR',asetpts=N/SR/TB` to two files and run `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -filter_script:v v.txt -filter_script:a a.txt out.mp4` → 4.01 s from 6 s. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Filter scripts on 6.1 vs 7+
section: Silence detection and cutting with ffmpeg
what: docs now load a filtergraph from a file with `-/filter:v file`; ffmpeg 6.1 here said "Unrecognized option '/filter:v'", while `-filter_script:v file` worked
how: use `-filter_script` on this box. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Install and version caveat
what: the docs say the CLI is no longer published on pip (use the release binary or Homebrew); in this test `pip install auto-editor` fetched the 29.3.1 binary. The website now documents newer flags (`-w:0`, `--cut`, `--keep`, `--transition`) that 29.3.1 rejected ("Unknown option"); 29.3.1 uses `--when-silent/--when-normal`, `--cut-out`, `--add-in`
how: check `auto-editor --help` before copying commands from the site. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Default edit
what: `auto-editor video.mp4` cuts silent sections and writes `video_ALTERED.mp4`; `-o` names it
how: a 6 s clip with a 2 s silent gap came out 4.43 s (`--no-open` keeps it from launching a player). (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Margin for natural pace
what: default 0.2 s padding around kept sections; `--margin 0.5sec` (or `0.3sec,1.5sec` before/after) lets speech breathe
how: `--margin 0.5sec` gave 5.03 s instead of 4.43 s. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Look before you render
what: `--preview` prints stats on how the input will be cut
how: it reported 1 cut of 0:00:01.57 (47 frames) and stopped. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Threshold: % or dB
what: `--edit audio:threshold=6%` or `--edit audio:-18dB`; raise it to cut more
how: on a -18 dBFS test tone, `audio:-18dB` cut far more (2.23 s left) than the default (4.43 s). (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Fast-forward silence instead of cutting
what: docs: `-w:0 speed:8`; on 29.3.1: `--when-silent speed:8`
how: `auto-editor in.mp4 --no-open --when-silent speed:8 -o ff.mp4` → 4.63 s (gap played 8x). (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Podcast pace
what: cut silence and speed speech slightly (`-w:0 cut -w:1 speed:1.15` in docs)
how: 29.3.1: `--when-normal speed:1.15 --when-silent cut` → 3.83 s from 6 s. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Manual ranges on top of the auto edit
what: range syntax: start inclusive, end exclusive, units frames or `sec`, `start`/`end` and negative indexes
how: 29.3.1 `--cut-out start,1sec` gave 3.43 s; `--add-in start,end` kept the whole 6 s; `--set-speed 2,0sec,2sec` sped the first 2 s. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Cut by motion for silent screen recordings
what: `--edit motion:threshold=2%` drops still parts
how: ran on a moving test pattern: nothing cut (3.0 s). (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Hand the cut to an editor instead of rendering
what: `--export premiere|resolve|final-cut-pro|shotcut|kdenlive`
how: wrote `ae.xml` (xmeml), `.fcpxml` for Resolve/FCP, `ae.mlt` and `ae.kdenlive`. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Each kept section as its own file
what: `--export clip-sequence`
how: produced `clips-0.mp4`, `clips-1.mp4`. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: v3 JSON timeline
what: `--export v3` writes a JSON timeline (version "3", timebase, resolution, `v`/`a` layers of clips with src/start/dur/offset/stream); `auto-editor input.v3 -o out.mkv` renders it
how: exported `ae.v3`, rendered it back to 4.43 s. (tested here 2026-10-24)
refs: auto-editor docs, "The v3 format", https://auto-editor.com/docs/v3, checked 2026-10-24

name: Inspect before editing
what: subcommands `info`, `levels`, `desc`, `cache`, `subdump` (plus `whisper` in newer docs)
how: `auto-editor info in.mp4` printed durations/bitrates; `auto-editor levels in.mp4` printed one loudness value per frame (183 lines for 6 s). (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Model choice for editing transcripts
what: `turbo` (optimised large-v3) is the CLI default and fast, but it is not trained for translation; use multilingual tiny/base/small/medium/large for `--task translate`
how: here `--model small` (cached in `~/.cache/whisper`) ran on CPU with `--fp16 False`. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: TSV in integer milliseconds
what: the TSV writer prints `start end text` in whole milliseconds so locale decimal commas can't break parsing
how: read it with `awk -F'\t'` to build cut ranges. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Cut out words from a transcript
how: load the word list from the JSON, mark words to drop (e.g. "test"), and emit keep ranges between them: the test produced `[(0.0, 1.4), (1.8, None)]`, ready for trim/concat or a select expression. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: What an EDL can carry
what: CMX3600-style EDLs hold reel + timecode events for simple decisions; FCP XML and AAF can carry more; EDLs use DF or NDF timecode at 24/25/30
how: for anything beyond cuts and dissolves hand over OTIO/XML plus a reference render.

name: Reel names: 8 characters, 7 with B-reels
what: CMX3600 on FCP allows 8 characters; the 8th may be replaced by B for same-reel dissolves, so keep reel names to 7
how: name reels like `A001C03` before exporting.

name: Player EDLs for skip/mute lists
what: MPlayer/Kodi-style EDL: `start end action` in seconds (0 cut, 1 mute, 2 scene marker, 3 skip) or frames with `#`
how: write `5.3 7.1 0` style lines from our silence/cut lists into `video.edl` for MPlayer/Kodi-style players; note mpv's EDL is a different format.

name: Install OTIO and the EDL/XML adapters
what: core OTIO has only otio_json, otiod, otioz; EDL, AAF, ALE, FCP XML come from OpenTimelineIO-Plugins or single packages
how: `pip install opentimelineio otio-cmx3600-adapter otio-fcp-adapter` (scratch venv) gave adapters `cmx_3600, fcp_xml, otio_json, otiod, otioz`. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Build a timeline in Python
what: Timeline → Stack of Tracks → Clips/Gaps; each Clip has a media reference (target_url, available_range) and a source_range
how: a 2-clip V1+A1 timeline with a 15-frame Gap: `tl.duration()` = 3.0 s and the second clip's `range_in_parent()` started at frame 60. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: trimmed_range vs available_range vs visible_range
what: trimmed = source_range if set, else available_range; visible_range adds adjacent transitions; `duration()` = trimmed duration
how: read `clip.trimmed_range()` for edit lengths, `available_range()` for media length.

name: Markers on clips
what: a Marker has a `marked_range` in the clip's time frame (duration 0 = instant) and a colour
how: a red "FIX LOGO" marker at frame 10 showed in `otiotool --list-markers` and in the EDL as `* LOC: 00:00:00:10 RED FIX LOGO`. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Gaps are transparent; black needs a generator
what: in multitrack timelines a Gap shows the track below; for solid black use a Clip with a GeneratorReference; a fade to black is a transition to a (possibly 0-length) Gap
how: use Gaps only for spacing on the top track.

name: Transitions don't change track length
what: in/out offsets borrow media from the neighbours; two transitions can't be adjacent; offsets beyond the available media are allowed but the result is app-specific
how: check handles before adding dissolves to an exported timeline.

name: otiotool reports
what: `--list-tracks`, `--list-clips`, `--list-markers`, `--list-media`, `--stats`, `--inspect NAME`
how: `otiotool -i demo.otio --list-tracks --list-clips --list-markers` printed V1/A1 with their clips and the marker; `--inspect cuts` showed range_in_parent etc. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Find missing media
what: `--verify-media` checks local file paths only
how: after moving `cuts.mp4`, it printed `MEDIA NOT FOUND: cuts.mp4` next to `MEDIA EXISTS: t.mp4`. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: List media references
what: `--list-media` prints each clip's media
how: `otiotool -i demo.otio --list-media` printed `MEDIA: t.mp4`, `MEDIA: cuts.mp4` per track. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Relink by name
what: `--relink-by-name DIR` matches clip names to file names (ignoring extension) and relinks with file:// URLs
how: `otiotool -i demo.otio --relink-by-name media -o rel.otio` → "Relinked 4 clips". (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Trim, concat, filter
what: phases: filter (`--video-only`, `--trim`, name/regex filters) → combine (`--stack`, `--concat`) → flatten → relink → redact → inspect → output; option order doesn't matter except input order for stack/concat
how: `--trim 0 1.5` gave 00:00:01:15; `-i demo.otio demo.otio --concat` gave 00:00:06:00. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Redact before sharing
what: `--redact` removes all metadata and renames objects generically
how: clip names became `Clip #1` … `Clip #4`. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Write a CMX3600 EDL
what: the adapter supports one video track (not multiple video tracks or nesting), audio, gaps, markers, transitions, linear speed and CDL; styles `avid` (default), `nucoda`, `premiere`; `reelname_len` default 8
how: writing a video-only copy gave events with reels truncated to `tmp4`/`cutsmp4` and a `* OTIO TRUNCATED REEL NAME FROM` comment; `style="premiere"` wrote reel `AX` with `* OTIO REFERENCE FROM`. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Read an EDL at the right rate
what: EDLs carry no rate, so pass `rate=` (default 24); `ignore_timecode_mismatch=True` tolerates overlapping record TC
how: `otio.adapters.read_from_file("demo.edl", rate=30)` returned clips t (00:00:00:00) and cuts (00:00:01:00). (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: FCP7 XML out
how: `otio.adapters.write_to_file(tl, "demo.xml", adapter_name="fcp_xml")` wrote an xmeml file. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Interchange is not guaranteed
what: OTIO's fcp_xml reader failed on auto-editor 29.3.1's Premiere XML (`float() argument ... NoneType` on a missing duration)
how: always re-open an exported list in the target (or `otiotool --stats`) before sending it. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: otioz bundles: cut + media in one zip
what: `content.otio` + `version.txt` + flat `media/` (unique basenames required); reading only parses content.otio (fast)
how: `otioconvert -i demo.otio -o demo.otioz` → zip with `content.otio`, `media/t.mp4`, `media/cuts.mp4`; `otiostat demo.otioz` read it. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: otiod directory bundles
what: same layout as a folder
how: `otioconvert -i demo.otio -o ./demo.otiod` worked; a bare `demo.otiod` failed with "Directory '' does not exist". (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Bundle without media
what: `-A media_policy=AllMissing` replaces all references with MissingReference (originals kept in metadata) and copies no media
how: `otioconvert -i demo.otio -o nomedia.otioz -A media_policy=AllMissing` → zip without `media/` files. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: Timecode helpers
what: `otio.opentime.from_timecode("01:00:00:00", 30).value` = 108000, `to_timecode(RationalTime(45,30))` = `00:00:01:15`; a 29.97 float rate raised "SMPTE timecode does not support this rate" (use `30000/1001`)
how: convert NLE timecodes this way instead of hand maths. (tested here 2026-10-24)

name: MoviePy 2 API names
